en: *Fozu Tongji*, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhipan of Donghu, Mingzhou, during the Jingding era of the Song dynasty. 1.
The Primary Chronicle of the Founder, Śākyamuni Buddha. The First Part of the First Section of the Primary Chronicle of the Founder, Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Preface to Elucidating the Fundamental and the Traces states:
When the Sage Tathāgata appears in the world for the benefit of beings,
there necessarily exists the subtle mystery of descending the fundamental to manifest traces, and opening up the traces to reveal the fundamental.
Now, the "root" refers to the Dharma-body;
the "traces" refer to—
This refers to what is called the "eight phases. The meaning is found in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning):
from the Dharma-body, the eight phases are manifested; through the eight phases, the Dharma-body is revealed.
The fundamental and the trace interpenetrate, both being inconceivable.
Since the discourse on the Lotus Sūtra’s revelation of the near to manifest the distant, and its disclosure of the traces to reveal the fundamental, has not yet appeared,
it is insufficient for a deep understanding of this principle; therefore,
the eight phases [of the Buddha's life] are set forth in full detail.
This section separately enumerates the five periods and excerpts from various sutras to converge them upon the single reality,
thereby clarifying the meaning of the beginning and end of the Buddha’s transformative activities throughout his entire career.
Thus, whether in terms of the fundamental or the derivative,
there are no remaining aggregates.
Master Sha Xuan explained that there are six meanings of the fundamental and the derivative.

As for "the fundamental," it refers to the fundamental principle, which is the true mark (*dharmatā*), the single ultimate path. Regarding this, the Buddha stated that there is only one ultimate path and not many ultimate paths. As for "the traces":
Apart from the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), everything else of various kinds is termed a "trace.
Furthermore, this refers to both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).

All are termed "the Original Text" (benke). It is said that principle is true and phenomena are conventional; speaking of principle and speaking of phenomena are both termed "teaching" (jiao). The *Shiyao* states: "True and conventional are principle; explaining this true and conventional is teaching. Furthermore, there is the teaching of principle and phenomena.
All of these are termed the "root.
Receiving the teachings and practicing them is termed the "trace."
Just as when a person relies on a location, there are tracks; by following the tracks, one can find the location. Furthermore, practice is able to realize the essence (*tattva*);
the essence is the foundation.
Relying upon the essence, function arises.
That which is employed as the trace is called the "trace.
Furthermore, that which actually attains the essence and function is called the "root."
The provisional application of essence and function is called the "trace.
Furthermore, that which is manifested today constitutes the "root."
What was previously explained constitutes the "trace" (jiji).
These six meanings provide a general discussion of the fundamental and trace aspects of all Buddhas.
As for its specific discussion,
it pertains solely to the present Buddha,
and therein there are also six meanings.
First, regarding the clarification of the fundamental and the manifested in terms of principle and phenomena:
all dharmas are established from the root of non-abiding;
this principle of non-abiding is precisely the true aspect (dharmatā) of the fundamental time.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
All phenomena are the myriad things as they were in their original state;
this is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This explains the characteristics of the fundamental and the manifested. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) says:
Ignorance serves as the basis for all phenomena;
ignorance itself is the dharma-nature (dharmatā),
and ignorance, in turn, takes the dharma-nature as its basis.
One should know that all phenomena likewise take the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as their basis.
The nature of phenomena is itself ignorance;
furthermore, the nature of phenomena takes ignorance as its basis.
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is itself ignorance;
the nature of phenomena has no place of abiding.
Ignorance is itself the nature of phenomena.
Ignorance has no place of abiding.
Although the dharma-nature of ignorance is itself entirely without abiding,
it serves as the foundation for all dharmas.
Therefore, it is said that "from the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.
Since this root of non-abiding is universal,
the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) points to the principle (li).
All dharmas are matters of phenomena.
Because the true essence of the ultimate reality descends into the traces of the conventional,
by investigating these conventional traces, the true essence is immediately revealed.
Although the origin (*hon*) and the trace (*shaku*) differ, they are inconceivably one.
The text states:

"Contemplate all phenomena as empty, their true reality (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*)," thereby clarifying that the origin and the trace manifest each other and that their principles are harmonized. The *Sub-commentary* (*Shih-ch'an*) says:
This is the fundamental and derivative aspects of the principle of suchness (*tathatā*).

It is through this that there is the external manifestation of these two aspects—the fundamental and the derivative. Regarding the clarification of the fundamental and derivative aspects through both principle and teaching:
that which was illuminated during the original time is such that both truths (*satya*) are ultimately ineffable; all of these are termed "fundamental."
In the past, the Buddha skillfully taught this as the doctrine of the two truths.
This teaching is called the "trace" (迹), which explains the relationship between the "trace" and the "origin" (本).
If there were no foundation of the two truths, then these two kinds of teaching would not exist.
If there were no manifest traces, how could the fundamental reality of the truths be revealed?
Although the fundamental and the manifest differ, they are one inconceivable mark; the revelation of principle harmonizes with the text, which says:
"This dharma cannot be shown."
The characteristics of speech are quiescent;
yet, by the power of skillful means,
for the sake of the five bhikṣus, he spoke, citing texts as evidence that the three teachings take practice as their fundamental reality while manifesting in provisional traces.
Taking the teachings of the ancient Buddhas as the foundation, there is the practice of cultivating causes to bring about results;

this explains the mutual correspondence between the fundamental and the manifested. [The phrase] "there should be three characters for 'manifested' based on the teaching" indicates that the teaching elucidates the principle.
One can give rise to practice through this;
by means of practice, one encounters the teaching,
and thereby the principle is revealed.

Although the fundamental and the manifested differ, they are one inconceivable mark; this reveals the principle that unifies the text, stating: "All phenomena have from the very beginning always been of the nature of quiescent extinction.
Once the Son of the Buddha has practiced the Way," and so forth.
Regarding the citation of scriptural evidence for attaining Buddhahood in future lives, the fourth section clarifies the fundamental and the manifested through the lens of essence and function:
because one first practiced in the past,
one accords with principle and realizes the *dharmakāya*, which constitutes the "fundamental."

Because one first attains the fundamental Dharma-body, the function of the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) arises from its very substance; this explains the relationship between the fundamental and the trace. [The phrase] "should have 'taking [the Response-body] as the trace'" indicates that it is through the Response-body that the Dharma-body is manifested.
Although the fundamental and the manifested differ, they are one inconceivable mark; the text clarifies this principle with harmonious phrasing, stating:
"Since my attainment of Buddhahood, it has been exceedingly vast and remote, just like this."

It is solely through skillful means that he teaches and transforms sentient beings, making such statements to cite texts as evidence. Fifth, regarding the clarification of the fundamental and the traceous based on the real and the provisional:
the "real" refers to—
Originally, from time immemorial, the attainment of the Dharma corresponds to the two bodies,
both of which are termed "original.
In the interim, there have been repeated proclamations of birth and death.
The various provisional manifestations of the Dharma correspond to the two bodies;

therefore, they are called "traces" (*ji*). To explain the relationship between the fundamental and the trace: if there were no fundamental reality of the Dharma to which one first attains, then there would be no intermediate traces of the Dharma's manifestation.
The provisional reveals the fundamental;
although the provisional and the fundamental differ, they are one inconceivable aspect. To clarify this principle, the text states:
"This is my skillful means."

The same applies to all Buddhas; this citation is used to provide proof for the sixth point. Having already discussed the provisional and the real, as well as phenomena and principle, within the various teachings presented thus far, we shall now treat the fundamental and the manifested aspects.
As for what has been previously explained in those various teachings regarding phenomena and principle, up to the provisional and the real:
All are traces; "already" refers to the traces themselves.
This points to the gate of traces as well as all teachings of the traces.
"The present is precisely the fundamental" refers to the Fundamental Gate (Honmon);
that which precedes the Fundamental Gate is [the Trace Gate].
All are designated as "past.
Only after they have surged forth are they designated as "present.
What is taught in this sutra regarding the principles and events of the distant past, up to the provisional and the real, [is explained accordingly].
All these are termed "original" (hon) and "traced" (shaku); the mutual relationship between the original and the traced is not what is being clarified here.
There is no "original" from the remote past that could serve to transmit the "traces" already explained, nor are there "traces" already explained that do not depend upon it.
Does this not manifest the present text?

Although the origin (*hon*) and the trace (*shaku*) differ, they are a single inconceivable unity; the characteristics of origin and trace mutually manifest one another, and their principle is harmonious. As the text says:
"After a long time, the Dharma of all Buddhas..."
One must speak of the reality that serves as the primary source for citation and evidence;
it is the fundamental source rather than the manifested trace, the original realization prior to all else.
Since the trace has not yet been bestowed, [the source remains].
Therefore, it has already been stated that [the teaching] belongs exclusively to the final stage of the fundamental [truth].
However, having already explained the Trace Gate— which is merely the trace and not the fundamental—
it has not yet revealed the fundamental [truth].
Therefore, it belongs solely to the trace; furthermore, within the intermediate stage, both the trace and the source are mutually related as source and trace.
Moreover, within this intermediate stage, there is the manifestation of traces.
That which is called "trace" is also called "origin" when the origin is revealed;
it is not an origin that exists prior to the manifestation of the origin.
One cannot attain the intermediate or final traces.

If there were no previously explained traces, the present Trace Gate (*jimon*) would be unable to reveal the essence of what is now being taught; for although the essence and the trace of this fundamental gate (*honmon*) differ, they are inconceivably one. The above constitutes the text on the sixfold essence and trace (*honji*). If one clings to the trace as the essence, [one fails to understand].
Thus, they do not understand the traces nor recognize the source.
Some speak of Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, or Devadatta,
or refer to them as teachers.
Some call them "disciples," yet those who are deluded do not understand;
if one brushes away this middle ground, [the truth is revealed].
There is nothing that is not a trace;
thus, the trace and the source can be understood.
If one clings to the trace and doubts the source, [one remains deluded].
In that case, both meanings would be lost.
The *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) contains a diagram of six levels of fundamental and phenomenal manifestations (*honjaku*).

Regarding the contemplation of all phenomena as empty and being the true aspect (*nyorai-sō*): [the first level] is Principle (*ri*), while [the subsequent levels] are explained as Phenomena (*ji*) because they exist through causes and conditions arising from inversion.

The principle and teaching of the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukhavihāra*) is this: the Dharma cannot be shown through words, for its characteristics are quiescent (*śānta*) (principle); yet, by the power of skillful means (*upāya*), it is taught to the five bhikṣus (teaching).

In the "Expedient Means" chapter, the traces of teaching and practice state that all dharmas have, from the very beginning, been characterized by constant self-quiescence (teaching); that once the sons of the Buddha have practiced the path, they shall become Buddhas in future ages (practice);

and that regarding the essence and function of these traces, [the Buddha says]: "Since my attainment of Buddhahood has been exceedingly long ago, I have merely used skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings" (essence and function).
In the *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*, [it says]: "The provisional and the real are my skillful means; all Buddhas are likewise so. (Provisional) Now I shall explain for you the most ultimate reality.
(Real) Regarding the *Bhaiṣajyavastu-upama-parivarta*, it has already been said that after a long time, the Dharma of all Buddhas must indeed be based on the truth.
(Now) Regarding the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*, the *Vyākhyā* states:
The sixth [category] is "that which has already been" and "that which is now. "Already" refers to the traces;
it indicates that the gate of traces consists of all teachings concerning those traces.
"The present is itself the original" refers to the Original Gate (Honmon);
that which precedes the Original Gate is [the Trace Gate].
All are designated as "past.
Only after they have surged forth are they designated as "present."
Therefore, it is said that what has already been explained regarding phenomena and principle,
up to provisional and ultimate, is termed the "trace.
Now, the phenomena and principle are being explained.
Even down to the provisional and the real,
all are termed the "root. Therefore,
one should know that if there were no phenomena or principles within the traces, nor even the provisional and the real, [there would be nothing].
How can this manifest the long-term fundamental nature?
Furthermore, although the terms "past" and "present" differ from the preceding five, [they still do not constitute a fault].
This is also a provisional indication;
referring to the lifespan,
it is called the "present text."
If one looks back to the original source,
one should further distinguish between the "already" and the "now," as they are not the same;
this refers to the period prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The various sutras of the past and present still belong to the stage of the traces;
that which is elucidated in the present sutra, however, is different.
This directly clarifies the fundamental reality of the long distant past;
that which was previously explained and that which is now being explained as the "traces" (the manifested) are now explained as the "fundamental" (the underlying reality).
This alone constitutes the true teaching.
Therefore, among the texts cited as evidence for the six gates,
the first three cite the traces (the manifested teachings).
What are the three latter [categories] that lead back to the fundamental?
Indeed, the former three further encompass both the fundamental and the provisional,
including both phenomena and principle, as well as teaching and practice.
Regarding the three categories of essence and function and so forth,
there is further distinction within the general.
Since it is stated that there are both "original function" and "original skillful means," [the distinctions are as follows].
The provisional traces cannot manifest this;
how much less can the "Trace Gate" (Jiben) be taken as the present context?
It is crystal clear that one must not cite the traces.
For this reason,
there are three citations of derivative texts and three citations of the root text.
Furthermore, since the first three phrases pertain to the cause,
and because the primary cause is narrow in scope.
However, because the traces serve as examples for the fundamental,
only the Trace Gate (jimen) is cited.
As the *Dujiaoji* states:
Of the six layers of fundamental and phenomenal (honji-suijaku),
there is only one layer concerning essence and function;
this is cited from the original text.
The remaining five are all "traces" (jì).
As for the statement in the *Shí* that "the first three cite the traces and the latter three cite the fundamental" (běn),
this is surely the profound intention of the commentator as he punctuated the sutra.
The "present" in "the reality of power has already been realized" refers precisely to the traces and texts as the "Root Gate.
Therefore, it is said that "what is now being taught is the present, which constitutes the Root"; this is the true teaching.
If so, why were the preceding three [teachings] not pointed out as the Root?
It is said: Since the first three are already general, they simply take the traces as examples for the fundamental;
the latter three, however, are specific instances within the general.
Therefore, one must take the traces as the basis;
one may observe the two characters "comprehensive" (tong) and "particular" (bie).
There are many such examples.
As the text clearly elucidates the fundamental and the manifested,
it first cites the *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*:
"Since my attainment of Buddhahood, an exceedingly long time has passed."
Furthermore, in the "Expedient Means" chapter, it says:
"I have originally established a vow to cause all sentient beings universally to attain this path together.
Also, in the "Five Hundred Disciples Receiving Predictions" [chapter].
"Internally they secretly practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, while externally they manifest as śrāvakas.
Regarding this, Miaole explains:
first, he directly cites the original text.
Next, the passage beginning with "The skillful means" cites the text concerning the traces (jì),
because within these traces the underlying intention (běnyì) is secretly revealed;
had it been taught explicitly, [it would not have been so].
This refers to the provisional and the fundamental within the traces;
as will be clarified in the following text,
this principle may be applied universally.
Furthermore, the *Myōryaku-sho* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) explains the ten pairs of provisional and real regarding the "Chapter on Expedient Means," stating:
"However, among these eight [pairs],
the first seven belong to the Gate of Traces."
The eighth is the Original Gate.
Although the original has not yet arrived,
the principle of the provisional and the real is all-pervasive.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "This is my skillful means; all Buddhas are likewise.
Thus, the term "skillful means" (upāya) applies to both the fundamental and the provisional.
Since these textual explanations differ in their profound implications, [the distinction between them must be understood].
Regarding the various scholars' deliberations today,
some say that the first three [periods] represent the manifestation of traces from the fundamental source,
while the latter three represent the revelation of the fundamental source through the manifestation of traces.
Therefore, it is said that these three citations are from the text concerning the traces (*traces*).
Alternatively, it is said that the first three are the causes as traces,
while the latter three are the fruits as the fundamental reality.
Some say that the general purport of the *Yuán* (Perfect) teaching does not distinguish between the fundamental and the manifested;
others say that it specifically contains the meaning of the fundamental.
Therefore, it is said that three passages cite the original text.
The *Mysterious Record of the Separate Practice of Avalokiteśvara* states:
"If one considers principle and phenomena,
or principle and teaching..."
The teaching and practice;
essence and function;
and the fourfold aspects of the fundamental and the trace.
This is not unique to this sutra;
it may also be found in other sections.
If [it refers to] before aeons as numerous as motes of dust, [then...]
The initial attainment of Buddhahood is the true foundation;
today’s manifestation of attaining Buddhahood is merely an intermediate display.
All are provisional manifestations.
This is called the provisional and the real, the fundamental and the迹 (traces).
The opening of the Fundamental Gate is complete.
This body has already been explained in the section on the Original and Traces (Honji-suijaku),
as well as in the various sections;
all of these are designated as "traces" (jaku).
These are called the present and the fundamental,
and these two layers are beyond the reach of discussion in all other sutras.
Therefore, it is said that the various teachings do not clarify this,
whereas the *Lotus Sūtra* alone explains it.
The "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" states:
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:
"In the Sahā world, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers;
each one has a retinue as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers."
After my parinirvāṇa, those who protect, uphold, recite,
and extensively expound this sutra will cause the earth of the Sahā world to split asunder,
and immeasurable bodhisattvas will simultaneously emerge from within it.
Hearing the Buddha’s voice emanating from below,
they each proceeded to the wondrous stupa of the seven treasures in the void and prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones.
At that time, Maitreya and the great assembly, wishing to resolve their doubts,
questioned the Buddha in verse:
"The great assembly of bodhisattvas..."
From where have you come?
From whom did you first resolve to attain enlightenment?
And what Buddha-way have you cultivated?
Among this assembly,
there was not a single person whom I recognized;
suddenly, [a being] emerged from the earth.
"I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for this.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"These bodhisattvas..."
Once I have attained bodhi,
I shall teach, transform, and guide them,
causing them to resolve upon the path; I shall briefly reveal the near and manifest the far, moving their attachments and resolving their doubts— at that time, Maitreya and the others.
A doubt arose in his mind,
and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
It has only been slightly more than forty years since [the Buddha's passing].

How is it that in such a short time he performed such great deeds of Buddha-work? At first, they suspected that his attainment of enlightenment was recent because those he had converted were so numerous; later, they suspected that his passing was recent because this assembly of bodhisattvas was so vast.
Even if someone were to spend thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, they could not exhaustively enumerate them;

for since time immemorial, these beings have constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Furthermore, one might wonder whether those who are transformed are numerous and whether their stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*) are profound and subtle.
This attachment distances [the truth] while doubting what is near.
In the "Chapter on Life Span," the Buddha addressed the great assembly:
All the worlds— gods, humans, and asuras—
say that I have departed from the palace of the Śākyas.

Not far from Gayā, sitting at the site of enlightenment, he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. He extensively opened up the near and manifested the distant, severing delusions and engendering faith; yet, in truth, since I first attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable and boundless.

Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, while concealing the distant and revealing the near, I have constantly been here in this Sahā world preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings;
I have also been in other lands, as many as asaṃkhyeya worlds.
The *Daolizhongsheng xuanyun* states:
"The fruit first realized is called the 'Original Fruit' and the 'Sublime Original Sahā.'"
This refers to the excellence of the native land.
The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states:
"The analogy cited above is extremely vast; where has he resided for such a long time?"
Therefore, it is said that he constantly remains in this land and performs buddha-work in other lands as well; during this interval,
I spoke of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and others.
Furthermore, when it is said that he has entered nirvana,
these are all skillful means of distinguishing phrases and sentences intended to sweep away doubts regarding the traces left behind.
As taught in the ancient scriptures:
in various places one practices the causes,
and in various places one receives the prediction.
This refers precisely to doubt regarding the fruit;
now, this doubt is dispelled by pointing to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
The phrase "entering nirvana" immediately dispels doubt regarding the cause;
it immediately dispels doubt regarding the fruit.
Such causes and effects are not of a single kind;
they are all my skillful means and not literal teachings.
Miaole says:
This refers to Śākyamuni Bodhisattva entering extinction;
one must not say it refers to Dīpaṃkara.
Nirvana is also not Śākyamuni;
at that time, during the era of Dīpaṃkara Buddha,
he had already attained Buddhahood.
And he enters parinirvāṇa,
because it is impossible for two Buddhas to appear simultaneously. Therefore:
I shall take only the attainment of the prediction [of enlightenment], the propagation of the Dharma, and the end of my life as the fruit;
if there are sentient beings who come to me, I shall observe with the Buddha-eye whether their faculties, such as faith and so forth, are sharp or dull.

According to those who were to be saved, he manifested different names in various places, different ages, and different sizes; he appeared as one already born or as one yet to be born, and likewise manifested the words that he would enter nirvana, though he was not extinguished, merely showing the appearance of extinction.

This is benefiting beings through his physical form; furthermore, by means of various skillful methods, he teaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma—this is benefiting beings through his voice. Thus, the Tathāgata perceives those sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings, whose virtues are meager and whose defilements are heavy.
For these people, I say that I left home at a young age and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, appearing to do so in this life;
yet in reality, the time since I truly attained Buddhahood has been exceedingly long and far-reaching, such as this.
It is only by means of skillful expedients (*upāya*) that he teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way;
thus he speaks in this way, [yet it is] not birth.
*Miaole* says:
The duration of their lifespan is so vast that even a kalpa would be but a speck of dust;
yet in the interim, they are swept away,
for the *kāya* is not real.
This treatise is the original version of the *Shen zhen shi ming yuan* (The True Illumination of the Body).
The "Chapter on Learners and Those Beyond Learning" states:
The Buddha said:
I and Ānanda simultaneously gave rise to the bodhicitta in the presence of the Buddha Śūnyarāja.
Ānanda always delighted in much hearing,
whereas I was always diligent and energetic;
therefore, I have already attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, Ānanda upholds the words and phrases of my Dharma;
in the past, he together with me resolved upon the Great Mind,
and is thus a fellow student.
By my diligence,
I have previously surpassed and attained Buddhahood;
by his extensive learning, he [has attained it].
It is as stated in the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" (*Sadāparibhūta-parivarta*):
"In the distant past, there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (*Vaiśvāsana-rāja*)."
After they had passed into extinction,
another Buddha appeared,
also named King of Majestic Sound.
In this way, there were twenty trillion Buddhas,
all of whom shared the same title:
the first was Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja).
There was a bhikṣu named Constantly Not Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta).
Whenever he saw the fourfold assembly, he...
They all prostrated and offered praise, saying:
"We do not dare to treat you with contempt."
"All of you shall become Buddhas.
Among the fourfold assembly,
there were those who gave rise to anger and spoke with harsh words and insults.
We do not require such false prophecies.
After many years have passed,
people may [strike us] with sticks, clubs, tiles, or stones.
He beat and threw him down;
[the victim] fled and stayed at a distance,
yet continued to cry out in a loud voice.
"I do not dare to treat you with contempt;
you shall all become Buddhas.
Because he constantly spoke these words, [he was called Never-Disparaging].
The fourfold assembly of those with overweening pride addressed that bhikṣu as "Never-Disparaging."
As he was about to pass away,
he heard in the midst of the void the entire Lotus Sūtra previously preached by the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
He immediately attained the purification of the six sense faculties,
further increased his lifespan,
and extensively expounded [the teaching] for others.
At that time, the fourfold assembly who possessed overweening pride,
having been given the name "Not-Disdainful" by him,
saw that he had attained great supernormal powers.
All believed, submitted, and followed him;
this was the Bodhisattva.
He further transformed and led tens of millions of billions of beings.
They shall be established in bodhi;
after the end of their lives,
they will encounter two thousand billion buddhas.
All were named Candrasūryapradīpa.
Within their Dharma,
they preached this Lotus Sutra.
Furthermore, he encountered two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas,
all equally named Cloud Sovereign Lamp King (*Megheśvarapradīparāja*),
who [taught] for the sake of the fourfold assembly.
Having preached this sutra,
he subsequently encountered billions of buddhas,
and under them as well, he preached this very sutra.
Having accomplished these merits,
he shall attain Buddhahood.
He who was then known as "Never-Disparaging" (Sadāparibhūta).
Thus, my own body is these words and phrases;
when Śākyamuni appeared in the world,
he hesitated and did not speak.
Why is it that Never-Disparaging always speaks impulsively upon seeing others?
What is the reason for this?
Answer: If one already possesses goodness, Śākyamuni protects them by means of his smallness;
if one does not yet possess goodness, [he protects them] by means of his greatness.
Do not, out of pride in your own greatness, forcibly oppress others.
From the *Dharmadatta-parivarta*,
the Buddha said:
Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past,
I sought the Lotus Sutra without ever succumbing to weariness or indolence.
Throughout many kalpas, he constantly served as a king,
making vows to seek unexcelled bodhi in order to fulfill the six pāramitās.
He diligently practiced giving,
not begrudging his own body or life,
and renounced his royal throne.
Having entrusted the crown prince with the regency,
he issued a proclamation seeking the Dharma.

One night, when the rain caused the waters to rise so that people could not cross,
the Master arrived at his destination in an instant, his body and robes remaining dry.
People realized that he possessed the supernormal power of *ṛddhi*.
The Dharma Master Wenju was of the Zhang clan of Dongyang.
He entered Guoqing Monastery to study the Way of Tiantai.
He thoroughly mastered all essential subtleties.
His form was like a mountain and his countenance like jade;
in motion he was like drifting clouds, and in stillness he was like tranquil water.
He did not glance about, nor did his mouth utter frivolous words;
throughout the four modes of deportment, there was nothing that did not conform to the monastic discipline.
The two assemblies of Dancheng looked up to him as their model.
Previously, Guoqing Temple had established the Guangming Daochang for Emperor Yang;
it was held annually,
but the number of people was large while food supplies were scarce.
The Master exerted his utmost efforts in its construction and established twelve *qǐng* of cultivated fields,
upon which the assembly relied for their sustenance.
The Dharma Master Jingyun was a native of Jianye. From his youth,
he studied the Way of Tiantai.
In the second year of the Gwanghwa era,
he lectured on the sutras at Yongga Temple,
where he expounded upon the five stages of entering the Way according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* for the sake of the Hīnayāna.
He composed the *Xuanji* (Profound Record) in two fascicles.
The Dharma Master’s conduct was sublime;
he initially studied the teachings of Tiantai.
Having entered and resided at Mount Tai,
he made clothing from woven grass and gathered fruit for food.
By practicing the Lotus Samādhi, he was moved by the manifestation of Samantabhadra, who appeared before him to bear witness.
Later, he specialized in reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
One night, he saw the Buddha Amitābha and two bodhisattvas emerge from the ground and stand suspended in mid-air.
Emperor Xizong heard of his reputation.
The Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him the title "Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent.
One day later, he saw the jeweled ground once more and said to his attendants:
"Without engaging in visualization, the precious ground appeared once more;
the time for my rebirth in An-yang has arrived.
That very day, he passed away while lying peacefully on his right side.
The Dharma Master Lishi was a native of Siming.
He lived during the second year of the Qingtai era of the Later Tang dynasty of the Five Dynasties period.
He traveled to the various kingdoms of Koguryŏ, Paekje, and Japan to assist Master Jñānaprabha.
Koguryŏ dispatched an envoy, Li Inil, to escort the Master back to the West.
[There, he met] the King of Wuyue, Qiu.
He established a monastery in the prefectural seat to provide a dwelling for his followers; it is now known as Dongshouchang.
This Dharma Master was like a dark lamp illuminating the world, possessing the qualities of preceptual virtue, meditative concentration, and the dharma-gates of wisdom.
In lecturing and chanting the teachings of the school, he stood uniquely preeminent in his time.
At the beginning of the Dàshùn era,
he transmitted the Dharma in the imperial capital.
Hundreds of disciples followed him with joy on all sides;
at that time, it was said that he could succeed Jingxi,
and he was respectfully honored as the Tenth Patriarch.
The Dharma Master Hao was of the Zhang clan of Jiahe;
he heard that Xuan was renowned in his time as the Tenth Patriarch.
He then went forth to study under various masters and immediately realized the principle of the single mind and the threefold contemplation.
He vowed to dwell in the mountains for over twenty years.
His body was without extra robes and his mouth tasted no exotic flavors;
he sat upon a single mat and kept no bolt upon his door.
This was at the beginning of the Jianlong era of the founding dynasty.
He passed away while seated without illness.
When his remains were cremated, the number of śarīra relics was beyond counting.
Those who attained the Dharma numbered eighty.
The Dharma Master Shanqin was a native of Tiantai.
Because he was without fixed form, he was invited to preside over the monastic seat in the commandery.
At that time, he was appointed to the position because of his teacher’s esteemed conduct.
When the post of Jingming was transferred,
Zhuan’an was appointed to succeed him on the seat.
Zhāngān moved to Chìchéng;
the assembly appointed Lìyūn to succeed him,
and Yūn went to Bǎozàng.
The provincial commissioner further disparaged him as being without marks; the Master, however,
considered that the assembly was insufficient to contain him.
He subsequently moved to another superior location and expanded the buildings there.
At that time, it was said that as An Qing purified the assembly and expounded the subtle teachings and contemplations,

The Dharma Master Yuan Ying was a native of Wuxing.
In the second year of the Zhenghe era.
In the capital city of Jun, he established the Zhizhe Monastery;

the Master did not feel resentment;
he wore a simple cloth cap and coarse hemp garments.
He wandered through the human realm,
rising and sinking according to the times.
In his later years, he resided at the Yanqiao Hermitage, where he recited the sutras and performed his Buddhist devotions.
One night, he sat upright facing west;
his spirit was joyfully transformed.
On the day his shrine was cremated, śarīra relics were strewn across the ground.
The Dharma Master Tanzhao was a native of Siming.
He studied the Fangguang (Vaipulya) scriptures.
At the beginning of the Xuánhuá era,
he composed the *Commentary on the Separate Tradition of Tiantai*,
which is the most detailed and comprehensive.
Scholars approved of this.
Because of the Dharma Master’s aspiration,
he was granted the title "Puzhao" (Universal Illumination).
In his youth, he studied the Way of Tiantai and practiced the path of the Pure Land.
For fifty years, he never removed his monastic robes from his body.
Once, due to disturbances caused by bandits, he entered the mountains to take refuge from the chaos.
Carrying only his robes for contact with the body,
he was just about to ascend to the latrine when the raiders were already close at hand.
The Master changed his robes on the rock and washed and rinsed his mouth with composed ease;
the raiders did not dare to attack him.
Those who recognized his virtue sighed in admiration.
This is what is called "wandering without fear.
Is this not such a person?
The Dharma Master’s resolve was illustrious.
While residing at Jakseong, he composed the *Sakyamuni-pu* (Genealogy of Śākyamuni),
stating that he had personally received the subtle instructions of his paternal uncle, Gaean.
He also compiled the *Yeokdae Jongseung Tu* (Chart of the Lineage of Succession through the Ages).
Later scholars thus have a basis for investigation.
Wang Tian was a native of Cixi in Siming.
He styled himself the "Old Man of No Merit" (Wugong Sǒu).
His family had been renowned scholars for generations;
he attempted the jinshi examination twice but failed to achieve his ambition.
Wearing simple robes and subsisting on plain vegetables, he traveled extensively to consult with lecturers at various monastic seats.
In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha's name).
Based on the insights he had attained, he composed the *Jingtu Zixin Lu* (Record of Self-Confidence in the Pure Land).
The preface briefly states:
"The fundamental minds of sentient beings inherently possess the four pure lands;
thus, even those ordinary worldlings bound by all fetters may rely upon them."
As for the remaining three lands,
only those noble ones who have severed their afflictions are able to attain entry therein.
Furthermore, there are two types of pure karma for the single gate of rebirth.
It is called "correct contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*);
it is the silent illumination of the fundamental mind.
It is called "auxiliary practice."
This means fully cultivating the myriad virtues.
When correct contemplation and auxiliary practices advance together,
one will thoroughly comprehend the four pure lands.
Regarding the goodness of practices such as the aspiration for cessation:
while they bring about proximity to dwelling together with ordinary beings and sages,
they also serve as the remote cause for the three higher lands.
Judging by this discourse,
the Pure Land is precisely the realm ascended by Bodhisattvas who have thoroughly investigated ultimate principle.
Rather, it is to encompass the vast multitude of sentient beings through dedication and gradual cultivation.
It is further said that for those with the capacity for the Perfect [Teaching], embodying the Way constitutes the supreme pure karma;
provided one adds vows to guide them.
They are thus included among the superior class.
Even those who are ignorant and simple-minded,
merely by reciting the Buddha’s vows, will surely be reborn there.
By contemplating this single gateway of the Pure Land,
one knows that the Sage discards nothing;
those [who reject it] are merely people who cling to a deluded emptiness.
By means of unimpeded non-cultivation,

Furthermore, during the Dajian era, he expounded the Six Profound Gates for Mao Xi,
the Minister of State; and during the Zhongnan era,
Master Sengzhi of Mount Huo preached the "Peaceful Practices" chapter of the Lotus Sūtra for the Dharma Master Xuanguang of Goguryeo.
He returned to his country to propagate the teachings,
marking the beginning of the transmission of the Dharma to Goryeo (Dongguk).
This was on the twenty-second day of the sixth month in the ninth year of the Dajian era.
The Chan Master of Mount Nanyue passed away.
[This occurred during] the first year of Zhide (Gui Mao), the fourth year of the reign of Emperor Xiaodi Shubao, the eldest son of Emperor Xuan, up until the third year of Zhide.
An imperial edict was issued to Chan Master Yi of Waguan Temple.
He proceeded to the Taiji Hall to open the lectures on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Benevolent Kings Prajñā Sūtra*,
then returned to Lingyao Monastery to conduct the formal lectures.
At that time, those of the hundred seats sat on the left,
while those of the five ranks sat on the right;
Huikuang and Hui bian [were among them].
All received the imperial decree to pose difficult questions.
The Son of Heaven presided at the assembly to listen to the Dharma,
while the hundred officials paid their utmost respects.
In the fourth year of the Zhide era,
an imperial decree was issued to welcome Master Zhiyi to reside at Guangzhai Monastery.
The Emperor visited the temple to listen to the lecture on the *Renwang jing* and personally performed three prostrations.
From the fourth year of Zhengming (dingwei) until the third year [of the following reign], Master Zhiyi...
At Guangzhai Temple, he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Zhāng'ān attended these lectures in advance.

During the Sui dynasty, Emperor Wén (Yáng Jiān), following the abdication of Emperor Jìng of the Northern Zhōu, established his capital at Cháng'ān. In the tenth year of the Kāihuáng era, the Gēngxū year, the Chen dynasty fell; this was the first year the Sui claimed the orthodox mandate. This continued until the twenty-first year, the eleventh year of Kāihuáng.
The Prince of Jin, serving as Governor-General of Yangzhou,
welcomed Master Zhiyi to the Great Audience Hall,
where he hosted a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks and conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon him.
The Master gave the Prince of Jin the title "King of Total Retention" (Dhāraṇī-rāja).
The Master was honored with the title "Wise One" (Jñānin).
In the twelfth year of the Kaishuang era.
In the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era, the Dhyāna Master Zhiyi conferred the precepts upon Guan Yu and his sons at Yuyuan Mountain in Dangyang,
Jingzhou. The Dhyāna Master Zhiyi...
At Yü-ch'üan, he preached the *Mysterious Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra* (*Fahua xuanyi*).
Ch'ang-an was present among those listening.
This was in the fourteenth year of the Kai-huang era.
The Chan Master Zhizhe expounded the *Mohe zhiguan* at Yquan Temple;
Zhang’an was present to listen.
In this year, he passed through Yueyang and received the Mahāyāna precepts from the Regional Inspector Wang Xuanwu.
He then lectured on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* for the scholar Tanjie and others.
In the seventh month of the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era.
The Dhyāna Master Zhizhe arrived at Chanzhong Temple in Yangzhou and presented his commentary on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
He presented [the treatise] to the Prince of Jin.
In the ninth month, he took his leave to return to Tiantai.
This was the ninth month of the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era.
In the eleventh month,
Master Zhizhe orally transmitted the *Guanxin lun* (Treatise on the Contemplation of the Mind) to his disciples at Fulong Peak on Mount Tiantai.
At Shicheng Temple, he expounded for his disciples the ten suchnesses,
the four non-arising,
and the ten dharma realms.
The three contemplations,
the four immeasurable minds,
and the four *siddhāntas*.
The Four Noble Truths,
the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination,
and the Six Perfections.
Each and every Dharma door was [expounded];
on the twenty-fourth day of the month,
he entered parinirvāṇa before the stone Maitreya Buddha statue at Shicheng.

From the first year of Renshou, the *xin-you* year, to the end of the fourth year; from the first year of Daye, the *yi-chou* year, when Emperor Yang of the Sui (the second son of Emperor Guangwen), to the twelfth year; and from the first year of Gōngdi, the *ding-chou* year, the son of Emperor Yang of the Sui, to the end of that year—during this period, the Fifth Patriarch, Master Zhangan, [resided].
At Tiantai Guoqing Temple, he expounded the Essentials of the Mind of *Zhi-guan* for Chan Master Wei of the Lotus School.

From the first year of Wude (the Wuyin year), when Li Yuan, the High Ancestor of the Tang, received the abdication from the Sui and established his capital at Chang’an, until the ninth year; and from the first year of Zhenguan (the Dinghai year) during the reign of Taizong Shimin—the second son of the High Ancestor—until the twenty-third year, specifically on the seventh day of the eighth month of the sixth year of Zhenguan, the Chan Master Zhang’an [expounded this].
At Guoqing Temple,
he manifested parinirvāṇa in the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era.
Emperor Taizong summoned the Chan Master Fahua Wei.
He was conferred the title of Chao-san Dafu (Grand Master of Audience Dispersal) and appointed as one of the Four Great Masters of the Imperial Procession.
During the reign of Gaozong, he served from the first year of the Yonghui era, the *gengxu* year, until the sixth year of Yonghui.

He summoned the Chan Master Weicong of the Heavenly Palace and conferred upon him the title of Chao-san Dafu (Court Scattered Great Officer) and the rank of Fourth-Rank Grand Master for Escorting the Imperial Procession,
placing him on equal footing with the Master of the Lotus Sutra.

From the first year of Xianqing, the Bingchen year, through the fifth year; from the first year of Longshuo, the Xinyou year, through the third year; from the first year of Linde, the Jiazi year, through the second year; from the first year of Qianfeng, the Bingyin year, through the second year; from the first year of Zongzhang, the Wuchen year, through the second year; from the first year of Xianheng, the Gengwu year, through the fourth year; from the first year of Shangyuan, the Jiaxu year, through the second year; from the first year of Yifeng, the Bingzi year, through the third year; and from the first year of Tiaolu, the Jimao year, through the first year of Yonglong, the Gengchen year, ending on the twenty-eighth day of the eleventh month.

Dharma Master Fahua entered nirvana during the following years: the first year of Kaiyao (Xinsi), the first year of Yongchun (Renwu), the first year of Hongdao (Guiwei)— during which Empress Wu Zetian, the consort of Emperor Gaozong, deposed the Crown Prince to become the Prince of Luling and ruled in his stead from the throne— the first year of Guangzhai (Jia Shen), the first year of Chuihong (Yi You) through the fourth year, the first year of Yongchang (Ji Chou), the first year of Caru (Geng Yin) through the second year, and the second year of Ruyi (Ren Chen) through the end of that second year.
The Seventh Patriarch, Chan Master Tiangong,
expounded the *Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) to Chan Master Liang of Zuoxi at Tiangong in Dongyang.

Yanchai Year 1 (Jiamu); Zhengsheng Year 1 (Yiwu); Wansui Tongtian Year 1 (Bingshen); Shengong Year 1 (Dingyou); Shengli Year 1 (Wuxu), lasting until the second year; Jiushi Year 1 (Gengzi); Chang’an Year 1 (Xinchou), lasting until the fourth year. [The reigns of] Zhongzong Xian and Gaozong’s seventh son, whose mother was Empress Wu, lasted from Shenlong Year 1 (Yisi) until the second year; Jinglong Year 1 (Dingwei), lasting until the third year. [The reign of] Ruizong Dan, Gaozong’s eighth son, lasted from Jingyun Year 1 (Gengxu) until the second year; Xuantian Year 1 (Renzi). [The reign of] Xuanzong Longji, Ruizong’s third son, lasted from Kaiyuan Year 1 (Guichou) until the twenty-ninth year—specifically, the eighteenth year of Kaiyuan.
The Eighth Patriarch, Master Zuoxi,
expounded the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) to Chan Master Ruan of Jingxi at Zuoxi in Dongyang.
In this year, Naropa, Fayong, and others from Silla [arrived].
Saicho returned to Japan.
From the first year of Tenpō (the Renwu year) until the fourteenth year, the ninth month, the nineteenth day of the thirteenth year of Tenpō,
Zen Master Sōsa of Saikō-ji entered parinirvāṇa.

Suzong (reigned from the first year of Zhide, Bingshen [756], to the second year; and from the first year of Ganyuan, Wuxu [760], to the second year; and from the first year of Shangyuan, Gengzi [762], to the second year; and from the first year of Baoying, Renyin [764]—these constitute the reigns of Suzong). Daizong (reigned from the first year of Guangde, Kaimao [765], to the second year; and from the first year of Yongtai, Yisi [766], to the fourteenth year of Dali, Bingwu [779]; this constitutes the period of the Dali era). Suzong was the third son of Xuanzong. Daizong was the eldest son of Suzong.
The Ninth Patriarch, Chan Master Jingxi,
was expounding the *Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) for Master Sui at Fulong Peak on Mount Tiantai.

This occurred from the first year of Jianzhong, the Gengshen year (780 CE), during the reign of Emperor Dezong— the eldest son of Emperor Daizong— until the fifth day of the second month in the third year of Jianzhong (783 CE).
Chan Master Jingxi entered parinirvāṇa at Fulong.
This spanned from the first year of the Xingyuan era (Jiazi), through the first year of the Zhenyuan era (Yichou), up until the twenty-first year of the Zhenyuan era.
The tenth patriarch, Master Sui,
expounded the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation) for Master Xiu at Guoqing Temple.
In the first year of the Yongzhen era (805), during the reign of Emperor Shunzong—the eldest son of Emperor Dezong—Dharma Master Sui expounded the *Zhiguan* at Guoqing Temple for Saichō of Japan;
Saichō then transcribed the entirety of the treatises and commentaries of that school and returned home with them.
This marks the beginning of the transmission of the teachings to Japan.

From the first year of Yuánhé (the Bingxū year), the eldest son of Emperor Xiànzōng Chúnshùn, until the fifteenth year; from the first year of Chángqìng (the Xīnchōu year), the third son of Emperor Mùzōng Héng, until the fourth year; from the first year of Bǎolì (the Yǐsī year), the eldest son of Emperor Jìngzōng Zhàn, the second son of Emperor Mùzōng, until the second year; and from the first year of Dàhé (the Dīngwèi year), the second son of Emperor Wénzōng Āng, until the ninth year of the Dàhé era.
The eleventh patriarch, Master Xiufu,
expounded *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* for the external Dharma masters at Chanlin Monastery.

From the first year of Kaicheng, the Bingchen year, through the fifth year; and from the first year of Huichang, the Xinyou year—the fifth year of Emperor Wuzong’s reign, the son of Emperor Xianzong—through the sixth year: in the sixth year of Huichang, an imperial edict was issued to destroy Buddhist temples throughout the empire and purge the monks and nuns.
Xuánzōng was the thirteenth son of Emperor Xiànzōng.
When Wǔzōng intended to harm him,
he fled to seek refuge as a śramaṇa, taking refuge under the master Qī'ān.
Upon the demise of Emperor Wuzong, the ministers welcomed him back to the capital.

He ascended the throne, and in the first year of the Dazhong era (the Dingmao year), he issued an edict throughout the thirteenth year to restore the Buddhist monasteries that had been abolished during the Huichang era.

During the reign of Emperor Yizong, from the first year of the Xiantong era (Gengchen) through the fourteenth year, when Emperor Xuanzong’s eldest son [reigned]; and during the reign of Emperor Xizong, from the first year of the Qianfu era (Jiamu) through the sixth year, when Emperor Yi’s fifth son [reigned]—during the Qianfu period, the Twelfth Patriarch, Master Wai, expounded the *Zhi Guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) for Master Xu at Guoqing Temple.

From the first year of Guangming (the Gengzi year), through the first year of Zhonghe (the Xinchou year)—covering four years—through the third year of Guangqi (the Yisi year), through the first year of Wende (the Wushen year), and through the first year of Longji (the Jiyou year) during the reign of Emperor Zhaozong, the seventh son of Emperor Yizong: in the twelfth year [of this period], Dharma Master Xiu expounded the *Zhiguan* dharma-gate for Dharma Master Song at Guoqing Monastery.
From the first year of Dàshùn, the Gēngxū year, to the end of the second year; from the first year of Jǐngfú, the Rénzǐ year, to the end of the third year;

from the first year of Qiánníng, the Jiǎyīn year, to the end of the fourth year; from the first year of Guānghuà, the Wǔwǔ year, to the end of the third year; from the first year of Tiānfù, the Xīnyōu year, to the end of the fourth year;
and from the first year of Emperor Jǐngzōng’s reign (the ninth son of Emperor Zhāozōng), the Jiǎzǐ year of Tiānyòu, to its conclusion.
Three years of Liang. The Taizu of the Five Dynasties, Zhu Wen, received the abdication of the Tang and established his capital at Luoyang.
From the first year of Kaiping, the *dingmao* year, until the fourth year; and from the first year of Qianhua, the *xinwei* year, until the end of the second year.

Emperor Tai [Mendai], the fourth son of Taizu, reigned from the third year of Qianhua, the *guiyou* year, until the end of the second year; and from the first year of Zhengming, the *yihai* year, until the sixth year of Long.
From the first year of Dede, *xīn-sí* (1231), through the second year; Tang Zhuangzong Li Cunxū defeated the Liang dynasty and ascended the throne, establishing his capital at Luoyang.
From the first year of Tongguang, *guǐ-wèi* (1233), through the third year; Mingzong Duǎn was originally from the Qu-tú clan and was granted the surname Li, becoming a brother of Zhuangzong.
From the first year of Tiānchéng, *bǐng-xū* (1236), through the fourth year; and the first year of Chángxǐng (1237).
In the year Gengyin, at the end of the fourth year, Emperor Chengzu followed [the precedent]. Xu’s original surname was Wang; he was the adopted son of Mingzong.

From the first year of Qingtai (Jiawu) until the end of the second year, Shi Jingtang, the High Ancestor of Jin, extinguished the Tang dynasty and ascended the throne, establishing his capital in Bian.
From the first year of Tianfu (Bingshen) until the sixth year, during the Tianfu era, the Fourteenth Patriarch, Master Song, entered *nirvāṇa* at Guoqing.
The Dharma Master expounded on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

From the seventh year of Tenfu (Ren-yin), the second year, until the third year of Kaiyun (Jia-cheng), [the reigns of] Emperor Shao Di Li Gui, the grandson of Gaozu, and Han Gaozu Liu Zhiyuan came to an end.
The young Emperor of Jin was captured by the Khitans.
With no sovereign remaining in Central China, he subsequently ascended the throne at Jinyang and continued to use the era name of the Jin dynasty.

The capital was Bian. In the twelfth year of Tianfu (dingwei), the Emperor Yindu Chengyou ascended the throne; he was a paternal cousin of the High Ancestor (Gaozu). In the first year of Qianyu (wushen), spanning through the third year, Guo Tingwei, the Taizu of Zhou, received the abdication from Han and made Bian his capital. In the first year of Guangshun (xinhai), spanning through the third year, Shizong Rong, a nephew of the Empress Dowager of Taizu, succeeded to the imperial throne by testament. In the first year of Xiande (jiayin), spanning through the fifth year, Emperor Gongdì Chongxun, the son of Shizong, reigned. In the sixth year of Xiande (jimi), Song Taizu received the abdication from Zhou and made Bianjing his capital. In the first year of Jianlong (gengshen), spanning through the third year, the King of Wuyue, Qian Chu, [reigned].
In the second year of the Jiànlóng era,
he dispatched envoys to Goryeo and Japan to seek out lost and neglected scriptures, treatises, and commentaries.
The Kingdom of Goryeo dispatched the śramaṇa Digan to carry the commentaries on the Tiantai treatises to Luoxi, from the first year of Qiande (the year of Guihai) until the fifth year.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Dharma Master Jì of Luoxī, expounded the Dharma-gate of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* for Dharma Master Tōng.

This period began in the first year of the Kāibǎo era, the Wùchén year (948 CE), and ended in the eighth year of the Tàipíngxīnguó era, the Bǐngzǐ year (975 CE). Specifically, it spanned from the first year of the Kāibǎo era through the eighth year, up to the fourth year of the Tàipíngxīnguó era.
The sixteenth patriarch, Dharma Master Baoyun Tong,
expounded the various Mahāyāna teachings on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* for Dharma Master Li of Siming.
Dharma Master Luoxi passed away on the fourth day of the eleventh month in the fourth year of the Yongxi era (the year of Jia-shen).
Dharma Master Baoyun passed away on the twenty-first day of the tenth month in the second year of the Duangong era (the year of Wu-zi).

From the first year of Chunhua, the Gengyin year, to the end of the fifth year; to the first year of Zhaodao, the Yiwei year, to the end of the third year; to the first year of Xianping of Emperor Zhenzong, the Wuxu year, to the end of the sixth year; and through the sixth year of Xianping.
The seventeenth patriarch, Dharma Master Fazhi,
responded to Wanyuan Xinxin of Japan from Ba'en on the south lake.
Xinxin’s inquiries comprised twenty-seven points.
From the first year of the Jingde era (the Jiachen year) until the fourth year, he compiled the *Zhijiao chao* (Essential Excerpts on the Pointing-out).
He produced the *Bielixiuyuan ershi wen* (Twenty Questions on the Distinct Principle Following Conditions) to refute the errors of Jiqi’s indiscriminate application of the "pointing-out" method.
In the fourth year of the Jingde era,
Benru was dispatched with a letter concerning the Ten Meanings and two hundred questions to present them to Master Zhao of Qiantang.
This was to remedy the error of not establishing the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*) within the *Jiuguangming* (The Radiance of Salvation).
From the first year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, the Wushen year, until the third year of the same era, the Jiǔnián year.
He was granted the title Bao'en and had his name changed to Yanqing.
Together with the master Yiwen,
he composed two pieces of admonitory oaths.
He established it as a place for long-term lectures on the Tiantai school’s teachings.
In the seventh year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era,
he composed the *Guānjīng Róngxīn Jiè* (An Explanation of the Contemplation Sūtra for the Integration of the Mind).
In the first year of the Tianxi era (the Ding-si year), he practiced the Lotus Repentance rite together with ten monks for five years;
the three-year period was completed.
He intended to burn his own body as an offering to the Dharma;
however, because he was dissuaded by both public and private authorities, he did not obtain his wish.
He then composed the *Xiaofu San-yong* (The Three Uses for Subduing and Eliminating).
In the fourth year of the Tianxi era (1020), Li Zunxu,
the Prince Consort,
refuted the errors in the *Pogushan Chanyi*.
An imperial edict was presented, bestowing upon him the title of Dharma-Wisdom Great Master;
it proclaimed that he must remain in the world to expound the teachings and forbade him from relinquishing his body.
In the fifth year of the Tianxi era,
the Sovereign dispatched the palace attendant Yu Yuanqing to deliver an imperial decree to the temple.
Having practiced the Lotus Repentance for three days,
he composed an exposition on the essential principles of the repentance to respond to the Sage’s intent.
In that same year, he wrote the *Mysterious Record of the Separate Practice of Avalokiteśvara*.
The *Miaozongchao* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Contemplation Sutra) was completed;

in the first year of the Qianxing era, the Renxu year (1022), and from the first year of Emperor Renzong’s Tianstong era, the Guihai year (1023), until the ninth year, he composed the *Guangming Xuyiji* (Continued Record of the Remaining Works on the Light Sutra).
In the third year of the Tiānshèng era.
Previously, at the beginning of the Tiānxī era,
an imperial edict had been issued for the establishment of "fish-releasing ponds" throughout the empire.
The Master began on the Buddha’s birthday by releasing fish and birds for the sake of *fangsheng* (releasing life),
composing his own "Essay on Releasing Life" (*Fangsheng wen*).
In that year, the Prefectural Governor Zeng Hui reported the matter to the throne,
and an imperial edict was issued to Liu Jun of the Secretariat for Military Affairs.
The text was composed and engraved upon stone to reverently proclaim the Sage’s transformation.
The fifth year of the Tiānshèng era.
He compiled the *Wenzhuang Guangming Wenju Ji*.
Subsequently, Guanzhi continued it by adding one chapter on the Praise of the Buddha.
On the first day of the first month in the sixth year of the Tian-sheng era.
He established a seven-day period for the *Guangming* Repentance as the time for his peaceful passing.
On the fifth day, he sat in the lotus posture, preached the Dharma, and passed away while chanting the name of the Buddha.
His cremation was accompanied by the wafting fragrance of extraordinary incense.
The relics were innumerable;
the tongue remained intact,
like a red lotus flower.
From the first year of Mingdao, the Ren-shen year, until the seventh month of the second year of Mingdao,
his remains were enshrined in a stupa at Chongfa Monastery in the South City.
This concludes Volume Twenty-three of the *Fozu Tongji*.

Table of the Genealogical Succession of Buddhas and Patriarchs. Table of the Genealogical Succession of Buddhas and Patriarchs, Number Ten.
It is indeed true that the transmission of the Way is by means of the mind, not by means of outward traces.
Yet, when discussing the critical juncture of the successive transmission from patriarch to patriarch,
one must necessarily follow the traces before the mind can be known.
If one can truly know the mind, why need one necessarily eliminate its traces?
But what, then, constitutes these traces?
Is it not said that the teachings exist as their explanation?
There is contemplation which serves as their practice.
Their practice is necessarily reflected in their teaching, and their teaching is necessarily reflected in their practice.
The teaching and the practice correspond to their traces from the very beginning;
thus it is said, "One speaks of what one has practiced within one's own mind.
This is the trace of the transmission of the Way.
Knowing the traces, one necessarily knows the mind;
knowing the mind, one necessarily knows the Way.
It is only by virtue of knowing the Way that one may then discuss the occasions of transmission between successive patriarchs.

A Genealogical Table of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the Western Land: The Teacher of the Western Land, Śākyamuni Buddha; First Patriarch: Venerable Mahākāśyapa; Second Patriarch: Venerable Ānanda; Third Patriarch: Venerable Śaṇavāsa; Fourth Patriarch: Venerable Upagupta; Fifth Patriarch: Venerable Dhṛtaka; Sixth Patriarch: Venerable Miśraka; Seventh Patriarch: Venerable Buddhanandi; Eighth Patriarch: Venerable Buddhamitra; Ninth Patriarch: Venerable Pārśva Bhikṣu; Tenth Patriarch: Venerable Punyayaśas; Eleventh Patriarch: Venerable Aśvaghoṣa; Twelfth Patriarch: Venerable Kapimala; Thirteenth Patriarch: Venerable Nāgārjuna. [Note: Madhyāntika and Śaṇavāsa.]
They received the same transmission as Ānanda,
yet they were not his primary successors;
therefore, they are not listed here.
Since this land honors Nāgārjuna as its high ancestor,
it regards those from the fourteenth patriarch downward as being collateral branches.
The fourteenth patriarch of the Western Land likewise regards those from the Northern Qi dynasty onward as collateral lineages;
each [patriarch] discusses his own specific succession.
This is not a matter of mutual disagreement.
It is as when the Northern Qi master Wuzhi realized the *Zhilun* (Treatise on Wisdom) and its "one mind,
three contemplations," and transmitted them to Nanyue.
It is said that Yuanji succeeded Nāgārjuna and was ranked as the Second Patriarch; however,
the present school wishes to honor Siming as the true patriarch.
Thus, from Nāgārjuna onwards,
there are seventeen generations in total,
all of whom are equally honored in their respective positions.
Some may say that while the flourishing of the Way has reached its highest point,
the discussion of merit is slight; for indeed,
there are times of both openness and obstruction.
Thus, the Way may have its periods of decline and flourishing;
yet, what harm does this do to the Way?
It is simply that one does not possess such a father.
How could one obtain his son?
This merely records the traces of his transmission of the teachings;
should one wish to examine the underlying causes, [one must look elsewhere].
One should seek the esteemed patriarchs of the various schools in their discourses, views, and writings titled *Mingwen guangjiao zhi*.
[The lineages include: the Seventeenth Patriarch of the Eastern Land; the High Ancestor Nāgārjuna; the Second Patriarch, Master of the *Abhayapaddhati*;
the Third Patriarch, the Great Chan Master of Northern Qi; the Great Chan Master of Mount Heng; and the Chan Master Zhizhe of Tiantai. — Southern Lineage.
Chan Master Yue Dasha; County Magistrate Chen Zhengye; Chan Master Sengzhao of Nanyue; Chan Master Huicheng of Zhijiang;
Chan Master Hui-chao of Lan谷; Chan Master Hui-yao of Baqiu; Chan Master Hui-yong of Yunfeng; Chan Master Hui-wei of Jiangling;
Chan Master Zhi-guan of Zhongshan; Chan Master Hui-ming of Xiancheng; [and Chan Master] of Zhijiang.
Chan Master Huicui, Chan Master Lingbian of Nanyue, Chan Master Xuanwang of Silla, and Chan Master Huimin of Nanjian entered the hall to receive their prophetic mandates (*vyākaraṇa*):
one attained the fire-light samādhi, another the water-light samādhi, and the third was a lay attendant (*upāsaka*).
Lord of Nanyue, Prefect Liu Huibao, and Ba Zi of Guangzhou established portrait halls for them.
Twenty-eight individuals whose karma was exalted: four hundred who were deeply faithful and three thousand [others].
The Fourth Patriarch, the Great Zen Master Tiantai Zhizhe; Zen Master Guanding of Zhang’an; Zen Master Zhen guan of India;
Zen Master Faxi of Waguan; Zen Master Zhiyue of Guoqing; Zen Master Fashen of Waguan; Zen Master Puming of Guoqing; and [others] of Guoqing.
Chan Master Zhizao; Chan Master Zhixi of Fulong; Chan Master Fayuan of Guoqing; Chan Master Zhijian of Mount Lu;
Chan Master Dazhi of Mount Lu; Chan Master Daoyue of Yuquan; Chan Master Dengguan of Tiantai; Chan Master Banruo of Huading;
Chan Master Lizong of Kuaiji; Chan Master Faxiang of Qixia; [and Chan Master] Daoyue of Yuquan.

Now, our school has three types of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The first is called gradual,
which means that while the understanding is sudden, the practice is gradual.
This is precisely the dhyāna-pāramitā.
Second is the "indeterminate," which refers to sudden understanding.
Practice may be either sudden or gradual;
this refers precisely to the Six Sublime Gates.
The third is called the Perfect and Sudden.
This refers to the simultaneous practice of both understanding and application;
it is precisely the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
These three types of śamatha and vipaśyanā differ according to the capacities of practitioners.
Although their modes of practice differ, they both take the perfect principle as their fundamental tenet.

The Seven Patriarchs of the Lotus Society. The First Patriarch: Dharma Master Huiyuan (334–416), known as Bianjue, Zhengjue, and Yuanwu, of Mount Lu.

The First Patriarch was Master Dao’an; the Second Patriarch was Master Guangming of Chang’an, whom Śāṇanda (Shandao) declared to be an emanation of Amitābha; the Third Patriarch was Master Banzhou of Nanyue, Chengyuan; and the Fourth Patriarch was Master Fazhao of the Five Assemblies in Chang’an, who was a later incarnation of Śāṇanda.

The lineage of masters is as follows: the Fifth Patriarch, Dharma Master Xinding Taiyan Shaokang; the Sixth Patriarch, Dharma Master Yongming Yizhao Yongshou; the Seventh Patriarch, Dharma Master Zhaqing Yuanjing Shengchang; and Dharma Master Shiming Shizhi Xiaofa.
Those who, though belonging to different eras, equally cultivated the merit of pure practice until their achievements were preeminent, were established as the Seven Patriarchs;
we now follow this precedent,
regarding them as the masters and models for the school of the Pure Land teachings.
Even while possessing afflictions as ordinary beings,
one can manifest the Buddha of the original nature through the wisdom of the three contemplations,
as the masters of the Four Teachings have said.
It is said: Because the mind and its objects are ungraspable, defilement may be viewed as purity.
Because there is no obstruction to dependent origination, conceptualization gives rise to the manifestation of signs.
Because it is only form and only mind, they manifest right where they are.
This is the correct precept for the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha;
only those who have clarified the essence and attained its meaning can practice it.

As for such things as chanting auspicious titles, gazing upon and paying homage to the Honored Image, reciting the Mahāyāna scriptures, and upholding the pure precepts—these are [merely] auxiliary practices.
These are all the primary causes for pure karma and the auxiliary practices for right contemplation;
even those who merely cultivate the ten virtuous actions and possess benevolence and compassion can thereby achieve the merit of dedication and adornment.
Thus, whether in a state of concentration or distraction, wisdom or folly,

How truly credible this is!
