When the rain ceased and the waters receded, a great wind arose;
it blew the water's foam and cast it into the air,
where it formed the palaces of the Brahmā heavens, adorned with the seven precious jewels.
The waters receded further as before, and when the wind arose again,
it blew and cast up the water-foam to form the palace of Māra Pāpīyān;
next, he constructed the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
As it continued to recede, reaching the palaces of the Yāma Heaven,
the waters further withdrew.
A great wind blew upon the foam, forming Mount Sumeru, which is composed of the four precious substances.
Furthermore, he blew upon the water-foam to create the palaces of the thirty-three gods made of the seven treasures.
He also created the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings,
as well as the palaces of the sun and moon and the celestial palaces of the seven treasures, within the belly of the mountain.
He also constructed crystal palaces for the yakṣas dwelling in the sky,
and further built asura cities on the four sides of Mount Sumeru,
adorned with the seven precious jewels.
Furthermore, by blowing upon the water-foam, he fashioned the seven golden mountain ranges, the four great continents, and the eighty thousand minor continents,
surrounding them all with the Cakravāḍa mountains,
which are composed of vajra.
In this way, great winds blow and excavate the great earth, gradually penetrating deep within.
They deposit masses of water to form seven seas of fragrant water as well as the great salt-water ocean.
Furthermore, beneath the earth, they construct the palace of Yama and the abodes of the hells.
In this manner, the three thousandfold world-system is formed simultaneously;
beyond this, the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains are further created to encircle this great trichiliocosm.
Within these, there are ten trillion each of the six heavens of the desire realm, Mount Sumeru, the sun and moon, the four continents,
and even the Lesser Iron Encircling Mountains.
This is based on the sequence of twenty intermediate kalpas of increase and decrease as it is established in the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra*.
During the first small kalpa of decrease and increase, the past kalpa of destruction occurs;
at that time, all sentient beings had long since gathered within the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Since the hosts of devas were numerous and their dwellings cramped,
those whose merit had diminished should descend to lower abodes.
At the very beginning of this world, there was one devaputra.
Passing away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, he was reborn within the empty palace of Mahābrahmā;
thus he became the Brahmā King.
He remained there for one period of decrease and one period of increase.
He reflected:
"No son of Brahmā has come to be born in my abode since the Great King Brahmā passed away;
sixty minor kalpas have elapsed through the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness."
This constitutes their lifespan.
During the second intermediate kalpa of decrease and increase, the devas from the Ābhāsvara realm who are reborn in the Brahma-world [attain this same lifespan].
The lifespan of the Brahmapurohita devas is forty minor kalpas;
this corresponds to the second cycle of increase and decrease within the kalpa of self-formation,
and they pass away when the first cycle of increase and decrease arrives.
During the third intermediate kalpa of decrease and increase, the Ābhāsvara devas [diminish];
furthermore, there are those who come to be born in the Brahma-world,
becoming the Brahmakāyika devas with a lifespan of twenty intermediate kalpas.
This refers to the third cycle of increase and decrease within the *kalpa* of formation;
they perish at the time of the first cycle of increase and decrease of the *kalpa* of abiding,
or those who follow thereafter are reborn here.

Since the sequence of before and after is not fixed, the timing of their disappearance is likewise not fixed. Gradually descending, they are reborn among the various celestial beings of the six desire realms;
by the power of their evil karma, they gradually descend further to be reborn among the hungry ghosts, the animals, and the hells.
That which is formed later perishes first;
such is the natural law.
At that time, the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, their merit exhausted, descended to be born by transformation as human beings.
Alternatively, those who delight in observing new lands see light shining afar and travel with sovereign ease,
free from the characteristics of male or female.
Because they arise together as a multitude,
they are called "sentient beings" (sattva).
From the earth, sweet springs gush forth, their flavor like that of clarified butter and honey.
Having tasted it with his finger, he became attached to its flavor;
consequently, he lost his supernormal powers and his bodily radiance.
Then, a great darkness arose in the world, and a black wind blew across the ocean.
The sun and moon drifted forth and were placed within the belly of Mount Sumeru to illuminate the four continents.
At that time, when the people saw them emerge they rejoiced, and when they saw them enter they feared.
From this point onward, there came to be days and nights, the new and full moons, the seasons of spring and autumn, and the reckoning of years.
One cycle ends and another begins.
Because they became addicted to the flavor of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*), their complexions grew coarse and haggard.

Once the flavor of the earth had vanished, forest creepers (*vana-latā*) appeared. As the *Loutan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) states, "Two branches of grapevines [appeared], and they again became addicted to eating the forest creepers. Subsequently, the forest creepers also vanished.
Then there naturally grew non-glutinous rice without husks or chaff,
possessing all manner of exquisite flavors.
As this food became somewhat coarse, remnants and impurities remained upon the body.
Desiring to eliminate [the previous state],
it then becomes the two channels and forms the male and female organs.
Those with a preponderance of sensual desire become women;
by the power of habitual tendencies from past lives, they give rise to lustful desire and dwell together as husband and wife.
When those gods from the Ābhāsvara Heaven who were later to be reborn entered their mothers' wombs,
there subsequently arose birth from a womb.
At that time, the great city of Campā was first constructed.
Even throughout all the cities and towns,
non-glutinous rice grew spontaneously; it would ripen by evening after being harvested in the morning,
and once harvested, it would immediately grow back with grains four inches long.
At that time, sentient beings took provisions for two days' worth,
and even up to five days' worth;
gradually, husks and chaff began to appear.
Once the crops were harvested, they did not grow again.
The people were filled with grief and distress;
each person enclosed their fields and houses and began cultivating seeds for the next harvest.
Thereafter, many stole the rice from others' fields,
leading to mutual brawls that none could resolve.
They deliberated on establishing a single impartial king to reward the good and punish the wicked.
Thereupon, there arose the use of weapons and the slaughter of one another.
The multitude collectively provided for him and designated him as a Kṣatriya—this term meaning "Lord of the Fields. Since then, all kings have taken this as their primary title.
At that time, Jambudvīpa was wealthy, prosperous, peaceful, and secure.
In eighty thousand commanderies, kingdoms, populations, and villages, the sound of roosters could be heard from one to another.
There was no illness, nor extreme cold or heat.
They practiced the ten wholesome deeds and governed the country according to the True Dharma.
The people love and revere [the king], and his lifespan is exceedingly long;
many sūtras state that his lifespan reaches eighty-four thousand years, with figures increasing or decreasing from this.
It is not said that after such an extremely long time, the king would fail to practice the True Dharma.
Their lifespan gradually decreased until,
when it reached eighty-four thousand years,
their height was eight zhang.
The lifespan decreases by one year and the body decreases by one inch every hundred years.
When it has decreased in this manner until the lifespan is ten years and the height of the body is one foot,
it is called the limit of the *apacayakalpa* (the aeon of decrease).
Regarding the scriptural statement that after this period, the lifespan increases by one year every hundred years—
such that a son’s lifespan is double that of his father—
even if such a thing were to occur:
The periods of increase and decrease are not uniform; when the lifespan increases to eighty-four thousand years, it is called the culmination of an *utkalpa* (aeon of increase).
One decrease and one increase thus conclude and begin again.
When the lifespan increases to eighty-four thousand years,
a Golden Wheel-turning King appears,
possessing the seven treasures and a thousand sons.
The four continents of the world were governed with abundant prosperity and joy;
daughters did not marry until they were five hundred years old.
After this, at the beginning of every *vivartakalpa* (aeon of increase), it was likewise so.
In all cases, there is a Cakravartin King appearing in the world;

according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, this occurs during the increase and decrease of the fourth minor kalpa, continuing through the increase and decrease of the twentieth minor kalpa, remaining for twenty minor kalpas. During the increase and decrease of the first minor kalpa, the devas from the Ābhāsvara Heaven descend to be born in the Brahma-world.

Those who were originally among the Brahmakāyika devas reach a full lifespan of twenty intermediate kalpas here; they pass away from this kalpa during the second intermediate kalpa of decrease and increase, the third intermediate kalpa of decrease and increase, the fourth intermediate kalpa of decrease and increase, the fifth intermediate kalpa of decrease and increase, the sixth intermediate kalpa of decrease and increase, the seventh intermediate kalpa of decrease and increase, the eighth intermediate kalpa of decrease and increase, and the ninth intermediate kalpa of decrease and increase, at which time the human lifespan has decreased to fifty thousand years.
First, Krakucchanda Buddha appeared in the world;
his clan name was Kāśyapa,
and his father was named Lide (Līdeva).
His mother was Shan-zhi (Good Branch);
his attendant was Shan-jue-zi (Good Awakening Son); and his superior [disciple] was Ju-an-he-cheng (Dweller in the City of Peace and Harmony).
He sat beneath a śirīṣa tree and preached the Dharma;
in that single assembly, he delivered forty thousand people.
This occurred when the human lifespan had decreased to forty thousand years.
The second was Krakucchanda Buddha, who appeared in the world;
his clan name was Kāśyapa,
and his father was Mahāguṇa.
His mother was Bhadraśrī;
his attendant was Saumya;
his son was Śāstṛ.
He resided in the City of Purity and sat beneath an udumbara tree to preach the Dharma,
delivering thirty thousand people at a single assembly.
When the lifespan had decreased to twenty thousand years,
the third Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world;
his clan name was Kāśyapa.
His father was Brahmadatta;
his mother was Dhanavatī;
his attendant was Kalyāṇamitra.
The Son assembled his army and resided in the city of Vārāṇasī,
where he sat beneath a nyagrodha tree and preached the Dharma.
In one assembly, twenty thousand people were delivered.
When the lifespan decreased to one hundred years,
the fourth Buddha, Śākyamuni, appeared in the world.
Originally, when the human lifespan was ten thousand years,
he observed that sentient beings lacked the capacity to be saved; thus,
he waited until the end of the kalpa of a hundred-year lifespan, when they were oppressed by suffering.
Therefore, according to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Dīrgha Āgama*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
when the lifespan decreases to eighty-six years,
the True Dharma will come to an end.
One thousand four hundred years.
According to the *Dharmasthitistava*,
the Buddha told Ānanda:
After my parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall endure for one thousand years;
because women have gone forth, it shall be diminished by five hundred years.
The Semblance Dharma shall endure for one thousand years.
Regarding the ten thousand years of the Final Dharma (mofa),
the *Śāsanodbhāvana-śāstra* states:
"At the beginning, the Buddha did not ordain women."
Later, she was taught the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*),
whereby she regained her life for another thousand years.
The Fayuan zhulin states:
The deva replied to Nanshan,
"The Buddha’s *khakkhara* staff remains in the dragon cave,
having stayed there for forty years."
After the Tathāgata’s passing,
there was a flying rākṣasa who was able to expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
He falsely assumed the guise of a virtuous bhikṣu and consumed four hundred meals daily from those who observed the precepts;
in order to sever this evil, he was confined within a dragon cave.
Furthermore, it shall cause the True Dharma (Saddharma) to increase and abide for four hundred years;
the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpakadharma) to increase for fifteen hundred years;
and the Final Dharma (Śeṣadharmakāla) to increase for twenty thousand years.
The lifespan decreases until it reaches seventy-eight years.
This occurs during the eight hundred years of the Semblance Dharma (Saddharmapratirūpaka).

This is the present time when the lifespan is correctly reduced; based on the calculation that two thousand two hundred years have passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the lifespan has decreased by twenty-two years.
According to Zhili of the Zhi-li school,
it was calculated that the period of the Semblance Dharma would be reduced until it ended at sixty-one years.
The calculation of two thousand five hundred years is explained in the preceding text.
When the lifespan decreases to thirty years,
one enters the final dharma period (mappō) of three thousand one hundred years.
Humans were three feet tall.
At that time, a famine and disaster arose because the people all practiced the ten unwholesome deeds.
The five kinds of superior flavors— herbs, vegetables, rice,
and grains— all vanished;
they could do nothing but gather for banquets using only boiled, decayed bones.
If one encounters a single grain of millet or barnyard grass and guards it as if it were a treasure,
yet for six or seven years no rain has fallen from heaven,
one will still not obtain water.
How much more so regarding food and drink;
many people died of hunger,
and the commandery became increasingly desolate and abandoned.
The calamity will only cease on the seventh day of the seventh month in the seventh year.
At that time, there will be one person who gathers men and women possessing merit and virtue,
totaling ten thousand people.
They remain as the seed of humanity.
When people can practice goodness,
they obtain whatever food and drink they require.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Madhyama Āgama*, and the *Zhuangchun lu* all record that the heavens will send down rain mixed with [impurities] until the human lifespan diminishes to twenty years.
When the four thousand one hundred years of the final dharma age have passed,
humans will be two feet tall,
and at that time, the calamity of pestilence will arise.
Because people committed evil deeds with increasing intensity,
they all met their deaths and were buried without anyone to escort them.
The districts and towns lay desolate and abandoned,
with only a few families remaining;
it was not until the seventh day of the seventh month that the calamity finally subsided.
Only ten thousand people were left as a seed;
these people maintained virtuous conduct regarding food, drink, and clothing.
Then the heavens will send down rain,
and [the lifespan] will decrease until it reaches ten years;
this marks the entry into the five thousand and one hundred years of the Final Dharma (mappō).
Humans will be one chi in height;
women will marry at five months of age;
and at that time, the calamity of weapons will arise.
As people’s practice of evil became increasingly prevalent,
each gave rise to the intent to kill; thus,
those capable of committing evil acted accordingly.
They are held in contempt by others;
whenever they grasp grass, wood, tiles, or stones, these all turn into swords and blades,
whereby they slaughter one another and suffer countless untimely deaths.
There were also those who, out of revulsion, entered the mountains to hide;
after seven days and seven nights, the calamity finally subsided,
leaving only ten thousand people as the seed of the population.
The people emerged from their hiding places;
seeing one another,
they gave rise to hearts of compassion and kindness, and together practiced wholesome dharmas.
Whatever food and clothing they require, the heavens will rain down;
because they are able to practice virtue, their lifespan further increases.
Thus, from a hundred years, their life span increases by one year and so forth—this is called the minor three calamities (*kṣudra-saṃvartanī*).
It merely destroys the primary retribution;
however, if one encounters the three great calamities,
then both the environment and the primary retribution are destroyed together.
When the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa reaches ten years,
the kalpa of weapons arises and they slaughter one another;
at that time, the Buddha-dharma shall temporarily perish and disappear, according to the record of the duration of the Dharma.
When his age increased to forty-nine,
the ten-thousand-year period of the Semblance Dharma (mofa) began;
Bodhisattva Moonlight then appeared in the land of Zhendan— that is, the Eastern Land of China— and preached the Dharma for a full fifty-two years.
After he has extensively delivered sentient beings and entered nirvana,
the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* will first vanish and cease to appear;
the remaining sūtras will then disappear in succession.
One hundred years after the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* [is established], it will extensively deliver sentient beings and then vanish; this is the *Benqijing*.
According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, in a future age, the scriptures shall generally be extinguished.
Out of compassion and pity for them,
I shall now cause this sutra to remain for a hundred years.
Any sentient beings who encounter this sutra, [shall attain benefit].
One may attain deliverance according to one's wishes.
The *Vow Text of Nanyue* says:
"I now make this vow."
Maintain this sutra so that it does not perish,
until the appearance of Maitreya Buddha in the world,
and when the human lifespan has increased to one hundred years.
When fifteen hundred and one years of the final Dharma age have passed,
the people of Jambudvīpa will again practice wholesome deeds.
At that time, the sixteen Arhats, together with their disciples, [will appear].
Returning once more among human beings, he will manifest and proclaim the unsurpassed True Dharma, delivering immeasurable multitudes and causing them to leave the household life.

This record of the duration of the Dharma’s extinction states that after the Dharma has increased to two hundred and forty-four years, it will enter the period of the Final Dharma (mofa) for twenty-nine thousand five hundred years.
When the Dharma is nearing extinction, during the final five hundred years,
if one single-mindedly cultivates this Lotus Samādhi,
one will immediately attain the purification of the six sense faculties.
Thus, we know that even in the final age there are those with the capacity to enter the Mahāyāna; the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* quotes the *Samantabhadra-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra*,
which extends [the lifespan] to two hundred and forty-nine years,
at which time the three thousand years of the Final Dharma (mofa) will be exhausted.
When the human lifespan increases to seven hundred years,
the sixteen Arhats will have completed their propagation of the Dharma; they will then descend from the world of men to the present day,
where they shall continue to teach and transform beings for five thousand years by means of all the sūtras and śarīra relics.
Having gathered [the relics] to erect a stūpa,
he sat cross-legged and circumambulated this stūpa.
They all sank into the earth;
this was the sign of the complete extinction of the Buddha-dharma.
From that time forth, there were ten billion pratyekabuddhas.
The *Lokottara-dharmadeśanā-sattvārthakara-dharmakṣayavyaya-sūtra* and the *Dharmasthitigāthā*.
When the lifespan of humans was seventy thousand years,
sixteen arhats constructed a stūpa out of the seven precious gems.
The relics of Śākyamuni were all gathered within the city of Dhānyakaṭaka; there,
they made offerings of incense and flowers, speaking these words:
I have previously received the command to protect and uphold the True Dharma and to bring manifold benefits to devas and humans.
Now that the treasury of the Dharma has been exhausted and my karmic conditions have been fully fulfilled, [I shall depart].
Now, as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he first resolved his power of aspiration, whereupon flames arose and consumed his body.
At that moment, the stūpa immediately sank into the earth, coming to rest upon the vajra-limit.
At that time, when Śākyamuni’s True Dharma has utterly perished,
seven hundred koṭis of pratyekabuddhas will appear in this world simultaneously.
When the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, the assembly of Pratyekabuddha Āryas will again all enter parinirvāṇa.
Subsequently, Maitreya Tathāgata will appear in the world; the record states that seventy thousand [Pratyekabuddhas] will forever pass into extinction.
The period of the final Dharma (mofa) is too remote;
for now, we shall take the scripture’s statement of seven hundred years as the correct measure,
increasing it until the time of twenty thousand years.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, an Iron Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin) emerges to rule exclusively over the single continent of Jambudvīpa;
whereas those with Gold, Silver, and Copper wheels rule over one, two, three, and four continents respectively.
Thus, an Iron Wheel-turning King rules over one continent.
The Golden Wheel-turning King [rules] over the four continents when the human lifespan increases to forty thousand years;
the Copper Wheel-turning King appears to rule over the two continents of the southeast when the lifespan increases to sixty thousand years.
When the lifespan increases to eighty-four thousand years, a silver-wheel-turning monarch appears to rule over the three continents of the east, south, and west; when it further increases,
a gold-wheel-turning monarch appears to rule over the four continents.
A Wheel-Turning King accomplishes the seven treasures.
First, as for the golden wheel treasure:
when a noble king appears, [the golden wheel emerges].
The divine wheel-treasure suddenly appeared before him;
the wheel had a thousand spokes and was crafted by a celestial artisan,
with a diameter of one zhang and four chi.
The Sage-King saw it and stroked the wheel with his hand, saying,
"Turn toward the eastern direction according to the Dharma.
The wheel then turned eastward.
The king, leading his fourfold army, followed behind him.
The minor kings of the eastern regions came to visit and prostrated,
saying, "Excellent, Great King!"
"I wish for you to govern here.
Then the Holy King said,
"You should transform and govern by means of the True Dharma (saddharma)."
"Do not allow for partiality or injustice.
When the various kings heard this,
they immediately followed the Sage King on his tour of the various states as far as the shores of the Eastern Sea.
The same occurs in the south, west, and north, wherever the wheel reaches.
As for the second precious treasure, the white elephant:
while the king is seated upon his palace terrace, it suddenly appears before him.
He immediately tested it by mounting it;
departing from the city at dawn, he traveled around the four seas and returned by mealtime.
These were the three types of dark-blue horse treasures.
Suddenly appearing before him,
he returned at the time of the morning meal.
As for the four divine jewels:
Suddenly it appeared before him;
placed atop a high banner, its light illuminated one yojana.
All the people within the city arose to attend to their tasks.
It was said to be during the daytime.
Then, the five types of precious women suddenly appeared.
His countenance is upright and handsome; he is warm in winter and cool in summer.
As for the six treasures of the householder, various scriptures, classics, and wealth suddenly appear;
he perceives and knows all the treasuries hidden within the earth.
As for the seventh, the Treasure of the General of the Army:
it appears suddenly;
possessing wisdom, strategy, and heroic prowess, he is exclusively entrusted with the task of military expeditions.
This constitutes the accomplishment of the seven treasures of a Wheel-Turning King according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
During the tenth minor kalpa of the period of decrease and increase, when the human lifespan has decreased to eighty thousand years,
the fifth Buddha, Maitreya, appears in the world.
At that time, the land of Jambudvīpa was as level as a mirror of lapis lazuli.
Its forests were lush and flourishing, reaching thirty li in height.
Eighty-four thousand small cities made of various jewels surrounded the world.
Within it is a great city named Ketumatī,
featuring pavilions made of the seven treasures, seven rows of trees,
and gardens and bathing pools filled with water of eight meritorious qualities.
The streets, alleys, and lanes are twelve *li* wide.
The land is peaceful and secure, free from the calamities of enemies, bandits, robbery, fire, water, weapons, or famine.
There is a pillar of bright jewels, twelve *li* in height.
Its radiance surpasses that of the sun, shining constantly day and night.
Fragrant winds occasionally blow, causing jewel pillars to rain down precious necklaces;
the multitude takes these to use as clothing and ornaments.
A net of various jewels covers the city above.
When the wind blows, the jeweled bells proclaim the taking of refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
The height of a human body is sixteen zhang.
The lifespan reaches a full eighty thousand years;
there are none who die prematurely.
Women marry only at five hundred years of age.
They constantly experience sublime bliss and dwell deeply in meditative concentration,
as in the Heaven of the Third Dhyāna;
these people always possess a heart of loving-kindness, being respectful, harmonious, and compliant.
This is entirely due to Maitreya’s compassionate instruction and guidance;
because they observe the precept against killing,
they suffer from only three types of illness.
First, food and drink;
second, excretion; third, aging.
There was a species of fragrant and delicious rice that yielded seven harvests;
it possessed a hundred flavors and was digested as soon as it entered the mouth.
When they relieved themselves, the earth split open and produced red lotuses to conceal the foul odors.
When the people have grown old, they naturally go beneath the trees to recollect the Buddha and await their end;
they will be reborn in the Great Brahma Heaven and before the various Buddhas.
There was a wheel-turning sage king named Śaṅkha,
who possessed the seven treasures, a thousand sons,
and four great treasuries filled with precious jewels.
When the multitude saw this, their minds were not filled with greed or attachment;
each of them said to one another,
"In the time of Śākyamuni Buddha, sentient beings of the past committed the karmic offenses of birth and death by stealing and plundering one another for the sake of such jewels."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, who was about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven to become a Buddha,
was born into a great Brahmin family;
his father’s name was Śuddhama.
His mother was named Brahmavatī.
He descended to be born and took conception in her womb;
his body was the color of purple gold and possessed the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Seated upon a precious lotus flower, his radiance was immeasurable;
his body was thirty-two zhang tall,
like a mountain of yellow gold.
Observing with right mindfulness that [existence] is suffering, empty, impermanent, and not to be delighted in, he no longer found pleasure in the household life.
At that time, King Śaṅkha presented him with a palanquin made of the seven treasures;
having accepted it, Maitreya bestowed it upon the brahmins.
Even as they destroyed their respective shared portions,
Maitreya beheld this jeweled terrace momentarily subject to impermanence;
he realized that all conditioned phenomena are utterly subject to decay and extinction.
Cultivate the perception of impermanence and recite the verses on the impermanence of past Buddhas:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. Once arising and ceasing have ceased, nirvāṇa is bliss."
Having spoken this verse, he left the household life to study the Way.
He went to the Vajra-Adorned Bodhimaṇḍa outside the city of Ketumatī, beneath the Dragon-Flower Bodhi tree, whose branches were like precious dragons exhaling flowers of a hundred jewels.
Therefore, he is named Dragon Flower (Nāgapuṣpa). On that very day, during the first watch of the night, he subdued Māra and attained enlightenment.
Śakra, Brahmā, and the four heavenly kings requested him to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, King Śaṅkha, together with eighty thousand ministers, sought to leave the household life and become renunciants.
Their hair fell off naturally and they immediately became śramaṇas.
Then, Maitreya Buddha, together with King Śaṅkha and the assembly of bhikṣus, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings,
entered the center of the city of Ketumatī.
The diamond throne upon which the Buddhas of the past sat spontaneously emerged from that ground;
it was upon this seat that the Buddha turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma.
The brahmin and elder Sūḍana of that time was the present elder Sūḍana;
the precious woman of the wheel-turning king was Śyāmavatī, the precious queen.
The mother Viśākhā is she;
Sumati, a relative of Maitreya,
is the present bhikṣuṇī Bhadrikā.
Each of them ordained eighty-four thousand people to study the Path.
At that time, King Śaṅkha’s thousand sons all sought ordination together,
leaving behind only one son to succeed to the royal throne.
In the first assembly of the World-Honored One Maitreya, he will preach the Dharma upon a diamond throne,
and nine hundred and sixty million people will attain arhatship.

The Buddha told Bimbisāra:

Seeing an Arhat entering meditative absorption,

Having received the instructions as taught, the monkey leaped for joy;
while climbing a tree, he fell and died, reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
He encountered a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), who taught him the unsurpassed path.
From that time onward, he encountered countless Buddhas until his final existence.
After Maitreya, he shall attain enlightenment and be named Buddha Siṃhacandra.
He is the present Vāsumitra; this is the *Siṃhacandra-buddha-sūtra*.

animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras likewise perish in succession.

Within the human body there are no parasites;

Because it is produced by the power of karma and afflictions;

because it arises through the predominant influence of karma and afflictions; and because, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-kośa*, the first dhyāna is internally disturbed by the fires of vitarka and vicāra.

Because the second dhyāna is internally disturbed by the water of joy, it is externally swept away by the calamity of water. Because the first dhyāna is internally disturbed by the fire of vitarka and vicāra, it is externally consumed by the calamity of fire. Because the third dhyāna is internally disturbed by the wind of equanimity, it is externally destroyed by the calamity of wind. Because the fourth dhyāna is free from these internal disturbances, it is not destroyed by external calamities. Furthermore, because the first three dhyānas possess coarse and subtle forms, they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind; whereas the fourth dhyāna is formless and thus not destroyed by such calamities. Moreover, because the first three dhyānas are accompanied by the afflictions of vitarka, vicāra, and prīti, they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these afflictions and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Finally, because the first three dhyānas are characterized by the presence of the three elements of fire, water, and wind, they are destroyed by the corresponding calamities; whereas the fourth dhyāna is devoid of these elements and is thus not destroyed by external calamities. For these reasons, the fourth dhyāna is not destroyed by external calamities. Furthermore, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of suffering—namely, the suffering of change, the suffering of formation, and the suffering of suffering—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three sufferings and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Additionally, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of craving—namely, craving for form, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three cravings and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Furthermore, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of pride—namely, pride of superiority, pride of equality, and pride of inferiority—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three prides and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Moreover, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of delusion—namely, delusion regarding the self, delusion regarding phenomena, and delusion regarding both—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three delusions and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Finally, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of attachment—namely, attachment to form, attachment to sensation, and attachment to consciousness—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three attachments and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. For these reasons, the fourth dhyāna is not destroyed by external calamities. Furthermore, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of conceptualization—namely, conceptualization of the self, conceptualization of phenomena, and conceptualization of both—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three conceptualizations and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Additionally, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of latent tendencies—namely, the latent tendency of desire, the latent tendency of existence, and the latent tendency of ignorance—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three latent tendencies and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Moreover, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of fetters—namely, the fetter of desire, the fetter of existence, and the fetter of ignorance—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three fetters and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Furthermore, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of outflows—namely, the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three outflows and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Additionally, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of taints—namely, the taint of desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three taints and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Moreover, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of clinging—namely, clinging to sensual pleasure, clinging to views, and clinging to precepts and vows—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three clingings and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Furthermore, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of craving—namely, craving for form, craving for sound, and craving for touch—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three cravings and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Additionally, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of perception—namely, the perception of form, the perception of space, and the perception of nothingness—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three perceptions and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Moreover, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of consciousness—namely, the consciousness of the eye, the consciousness of the ear, and the consciousness of the body—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively; whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three types of consciousness and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Furthermore, because the first three dhyānas are associated with the three types of mental activity—namely, the activity of vitarka, the activity of vicāra, and the activity of prīti—they are destroyed by the calamities of fire, water, and wind, respectively;

whereas the fourth dhyāna is free from these three types of mental activity and is therefore not destroyed by external calamities. Because the third dhyāna is internally disturbed by the winds of inhalation and exhalation, it is destroyed externally by the calamity of wind.
The fourth dhyāna lacks such fixed continuity; its palaces arise simultaneously with the birth of the beings who dwell therein.

Circling to the right,

Within it, unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields are arrayed; the very first layer at the bottom is named Supreme Light Pervasively Illuminating.
It is shaped like a maṇi jewel and is surrounded by as many worlds as there are atoms in a buddha-field.
The Buddha’s name is Pure Eye, Lamp Free from Defilement.
The second tier is named the World of Various Fragrant Lotus Flower Exquisite Adornments;
it is shaped like a lion throne and is surrounded by world-systems as numerous as the atoms within two buddha-fields.
The Buddha’s name is Lion-Light Supreme Illumination.
The third tier is named Jewel-Adorned Universal Radiance World;
its shape is octagonal.
It is surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in three buddha-fields;

The fourth layer is named the World Adorned with Various Radiant Flowers.
Its form is like a mani-lotus,
surrounded by as many world-systems as there are atoms in four buddha-fields.
The Buddha’s name is Vajraprabhāpramāṇavīryasunirmita.
The fifth layer is named the World of Universally Radiating Sublime Flower Light.
Its shape is generally square with many corners,

The Buddha’s name is Fragrant Light Joyful Power Ocean.
The sixth layer is named World of Pure and Wondrous Radiance;
its shape is square.
It is surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in six buddha-fields;

The seventh layer is named World Adorned with the Flames of Various Flowers.
It is shaped like a multi-storied pavilion and is surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms within seven buddha-fields.
The Buddha’s name is Sovereign Light of the Fame and Merit of the Ocean of Joy.
The eighth layer is named the World-Sphere of the Birth of Sovereign Power;
its form is like Indra’s net,
surrounded by as many world-systems as there are atoms in eight buddha-fields.
The Buddha’s name is Wisdom-Ocean Banner of Vast Renown.
The ninth layer is named World of Emanating Exquisite Sounds;
its shape is like the body of Brahmā.
It is surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in nine buddha-fields.
The Buddha’s name is Pure Radiant Mark Unconquerable.
The tenth layer is named Vajra Banner World.
Its form is perfectly circular,
surrounded by as many worlds as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields.
The Buddha’s name is Sovereign King of the Ocean of All Dharmas.
The eleventh layer is named the World-Sphere of Constantly Manifesting Sapphire Radiance;
it is shaped like a half-moon and is surrounded by world-systems as numerous as the atoms within eleven buddha-fields.
The Buddha's name is Immeasurable Merit Dharma.
The twelfth layer is named World of Radiant Illumination;
its shape is like a swirling flower.
It is surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in twelve buddha-fields.
The Buddha there is named Surpassing Śakra and Brahmā.
The thirteenth layer is named the Sahā World.
Its appearance is like empty space,
covered above by a universally perfect celestial palace,

The Buddha’s name is Vairocana; he is the Thousand-Petaled Rocana whose number of marks is equal to the atoms within ten Lotus Treasury Worlds.
This corresponds to the thirteenth world among the hundred billion lands of a single flower. The fourteenth layer is named the World of Tranquil Dust-Transcending Light.
