one puts on whatever garment is encountered and does not seek out one's original clothes.
Next, they arrived at the incense trees,
where they took up musical instruments and proceeded while harmonizing their strings with exquisite voices;
those people were free from all ailments.
Their facial features were identical, and their hair was a deep blue-black, reaching down to their eyebrows.
When a man felt desire, he would gaze intently at a woman;
she would then follow him to the pleasure groves.
If the father and mother were such that sexual intercourse should not take place,
the tree would not bend its shade over them,
and they would each disperse.
If they were not kinsmen, the tree would bend its shade over them so that they might enjoy themselves as they pleased for one day up to seven days.
Thereupon, she departed.
After that woman had been pregnant for seven or eight days, she gave birth;
as soon as the child was born—whether male or female—she placed it at a crossroads.
There were practitioners who, upon emerging, would take up their fingers to rinse their mouths;
sweet milk issued from their fingers, filling the child's entire body.
After seven days had passed, the child grew to maturity.
They associate with their own kind:
men among the male community and women among the female community.

When such a person reaches the end of life, they do not weep or wail for them; because the human lifespan is fixed at one thousand years, they do not mourn the dead, but instead adorn the corpse and place it at a crossroads.
There is a bird named Uccaiḥśravas (or Ucchvāsaka); as the Abhidharma states,
this bird pecks at corpses.
When they went outside the mountain to eat, the ground was soft and rose up to meet their feet;
when they voided excrement or urine, the earth would open and split apart,
and once finished, it would close back together again.
That person, having cultivated the ten wholesome actions in previous lives, was born in this continent.
Their lifespan is one thousand years, neither increasing nor decreasing.
After the end of their life, they are reborn in a heavenly realm. According to the Abhidharma:
Regarding those among the inhabitants of the Northern Continent who possess much desire:
they may experience it several times during a single lifetime, up to four or five times;
yet there are also those who practice cultivation so that they remain free from desire until death. (From the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*).
There are two intermediate continents:
first, Kūṭāhva; second, Krauñcāhva.
Both are inhabited by humans. According to the Abhidharma:
The people of Jambudvīpa are three and a half cubits tall,
or four cubits;
those of Pūrvavideha are eight cubits.
The Western Continent is sixteen cubits;
the Northern Continent is thirty-two cubits. The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states:
"The Southern Continent is three and a half [cubits]."
The eastern and western continents are equal in measure.

On the northern continent, seven *zhǔ* (one *zhǔ* equals eight-tenths of a *chǐ* according to the scale of King Jī of the Zhōu dynasty). The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that the southern continent excels in three respects.
First, being courageous and possessing a powerful memory, one is able to perform karmic deeds;
second, diligently cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
third, a Buddha appears in that land. (From the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*).
In the four great continents and the eight intermediate continents,
human forms are short and small.
Some say that on Camara Island, only rākṣasas dwell.
Furthermore, there are five hundred small islands,
some inhabited by humans and others inhabited by non-humans.
In the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, there is one who speaks of emptiness.
The Buddha said:
"I observe the sentient beings in the world."
They are constantly oppressed by ten kinds of suffering:
first, birth;
second, old age.
Third, illness;
fourth, death;
fifth, sorrow.
Sixth, the enemy.
Seventh, painful sensation.
Eighth, sorrow.
Ninth, the affliction of pain;
tenth, the cycle of birth and death.
Sentient beings undergo such oppressions in order to attain the liberation of Bodhi. (From the *Sijiao yi*).
When practicing the five constants, the five precepts, and the medium grade of the ten wholesome actions during the causal stage,
one receives a human body.
The commentary states:
The inhabitants of the northern continent have a fixed lifespan of one thousand years; therefore,
they do not weep or offer condolences at death,
and the Buddha does not appear there.
Therefore, one does not hear the Buddha-dharma;
this is why it is considered one of the eight difficulties.
As people of old have said:
The *Liezi* records that the Yellow Emperor dreamed of traveling to the land of Huaxu;
this is none other than the Northern Continent (Beizhou).
Whether this can be accepted as fact remains unknown.
Because there is the Buddha-dharma to be studied in Jambudvīpa,
many individuals with the capacity for the Mahāyāna are born therein;
this is because their lifespans are short and they are oppressed by manifold sufferings.
Out of fear, they resolve their minds [on enlightenment] and diligently cultivate the path of practice;
this is why they are the most excellent among those of the four continents.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
The great trichiliocosm is formed as the vast earth through immeasurable causes and conditions;
it rests upon the water wheel, the wind wheel, and the space wheel;
yet space itself has no support.
The world is established through the karmic retribution of sentient beings.
According to the *Nava-bodhisattva-piṭaka-sūtra*,
it is because all Buddhas have accomplished inconceivable wisdom.
He is able to discern the signs of all winds and rains,
and he knows that there is fire and wind in the world called Ulūka.
Whatever sensations sentient beings experience are all stirred by this wind;
this wheel of wind is three *krośas* in height, with each *krośa* being [the standard measure].
This is called "the question of the sound of one drum-beat.
According to the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*,
five li constitute one krośa.
In the Abhidharma-śāstra,
eight krośas constitute one yojana;
this is the "medium" yojana mentioned in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
At a distance of forty *li* above this wind, within the midst of space,
there arises another wind named Cāpaka.
"The height of this wind-circle is ten yojanas," and so forth.
In this manner, he is able to fully comprehend the characteristics of the sixty-eight thousand koṭis of wind-circles upon each successive wheel.
The supreme wind-circle is named "Pervading the Upper Realm" (Samantaparivāra).
It serves as the support for the water-circle,
which has a height of six million eight hundred thousand yojanas.
It is that upon which the great earth rests;
the height of this earth is sixty-eight thousand yojanas,
and this is the measurement of its surface.
There is a trichiliocosm.
Its earth, water, and wind wheels differ from those of other trichiliocosms. [The earth wheel, gold wheel; the water wheel; the wind wheel. *Abhidharmakośa*.
The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) is three hundred and twenty thousand yojanas;
the *Xin pusa zang* (New Bodhisattva Piṭaka) is four hundred and eighty thousand yojanas;
and the *Lou tan jing* (Loutan Sūtra) is sixty-eight thousand yojanas.

Above [this], there are twenty billion *li* of gold dust and twenty billion *li* of golden vajras; together with the *Lishi* (Abhidharmakośa), they total three million two hundred thousand *yojanas*. — *Prabhāsa-sūtra*.
The earth is eighteen thousand yojanas deep,
beneath which lies golden sand;
this is according to the *Lokotpatti-sūtra*.
480,000 [yojanas]. This likely omits four characters.
According to the *Qishi yinben jing* (Sūtra on the Causal Origin of the World), winds blow upon the water, causing it to circulate.
Above this, it becomes gold, like the cream that forms from boiled milk;
this is called the Golden Wheel. (From the *Ekottarika Āgama*).

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* states that the earth is sixty-eight thousand *yojana* deep. The *Dharmakṣema’s Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states that the earth is one hundred and sixty-eight thousand *yojana* deep.
The *Abhidharmakośa* [states...].
The *Lokotpatti* (Arising of the World) is eight hundred thousand *yojanas*;
the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka* is six hundred thousand *yojanas*;
and the *Loutan* (Ratnakūṭa/Loka-dhātu) is six million eight hundred thousand *yojanas*.
Eighty billion *li*. According to the *Lokasthāna-hetu-mūla-sūtra*,
by the karmic power of the various kings, the water does not flow away or disperse,
just as food that has not yet been digested does not fall into the receptacle for digested matter (*pakvāśaya*).
The *Abhidharmakośa* states it is 1,600,000 yojanas; the *Lokadhātunirdeśa* states it is 360,000 yojanas;
and the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka* [states it is 400,000 yojanas].
Sixty-eight thousand *koṭi* wind-circles (according to the *Loutan jing*),
five hundred twenty billion *li* (according to the *Zhilun*),
and the great trichiliocosm.
All are based upon the wind-circle as their foundation.
The commentary states:
What is set forth in the sūtras and śāstras cannot be made uniform; only the *Abhidharmakośa*’s presentation of the world-system is roughly consistent [with the sūtras].
The meaning taught by the Buddha should not differ;
rather, it is that the masters of the various schools have distinct lineages of transmission and perspectives,
and the translations produced by translators in different eras vary in their phrasing.
Ascending ten thousand yojanas from the base of Mount Sumeru,
with a circumference and breadth of ten thousand yojanas,
there dwells the Heaven of Firm Heads (Sudarśana).
Ascending another double [the previous height], based on the original [circumference], it is twenty thousand [yojanas] high and encircles the mountain for eight thousand yojanas;
this is where the Mālyaprabha devas dwell.
Ascending yet another double, based on the original, it is thirty thousand [yojanas] high and encircles the mountain for four thousand yojanas.
This is the abode of the gods who are constantly heedless.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "ascending one more level, the three heavens are each 'one-fold,'" this means that each increases by ten thousand times.
The Four Heavenly Kings [reside] at a height of forty thousand yojanas. According to the *Yinben* (Original Text), it says:
"At the midpoint of the mountain, forty-two thousand yojanas [from the base], the abodes of the Four Kings surround the mountain for four thousand yojanas."

Regarding the Sun, Moon, Constellations, and the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Beneath Mount Sumeru there are three distinct tiers, which are the abodes of various deities;
each is surrounded by sevenfold walls and courtyards."
All [these] are inhabited by yakṣas; according to the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra*, these three heavens are all inhabited by yakṣas and are under the jurisdiction of the Four Great Kings.
(From the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*): The palace of the Sun Deity.
It is composed of celestial gold and crystal, measuring fifty-one yojanas in length and breadth;

it is square like a house, yet appears round from a distance. According to the Treatise on Wisdom (*Jñānaprasthāna*), the sun and moon travel at a distance of five hundred li, driven and rotated by five kinds of winds.
A magnificent palanquin made of Jāmbūnada gold,
sixteen yojanas in height and eight yojanas in square.
The Sun Deity and his retinue dwell therein, enjoying the five celestial sensual pleasures.
The lifespan of the Sun Deity is five hundred years;
his descendants succeed one another in turn.
They all dwell in palaces within that realm for the duration of one kalpa, passing through the four phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness,
as well as eighty minor kalpas.
This constitutes one great kalpa. The radiance of the Sun Deity’s body and the light of his wondrous palanquin and palace illuminate one another;
there are a thousand rays of light.
Five hundred [yojanas] it shines sideways, and five hundred it shines downward.
The celestial palace of the Sun God (Sūryadeva) moves constantly without ceasing;
for six months it travels northward, and for six months it travels southward.
The celestial palace of the Moon Deity is composed of silver, lapis lazuli, and blue beryl;
it is sixteen yojanas in height.
It is eight yojanas in width.
Within this palanquin, the Moon Deva and his celestial maidens enjoy the five heavenly sensual pleasures.
The lifespan of the Moon Deva is five hundred years.
The palace is inhabited by descendants in succession for the duration of one kalpa.
The body-light of the Moon Deity transforms the palace into a thousand-fold radiance that shines forth in five hundred directions.
The five hundred lower lights shine forth.
By what causes and conditions does the celestial palace of the Moon God gradually appear?
The orb of the moon is obscured by sixty rays of the sun;
as it gradually moves further away from the sun,
it becomes increasingly visible.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it that on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon, the lunar palace reaches its full perfection and clarity,
as it is at its greatest distance from the sun such that its light cannot be obscured?
And by what causes and conditions is it that on the fifteenth day of the waning moon, nothing at all appears?
At this time, the lunar palace is closest to the sun;
the sunlight obscures it so that it does not appear at all.
By what further causes and conditions, then, does the shadow of the lunar palace manifest?
On this continent there is a Jambu tree;

because it is so tall, its shadow appears as the lunar disc. In the past, when the Bodhisattva was practicing the conduct of a rabbit, Śakra, Lord of Devas, tested him by requesting his flesh for food.
He cast his body into the fire.
Out of pity for him, Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
took the scorched rabbit and placed it within the moon.
He causes sentient beings to behold him,
so that they may know this is the body of a bodhisattva practicing loving-kindness. According to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), when the sun is at its zenith in Jambudvīpa,
it is just beginning to set in Pūrvavideha.
When the sun first rises over the western continent, it is midnight on the northern continent;
the other three directions may be understood by analogy. According to the *Qishi yinben jing*, the walls and ground of the Sun Deity’s palace are as thin as flower petals.
Sustained by five winds, the Great Discourse on the Long Agama states that the sun and moon are five hundred *yojanas* in circumference;
yet what we actually see does not exceed the size of a fan. According to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the palatial abodes of the great stars are seven hundred and twenty *li* in circumference.
The medium-sized stars span four hundred and eighty *li*,
and the small stars span one hundred and twenty *li*. According to the *Loutan jing* (Kālacakra-sūtra),
the past Bhagavān Seer distributed the various lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and planetary deities (*graha*), each with its own presiding deity to protect the state and nourish the people.
The seven lunar mansions of the eastern quarter are Jiao (Horn), Kang (Neck), Ding (Shoulder), Xin (Lord), Fang (Palace), Xin (Heart), Wei (Tail), and Ji (Broom).
The seven lunar mansions of the northern quarter are... [as listed above].
The seven lunar mansions of the western quarter are Dou (Dipper), Niú (Ox), Nǚ (Woman), Xū (Emptiness), Wēi (Danger), Shì (Room), and Bì (Wall).
The seven lunar mansions of the southern quarter are Kuí (Donkey), Lóu (Hare), Wèi (Stomach), Mào (Mao), Bì (End), Zǐ (Beak), and Shēn (Forest, pronounced *zī* and *sēn*).
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* contains the forms, surnames, sacrificial offerings, ritual regulations, presiding deities,
and sovereigns of the various constellations— Jing (井), Gui (鬼), Liu (柳), Xing (星), Zhang (張), Yi (翼), and Zhen (軫).
All of these are fully detailed in this sutra, which was preached by the Buddha while residing in the Palace of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
He addressed the various lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*),
the celestial hosts who roam the sky, the nine planetary deities (*navagraha*), the twenty-eight lunar mansions, and the twelve zodiacal signs (*dvādaśa-rāśi*):
"I shall proclaim the method for removing calamities and difficulties through the *Candraguhyaprabhāsa-mahāteja-dhāraṇī*, as taught by the Tathāgata Śālarāja in the past."
If there are kings, ministers, their residences,
or their realms that are oppressed by the five planets,

or visited by Rāhu, comets, meteors, or malevolent stars; or if these afflict the zodiacal signs and constellations belonging to one's natal horoscope, or various stellar positions, or even the imperial throne itself.
When there is oppression within the nation, the family,
or the regional domain, those who cause various obstacles by either retreating or entering shall [be dealt with].
Simply establish a *maṇḍala* in a pure place and recite this *dhāraṇī* one hundred and eight times, or one thousand times.
Regarding the *Xiāozāi jīng* (Sūtra on the Elimination of Calamities), there are nine types of *graha* (planetary deities).
They are able to cause the increase and decrease of days and nights, as well as the abundance or scarcity of the world.

Their names are: the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu (the residual energy of fire), Ketu (the residual energy of earth), the *Mayūra-sūtra*, and the eighty-four thousand calamitous evil stars in the Sahā world. According to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, Vaiśravaṇa is the lord of the constellations; according to the *Fahua wenju* [Commentary on the Lotus Sutra]; and as the *Analects* says:
Regarding the North Pole:
the *Tianwen zhi* (Treatise on Astronomy) states that the North Pole is located halfway up Mount Sumeru, at forty-two thousand *yojana*.
The account of the Four Heavenly Kings residing [there] is the same as in the *Jñānaprasthāna-sūtra*.
If one follows the *Abhidharma* treatises,
such as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:
It is said that they all measure forty thousand yojanas: the city in the east is named Uttarakuru,
the city in the south is named Sudarśana,
and the one in the west is named Aparagoyānī.

In the north, he is named Devapūjita (Heaven-Worshipped); according to various sūtras such as the *Pūrva-videha-rāja-sūtra*, he is generally called Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Holder of the Realm), who leads the gandharvas—translated here as "those who travel seeking fragrance"—the celestial musicians of Śakra; the piśācas—translated here as "demons that devour the vital essence of humans," or "mad demons"; and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* identifies him as a pūtana, who protects the inhabitants of the eastern continent.

In the south, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka leads the kumbhāṇḍas—translated as "ghosts of enchantment" (or "hypnotizing ghosts")—who cause those who are sleeping to be possessed by spirits; he also protects the people of Jambudvīpa from the preta, translated as "the first of the hungry ghosts."

The *Kokālika-sūtra* (孔雀經) states that the Heavenly King of Miscellaneous Speech in the Western Quarter is translated as "Broad Eyes" (*Virūpākṣa*) and also as "Not Retribution. He is able to take charge of sentient beings who have committed grave transgressions for whom retribution cannot manifest in this life, as well as nāgas and pūtana-demons—these latter being called "stench-ghosts" (*gandharva*). According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he protects the inhabitants of the Western Continent (*Aparagoyānī*).

In the north, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa (Multihearing) leads the yakṣas—here translated as "the swift"—who are the class of messengers currently transmitting talismanic writs at this Dharma assembly. The rākṣasas—here translated as "the violent and evil," ghosts who devour humans—protect the inhabitants of the northern continent. This is recorded in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa (known here as Duowen; he is so called because his fame for merit and virtue spreads in the four directions); King Dhṛtarāṣṭra (known here as Chiguo; he is so called because he protects and sustains the land); King Virūḍhaka (known here as Zengzhang; he is so called because he causes the roots of goodness in himself and others to increase); and King Virūpākṣa (known here as Zayu; he is so called because he can speak various kinds of diverse words, or "Broad Eyes," or "Evil Eyes"; he is specifically charged with punishing the wicked and causing them to encounter suffering so that they may resolve their minds toward awakening)—all rose from their seats and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the king of all sūtras...
We, the four kings and the twenty-eight divisions of hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities, with our pure divine eyes, shall constantly observe and protect this Jambudvīpa."

For this reason, we call it the *Sūtra of the Golden Light of the World-Protecting Kings*. Regarding the fact that the scribe first designates the North: in the Western lands (India), the North is considered the superior direction. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* provides a clear analogy for this, stating that "just as the North is to the East, so it is the unsurpassed supreme. This is precisely what the four clarifications rely upon. Bodhisattvas of the First Ground often manifest as the Four Heavenly Kings; according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, all four heavenly kings engage in marriage and sexual desire just like humans.
The spontaneously born infants appear upon his knees like two-year-old children.
Before long, celestial vessels filled with food of a hundred flavors and divine nectar spontaneously appear.
Those with greater merit are white in color.
The middling is blue in color;
the inferior is red in color.
Once consumed, it becomes equal in measure to that of the various devas.
Upon first birth, they remember their past karma;

having played, they forget. According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, when the sons and daughters of the Four Heavenly Kings are born, if they are born upon the knees or at the eyes of a female [deity], [they remember their past].
The goddess thinks, "This is my son," and the god also says, "This is my son.
If he is born on the lap where he was sleeping,
he has only one father.
All the wives may become mothers;
the sexual activities of the gods of the Four Great Kings are innumerable.
Yet there are also those who practice cultivation until death remains free from desire.

It is the same for all the devas of the desire realm. According to the *Lokasthiti-śāstra*, each of the Four World-Protecting Kings has ninety-one sons of great power, all of whom are named "Emperor" (Devendra).
They are able to protect the ten directions.

All mountains, rivers, trees, lands, cities, and walls, as well as all ghosts and spirits, belong to the Four Heavenly Kings (*Catur-mahārāja*). [From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: Beneath each king are eight generals.
The Four Heavenly Kings and their thirty-two generals surround the four worlds to protect and assist those who have left the household life;
among these thirty-two generals, General Wei is foremost in his vast protection.
Monks whose power of the Path is weak are deluded by Māra.
When the General [Vaiśravaṇa] rushed forward in distress, he responded to the situation to eliminate and prune [the obstacles];

this was a matter of the resonance between Heaven and Man, as recorded in the *Tuolitian Gong Zhi Tu* (The Diagram of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven Palace). Formerly, a Brahmin of the Kauśika clan, together with thirty-two companions, jointly cultivated merit and virtue.
At the end of their lives, they were all reborn on the summit of Mount Sumeru, where Kauśika became the Lord of Devas and thirty-two people served as his ministers.
[From the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*]: Once, after the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a woman.
Having resolved to build a stupa as an act of merit, he was reborn as a lord of devas;
thirty-two people who assisted in the construction were reborn as his ministers.

The combination of the sovereign and his ministers constitutes the thirty-three [deities] in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*. ○ In Sanskrit, *Trāyastriṃśa*; this is translated here as the Heaven of the Thirty-three. ○ Śakra dwells in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
In the future, when he attains Buddhahood, his name shall be Wu-zhuo (Unattached).
At each of the four corners of Mount Sumeru, there is a peak five hundred yojanas high and broad, as described in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, where the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi dwells.
The Trāyastriṃśa gods protect [this realm].
At the summit of the mountain is the great city of Sudarśana, ten thousand yojanas in circumference (*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*).
The summit of the mountain is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and breadth (*Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*).
Of these, the area level enough for habitation is only forty thousand yojanas; its double gates are one and a half yojanas high.
The city has a thousand gates, each guarded by five hundred blue-clad yakṣas.
They were strictly armed and on guard.
Within the city was the Palace of Supreme Excellence (Viśeṣavati), measuring one thousand yojanas in circumference;
its ground was adorned with pure gold and various precious jewels.
It is as soft as *tūla* cotton.

Following the contours of the ground, it conforms to the principles of correct reasoning. In the center of Śakra’s abode is a golden city one thousand *yojanas* in circumference; within it is the Palace of Excellence (*Vaijayanta*), which has five hundred gates.
Within it is a multi-storied pavilion named Piśācayan.
On its four sides are one hundred and one jeweled towers.
There were seventeen thousand chambers.
In each chamber there were seven celestial maidens,
and each maiden had seven handmaidens.
All those celestial maidens were the principal consorts of Śakra.
Śakra dwells together with the Aśura maiden Śacī;
manifesting emanated bodies, he dwells together with his various consorts. According to the Abhidharma-śāstra, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana traveled throughout the small thousandfold world system.
There is nothing as magnificent as the Vaijayanta Hall (*Vaijayanta-śālā*)—the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
[This refers to] the city streets and alleys;
according to the merit of devas and humans, there are various dwellings of varying sizes.
The city roads are five hundred [yojanas] long.
Within them are seven markets for grain, clothing, various incenses, food and drink, flower garlands, crafts, and courtesans.
There was also a market official;
the Son of Heaven and his celestial consorts came and went to trade,
negotiating the prices of goods, high and low.
It possesses the characteristics of a marketplace;
although such things are made there, there is no taking and no giving.
If one wishes to satisfy a need, one may simply take it away.

This city of Sudarśana is further surrounded on all sides by celestial districts, celestial counties, and celestial villages. Outside the city, as described in the *Qishi yinben jing*, there are four gardens on its four sides.
The first is the Caitraratha Garden (the *Qishi yinben* refers to it as the Citra-ratha Garden).
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that outside the eastern gate, various chariots appear according to the merit of the devas.
The *Lokadhātunirdeśa* refers to the second as the Coarse and Wicked Garden (*Raudra-udyāna*), while the *Lokaprajñapti* calls it the Rough and Harsh Garden (*Karkaśa-udyāna*).
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that when the devas outside the southern gate were about to go to war, their armor and weapons appeared spontaneously.

The *Lokaprajñapti* mentions three groves: the Grove of the Three [Heavenly] Miscellaneous Trees (*Trāyastriṃśa-miśraka-vana*), the Grove of Arising in the World (*Lokotpatti-vana*), and the Grove of Confusion (*Saṃkara-vana*).

On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, the celestial maidens from the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter this garden to mingle with the heavenly hosts, sporting and enjoying the five celestial sensual desires. The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that outside the western gate, when the various devas enter therein, they are accompanied by all manner of most exquisite objects of desire.

Regarding the four pleasure groves, the *Lokaprajñapti* states that upon entering them, one experiences joy; the *Saṃyukta Āgama* says they are located outside the northern gate, where the devas sport and all give rise to delight.
Each of the four groves is one thousand yojanas in extent.
Each has a wish-fulfilling pond, fifty yojanas in circumference,
filled with water of eight virtues.
To the southwest outside the city is the Sudharmā Hall.
When the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three assemble to deliberate upon and adjudicate matters of what is lawful and unlawful regarding the subjugation of the asuras,
there is to the northeast a tree called the Pārijāta.
On the day its flowers bloom, their fragrance wafts with the wind for a hundred yojanas.
Even against the wind, it can be reached from fifty *li* away; according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in the center of the Sudharma Hall there is a lion throne.
According to the *Vaiśravaṇa-ṛṣi-sūtra*, the Sudharma Hall has eighty-four thousand pillars.
Those who enter this hall are free from the faults of unpleasant tactile sensations, drowsiness, and groaning.
When Śakra ascends the throne,
sixteen celestial kings sit on his left and sixteen on his right.
There were two crown princes,
who were these two great generals,
seated at the left and right sides of the various heavenly kings.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, King of the Heavenly Kings, together with his ministers and military forces, sat respectfully at the eastern gate for the sake of the various devas.
Virūḍhaka, King of the Heavenly Kings, sat at the southern gate.
Virūpākṣa, King of the Heavenly Kings, sat at the western gate.
The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa sits at the northern gate.
These Four Heavenly Kings report upon the good and evil of the world to Śakra and the various heavenly kings.
On the eighth day of the month, the ministers of the Four Great Kings travel throughout the world;
on the fourteenth day, the princes of the Four Great Kings travel;
and on the fifteenth day, the Four Great Kings themselves personally observe the good and evil [of sentient beings].
If there are not many people receiving the precepts or practicing giving,
Śakra hears this report and speaks with distress, saying:
"The host of devas is diminishing."
The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states that the Asuras increase daily. First is the Heaven of the Hall of Wholesome Dharmas (*Sudharmā-deva*), which is Śakra;
second is the Heaven of the Peak Dwellers (*Kūṭāgāra-deva*);
third is the Heaven of the Mountain Summits (*Śikhara-deva*).
Fourth, the gods of the city of Sudarśana;
fifth, the gods of the earth of Pariṣaṇḍā;
sixth, the gods dwelling on Mount Kūṭaka.
Seventh, the gods of the Miscellaneous Palaces;
eighth, the gods of the Joyful Garden;
ninth, the gods of the Luminous Heaven.
10. The gods of the Pārijāta Grove; 11. The gods of the Saṃjīva Tree; 12. The gods of the Dangerous Shore;
13. The gods of the Variegated Dangerous Shore;
14. The gods of the Maṇiguhya Treasury.
14. The gods of the Revolving Ground (Cakravāḍa-bhūmi).
15. The gods of the Secret Palace (Guhyamandira).
16. The gods of the Garland Reflection (Mālāpratibimba).
17. The gods of the Soft and Supple Ground (Mṛdumṛdu-bhūmi).
18. The gods of Miscellaneous Adornments (Vicitravyūha).
19. The gods of the Ground of Fulfilling Wishes (Cintāmaṇi-bhūmi).
Twenty: the gods of Subtle Conduct;
twenty-one: the gods of Musical Song;
twenty-two: the gods of Majestic Power and Wheels.
Twenty-third, the Candra-devas;
twenty-fourth, the Sūrya-devas; twenty-fifth, the Śīghraga-devas;
twenty-sixth, the Ābhāsvara-devas.
Twenty-seven: the Heaven of Wisdom;
twenty-eight: the Heaven of Multitudinous Parts;
twenty-nine: the Heaven of Abiding on the Wheel.
30. The Heaven of Superior Conduct;
31. The Heaven of Majestic Splendor and Countenance;
32. The Heaven of the Wheel of Majestic Splendor.
The Sūtra on Mindfulness of the True Dharma of the Thirty-three Pure Heavens: Because he gave food, drink, lamps, and wealth when he was formerly a human being, he is named Śakra Devānām Indra;
this means "Lord of the Gods. Because his clan name when he was formerly a human being was Kauśika, he is also called Kauśika.
Because Śacī was his first queen, he is named Śacīpati.
Because he contemplates a thousand meanings within a single sitting, he is named Sahasranetra.
Because he is the sovereign of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, he is named Indrāli. In the *Madhyama Āgama*, he originally had a thousand names.

The *Vajrapāṇi-balopama-mayūra-vidyārājñī-sūtra*: When Śakra was insufficient in his translation [of merit], he possessed the power of the vajra-pestle. Regarding the birth of those born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three:
when they are born, lotuses grow in the hands of the celestial maidens, and they know for themselves that they have sons.
He immediately bestowed it upon her husband.
Seven days later, she gave birth to a son who was born with a natural knowledge of celestial laws.
Within the palace, he saw a mistressless goddess who came and said, "Welcome, noble son, to this palace of yours. I have no husband;
I now offer myself to you for worship. She was like a twelve-year-old girl, as described in the *Vidyādhara-siddha-ṛṣi-sūtra*, at the time of her first birth from heaven.
Suddenly, within the birthplace of his parents— either between their two knees or their two thighs—
a precious vessel appeared, filled with celestial *sudhā* and celestial wine.
According to whether one's merit is superior, middling, or inferior, there are white, red, or black colors [of the body].

Once the meal is finished, the physical stature immediately becomes equal to that of the original men and women. According to the *Sūtra on the Primary Causes of the World’s Arising*, those who practice the ten wholesome paths exclusively in their superior grade are reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. (From the *Fourfold Teaching Ritual*).

A general discussion on the physical dimensions of the various devas: the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* [provides the measurements]. Regarding the size of their robes: the *Dīrgha Āgama*. Regarding their lifespan: the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, which agrees with the *Abhidharmakośa*. Regarding bodily radiance: the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. Regarding food and drink: the *Karma-hetu-tridhātu-vibhāga-sūtra*. Regarding the fruits of retribution: the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Regarding ordinary beings and sages: [the same source]. Regarding the location of the formless bodies: [the same source]. Regarding the Lord of Devas: [the same source]. Regarding the four dhyānas, the four stages, and the height of the Four Heavenly Kings’ bodies: half a *li*.
The garment weighs half a *liang*.
Fifty years in the human realm constitute one day and night for the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*).
Thus, the lifespan of the Four Great Kings is five hundred such years.
Nine million human years constitute one day and night in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell; by such reckoning,
the lifespan in the Saṃjīva Hell is five hundred years.
Three hundred twenty-four billion years for humans constitutes one year in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) hell.
The bodies of those in the Trāyastriṃśa (Heaven of the Thirty-three) are one *li* in height.
Their garments weigh six *zhū*.
One hundred years in the human realm constitutes one day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa devas;
they live for one thousand such celestial years.
Three hundred and sixty million years among humans constitutes one day and night in the Black Rope Hell; by this reckoning,
the lifespan in this hell is one thousand years.
The bodies of the deities in the Yāma Heaven are one and a half *li* in height,
and their garments weigh three *zhu*.
Two hundred years in the human realm constitute one day and night for this heaven.
Taking one thousand years of the lifespan of those gods as the measure,
it corresponds to fourteen hundred and forty million years in the human realm;
this constitutes one day and night in the Saṃghāta Hell.
Counting in this manner, the lifespan in this hell is two thousand years.
The inhabitants of the Tuṣita Heaven are two li in height,
and their garments weigh one and a half zhu.
Four hundred human years constitute one day and night for this deva realm;
using this reckoning, the lifespan of this deva is four thousand years,
which calculates to five billion seven hundred and sixty million human years.
One day and night in the Raurava (Crying) Hell is equivalent to four thousand years by such reckoning; this is the lifespan in that hell.
The gods of the Nirmāṇarati (Delighting in Emanation) Heaven are two and a half *li* in height.
Their garments weigh one *zhu*.
Eight hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for this heaven,
and they live for eight thousand years by that celestial reckoning.
Two hundred and thirty billion years among humans constitutes one day and night in the Great Crying Hell (*Mahāraurava*).
Calculated in this manner, the lifespan in this hell is eight thousand years.
The beings of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations are three li in height,
and their garments weigh half a zhu.
One thousand six hundred years in the human realm constitutes one day and night for this heaven.
Taking those sixteen thousand celestial years as a single day and night,
this corresponds to nine hundred twenty-one billion six hundred million human years.
This constitutes one day and night in the Hot Hell (Tapana-naraka).
Calculating in this manner, the lifespan in this hell is sixteen thousand years.

The lifespan of Māra Pāpīyas, the Lord of the Maras, is thirty-two thousand years. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, the *Dīrgha Āgama*, and the *Abhidharma*, the measure of lifespan in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) is calculated in terms of *kalpas*.
The gods of the Brahmakāyika heaven have a lifespan of half an eon—twenty minor eons—and their bodies are half a yojana in height.

The gods of the Brahmapurohita heaven have a lifespan of one eon—one minor eon being counted as part of that eon—and their bodies are one yojana (forty *li*) in height. The Mahābrahmā gods have a lifespan of one and a half eons—sixty minor eons—and their bodies are one and a half yojanas in height.
In the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*), two great eons (*mahākalpa*) elapse;

hereafter, all instances refer to "great eons," which collectively comprise eighty minor eons (*antarakalpa*) consisting of the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. Their bodies measure two *yojana* in height; from this point downward, the dimensions of the body correspond to the lifespan. In the Heaven of Infinite Light (*Apramāṇābha*), four great eons elapse.
The body [of the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings] is four yojanas;
that of the Ābhāsvara Heaven is eight great kalpas;
and the body [of the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven] is eight yojanas.
The Śuddhāvāsa devas have a lifespan of sixteen great kalpas and a body sixteen yojanas in height;
the Apramāṇaśubha devas have a lifespan of thirty-two great kalpas.
The body [of the Śubhakṛtsna devas] is thirty-two yojanas;
for the Śubhakṛtsna devas, it is sixty-four great kalpas,
and their bodies are sixty-four yojanas.
In the Anabhraka Heaven, there are one hundred and twenty-five great kalpas;

the body is one hundred and twenty-five yojanas. When this heaven’s body and lifespan both perish, it is three kalpas and three yojanas. In the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, there are two hundred and fifty great kalpas.
The body [of the beings in the Heaven of No-Thought] is two hundred and fifty yojanas;
those in the Heaven of Vast Fruit both have five hundred great kalpas [of lifespan],
and their bodies are five hundred yojanas.
In the Avṛha Heaven, the lifespan is one thousand great kalpas and the body is one thousand yojanas;
in the Atapa Heaven, it is two thousand great kalpas.
The body [of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three] is two thousand yojanas;
the gods of the Sudarśana Heaven [have a lifespan of] four thousand great kalpas,
and their bodies are four thousand yojanas.
In the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the lifespan is eight thousand great kalpas,
and the body is eight thousand yojanas in height;
in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, it is sixteen thousand great kalpas.

The bodies [of the gods] are sixteen thousand yojanas long; as for the Abhidharma treatises on the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, the garments they wear change in size and weight according to their minds.
The devas of the form realm do not wear clothes;
though they appear as if wearing them, it is no different from being naked.
Although their heads have no topknots, they appear as if wearing celestial crowns.
There is no distinction of male or female; they arise as a single kind from the causal origin of the world. Regarding the lifespan in the formless realm:
it is twenty thousand kalpas in the Sphere of Infinite Space, and forty thousand in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.
The Sphere of Nothingness lasts for sixty thousand kalpas;
the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception lasts for eighty thousand great kalpas.
In all three realms, there are those who die prematurely.
Only those in Uttarakuru, the Tuṣita Heaven, those in their final existence as Bodhisattvas, and those in the Heaven of Non-conception have fixed lifespans;

it is not said that they die prematurely. According to the Abhidharma, those who practice the concentration of the Sphere of Infinite Space and those who practice wisdom each attain a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas.
In the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the two practices of concentration and wisdom each attain twenty thousand *kalpas*.
In the two higher stages, there is only the practice of concentration, which is doubled;
thus, they are sixty thousand and eighty thousand [kalpas], according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Regarding the light of the bodies born from karmic retribution among the various devas:

The gods of the desire realm possess constant bodily radiance because they have practiced giving lamps, candles, and bright jewels, as well as maintaining the purity of ethical discipline and meditative concentration.
The gods of the form realm possess it because they practice dhyāna, transcend desire, and cultivate the fire-light samādhi.
The constant radiance of their bodies surpasses that of the desire realm.
If the constant light of Śākyamuni extends one *zhang* in each direction,
the greatest radiance of the various devas is even greater than this.
Although they may extend for immeasurable yojanas,
they are eclipsed and do not appear before the light of a single zhang.
The Four Heavenly Kings possess four kinds of colors.
Dark blue, red, yellow, and white:

the colors of the deities in the various heavens of the desire realm are all like this, just as when one first sees a dark blue flower at birth, the body becomes dark blue in color. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle [number missing], and the *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma) state: [as above].
The gods of the form realm take joy as their food;
those of the formless realm take mental activity as their food.
Furthermore, it is said:
Those in the realms of form and formlessness take the joy of meditative concentration and the delight in the Dharma as their sustenance.
As for the gods of the desire realm whose merit is profound,
their cups are filled with ambrosia and a hundred flavors arrive together.
Those of meager merit, though they possess food and drink, never find them to their satisfaction.
Thus, a sutra says:
"For example, when the various devas partake from a common vessel, the color of the rice differs according to their respective merits."
Those of superior capacity see white;
those of middling capacity see yellow;
and those of inferior capacity see red.
According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*,
from the Yāma Heaven upward through all the heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*),
both the poor and the wealthy are equal.
From the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven downward, the retributions received vary in degree.
Thus, a sūtra states:
"There are gods of meager merit who suffer from hunger and descend to Jambudvīpa to pick sour jujubes for food."
It is further said:
"The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings consume the divine *sūdā* flavor;
they possess gardens, groves, ponds, and parks."
All flavors also arise spontaneously.
The food of the various devas in the desire realm is likewise. Sentient beings who fully cultivate the ten wholesome actions obtain the retribution of the heavens of the desire realm;
those who cultivate the ten wholesome actions associated with outflows and corresponding to meditative concentration obtain the retribution of the heavens of the form realm.

Furthermore, there is the *Sūtra on the Distinctions of the Three Realms*, which states that by practicing the four dhyānas of the formless realm, one obtains rebirth as a deity in the formless heavens;
whereas by single-mindedly practicing the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade, one is born in the realms of the Four Heavenly Kings or the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

If those from the Yāma Heaven upward also cultivate the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi), yet have not yet entered the fundamental dhyānas, this preparatory concentration is also called the "desire-realm concentration" (kāmadhātu-samādhi).
This method is fully explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*; "Yāma" is translated as "Good Time" (Kṣema-kāla).
Because they frequently proclaim joy;
Tuṣita is translated here as "Contentment," for its inhabitants give rise to satisfaction regarding the objects of the five desires.
The Nirmāṇarati gods are so called because they take pleasure by themselves through the transformation of their objects.
The Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods are so called because they possess sovereign mastery over the transformation of both their own and others' objects.

The four heavens mentioned above all dwell in the sky. According to the *Fan shen tian xia you mo luo bo xun zhu gong dian* (The Palace Halls of Māra-pāpīyas beneath the Brahma-body Heaven) in the *Qi shi yin ben jing* (Sutra on the Origin of the Causes and Conditions of the World), within the two realms of desire and form, there exists separately the palace of Māra.
That Māra harbors jealousy;
like a stone mill,
he grinds away and destroys their merit.
It is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
it has seven layers of palace walls as described in the *Loutan jing* (Sūtra on the Burning House) and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
"Māra" is translated as "that which seizes life."
Pāpīyān is the name of the Māra king;
Kumārajīva translated this as "the Killer," for he constantly seeks to sever the life-force of wisdom in human beings.
The Nirvāṇa Commentary states:
"Having obtained wholesome benefit by relying on the Buddha-dharma,
one fails to contemplate the debt of gratitude and instead seeks to inflict harm."
In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), the character for "māra" (魔) is written with the "stone" radical.
Since the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
it has been said that because [Māra] can afflict people, the character was changed to "ghost" (鬼).
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"For the most part, these are bodhisattvas of inconceivable liberation who should manifest as Māra kings."
The *Chuiyu ji* states:
"On the sixth heaven there is a separate abode where Māra resides; it is subsumed under the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*)."
This refers to the Devaputra Māra. ○ Mahābrahmā is here translated as "Free from Desire" (Vītarāga).
Having severed the fetters of the lower realms, he ascends to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). According to the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), the Brahma King has no separate abode.
However, regarding those who possess high towers and pavilions within the heavens, according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the Great Brahmā (*Mahābrahmā*) is the sovereign,
the Ministers of Brahmā (*Brahmapurohita*) are the ministers,
and the Retinue of Brahmā (*Brahmakāyika*) are the subjects. According to the *Fayuan zhulin*, these correspond to the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*).
The light is least in the [Heaven of] Limited Light;
in the [Heaven of] Immeasurable Light,
the radiance surpasses the former.
In the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
there is no speech consisting of vitarka and vicāra;
they communicate by means of light.
Furthermore, when this deva speaks, pure light issues from his mouth.
For the Śuddhāvāsa devas,
the departure from the sensation of joy constitutes purity.
Those who have not yet reached the higher stages are few;
the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity is more pure and superior than the former.
The Śubhakṛtsna Heaven is pure and all-pervading, free from any defects.
Below the Anabhraka Heaven, all three levels of the third dhyāna abide upon clouds.

Upon reaching the fourth dhyāna, one then dwells in the heavens of empty space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). According to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, those who generate merit are born in the Heaven of Merit-Born (*puṇyaprasava*);

those with superior meritorious power are born in the Heaven of Merit-Loved (*puṇyapriya*); and [those who attain] the state of non-conception are born in the Heaven of Non-Conception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Dwelling among the non-Buddhists,
they merely undergo a single period of existence where mental activity does not function;
they receive the retribution of five hundred kalpas of mindlessness.
When their retribution is exhausted, they will inevitably give rise to false views and be reborn in hell.
As for the Bṛhatphala Heaven,
its karmic fruit is most supreme.
Anabhraka (Cloudless), Puṇyaprasava (Merit-born),
and Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit).
These three heavens are the abodes of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Those who cultivate the ten wholesome courses of action in their highest degree and practice dhyāna will be reborn in the Heaven Free from Affliction (Avṛha),
because it is unmixed with the afflictions of views and thoughts;
and in the Heaven Free from Heat (Atapa).
Because they are free from the affliction of heat,
the gods of Sudṛśa Heaven have their meditative hindrances gradually diminished, and their vision becomes extremely clear and penetrating.
The Śubhakṛtsna Heaven,
where forms and colors become increasingly excellent and one is highly skilled in transformations;
and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is the ultimate limit.
These five heavens are called the Five *Anāgāmins* (here translated as "Non-returners"),
which is the dwelling place of those noble ones who have attained the third fruit.
They are also called the Five Pure Abodes.
Regarding the five heavens of the Non-returners (anāgāmin) in the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu):
as for the Heaven of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana), practitioners who weary of the cage of form and desire to escape from it [attain this state].
In the cultivation of contemplation, one destroys three kinds of form (*rūpa*):
visible and resistant form, which refers to the visual object-field perceived by the eye;
and invisible but resistant form.
These are the objects of sound, taste, and touch.
They are forms that are invisible and non-resistant.
The mind takes mental phenomena (dharmas) as its object.
This refers to non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*). As for the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*),
being weary of infinite space,
they cultivate contemplation and relinquish the previously external emptiness to further take internal consciousness as their object.
Regarding the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*):
external objects are termed "space" and internal objects are termed "mind.
By relinquishing these two objects, one enters into nothingness.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not the presence of perception found in the sphere of infinite consciousness,
nor is it the absence of perception found in the sphere of nothingness.
Having abandoned the two extremes of existence and non-existence, they enter the higher meditative concentrations.
All the celestial hosts speak with noble speech,
for their language is identical to that of Central India.
However, if one does not understand the words of the scriptures through study but instead follows the *Nyāyapravēśa-śāstra* (Treatise on Entering Righteousness), and commits the karmas of killing,
stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, then if one is born among humans, one’s physical appearance will be haggard and devoid of majesty.
If there were other karma by which one obtained a body among the gods, it would be inferior in form and appearance to that of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
the brilliance of its precious ornaments and adornments would be faint,
and the celestial maidens would all abandon it.
The other devas laugh at them in derision.
When they engage in battle with the asuras and are slain by them, or when their lives among the devas come to an end according to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, the five signs of decay appear.
The first is that their garments become soiled and stained.
Second, the flowers upon his crown wither;
third, sweat flows from both armpits;
fourth, a foul odor arises from his body.
Fifth, they do not delight in their original seats (*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*). Regarding these thirty-two heavens, two are inhabited solely by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
that is to say, the Great Brahmā King does not comprehend the causes of karma.
They claim that they can create all of heaven, earth, people, and things;
relying on this, they become arrogant and conceited,
and the sages do not dwell with them.
The Heaven of Non-conception belongs exclusively to non-Buddhists;
by practicing the attainment of non-conception, they receive the retribution of five hundred kalpas without mind.
Once this retribution is exhausted, they inevitably give rise to false views and fall into hell.
For this reason, the Noble Ones are not born therein.
The five abodes of the noble ones are the five Pure Abode Heavens (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Generally, those who are born there must be those progressing toward the state of an Anāgāmin.
Having attained the four dhyānas in this body, they give rise to untainted (anāsrava) states and initiate the karma of perfumed dhyāna (vāsita-dhyāna),
whether initiating one grade up to nine grades.
Only then can one be born there.
Ordinary persons lack this cultivation of meditative karma;
therefore, they cannot be born there.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the remaining twenty-five heavens are inhabited by both ordinary beings and sages.
The commentary says:
[This] discusses the physical locations within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the initial statement that there is "no location," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The four formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*) are free from physical form; as retributive fruits, they have no distinct locations."
However, regarding those who accomplish the karma of the four formless attainments within the desire and form realms,
the statement that they are "without body" is explained in the *Abhidharmakośa* as follows:
"Formless and bodiless.
Zuǎn says:
"There is no form that is the fruit of karma; it is not a body of maturation (vipāka)."
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra states:
"In these four heavens of the Sphere of Infinite Space,
the body and mind are extinguished, and a fixed nature manifests before them."
"There is no matter that is the fruit of karma.
The Gloss of Gushan states:
"The negation of matter that is the fruit of karma indicates the existence of matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration."
Next, regarding the phrase "there is a place," the *Lokotpatti-sūtra* states:
"Twofold the Akaniṣṭha."
From the Realm of Infinite Space up to the Realm of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception,
all are called the dwelling places of the devas.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
The bodhisattva’s faculty of the nose perceives the fragrance of the palaces of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding those who "possess a body," the *Āgama* states:
When Śāriputra passed away,
