From the mouth of the golden elephant flows the Indus River;
it circles the lake once and enters the southwestern ocean.
From the western side of the lake, the Vārakṣa River flows out from the mouth of a Vaiḍūrya horse;
it circles the lake once and enters the northwestern ocean.
From the lion’s mouth on the northern side of the pond, the Hiraṇyavatī River flows out,
circling the pond once.
It flows into the Eastern Sea.

Some say it flows underground and emerges from Mount Jishishan (Mount Tsikshi) as the source of the River Donghua (Eastern Flower). For an explanation of Jambudvīpa, see the preceding diagram of the four continents and nine mountains.
Anavatapta, which in this language means "Without Heat or Torment," is a lake adorned with the four precious substances;
its waters flow forth from the mouths of four animals.
Gaṅgā is here translated as "Coming from Heaven," signifying that its source is high.
Sindhu is here translated as "River of Verification."
Bāhū (縛芻) is translated here as "Blue River" (Qinghe).
Sītā (徙多) is translated here as "Singing River" (Yinhe). Jambudvīpa is also known as Yañbūtí.

Starting from Gaochang, the nearest [country] is the kingdom of Ākṣiṇī, which possesses several dozen monasteries. The *Hanshu* states that nine hundred li southwest of Yanqi is Quzhi, where there are one hundred monasteries.
The character "qu" (屈) is pronounced with the tone of *fu* (勿) reversed.
Formerly called Qiuci (龜茲), its pronunciation is Qiu-ci. Six hundred li southwest is Baluka (跋錄迦), formerly called Gumu (姑墨). Six hundred li northwest one reaches Mount Ling (凌山).
Traveling four hundred *li* north of the Pamir Mountains (Congling), one reaches Qingchi.
Traveling five hundred *li* further north, one reaches Suyab Shuicheng.
Four hundred *li* to the west is Qianquan.
To the south lies the Snow Mountains;
on three sides it opens onto level plains.
The Turks come here to escape the summer heat.
To the west lies Talaśī;
to the southwest is the White Water;
and to the southwest is the city of Gongyu.
To the south is Nanzhu Chijian;
to the west is Shiguo and Xisu Dulili;
to the northwest is Kangguo.
To the south it reaches the country of Mi;
to the north, the country of Cao;
and to the west, the country of He.
Peaceful in the west and east;
peaceful in the center of the west;
reaching as far as Xi'an in the west.
Southwest: Huoluo (Tocharians). From Kangguo (Sogdiana) to the southwest, one reaches Shiguo (Wakhan);
to the southeast, one enters the Iron Gate;
to the south, one emerges at Duhuoluo (Tokhara), which is what was previously cited from the *Sui Shu* as "easternly hemming in the Pamir Mountains."
To the west it borders Persia;
to the south it faces the Snow Mountains;
to the north it rests upon the Iron Gates. Following the northward flow of the Oxus River, one arrives at the eastern part of Tāxmīsh.
Reaching Chigöyen,
he proceeded further east to Huluma,
and further east again to Yuman.
To the southwest, it borders the river and reaches Juhoyan;
further east, it reaches Hosha;
and further east, it reaches Kodhula.
To the east, it borders the Pamir Mountains and extends to Kūrmīta;
to the south, it reaches Śrīkaṭā;
crossing the river, one arrives at Dharmasthiti; from the kingdom of Huo, it extends southeast to Kaśmīra.
To the west it reaches Bāgalang;
to the south, Hṛṣṭikaṇṭha;
and to the southwest, Huḷiṅga.
To the east it reaches Bāhīka;
to the north it borders the river.
There are one hundred monasteries.
People call it the Lesser Rājagṛha.
From here, one enters the Snow Mountains to the southwest and reaches Ārāmārdha; proceeding further southwest, one arrives at [the destination].
From Bāhīka to Kapiśa, one enters the Great Snow Mountains toward the southeast and reaches Bāmiyān, where there is a reclining Buddha one thousand feet long;

the nine-striped robe of Śāṇakavāsin, born from a womb, still remains there. To the east, crossing the Black Ridge, one reaches Kāpiśī; facing north toward the Snow Mountains, there are a hundred monasteries. Proceeding eastward, one enters the borders of North India and arrives at Lampāka.
To the east is the Great Stūpa of Gandhāra, five hundred feet high;
during the Yuan-Wei dynasty, the Hu Empress Dowager dispatched an envoy carrying a great banner five hundred feet long to hang it there.

His feet barely touched the ground as he traveled south to the borders of Nāgara in North India, and north to Oḍḍiyāna, the realm where the Śākya king was exiled—this being called "The Garden of the Former Wheel-Turning King."
The monastic community has always numbered ten thousand. To the east lies the Great Snowy Mountains of Parvata; to the south, crossing the Indus River, one reaches Takṣaśilā;
and to the southeast, one arrives at Siṃhapura.
To the southeast lies Uraśā;
to the southeast lies Kaśmīra (formerly called Jibin), with one hundred monasteries; to the southeast lies Haṣṭanāga;
to the south lies Takka.
To the east lies Cina-puti;
to the northeast lies Jalandhara;
and to the northeast lies Kuruta.
To the north it reaches Lokhula; further north it reaches Mālava.

From Kurukṣetra to the south it reaches Śatadru. All the regions above these belong to North India. To the southwest it reaches Pārśvata, which marks the border of Central India. To the east it reaches Mathurā, the place where the stone chambers for counting people were filled with tally-sticks. To the northeast it reaches Śrāvastī.
To the northeast lies Sru-na, bordering the Gaṅgā River on its eastern side; crossing the river to the east, one reaches Mathurā.
To the north lies Vārāṇasī, where there is a kingdom of the Kāśyapa clan ruled by a queen from among the women of the Northern Snow Mountains in North India.
This was because the king was ignorant of the affairs of government.
This country borders on Tufan to the east and on Khotan to the north.
To the west it borders Mālava; from Mṛttikāvatī to the east it reaches Goviśaṇḍa.
To the southeast, at the place where the Buddha Akṣobhya preached the Dharma for seven days to the nāga king Śaṅkhapāla, one crosses the Gaṅgā River to the south and arrives at Virāṭa.
To the southeast is Kapitha, the place where the Buddha, while residing in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, preached the Dharma for his mother;
and to the northwest is Kanyākubja, where Śakra offered the triple-jeweled staircase.
To the southeast, crossing the Gaṅgā River, one reaches Ayodhyā;
to the east, Anāma; to the southeast, Prayāga;
to the southwest, Kauśāmbī; and to the north, Vaiśālī.

To the northeast, five *li* south of the city of Śrāvastī, is the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden; to the southeast, it reaches Kapilavastu, the birthplace of the Buddha, where the palace of King Śuddhodana stands.
He also constructed vihāras for both the palace of Queen Māyā and the place where the Bodhisattva descended into the womb.
The Buddha returned to his native country and stayed at the Nyagrodha Monastery,
where he accepted a gold-threaded *kāṣāya* from his maternal aunt.

To the northeast, it spans from the place where the Buddha passed away in the Śāla Grove of Kuśinagara to the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, the site where he turned the Wheel of Dharma; to the southwest, it likewise extends between these two points. It accommodates eight princes and five hundred members of the Śākya clan.
Near the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva) is the Zhina Temple (China Monastery), which was built by the king for the monastic community of the Great Tang. "Zhina" here refers to the Great Tang.

Following the Ganges River northeast, one reaches Vaiśālī (formerly called Viśālī); there is the chamber of Vimalakīrti. To the northeast is Pūrvavideha; to the north is the territory of Northern India; and to the northwest is Nepal. The northern border of that country is the kingdom of Tönpa-nyo (East Woman).
It borders with the Tufan (Tibetans).
When people come from or depart for that country,
they generally pass through this region.
China and India are separated by ten thousand *li*;
since ancient times, the routes have been circuitous, resulting in great distances and obstacles. From Vaiśālī, traveling south across the Gaṅgā River, one reaches Magadha, also known as Māgadha.
This is the border region between China and India.
The city of Rājagṛha is located within this country;
the city of Pāṭaliputra is on the southern bank of the river.
Crossing the Nairañjanā River to the southwest,
one reaches Gayā City;
six li to the west of the city.
He arrived at Gayāśīrṣa Mountain,
which is popularly called Ling-shan (Spiritual Mountain).
To the southwest was the Bodhi tree.
This is the place where the Buddha attained enlightenment.
The tree is fifty zhang high,
and the surrounding wall is five hundred paces in circumference.
Within it is the Vajrāsana,
where a thousand Buddhas sit and enter the vajra-samādhi.
There is also the Kukkuṭārāma monastery.
King Aśoka established [this] and constantly provided offerings to a thousand monks at Nālandā Monastery.
The five kings jointly constructed it.
There were several thousand monks,
all of whom were men of outstanding talent and profound learning, extending as far east as Campā.
To the east lies Kezhuzhi;
crossing the Ganges River to the east, one reaches Punyavardhana—these regions all belong to Central India. To the east lies Kāmarūpa, a kingdom that has passed through a thousand generations.
To this day, they do not believe in the Buddha-dharma.
To the eastern border of the country, the hills and mounds are continuous;
one can travel for about two months to enter the southwestern border of Shu. Going south from there to Samataṭa, and then northeast to the shores of the great ocean, one reaches Śrīlaṅkā.
From the southeastern corner of the great ocean to Kāmarūpa;
to the east, to Tāmralipti;
and further to the east, to Iṣaṅku.

Proceeding further east, one reaches Mahācampā, which is the present-day Lin-yi (Linyi) of this region; proceeding southwest from there, one reaches Yamunā. These six kingdoms have difficult and obstructed roads, such that [the author] was unable to travel there. From Samataṭa westward to the eastern border of Damalipti, which borders the sea, and northwest to Kerala.
To the southwest lies Oḍra, bordering the great ocean to the southeast; it contains a city that serves as a resting place for sea merchants.
It is twenty thousand *li* to the south of Siṃhala (Lion Island).
One may behold this country from afar on a clear night.
The light of the precious jewel atop the Buddha-tooth stūpa is like a great torch;
from there, traveling southwest to Koṅgoda and further east, one reaches East India,
bordering the seashore.
To the southwest of the land of non-believers in the Buddha-dharma lies Dakṣiṇāpatha (Southern India), and to the northwest lies Kośala (Central India).
There, the king was named Yaśas, who built a monastery for Nāgārjuna.
He assembled a thousand monks.
Calculating the cost of the salt consumed by the laborers,
he spent nine hundred million gold coins as far south as Andhra— this being the southern part of India— and as far as Dhānyakaṭaka.
To the southwest it reaches Julliar, and to the south it reaches Darab.
To the south it reaches the southern border of Mālava, which adjoins the sea.
There is Mount Malaya.
To the east of this mountain is Mount Potalaka.
At its summit is a lake,
and by the side of the lake is a stone celestial palace.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara dwells here.
Those who wish to see him must wade through waters and climb mountains to travel southeast to the Kingdom of Siṃhala; this is not within the borders of India.
There is a shrine for the Buddha’s tooth relic,
atop which a flagpole is erected bearing a great precious gem like the King of Stars; beside the palace, a large kitchen has been constructed.
Every day, they provide meals for eighteen thousand monks.
At mealtime, the monks come with their alms bowls to receive food,
each returning to his own quarters.
Since the advent of Buddhism, this offering has been established.
To the north of Dāravī and south of Koṅkaṇapura, within the territory of South India, there is a forest of tārā trees;
their leaves are long and broad.
In all the various kingdoms, there are none who do not adopt [this script] for writing;
it extends northwest to Mahārāṣṭra, west to the sea where salt is boiled at Valabhī, and northwest to Mālava, the realm of the Five Indias.
There are two kingdoms that value learning:
Mālava in the southwest and Magadha in the northeast.
Famous monks were extremely numerous.
From this country, traveling south to the sea and northwest to Aṭali, and from Mālava northwest to Kiṭa.

To the north, reaching Vārāṇasī, this is South India; to the northwest, reaching Puruṣapura, this is West India. From Vārāṇasī to the north, reaching Gajapura, this is West India; to the southeast, reaching Ujjayinī, this is South India; to the northeast, reaching Takṣaśilā, this is South India; and to the north, reaching Mahīpura, this is Central India. From Gajapura to the north, crossing the Indus River, one reaches the country of Sindhu (West India); to the east, crossing to the eastern bank of the river, one reaches Mūlasthāna (West India); and to the northeast, reaching Pārvatī, this is North India. From the country of Sindhu to the southwest, reaching Amarkaṭaka, this is West India; bordering the great ocean to the west, reaching Laṅkā, this is West India; along the shore of the great ocean to the northwest, reaching Persia, this is the border of North India; to the northwest, reaching Ferghana (Fulin), this is North India; and to the southwest, reaching the islands of the sea, this is the Kingdom of Women, where there are only women.
Fuli sent men every year. By chance, they found a male child but did not raise him.

From A-mo-qi (Amarkot) in the north to Pi-du-shi (Badakshan) in the west, extending northeast to A-tu (Attock) in the western region of India, and further northeast to Fa-la-na (Varanasi) in the western region of India, this territory belongs to Kāpiśī; to the west lies Ji-giang-na (Khaṅjana).
To the northwest, one exits the borders of India and reaches Caukūṭa;
to the north, one reaches Vṛji;
and to the northeast, one reaches the great snowy mountain range of Siṃhala.
Among the ranges of Jambudvīpa, this mountain range is particularly high.

From the lower reaches of the range to Andara belongs to the Turks; to the northwest is Kustana, which also belongs to the Turks; and to the northwest is the country of Hu (Khotan), which likewise belongs to the Turks. These [territories] govern all the small kingdoms south of the Iron Gates; from here, one enters the Pamir Mountains to the east.
This ridge lies in the center of Jambudvīpa;
to the south it adjoins the Great Snow Mountains,
to the north it reaches the Thousand Springs of the Hot Sea, and to the west it extends to the Kingdom of Huo.
To the east it reaches the kingdom of Ukā;
each of its four sides extends for several thousand li,
with hundreds of layers of cliffs and ridges.
Because the snow and wind are perpetual yet the mountain ridges remain lush and verdant, it was named for this reason.
To the east it reaches Mengjian, belonging to the Turks; to the north it reaches Alini.
To the east lies Halaho; from Mengjian, one travels east to Kṛśa, and to the northeast to Parika;
from Kṛśa, one travels east to Himatala.
To the west it reaches Pāṭana;
to the southeast it reaches Yimabojian;
and to the southeast it reaches Kulūta.
To the northeast it reaches the Great Iron Diadem Mountain (Cakravāḍa) to the north of Śītavana;
to the south, it reaches Śāmbi;
to the northeast, it reaches the Pāmśu River, spanning one thousand li from east to west; and to the south, it reaches Bolor.
From the river, one ascends the mountains to reach Jiebanduo (Khotan).
Descending from the eastern ridge of the Pamir Mountains, one arrives at Uska.
To the northwest lies Kasha (formerly known as Shule); to the southeast lies Juqu; the Buddhist scriptures flourish there to the extreme; and to the east lies Yutian (Khotan).
To the east, he entered Sha-shi and reached the city of Ni-rang,
which served as a frontier pass for the eastern region.
Continuing further east, he entered the Great Flowing Sands.
The sand gathers and disperses according to the wind,
causing many people to lose their way;
travelers collect the remains of the deceased to mark their path.
To the east it reaches Qiumo;
to the northeast it reaches the old site of Loulan, which is the kingdom of Shanshan. As for India, this is the formal name for Tianzhu (India);
here it is called Yuebei (Moon-Backed), as it has its back turned toward the Snow Mountains.
It borders the great ocean on three sides;
its terrain is narrow in the south like the crescent moon of the waxing phase,
with plains that are level and broad.
It is ninety thousand *li* in circumference.

More than seven thousand cities are situated within it, extending to the edges of the three seas, all under the same royal command. (From the *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions* by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang.)
The *Prabhāsa-sūtra* [mentions] eighty-four thousand cities, towns, and villages;
the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*.
There are sixteen great nations, five hundred middle nations, and one hundred thousand small nations.
According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*,
there are two thousand three hundred great nations in this Jambudvīpa.
The *Loutan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) states that the area east of the Onion River is called Zhendan.
The Dharma Master Yancong of the Tang dynasty said:
To the west of the Pamir Mountains, all regions belong to the lineage of Brahmā;
to the left of the Iron Gate, they are all called the lands of the Hu. Some even point to the Five Indias as being Hu kingdoms.
To claim that the Sanskrit scriptures are "Hu" (Chinese) sutras,
and that Indian monks are "Hu" monks—
such views are all great errors. This was the case with the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Tang dynasty.
In the second year of the Xianheng era, he boarded a merchant vessel in Panyu—present-day Guangzhou—and traveled west to Ho-ling;
next to Śrīvijaya; and then to Malayu.

Next is Keḍā. Traveling north for ten days, one reaches the land of the naked people (Nagna), located to the southwest of Shu; both men and women there go about entirely naked. Half a day’s journey to the northwest is Damalipti, a seaport on the eastern border of India from which one boards a ship to return to Tang China. Traveling due west from there, one arrives at the country of Mahābodhi, which is Magadha. There is the Nālandā Monastery, reached via seventy postal stations (*yājia*). It is also said that Damalipti is ten days’ journey from Mahābodhi; at Nālandā, one pays homage at the Root Stūpa.
The place on Vulture Peak Mountain where the robes were folded;
the Great Enlightenment Temple where one pays homage to the true image, which is the site of the Bodhi-maṇḍala and the Diamond Throne;
and the chamber of the final nirvana at Kuśinagara.
He visited the Deer Park and Chicken Hill,
paying homage to all the sacred sites,
and resided at Nālandā for ten years.
Seeking the scriptures, he returned to Dharmalīti;
embarking on a ship, he passed through Kāñcī and entrusted the Sanskrit manuscripts to Fo-shi (Śrīvijaya).
He composed the *Nanhai Jiguī Zhuan* (Record of the Inner Sea Sent Home) and the *Qiufa Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks Who Sought the Dharma).
In the autumn of the first year of the Yongchang era, he returned to Guangzhou;
by winter, he again boarded a ship and arrived at Fo-shi (Bhoja).
He resided there for three years.
In the first year of the Zhengsheng era, he returned to the capital city of Luoyang to translate scriptures.
He recorded this, saying:
Jambudvīpa is located to the west and consists of the five regions of India;
it is the domain governed by the *cakravartin* who travels by flight,
and its inhabitants belong to the lineage of Brahmā.
To the east lies Zhendan,
the land transformed by the sovereigns and sages Zhou and Kong;
it is the country of the gentleman.
To the north lies the territory of the Di tribes—
the lands of the Xianyun, the Xiongnu, and other Hu peoples—
whose boundaries and domains are distinct and separate.
One should not take "Hu" (the term for foreigner) as synonymous with "Fan" (Sanskrit) to create confusion and conflation.
Such instances as the old designations "kneeling in the Hu manner," "Hu scriptures," and "the Old Hu" are all unfounded statements and are unworthy of use.
Regarding the fact that the number of kingdoms and cities mentioned in various sutras is not fixed:
this is because their boundaries have differed throughout antiquity and the present in terms of merging and splitting.
For example, in this region, there were eighteen hundred kingdoms during the Zhou dynasty.
In the Spring and Autumn period, there were over seventy states;
in the Qin era, seven kingdoms;
and in the Wei era, three states.
During the Sixteen Kingdoms period of the Jin dynasty,
these states were sometimes divided and sometimes united;
thus, they did not constitute a single unified state.
It does not go beyond this single realm.
Furthermore, regarding the differences between the Chinese and Sanskrit names for various sūtras,
[the name] "Ganges" was consistently used by Kumārajīva.
Master Xuanzang [translates it as] Gaṅgā;
Kumārajīva says *Sumeru*;
Xuanzang says *Sumeru*.
Furthermore, the claim that Kumārajīva’s translations are erroneous cannot be taken as definitive.

This is likely because the local dialects inquired about by the dharma-seeking śramaṇas differed between the central and peripheral regions, and because there were variations between ancient and modern times.
Yet, when one explains their actual reality, they are one and the same.
This is just as in this region, where sounds shift between north and south so that names for places and things differ in their respective dialects;
and again, as within this same land of Zhendan (China), the designations differ according to whether it is called Zhou, Qin, Han, or Jin.
How could one possibly determine right and wrong at the juncture between the ancient and the modern?
If one can understand this meaning,
then the Chinese and Indian traditions, though different, will not be in conflict.
This can be understood through one's own mind.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
the southern continent extends downward as far as the Avīci Hell.
It is forty thousand yojanas in extent,
tapering at the top and broad at the base like a heap of grain. According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-ksudraka-vastu* (Sapoduo lun),
the soil beneath Jambudvīpa is five hundred yojanas deep.
The White Clay [Hell] is five hundred yojanas [in extent].
From the Reviving Hell up to the Extremely Hot Hell,
the seven hells together have a total height of nineteen thousand yojanas.
Each is ten thousand yojanas in width;
the Avīci hell is twenty thousand yojanas in both height and breadth,
according to the Abhidharma-śāstra.
In the Saṃjīva hell, the lifespan is five hundred years;
in the Kālasūtra hell, it is one thousand years;
and in the Saṃghāta hell, it is two thousand years.
One cries out for four thousand years;
one shrieks loudly for eight thousand years;
and in the Reviving Heat Hell, one remains for sixteen thousand years.
The Extremely Hot Hell lasts for half an eon;
the Avīci Hell lasts for one eon.
(Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya)
One day and night in Saṃjīva corresponds to five hundred years in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

Following this sequence, one day and night in Tapana corresponds to sixteen thousand years in Paranirmita-vaśavartin. The remaining hells follow this same pattern of correspondence, as established in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Regarding the five immediate transgressions (*pañcānantarya*):
first is the immediacy of proceeding toward the fruit,
because one is reborn there immediately upon casting off the body.
Second, there is no interval between sufferings,
because there is no pleasure in between. Third,
there is no interval throughout the three periods of time.
Because it is fixed as lasting for one kalpa;
because life is uninterrupted,
being continuous throughout the interval.
The five forms of uninterrupted suffering.
This hell is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
and it is filled with even a single person.
Many people also fill the many treatises [extending] twenty thousand yojanas.
Regarding the eight hot hells, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* [states]:
"The eight hot hells..."
Each hell has four gates.
Outside each gate are four *pariṣaṇḍas* (encircling terraces);
because sentient beings who roam there experience an intensification of their suffering, they are so named.
The beings in the hells have forms like those of humans.
According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*,
the suffering in Avīci is a thousand times greater than that of the preceding seven great hells.
Five: *Utkrośa*; Six: *Utpala*; Seven: *Padma*;
Eight: *Puṇḍarīka*. These eight hells are situated at the base of the Cakravāḍa Mountains, dwelling facing upward and suffering from the pain of freezing cold.
According to the *Tridharmaka Sūtra*, the lifespan in the Arbuda hell is [as follows].
Suppose there were twenty *droṇas* of sesame seeds, filled to capacity according to the measure of the kingdom of Kośala;
and suppose a man were to remove a single sesame seed every hundred years.
When those [years] are thus exhausted,
twenty *arbuda* lifespans constitute one *nirarbuda* lifespan.
The remaining [terms] follow this sequence: according to the *Lokadhātu-hetu-mūla-sūtra*, *niraya* means "non-path" (*amārga*), because it is the most inferior part of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
According to the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, *naraka* means "evil person" (*pāpapurusa*). According to the *Abhinava-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it refers to the good and evil deeds performed by persons.
It follows a person just as a shadow follows a form or a reflection follows the body.
When a person dies, only their physical body perishes, but their conduct does not perish.
It is like writing at night by the light of a fire: when the fire is extinguished, the characters remain; when the fire returns, they are once again visible.
The *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Praśna Sūtra* states that actions performed in this life are completed in the next life.
There are three types of hells:
first, the hot [hells].
Two cold hells and three peripheral hells.
As for the eight hot hells: [they are as follows].
The first is named Saṃjīva (Reviving).
When the sinners' hands grow iron claws, they tear at one another until the flesh falls away;
or else, the hell-wardens cry out, "Live! and they are restored.
Alternatively, they may be revived by a cold wind;
though the two conditions for reviving them differ, the result is the same.
After the person has finished suffering there, they proceed again to the Black Sand Hell, and so on, until the Boiling Excrement Hell.
Proceeding in succession to the Hell of Cold Ice,
they eventually pass away;
having created unwholesome karma through body, speech, and mind, they fall into this hell.
Each of the great hells is surrounded by sixteen minor hells;
according to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, these are the sixteen *Utsada* (Augmented Hells), two of which are named Kālasūtra.
There, the limbs and bodies are first measured out with glowing iron cords and subsequently cut and sawn apart.
Having long endured suffering, they proceed from the Black Sand Hell to the Cold Ice Hell;
thereafter, their life comes to an end,
and according to the previous pattern, their suffering is intensified.
One falls into this hell by harboring malicious intent toward one's parents or the śrāvakas.
It is called Saṃghāta (The Crushing Hell).

Many instruments of torture, blazing and fiercely hot, come together to oppress and afflict [the inhabitants]. The remaining details are to be understood according to the previous explanation. One falls into this hell by having committed the three types of evil karma.
The fourth is named Crying Out.
There, the hell-wardens seize people and hurl them into iron cauldrons;
they boil and bubble, and the victims cry out.
Due to harboring the poison of hatred, one falls into this hell.
The fifth is named Great Wailing;
cast into iron cauldrons, one shrieks and wails loudly.
Due to the habitual practice of wrong views and evil conduct, one falls into this hell.
The sixth is named Intense Heat;
one is placed within an iron city where fires blaze, causing the body to be scorched and consumed.
Because they roasted and scorched sentient beings, they fall into this hell.

The eighth is named Avīci (in Sanskrit, *Avīci*, or alternatively *Abīci*). The hell-wardens seize those transgressors, flay their skin, wrap it around their bodies, and place them upon flaming chariots.
When ten thousand poisons converge, there is no moment that is not painful;
one falls into this hell for committing the most grievous sins—the ten evil deeds and the five rebellious acts.
The above is a composite rendering based on the *Dīrgha Āgama*, wherein these eight hells are situated beneath Jambudvīpa.
Stacked one upon another, they dwell there experiencing the suffering of heat and affliction.
Of these, the first two have predominant rulers,
while the subsequent three have minor rulers.
The latter three have no presiding ruler.
Second, there are eight cold hells.
The first is named Arbuda.
The flesh, tormented by the bitter cold, develops small blisters;
this second stage is called Nirarbuda.
Blown by the freezing winds, the entire body becomes covered in blisters.
These two derive their names from bodily characteristics.
The third is called Aṭaṭa;
it is a sound produced by the tongue while the lips move but cannot meet.
The fourth is called *āpa-āpa*;
the tongue does not move, but the lips produce this sound.
The fifth is called *au-hu*.
Vibrating the breath within the throat to produce sound—
these three receive their names from the characteristics of their sounds.
The sixth is named *utpala*.
This is the blue lotus (*utpala*).
The flesh-colored [tongue] is finely split like this flower.
The seventh is called the *padma*.
This is the red lotus (*padma*).
The flesh-colored [lotus] blooms like this flower when it is fully opened.
The eighth is called the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*).
This is the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*).
Because its bones split open like the blooming of this flower,
these three [stages] receive their names from the appearance of the wound.
These eight hells are located at the base of the Cakravāḍa Mountains;
dwelling there facing upward, the inhabitants suffer from the misery of freezing cold.
As for the hells situated on three sides, there are three such types.
In mountain valleys, by waters, and in wildernesses,
they undergo the retribution of distinct karmic actions.

This refers to the experience of cold, heat, and mixed sensations, as described in the *Sāndṛṣṭika-dharmapada-sūtra* (or *Sāndṛṣṭika-śīla-sūtra*), where "fǒu" (鍑) is pronounced as *qiāng fāng yòu qiè*, meaning a large cauldron.
To the south of Jambudvīpa,
beyond the two Cakravāḍa mountains, lies the palace of King Yama;
it is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth, being perfectly square.
There were sevenfold railings and seven rows of trees;
within the gardens and groves were various flowers, ponds, and diverse beautiful fruits.
A fragrant breeze wafted from afar, and flocks of birds sang in harmony.
Due to his evil karma,
six times throughout the day and night, molten red copper naturally appears before him.
The palace immediately transforms into iron.
The hell-wardens seize the king and throw him onto the glowing-hot iron ground,
pouring molten copper into his mouth.
At that time, the king was struck with fear and made this aspiration: "May I relinquish my body here and be reborn among humans;
may I go forth from the household life with right faith within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Having formed this virtuous thought, he passed away.
The palace is restored as the seven treasures,
complete with the five desires, according to the *Qishi jing* (Sutra on the Arising of the World).
King Yama was formerly King Viśāṇa.
When he fought against King Vitatādi, his military forces were no match for the enemy.
Consequently, he made a vow to become the lord of hell,
accompanied by eighteen ministers and a host of one million followers.
They made a vow together, saying:
"In the future, we shall assist in governing these sinful persons.
The King Vaiśravaṇa is none other than the present King Yama.
The eighteen ministers are the various minor kings of today;

the million-fold multitude are the *āpāṅgas*. Regarding the *Diyu Jing* (Sūtra on the Hells), *āpāṅga* is translated here as "Uninterrupted" (*Avīci*), and *Yanmaluo* is translated as "Twin Kings" (*Yama-rāja*).

The elder brother presides over the prison for men, while the younger sister presides over the prison for women; according to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, both brothers and sisters serve as jailers.
Therefore, they are called the "Twin Kings."
Furthermore, because both suffering and pleasure are experienced together, according to the *Jing yinyi* (Meanings and Pronunciations of the Sūtras),
the Avīci Hell is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
There are seven layers of iron walls and seven layers of iron nets.
There are eighteen cauldrons— *líg* (pronounced *lìng*)— surrounding these seven layers on all sides.
These are all forests of blades,
four great copper dogs,
and eighteen hell-wardens.
It has eight heads and sixty-four horns;
it has sixty-four eyes.
There are seven iron banners from which fire surges like boiling water.
If there are those who have committed transgressions or rebellious acts,
at the time of their death, copper dogs will transform into eighteen chariots shaped like precious canopies,
and all the flames will transform into jade maidens.
Seeing them from afar, the sinner’s heart rejoices and he wishes to go toward them;
yet as the wind-bladed knives dismember his body, the intense cold causes him to cry out,
"How wonderful it would be to have a good fire!"
As soon as he places it upon the chariot,
it immediately bursts into flames;
when the sinner’s life ends, he is reborn in the Fire-Chariot Hell.
In the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, they enter directly into Avīci;
from the upper partition to the lower, they descend like a whirling wheel of fire.
There, they transform into King Yama and issue a loud proclamation and command.
"You are a foolish person, a seed of hell.
While you were in the world, you were unfilial toward your parents, held wrong views, and lacked the Way.
Therefore, the place where you are born now is named Avīci Hell."
Such great suffering lasts for one day and one night,
which is equivalent to sixty minor kalpas in the human realm;
such a lifespan extends to the end of one great kalpa.
Those who have committed the five heinous crimes shall undergo retribution for five kalpas.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who violate the four grave prohibitions and consume the offerings of the faithful in vain.
They slandered [the Dharma] with false views and failed to recognize cause and effect;
they severed their study of Prajñāpāramitā and reviled the Buddhas of the ten directions;
they stole the property of the Saṃgha and were licentious and devoid of the Way.
This person’s retribution for their sins will last for eighty-four thousand great kalpas;
they shall then enter the eighteen compartments in the eastern direction and undergo suffering as before.
The same applies to the south, west, and north.
"Avīci" means "without rescue. From the *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha’s True Ocean* (the character for "vī" is pronounced as a nasal, *bi*).
From the *Sūtra of the Wisdom Torch*.
The Avīci Hell shall be destroyed at that very moment;
one should know that the pronunciation of "Vī" is beyond doubt.
*Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Since it is called "Avīci" and also termed "Uninterrupted" (Anantara),
Avīci itself now declares that there is no rescue.
One should know that the Avīci Great Hell lies outside of the Uninterrupted (Avīci) realm.
The *Fozu Tongji*, Volume 32, ends here; it was during the reign of Emperor Xiaowu that the Western Regions were first opened to communication.
There are thirty-six kingdoms,
all situated to the west of the Xiongnu and to the south of the Wusun.
To the northwest lies a great mountain range.
In the center there is a river,
over six thousand li from east to west and over one thousand li from south to north.
To the east, it connects with the Han Pass;

the two passes of Yumen and Yangguan both lie on the western frontier of Dunhuang. To the west, it is bounded by the Pamir Mountains (Congling); these mountains are verdant, and it is also said that they abound in "congcong" (luxuriant growth), hence the name.
Its southern mountains extend eastward to the Golden City,
connecting with the Southern Mountains of Han (the word "shu" means "to connect").
Its river has two sources, one of which issues from the Pamir Mountains.
First, there is the region of Khotan (Youtian), where "Youtian" is pronounced "Tian. It lies at the foot of the Southern Mountains.
Its river flows northward and joins with the river of the Pamir Mountains (Congling), emptying eastward into Lake Lop (Puchang Hai), also known as the Salt Sea.
It is three hundred li from the Yumen and Yangguan Passes.
It is three hundred li in breadth and extent.
Its waters neither increase nor decrease throughout winter and summer.
All believed that it flows secretly beneath the earth,
emerging from Jishi (Accumulated Stones) in the south as the source of the Yellow River in the Middle Kingdom.
From Yumenguan and Yangguan, there are two routes leading out to the Western Regions.
One proceeds from Shanshan along the southern mountains, following the river westward to Shache; this is the Southern Route.
Traveling west from the Southern Route across the Pamir Mountains leads to Daxuèyuèzhī (Great Yuezhi) and Ānxī (Anxi).
From the capital of the Former King of Cheshi, following the northern mountains and proceeding west along the river to Shule constitutes the Northern Route.
Traveling west from the Northern Route across the Pamir Mountains, one reaches Daxiawan (Fergana), Kangju (Sogdiana), and Yanchai (Sakastan).
The various kingdoms of the Western Regions possess walled cities, cultivated fields, and livestock;
their customs differ from those of the Xiongnu and the Wusun.
All were subject to the Xiongnu.
To the west of the Xiongnu, the King of Ruzhu established a Commandant to govern the Western Regions.
Later, the General of the Flying Cavalry (Biaoji Jiangjun) defeated the Xiongnu at Gu-di and captured the Kings of Kunya and Xiutu (Piao-pin-miao-fan).
*Kun* is pronounced like *hun*;
*tu* is pronounced like *chu*.
The two kings of the Xiongnu first built fortifications west of Lingju (Ling pronounced like *ling*) and initially established the commandery of Jiuyuan, where the water was sweet in taste.
Later, these territories were gradually divided and established as the four commanderies of Wuwei, Zhangye, Dunhuang (the "dun" in Dunhuang is pronounced *tún*),
and Jiuquan, which occupied two strategic passes.
This occurred after General Li Guangli, the Second General, campaigned against Dayuan and obtained the divine horse.
The Western Regions were struck with awe and sent many envoys to present tribute.
During the reign of Emperor Xuan, the Yuezhi ruler Yu came to surrender.
He then ordered the envoy Zheng Ji to concurrently oversee the northern route, being titled the Protector-General (Duhu), stationed at the city of Wulei.
It was located two thousand seven hundred li from Yang Pass;
it served as the central hub for the Western Regions during the Western Han, as recorded in the "Account of the Western Regions" in the *Hanshu*.
During the Yongping era of Emperor Ming, Ban Chao was dispatched as an envoy to the Western Regions; upon arriving in Shanshan, he executed the envoys of the Xiongnu.
Terrified, the King of Shanshan accepted his son as a hostage.
Subsequently, he dispatched troops from various kingdoms to attack Shache, where they executed the King of Shule;
they also defeated the viceroy of the Yuezhi and brought Guizi, Gumu, and Wensu under submission.
He executed the two kings of Yanqi and Yuli;
his majesty shook the Western Regions, and more than fifty kingdoms all submitted hostages and became tributary subjects. (From the Biography of Ban Chao in the Eastern Han History).
*Fozu Tongji*, Scroll Thirty-Three, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhipan of Donghu, Mingzhou, during the Jingtai Era of the Song Dynasty. Section Sixteen:
Record of the Radiance of the Dharma Gate. Section Sixteen: Record of the Radiance of the Dharma Gate.
The Buddha-dharma is inconceivable;
for now, let us bring these two together at the juncture where the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual.
As for that which is revealed as the gateway for establishing transformation:
One must then rely upon Buddhist ritual activities to assist in clarifying the characteristics of the Three Jewels as they abide; thus,
through phenomena, one realizes the ultimate truth.
Composed by Fazhen, with the aspiration for illumination.
He fashioned a statue depicting Śakra inviting the Buddha to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother.
King Udayana of the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, longing to behold the Tathāgata,
immediately fashioned an image of the Tathāgata out of sandalwood,
five feet in height. (According to the *Ekottarika Āgama* [as cited in the *Xiyu ji*]).
King Udayana invited Maudgalyāyana,
who used his supernatural powers to transport the artisans to heaven so that they might personally observe the wondrous marks [of the Buddha].
He used sandalwood to carve a statue five feet in height.
As for cast metal statues, King Prasenajit heard that King Udayana had carved such an image.
He then cast an image of the Buddha out of purple-polished gold, also five feet in height.
At that time, there were for the first time two images within Jambudvīpa. As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama* and the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi Sūtra*:
King Udayana cast a golden image and produced painted images.
During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, Qin Jing was sent to the country of Moji (Yuezhi), where he obtained the fourth model for painting from the sculptor of King Udayana’s image.

This marks the beginning of painted images in the Western Regions; by imperial decree, they were first depicted at the Xiyang Gate in Luoyang and on Mount Xianjie for veneration, marking the beginning of painted images in the Eastern Land.
The Relic Stūpas: After the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, Śakra built four stūpas in the great city of Sudarśana.
To the east of the city, in the Ālokaka Garden, was the Hair Stūpa.
The Caitya of the Robe at the Initial Aśoka Garden in the south of the city,
the Caitya of the Almsbowl at the Nandana Garden in the west of the city,
and the Caitya of the Tooth at the Vaibhrāja Garden in the north of the city— these are known as the Four Caityas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Furthermore, there is the Birthplace Stūpa in the kingdom of Kapilavastu;
the Enlightenment Stūpa in Magadha;
and the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma Stūpa at Rṣipatana in Vārāṇasī.
The Nirvana Stupa between the twin trees at the city of Kuśinagara is called one of the four stupas among men; according to the *Ekottarika Āgama*,
it was established one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
King Aśoka took the Buddha’s relics;
at night, he employed spirits and deities to grind them into powder from the seven precious gems and construct eighty-four thousand stūpas.
The Venerable Yaśas extended his fingers and emitted light.
He caused eighty-four thousand spirits with feathered wings to each follow one ray of light to its end, establishing a stūpa at every location;
in a single day, they did so throughout the entire realm of Jambudvīpa.
Regarding the nineteen locations in the land of China mentioned in the *Aśokarāja-avadāna*, five sites where stūpas can be identified are known:
the Holy Mound to the east of Baima Monastery in Luoyang; [and others].
The stupa at Changgan Temple in Jiankang;
the Aśoka Stupa in Siming;
and those in Linzi and Chengdu.
There is also the stupa of King Aśoka.
Liu Sahe heard Avalokiteśvara speak in a dream, saying:
"The eighth day of the fourth month is the Buddha’s birthday; it is the day for bathing the Buddha."
When the people recite the *Mahāsthāmaprāpta Sūtra* while bathing the Buddha’s image, they chant the verse:
"I now bathe all the Tathāgatas,
the assembly of merit adorned with pure wisdom."
May the sentient beings of the five turbidities be freed from defilement.
May they realize the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body. [From] the *Buddhabhiseka Sūtra*.
Bathing the Sangha. The devas of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven invited the Buddha and the Sangha to bathe and made offerings.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This deva, by virtue of these meritorious deeds, shall attain Buddhahood in the future, and his name shall be Śuddhāṅga.
(From the *Xianyu jing*; Śuddhāṅga is the name of a son of heaven from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.)

Generally, those referred to as "Heavenly Beings" (*devaputra*) who are not designated by the names of the six classes of desire-realm heavens or the eighteen Brahma-heavens are all sons of the gods (*devaputra*).
For instance, Jīvaka, Viśvakarman, and others were all sons of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
This is because they frequently bathe and are born into the world for the sake of performing good deeds; thus it is stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

The Wheel Repository (Lun-zang): During the Liang dynasty, the Great Master Fu, out of compassion for those in the world who lacked the leisure to recite the sutras or were illiterate, first established the Wheel Repository at the Shuanglin Monastery.
He offered it as a scripture scroll.
His vow stated:
"Should there be those who ascend my storehouse gate three times,"
One will be reborn life after life without losing human form.
If one can, with a faithful heart, circumambulate it once,
its merit shall be exactly equal to that of reciting the sutras.
If there are those who can rotate [the wheel] beyond counting,
the merit they obtain is exactly equal to that of reciting the entire Tripitaka. Prior to the Tripitaka,
images of the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) were traditionally displayed.

He was depicted wearing the ceremonial headgear, robes, and vestments of Confucianism, Daoism, and Buddhism, as the Great Being (Mahāsattva) frequently assumes such an appearance. When Wang Jinggong praised his portrait, he wrote:
"A Daoist cap, a Confucian shoe, and a Buddhist cassock."
Synthesizing the three families into one family,
they forget the path to the Tuṣita Heaven;
sitting dully by the Twin Śāla Trees, they await the Dragon Flower Assembly and array the eight great divine generals.
These are the eight classes of celestial deities.
As for the General Who Protects the Realm,
he was formerly the Magistrate of Wushang during the Jin dynasty.
The one who took a vow to protect the treasury resides in Yiwu County.
Its former name was Wushang;
details may be found in the biography of Master Fu Dashi.
The Divination Sticks of the Mahāsattva: One hundred sticks from India,
supplemented by thirty more from Yuantong, totaling one hundred and thirty sticks,
used to determine fortune and misfortune.
Its responses are like echoes.
It is traditionally said to have been composed by a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of a Great Being (*mahāsattva*), representing the orthodox lineage of the Śākya school.
[Regarding] the Offering of Lamps: The Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
If there is someone who offers lamps to a stupa, a temple, or an image—
even with just a small torch—
the merit of such an act can only be known by a Buddha; this is as stated in the *Dīpadāna-sūtra*.
Regarding the "Lamp of the Body," the Buddha said:
"In the past, when I was a king in Jambudvīpa,
I cut flesh from my own body, making it as deep as a large coin."
He poured ghee into the center and prepared a thousand lamp wicks.
He then said to the brahmin,
"I request that you preach the Dharma."
The *Sūtra on the Original Conduct of Bodhisattvas Seeking the Unsurpassed Way*, in which the Bodhisattva carves his own body for the sake of the Dharma as a lamp; the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*;
the "Inexhaustible Lamp"; and the Master Xianshou Fazang.
Empress Wu placed ten mirrors in the eight corners and installed a Buddha image in the center;
when lamps were lit to illuminate them, the image appeared in every mirror.

This was intended to symbolize the principle of the infinitely layered and inexhaustible ocean of lands (*kṣetrasamudra*), representing the intent behind the establishment of the teachings by the various schools.
Lighting Lamps: When Buddhism first arrived, it competed with the Daoists in a trial of powers.
[The Buddhists] burned scriptures which emitted light, yet the volumes remained undamaged.
This occurred on the fifteenth day of the first month.
Emperor Ming then ordered that lamps be lit on this day every year to symbolize the great illumination of the Buddha-dharma.
From then on, successive dynasties invariably held lantern festivals during the Yuanxiao festival.
In the sixth year of the Taiping Xingguo era of our own dynasty, [the practice was continued].
The imperial edict was originally issued to permit lanterns to be lit for three nights, praying for the blessings of the military and the people (*Sengshilüe*). Wujincai [noted]:
"In making offerings to the Buddha with many flowers, one may listen to [the rules] regarding the buying and selling of fragrant oil."
Regarding the "Inexhaustible Wealth" (wújìn cái) mentioned in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* as being frequently resold:
the *Shìshì yàolǎn* states that this is what is commonly referred to in the world as "longevity money" (*chángshēng qián*).
It is called "inexhaustible" because it increases through the accumulation of principal and interest.
On the Ritual for Preaching and Repentance:
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states that since the Han and Wei dynasties, the practice of inviting monks to offer food had become similar to ancestral sacrifices;
the etiquette regarding rising and sitting lacked almost any formal rules.
Reaching the Jin dynasty,
Master Dao’an was the first to establish ritual protocols for responding to invitations, performing prostrations, and offering praises based upon the sutras and vinaya,
organizing them into three categories.
First, the practice of offering incense and lecturing while seated in meditative concentration;
second, the performance of repentance rituals throughout the six periods of the day and night;
third, the observance of the *poṣadha* and other such dharmas.
Subsequently, Master Huiyuan again established the regulations for the Dharma-society; the texts concerning these are found in the *Lushan ji*.

Master Daoxuan of the Tang established the *Wufenwu yi* (Rituals for the Distribution of Property among the Five Assemblies), the *Yizhangfu yi* (Rituals for Robes and Vestments), the *Guijing yi* (Rituals for Paying Homage), and the *Mingzhong jiandu* (The *Kṣudraka-vastu* on Ringing the Bell).
The Vinaya Master Zhao composed the *Luofa yi* (Ritual for Tonsure), all of which were appended with contemporary auxiliary teachings to serve as the orthodox tradition of the Śramaṇa school.

Regarding the various scriptural practices, Zhiyi composed the *Fahua sanmei yi* (Ritual for the Lotus Samādhi). The *Guoqing bailu* (One Hundred Records of Guoqing) records the *Buzhu yi* (Supplementary Ritual) described by Jingxi [Zhanran] to assist in contemplative visualization.
Fazhi compiled the *Ritual for the Practice of the Mantra of Great Compassion* and the *Repentance Ritual of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
Ciyun compiled the *Golden Light Ritual for Protecting the State*.
Based on the *Bai lu*,
he composed the *Supplementary Rituals* as well as the *Amitābha Sūtra Repentance Rite* and the *Pure Land Repentance Rite*.
The Ritual for the Repentance of Avalokiteśvara;
the Ritual for the Repentance of the Blazing Radiance;
and the Ritual for the Repentance of the Benevolent Kings compiled by Shenzhao.
Jingjue compiled the *Lengyan Chan yi* (Ritual for the Śūraṃgama Repentance) and the *Ruyilun Ke* (Daily Recitation of the Cintāmaṇicakra).
Fazhi Yong compiled the *Gongdetian Chan yi* (Ritual for the Repentance of Śrīdevī).
All these are the methods by which the various patriarchs, relying upon the four samādhis, practiced for themselves and transformed others.
Those who make offerings to the Buddhas— the Tathāgatas—
are all making offerings to the Dharmakāya.
Whether during his lifetime or after his parinirvāṇa, there is no difference in the merit of all offerings made;
as stated in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*, those who make offerings to the Buddha obtain great merit and swiftly accomplish awakening.
Furthermore, according to the *Acintyavimokṣa Sūtra*, if one gives to an animal, one obtains a hundredfold reward.
Giving to one who has broken the precepts yields a thousandfold reward;
giving to one who upholds the precepts yields a ten-thousandfold reward.
Even giving to the Buddha yields immeasurable retribution.

In order to distinguish among the various fields of merit, I have made this statement in the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*: "The field of respect is supreme. If one makes offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, to the bodhisattvas, and to the śrāvakas—
It is not as good as someone giving a single mouthful of food and drink to an animal, even down to giving to a starving dog or an ant.

The *Juedi yi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma) states that the field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*) is most supreme; this teaching that the field of compassion excels even a one-part offering was spoken by the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha.
One portion is given to the lowliest beggar.

Regarding the statement in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* that "there is no duality between the field of merit," this refers to the non-duality of compassion and reverence. As for the worldly saying that one makes offerings to three thousand Buddhas, this refers to the past *Kṛta* (Adornment) Kalpa.
From the Buddha Prabhūtaratna at the beginning to the Buddha Viśvabhū at the end,
there are one thousand Buddhas;
this is the present Bhadrakalpa.
From Krakucchanda Buddha at the beginning to Ruci Buddha at the end,
there are one thousand Buddhas;
this is the future Star宿劫 (Nakṣatra Kalpa).
Beginning with Buddha Sūryaprabha and ending with Buddha Merudhvaja,

there are one thousand Buddhas across three kalpas, each having a single fascicle of scripture; those who speak of making offerings to the "one thousand Buddhas" refer to the one thousand Honored Ones of the present Bhadrakalpa.
The *Sudhana-vidyādhara-pitaka* (The Collection of the Knowledge-holder Sudhana):
Mañjuśrī traveled south to the eastern outskirts of Puṇḍravardhana and taught the Dharma to the youth Sudhana, instructing him to seek awakening by attending upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
From here, he traveled through one hundred and ten cities,
attended fifty-three spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra),
and entered the Bodhimanda of Samantabhadra.
He attained as many gates of samādhi as there are motes of dust; [this is from] the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Regarding the offering to the arhats: at the time of the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, [the teachings] were entrusted to the sixteen arhats.
They served as true fields of merit for all donors.
At that time, the Arhats, all receiving the Buddha’s command,
used their supernormal powers to extend their own lifespans.
If one invites the Sangha of the four directions to offer an unrestricted almsgiving (vaiyāvṛtya),
whether at one's own residence or by going to a monastery.
These venerable ones and their retinues dispersed and proceeded there;
concealing their noble deportment, they secretly accepted the offerings.
The Dharma-abiding prophecy concerning the superior karmic fruits obtained by various donors,
beginning with Pindola and ending with Upavāna,
consists of sixteen ranks; these sixteen arhats exclude the four great arhats.
The others all entered parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the four great arhats,
the *Maitreya’s Descent Sūtra* (*Mile xiasheng jing*) states:
Kāśyapa, Piṇḍola-bharadvāja,
and Rāhula.
The *Bao yun jing* (Ratnamegha Sūtra) lists sixteen arhats, including Piṇḍola Bharadvāja;
however, Piṇḍola-bharadvāja is already included among those sixteen.
Now, there are those who speak of eighteen [arhats];
that is, adding Kāśyapa, the host of his followers, and Maudgalyāyana (Miaole), as well as Piṇḍola—here translated as "Immovable" (Abhedyaka)—to the sixteen.
There are also those who add Piṇḍola to the sixteen.
This refers to Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja.
As for those who composed the *Dharmasthitistava* (Record of the Abiding Dharma) one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is they.
In describing the sixteen arhats who received the entrustment to remain in the world,
it is evident that Guṇamitra is not included among those dwelling in the world.
Now, I wish to discuss the eighteen who dwell [in the world].
One should take *Myōraku* as the testimony.
When Jōgaku composed his liturgical hymns,
he likewise excerpted from *Myōraku*.

Regarding the Monastic Meal:
The Buddha said, "There are five kinds of merit in offering food to the Sangha."
Regarding physical form, strength, lifespan, peace, and eloquence:
when an elder bestows food, he should recite this verse:
"May both the giver and the receiver obtain the five constant virtues."
Regarding the *Sūtra on the Five Meritorious Virtues* concerning physical form, vitality, life, peace, and unimpeded eloquence, the Buddha said:
"There are five blessings from giving food:
it bestows vitality, physical form, strength, peace, and eloquence."
What is meant by "bestowing life"?
If a person does not obtain food for seven days, their life will come to an end;
when a wise person bestows food, they are thereby bestowing life.
As for those who give life,
they shall enjoy long life and immeasurable wealth in every lifetime.
What is meant by "giving form"?
When people do not obtain food, their complexions become haggard;
when a wise person gives food, they are giving complexion.
As for this giving of complexion:
From lifetime to lifetime, one is handsome and one’s complexion is radiant.
What is meant by "the power of giving"?
Without food, a person is unable to perform their tasks.
When a wise person gives food, they bestow strength.
As for this bestowed strength,
when one is born among gods or humans, their power is peerless and without equal.
What is meant by "bestowing peace"?
When people do not obtain food, their minds are distressed and their bodies are endangered, such that they cannot find peace for themselves.
When a wise person bestows food, they are thereby bestowing peace.
As for those who bestow peace and security,
they will be safe and secure in every lifetime and shall not encounter various calamities.
What is meant by "bestowing eloquence"?
When a person cannot obtain food, their body becomes emaciated and their mind weakens, such that they are unable to speak.
When a wise person gives them food, they are thereby giving eloquence.
As for this gift of eloquence:
Their wisdom and eloquence are thorough and penetrating, bringing joy to those who hear them.
These are the five blessings. Regarding the five blessings of giving food, the *Sūtra on the Five Blessings of Giving Food* states there are three methods.
The first is to send the food to the monastery; this is called "superior."
Regarding the names for making offerings by constructing a dwelling:
"Constructing a dwelling" and "Giving with a resolute mind" are names for making offerings; these are found in the *Ekottarika Āgama*. As for when a donor prepares food and invites the Saṃgha:

They dispatched guards to man the gates, obstructing and barring monks who were elderly, infirm, or poor from begging; they did not permit them to enter the assembly, resulting in the mere waste of food and drink with no portion of merit whatsoever.
According to the *Xiangfa jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma), if the disciples of the four assemblies practice fasting and precepts...
One should maintain this visualization in the mind:

when inviting the Sangha from the ten directions to various stupas and temples, one should not discriminate between those who are good or evil, or those who observe or violate the precepts, nor between those of high or low conduct.
This is the time for inviting the Sangha.

The merit of providing offerings according to the order of the monastic assembly is greatest. According to the *Puguang jing* (Sūtra on Universal Radiance), when a donor invites the monastic community, visiting monks receive a share of the offerings;
the abbot of the monastery should assign them in sequence. Furthermore, when worldly people separately invite five hundred arhats or bodhisattvas, [the same principle applies].
It is not as good as [receiving alms] according to the monastic order from even a single ordinary monk.
According to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, when the Buddha entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food, there was a brāhmaṇa who [complained] because the Buddha frequently came to his house.
The mind formed this thought:
"Why does this śramaṇa come so frequently, as if he were burdened by a debt?
At that time, the Buddha spoke a verse, saying:
Then rain falls frequently;
the five grains ripen repeatedly;
and meritorious deeds are cultivated again and again.
Having repeatedly received the karmic retribution,
the brāhmaṇa, upon hearing this,
felt shame and remorse; he took his alms-bowl, filled it with food, and offered it to the Buddha.

*The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra)* states that if one can establish a daily vow to first offer food to the Sangha and only then eat oneself, this is the most supreme among all forms of giving.
Regarding the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*: as for those who now offer bowls of rice in cities, [this practice follows that tradition].
The incident originated from this.
At Śrāvastī, Nanda’s mother was cooking rice in a cauldron to provide gruel.
He drank the strained broth himself.
He felt that the wind within his body was dispelled and his food digested.
Thereupon, he thought:
"Upādhyāya, you are one who eats but once a day;
you ought to eat gruel.
Therefore, take much water and little rice."
Having fried it until two-fifths were removed,
he added pepper and *bījaka* and went to the Buddha's presence, saying:
"May the Blessed One permit the bhikṣus to eat gruel.
The Buddha granted this permission and spoke a verse, saying:
Those who maintain pure precepts and are honored and respected by others should offer gruel at the appropriate time.
This brings ten benefits and advantages to the practitioner:
it enhances physical appearance, strength, longevity, and happiness; it clarifies speech and eloquence; and it eliminates undigested food, wind-disorders, hunger, and thirst.
This is called "Medicine," as taught by the Buddha. Those who wish to obtain the long life and happiness of humans and devas should offer congee to the Saṃgha.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, if the characters on the surface of the boiling pot cannot be discerned, it is called "improper food. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* further clarifies that one may only consume the congee once the dawn light has appeared.
All other times are considered improper. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, when the sun shines upon the *śālmali* tree, it appears white;
when one extends the hand, the lines on the palm are clearly visible—this is known as the "sign of light" (*āloka-nimitta*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that "gruel" is called "light food" (*prātarāśa*). *Zenghui ji*.
Begging for food (*piṇḍapāta*; Sanskrit: *piṇḍapāta*;
Chinese: *qǐshí*). In the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, begging for food is divided into four parts:
first, offering [a portion] to fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*).
One portion is given to the destitute and beggars;
one portion is given to the spirits and deities;
and one portion is eaten by oneself. According to the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* and the *Dharmasaṃgīti Sūtra*, there are three kinds of alms-food for those who practice walking meditation while begging.
First, eating when invited;
second, eating with the community of monks;
third, constantly begging for food.
The first two types of food give rise to various causes for contemptibility:
if one receives an invitation, one claims to possess virtue;
if not invited, one harbors resentment toward the other.
If one disparages this craving for the Dharma oneself,
it will obstruct the Path;
this is especially so regarding food belonging to the Sangha.
One should follow the communal rules of the Sangha; however,
when adjudicating legal cases or expelling individuals,
the mind becomes distracted while managing such monastic affairs, thereby obstructing and causing the abandonment of spiritual practice.
Regarding such afflictions and disturbances, one should observe the twelve dhūta practices of the *Piṇḍapātika-dharma-sūtra*.

The *Zhongshìsānshìfóshí Pílósānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Three Times Buddhas Eating at Midday) states that "midday meal" (*zhōngshí*) refers to the time when the sun's shadow has passed by the width of a hair or a single instant. This is what is meant here by "midday meal.
If it is the hour of noon, even if the shadow has moved past a hair’s breadth or a moment, [it is still considered midday].
This refers to the *Asamaya* (non-time) rule in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: "If a bhikṣu eats at a non-time, it is a *pāyattika*.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the meaning of *pāyattika* is translated as "falling" (*duo*). In the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, it is likewise a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the fast (upavāsa) that falls within the Burning Hell, its essence consists in not eating after midday. As the Buddha stated in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*:
"One day of observing the fast provides sustenance for six million years."
Furthermore, there are five blessings:

having little illness, physical ease, little sleep, little lust, and attaining rebirth in heaven with the knowledge of past lives. From the *Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables*: "To fast (*zhāi*) means to align (*qí*);
it is to align the karma of body and speech."
"Equanimity" (*śīta*) refers precisely to the Middle Way.
The statement that "one must not eat thereafter" indicates that outside of the Dharma-realm of the Middle Way, there is no other separate dharma. (From the *Commentary on the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*).
The "Food for Birth" (Chusheng fan): This has two conditions.
First, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, one should cause it to be given to the hungry ghosts of the wilderness (*āṭavika-preta*).
According to the Vinaya-vinaya,
one should give [offerings] to Hārītī and her sons;
these beings originally subsisted on eating flesh and devouring people.
The Buddha transformed them so that they received the precepts and refrained from killing;
he then instructed his disciples to provide food for them wherever they went,
which is why today each vegetarian hall provides food for sentient beings.
This is practiced exclusively by those who have left the household life.
Second is the *Yankou Jing* (The Scripture of the Flaming Mouth),
which takes Ānanda as its narrative occasion.
He ordered that food be given to the hungry ghosts (preta).
Now, small measures of grain are prepared separately in the hall for the vegetarian feast;
once the meal is finished, the assembly performs the ritual to bestow it as a Dharma-gift.
Alternatively, one may prepare small *janmahūḍaka* (birth-measures) for each [deity] and perform the rite of consecrated offering at night;
this is a practice common to all families of the lineage.
The Three Long Fasting Periods: The Buddha said to the elder Trapusa,

It is performed six times each month.

Regarding the "Committing of Minor Defilements" in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*: as for why worldly people observe the prohibitions during these three months, it is because those in authority avoid carrying out executions during this time.
Regarding the Six Fasting Days (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*):
Śakra commanded the Four Heavenly Kings to each govern one of the four directions.
On the eighth day of the waxing moon, he dispatches a messenger to inspect the good and evil of sentient beings;
on the fourteenth day, he dispatches his crown prince;
and on the fifteenth day, the king himself presides over the assembly.
It is likewise on the third day of the dark fortnight.
If the king himself descends,
the constellations and spirits all follow him at that same time.
If one encounters the practice of observing fasts and precepts,
all the devas will rejoice and bestow upon them longevity and increased merit (see the *Sūtra of the Four Heavenly Kings*). If kings and great ministers,
on the six days of fasting, issue a decree throughout their realms to prohibit killing (see the *Universal Worthy Contemplation Sūtra*).
The Ten Fasting Days (*daśa-upavāsa*): These are the ten days of fasting each month.
By maintaining the recitation of the names of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one seeks blessings and extinguishes transgressions.

According to the *Yizhai jing* (Sutra on the Day of Fasting), these consist of the six fasting days (*ṣaḍ-upavāsa*) plus the first day of the month, the eighteenth, the twenty-fourth, and the twenty-eighth.
According to the current national laws and regulations,
judicial executions may not be carried out on the ten designated days of the month in all provinces;
this is based precisely upon this principle.
The Forty-nine Day Memorial Services: When a person dies, if the intermediate state body (antarābhava) has not yet obtained the conditions for rebirth, it remains for a maximum of seven days;
having died, it is born again.
In this manner, transmigrating through birth and death for up to seven weeks,
one will certainly attain rebirth;
however, if there are conditions for birth, it is not fixed.
Now, examining the purport of the sūtras:

regarding the ultimate states of goodness and evil, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*). According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the intermediate state is also called the "intermediate shadow" (*chāyā*);
those of ultimate goodness are reborn in a pure land.
Those of intermediate virtue will be reborn among humans or devas;
those of extreme evil will immediately enter hell or be born into the three evil realms.

Those who die on that very day do not pass through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Nowadays, it is customary to perform memorial feasts every seven days after a person’s death to cultivate merit for their benefit.
Regarding what is called the "Sevenfold Fast" (*saptāha-śīla*):
it is intended to prevent the seeds within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) from being reborn in the evil destinies (*durgati*).
The *Shishi Yaolan* states:
Confucius said:
"A child is born and only after three years is it released from the parents' embrace;
therefore, one repays them with a three-year mourning period."
The Buddhist scriptures state that after a person dies,
they remain for seven times seven days before finally escaping the realm of the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Therefore, the ritual procedures for the seven-day purification period are fully prepared;
as for the contemporary practice of performing Buddhist services during the one-hundred-day, small-anniversary (xiaoxiang),
and great-anniversary (daxiang) rites.
Although it was due to the Confucian texts on mourning rites,
one was able to cultivate the merit of upholding the solemn observances of the Buddhist gate;
how can this not be believed?
On the Topic of Preparing for the Ritual of Fasting: Bodhisattva Puguang addressed the Buddha, saying, "If good men or women, before their death,

prepare in advance by performing the *shengqi* (seven-day) rites, lighting lamps, hanging banners, and inviting the Sangha— meaning they invite the monks in succession to receive offerings— and recite the sutras, taking these four as examples, will they obtain much merit?"
The Buddha said,
"That merit is immeasurable.
He further said:
"When parents or kinsmen have passed away and are undergoing suffering,
if one performs meritorious deeds on their behalf, will they obtain much merit?
The Buddha said:
One obtains one-seventh [of the merit],
because in a previous life they lacked faith in the Way and its Virtue. If, however,
one offers the deceased's ornaments for the body, houses, or gardens and groves...
By making offerings to the Triple Gem,
one may be uprooted from the sufferings of hell and be reborn according to one’s vows. The *Suiyuanwangsheng jing* (Sutra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows) states:
According to the *Yijian zhi*,
an old woman named Wang from E-zhu used to purchase paper money to deposit in the treasury.
The Grand Secretary Li Da was ordered to draft the document and affix his seal.
After the old woman passed away, Li suddenly fell ill and collapsed to the ground;
after three days, he revived and said:
He was arrested by the authorities of the underworld and brought before the treasury office to identify his signature.
Li said:
"This was written by me on behalf of the mistress of the household.
He was introduced to the Golden-Purple-Rank Official;
the questions and answers were as they had been at the beginning.
The official said,
"Simply pursue the evidence of this matter and let him return.
He was then led out.
The old woman was overjoyed and said,
"I am grateful that you have come; now my deposited money has finally returned to me."
Regarding those people of today who delight in preparing for the future by depositing funds in advance,
one should take the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* as the scriptural authority and the *Yijian zhi* as the empirical verification.
Among the relics of the Dharma left by Vipaśyin Buddha,
there were bhikṣus who set out seats and placed their alms bowls upon them at the crossroads.
He spoke these words:

He refined the elixir according to the dharma for three years before it was perfected.
He said to his disciples:

As a subject serving the Three Realms, he hoped to be free from shame.

The Lord of the Old Man again commanded Lingcan to mount his carriage and attend upon the Great Lord of the Jade Dawn.

He was invested with the seal and ribbon of the Heavenly Master, the two swords—male and female—the secret registers of the "Correct Unity and Subduing Power," and the various scriptures, talismans, and diagrams of the Three Clarities.

When people suffered from illness or calamities from the authorities, they would provide grain according to their circumstances to redeem their offenses, recounting their transgressions and repenting.
His disciples numbered in the tens of thousands.

The Jade Bureau (Yùjú) sank again to become a well; the present-day Yùjú Guān (Jade Bureau Abbey) is the site of this ancient trace. Zhang Ling studied the Way on Mount Heming.

Heng’s son was Lu;
Lu styled himself Shijun (Master Lord).
Those who came to study under him...
Initially they were called *guizhu* (ghost-soldiers),
