each led their own retinue.
He ordered those who had committed transgressions to undergo penance before the various sacrificial officers.
He established charitable rest-houses (*yi-she*) along the roads,
providing rice and meat to supply travelers.
The common people and the ethnic minorities placed their faith and allegiance in him.
The imperial court appointed him as General of the Household for the Pacification of Yi (Zhēnyí Zhōnglángjiāng) with concurrent command of Hǎnnìng Commandery.
When Cáo Cão entered Nánzhèng, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lùgàngzhōng.
He was posthumously titled Marquis Yuan.
His son Fu succeeded him; this is recorded in the "Biography of Liu Yan" in the *Book of the Later Han*.
During the Xiping era, [he]...
In Hanzhong there was Zhang Xiu,
who practiced the Way of Great Peace;
Zhang Jue practiced the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice.
The masters of the Tàipíng Dào taught people to prostrate themselves and contemplate their transgressions;
they then administered consecrated water to them and required the families of the sick to provide five *dǒu* of rice.
Later, Jue was executed and Xiu also perished.
Lu, relying on their personal integrity and conduct, [prospered].
He subsequently embellished it.
He composed the *Jiaoyiqieshan dianlü* (Abridged Classic on the Erection of Almsgiving Halls).
Zhang Lu’s grandfather, Zhang Ling, had traveled to Shu to study the Dao at Mount Guming.
He composed books on the Way to delude the common people;
those who received his teachings had to provide five *dǒu* of rice,
and thus he was popularly known as the "Rice Bandit."
Ling died, and his son Heng transmitted his teachings;
after Heng died, Lu again transmitted them. (From the *Wei Zhi* of the Three Kingdoms).
Initially, Zhang Jue of Julu served the Yellow Emperor and Laozi.
He taught them by means of sorcery,
calling it the Way of Great Peace (Tàipíng Dào).
He used incantations, talismans, and consecrated water to treat illnesses.
He had the patient kneel and prostrate themselves to confess their transgressions;
sometimes the illness would be cured,
and the assembly all regarded him as a divine being.
Jue dispatched his disciples to travel throughout the four quarters, deceiving and enticing one another in turn.
Within ten years, their followers numbered hundreds of thousands;
from the eight provinces of Qing, Xu, You, Ji, Jing, Yang, Yan, and Yu, there were none who did not respond.
There were thirty-six generals in total;
"general" (fang) here refers to a military commander.
Each major general commanded more than ten thousand men.
Xiaofang was about six or seven thousand *li* away.
His disciple Tang Zhou submitted a memorial denouncing him.
An imperial edict was issued to pursue and arrest Jiao and his associates.
The various regions all rose up simultaneously at the command of [Zhang] Jue;
they all wore yellow turbans as their insignia,
and thus the people of the time called them the "Yellow Turban Rebels."
Within a month, the whole world rose up in response; Zhang Jiao began his rebellion in the first year of the Zhongping era of Emperor Lingdi.
An imperial edict was issued for Huangfu Song to suppress Jiao.
Song engaged in battle with Jiao’s younger brother, Liang.
He utterly defeated him and beheaded Liang Jiao;
as Jiao had already died of illness,
his coffin was opened and his corpse executed.
The *Hou Han shu*, in the biography of Huangfu Song, records that his head was sent to the capital,
stating: "In affairs,
there are indeed instances where the true and the false are intermingled."
As for those who have lost its true essence:
the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice is but one aspect of the "Correct Unity and United威 (Majestic Power) Dharma" bestowed by Lord Lao upon the Celestial Master.
The Celestial Master practiced it in Shu during the reign of Emperor Shun.
The Celestial Master and his son attained the Way and were summoned as immortals;
to this day, the sacred traces of Longhu Mountain remain majestic,
and those who serve as lineage masters among their descendants have never ceased.
This was also truly that which successive dynasties have revered.
During the time of Emperor Ling, Zhang Xiu and Zhang Jue followed in the wake of the Celestial Masters;
they feigned the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice to convert the masses.
Throughout the eight provinces, there were thirty-six generals, each acting as a commander-in-chief.
At one point, they all rebelled and were ultimately executed; this is the "false" account.
However, because some historians have occasionally offered exaggerated arguments, later generations have been unable to discern the truth from the falsehood between them.
Now, examining the account in the *Book of Han*,
the biography of Liu Yan states that those who received the Way from [Zhang] Ling had to provide five *dǔ* of rice.
Three generations passed from the time Ling arrived in Lú.
He was initially enfeoffed as Marquis of Langzhong,
and his son Fu succeeded him;
this is what Fan Ye recorded, with no further words.
Furthermore, upon examining the *Wei zhi*,
it states that Lü composed Daoist texts to delude the common people, requiring them to contribute five *dǔ* of rice; thus,
he was popularly known as the "Rice Bandit."
This account, as recorded by Chen Shou, contains considerable disparagement;
furthermore, regarding the narrative in the *Dianlüe*,
it further states that Zhang Jue was executed for practicing the Five Pecks of Rice Way (*Wudoumidao*).
The state of Lu relied on those people's beliefs and embellished them;
this interpretation is profoundly erroneous.
For it was in Lu that the Way of Rice was practiced.
This has been the ancestral tradition;
why must it be practiced solely because of the horns?
Thus we know that both the *Weizhi* and the *Dianlüe* lack comprehensive insight.
As for the truth or falsehood of these spurious matters,
they do not compare to the *Book of Han*, which is a treasure trove of records.
As for Li Ying’s *Record of Shu*, it is unknown what era its text belongs to.
To insult and treat others with contempt is to be swallowed by a great python of ghosts and spirits.
How can you bear to so recklessly utter such blasphemous and profane words?
When some in the world refer to them as the "Three Zhangs," they equate the venerable status of the Heavenly Master with the followers of the Yellow Turbans;
this is something those with discernment ought to avoid.
In the eighth year of the Yanxi era,
the eunuch Lao Xiu submitted a memorial accusing Li Ying,
the Inspector of the Imperial Clan (Sili Xiaowei), for harboring scholars from the National University.
They formed alliances with students from various commanderies to constitute factions that slandered the imperial court.
The Emperor was struck with indignation and issued an edict to all commanderies and kingdoms to arrest the members of these factions.
Zhang Heng, Ma Ying, and others—along with over two hundred people including Du Mi, Chen Xiang, Chen Shi, and Fan Pang—were all renowned worthies of the realm;
yet Ma Ying and the others frequently brought in the sons and younger brothers of eunuchs.
The eunuchs, fearing [the consequences], petitioned the Emperor that, according to the timing of Heaven, the members of the Party should be pardoned so they might all return to their villages.
Their names were recorded in the three government offices (*sanfu*) and they were subjected to lifelong prohibition from office.

The eunuch Cao Jie dispatched Zheng Sa to arrest the Grand Marshal Chen Fan at Beisi Prison and have him executed.

Cao Jie requested that the various provinces be ordered to investigate and prosecute those involved in the "Hooked Party.

Those at the gates of death and former officials were all subjected to prohibition and confinement.
Among the party members, more than a hundred died.
As for the heroes and talents of the realm, as well as those of Confucian learning and righteous conduct—
The eunuchs designated everyone as members of the faction.
Those who were executed, exiled, dismissed, or imprisoned numbered another six or seven hundred.
This was in the second year.
The Lord of the Old descended upon Mount Tiantai and bestowed the *Dadong lingbao jing* (Scripture of the Great Cavernous Treasure) upon the immortal Ge Xuan,
as well as the methods for the Upper Clarity Retreat (*shangqing zhai fa*) and the three registers— the Golden Register (*jin lu*) included— thereby securing and stabilizing the national destiny.
The Jade Register protects and blesses the nobility;
the Yellow Register delivers the seven generations of ancestors.
Furthermore, the "Treatise on Resonance and Response" was bestowed.
It demonstrates to the people of the world the matters of sin and merit, and how to cultivate goodness and abandon evil.
The commentary states:
In our own dynasty, Li Changling composed a commentary on the *Ganying pian*.
Citing extensively from Buddhist and Daoist scriptures and treatises, as well as secular biographies,
he provides the most illuminating evidence for the retribution of good and evil deeds.
In recent times, when high officials and nobles have offered praises to those who practice alongside them,

Cí said, "To study the Way, one must be pure and tranquil."

In the Jin dynasty, when the capital was Luoyang, during the Taishi era of Emperor Wu (Sima Yan), who had received the abdication from Wei,

In the fourth year,
the śramaṇa Zhu Fachong [arrived].
He arrived at Lushan in Xiangzhou,

Hou said,

The commentary states:
The Book of Jin says:
Yang Hu recognized that his previous life had been the son of the Li family,
as he was able to retrieve a gold ring that had been played with.
This current statement regarding his having built this temple in a previous life refers to that same individual.
This is indeed the prior body of one's former life.
The retributions for sins and blessings in this world do not err;
how could one fail to take this as a mirror for reflection?
That Hu was able to know his previous lives is what Buddhism calls the supernormal power of knowing past existences (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
It appears that Hu had studied Buddhism and attained realization, manifesting himself in this world.
In the second year of Taikang,
Liu Sahuo of Bingzhou was engaged in hunting when he died a sudden death.
The two men reported that they had traveled toward the northwest and,
upon reaching hell, saw a golden-colored holy man.
Those on his left and right said:
The Great Being Avalokiteśvara addressed him, saying:

You may go to the five locations where the Aśoka Stūpas are situated—Luoyang, Linzi, Jianye, Minyin, and Chengdu—to pay homage and repent.
Furthermore, there are two stone statues in the region of Wu.
It was constructed by spirits sent by King Aśoka.
Those who are able to go there to pay homage shall not fall into hell.
It is also said:
Whenever one establishes merit for the deceased,
the mid-autumn day of the seventh month is when the śramaṇas receive the summer retreat;
offerings made at this time are most excellent.
If one prepares ritual implements or vessels for offerings,
they should be inscribed with the title alone, stating:
"Offered to the Triple Gem by [Name]."
The bestowal of merit is vast.
When śramaṇas and laypeople see their past transgressions, they are able to reveal them themselves;
by not neglecting the prescribed procedures and repenting with diligent sincerity, their offenses are immediately extinguished.
If one feels ashamed to recite it aloud before a crowd,
one may silently recite it to oneself while facing an image;
if the ritual is thus not neglected, one's transgressions will likewise be extinguished.
If there are omissions or accidental concealments, the retribution received will still be light.
If a virtuous person recites the sutras,
that ground shall all become diamond.

There has never been one [account] that does not enumerate these matters in detail.
Thus, Fan Ye’s discussion of the Western Regions states:

"The divine transformation of the Buddha-way originated in Shendu (the sound *Gandhāra* refers to Tianzhu, or India); during the Han Dynasty of the West, it was not mentioned in any geographical records."
How could it be that the Way was closed during the past era and its fortune opened only in this later age?
Yuan Hong, in his *Han Ji*, states:
"In India, there is the Way of the Buddha."
Able to transform and pervade the myriad things,
he brought great salvation to all living beings.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, an imperial edict was issued to compile the Book of Jin (Jin Shu).
Dharmarakṣa, Kumārajīva, and Fotudeng are all listed in the biographies,
and they were praised with these words:
"They transmitted the written word and expounded the teachings, penetrating the profound and fathoming the mysterious."
Wei Shou compiled the *Weishu*.
In its "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism" (*Folao zhi*), it states:
"The Buddha taught that the spiritual consciousness of the three periods of time is eternally indestructible."
In all cases, good and evil deeds inevitably entail retribution;
by gradually accumulating superior karma, one eventually reaches the stage of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
These are all the clear teachings of the Buddha as recorded in various historical chronicles.
It is merely said that the fruit of the Buddha-way can benefit all things and save the world.
How strange!
This is like the way the Ouyang clan compiled the *History of Tang*.
Regarding all matters concerning the Śākya clan that might benefit state administration or enlighten the human mind,
I have deleted them entirely;
this serves precisely to preserve the comprehensiveness and richness of the original historical records.
To be deficient in comprehensive learning and to adhere to narrow views while claiming to possess such [understanding] is called "believing in history," yet it is not true belief.

Northern Qi: The Northern Qi capital was Ye. In the first year of the Tianbao era (550 CE), when Gao Yang ascended the throne of the Eastern Wei through abdication and became Emperor Wenxuan, he issued an edict inviting the eminent monk Fachang to enter the palace to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
He was appointed as State Preceptor; this was the beginning of the office of State Preceptor.
The Dharma Master Tanyan stood nine chi and six cun tall.
The Emperor summoned him frequently to inquire about the Way.
During the reign of Emperor Zhou, Zhou Hongzheng came on a diplomatic mission.
The high ministers appointed the Master to receive him as an escort.
Hongzheng, however, relied upon his own talent and acted with haughty arrogance.
Upon seeing Yan Yian, his [Dai's] doubts were naturally dispelled;
he sought out the master’s painted portraits and the commentaries on the sutras he had authored to take back with him.
The Emperor treated him with even greater honor.
While Jinwei was serving as the High Patriarch of Shaoyuan, Master Baogong of Mount Song was traveling toward Mount Bailu.
Suddenly, he heard the sound of a bell and saw a gate inscribed with the words: "Lingyin Monastery."
A Brahman monk arrived from abroad;
Bao followed him into the temple and sat upon a couch in the Dharma Hall.
Looking up at the ceiling, he saw an opening in the roof that resembled a well.
There were monks who flew down through the opening;
when they had reached more than sixty people,
they sat down and each was questioned.
"Where is today's fast being observed?
Some replied, "In Yuzhang, Chengdu, the South of the Yangtze, the North of Beiji, or the Five Indias—
distances spanning thousands of miles."
When the last monk arrived,
the assembly asked why he was so late.
He replied:
At a dharma assembly at Bican Temple in Xiangzhou presided over by Chan Master Jian,
each participant presented their formal thesis.
There was one young monk among them.
Difficult questions arose one after another;
it was truly a sight worth beholding,
and before one realized it, the sun had set.
Baoci said,
"Master Jian is my preceptor.
The monks stared directly at Bao.
Shortly thereafter, he suddenly lost his temple.
He then sat alone atop an oak tree—*zuo* (pronounced *zuo*), meaning *liè*—and went into the mountains to inquire of Dàtǒng Fǎshàng.
Fǎshàng said:
This temple was built by Fotudeng;
sages and saints dwell therein,
sometimes remaining hidden and sometimes appearing.
To this day, the sound of bells is still heard when traveling through the mountains.
In the second year [of the reign],
Emperor Wen issued an edict for Chan Master Chou to travel to the capital of Ye to establish Yunmen Temple as his residence.
The Master sat in meditation in a single room and never went out to see anyone off or welcome them.
When the Emperor arrived,
his disciples urged him to do so.
The Master said:
"Piṇḍola welcomed the king for seven paces,
which caused the king to lose his kingdom."
Although my virtue does not equal that of [the Emperor], it resembles his;
for this reason, I dare not deceive myself,
hoping only to bring blessings upon His Majesty.
The Emperor was deluded by his attendants;
out of arrogance toward the Master, he desired to harm him personally.
At dawn, the Master departed from the monastery for twenty li and stood with palms joined beside the road.
The Emperor questioned him in wonder.
The Master replied,
"I fear only that the blood might defile the monastery."
The Emperor immediately repented and apologized,
saying to the Vice President of the Secretariat,
Yang Zuyan: "How can one slander such a True Man?"
They then returned to the palace together in the same carriage.
[The Emperor] asked,
"Who was my disciple in a previous life?"
The Master said, "He was once a Rākṣasa king;
even now he still loves to kill. He then consecrated water in a basin and had him look into it.
Seeing a multitude of rākṣasas following behind him,
the Emperor felt great reverence and faith;
he requested and received the bodhisattva precepts.
Henceforth, meat shall never be eaten.

All instruments for harming living beings, such as the hawks and dogs of the Five Workshops (wǔfáng), and all slaughter within the realm are hereby suspended. An edict was issued to establish the position of Chief Overseer of the Buddhist Clergy (zhāoxuán shàngtǒng), with the śramaṇa Fǎshàng appointed as the Great Overseer (dàtǒng).
The clerical staff numbered more than fifty people.
Under his jurisdiction were over four million monks and nuns and more than forty thousand monasteries.
All received his moral instruction.
The Emperor constructed an altar and prepared the rites,
honoring him as National Teacher.
He spread his hair upon the ground and invited Shangtong to tread upon it as he ascended the seat.
The empresses, consorts, and high ministers all received the Bodhisattva precepts.
When the Emperor was in Jinyang, he sent a man riding a single camel.
The imperial edict stated:
"You may go to the temple to retrieve the scripture cases;
have someone inquire as to their location."
The Emperor said,
"When Ren-tuo left the city,
as soon as he had gone out, it was suddenly as if in a dream."
Upon reaching the mountain slope, there was a temple.
A group of śrāmaṇeras saw it and said,
"Gao Yang has come on a camel."
He then led him to see an elderly monk.
The monk asked,
"How is it that Gao Yang has become the Son of Heaven?"
The messenger said,
"O Sage and Illustrious One.
The monk said:
"Why have you come?
The messenger replied,
"I am sent to fetch the scripture case."
The monk said,
"Yang is at the temple and is too lazy to read the sutras;
have him go north to fetch them."
The envoy returned with his report.
In the sixth year,
the Daoist master Lu Xiujing first [arrived].
Because Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty abandoned the teachings of Laozi,
he subsequently fled to the Wei state;
by the time Emperor Wenxuan of the Northern Qi practiced Buddhism, [he was received there].
Jing and others feared him and went to the palace gate to petition for an audience,
requesting that he compete with the Śramaṇas in debate.
The Emperor granted his permission.
Jing used incantations and sorcery to cause the monks' robes and alms bowls to fly up, and the beams and pillars of the palace to tremble.
The Emperor turned to the Grand Steward Fashang and said:
"How could there be no one in the Buddha-dharma?
Thus, Shangtong recommended Tanxian;
however, at that time, Tanxian had been drinking wine.
He came out and said,
"You who ask such questions dare to indulge yourselves in mere minor arts.
He then placed Master Chou’s robe on the ground.
The Daoist practitioners exerted their combined strength but could not move it.
Xian took the beam himself and placed it between two pillars to have them perform the incantation;
yet the beam and pillars remained motionless.
Jing said:
"The Buddhists themselves designate their teachings as 'internal' (neijiao).
'Internal' refers precisely to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna)."
Xian said,
"When the Son of Heaven resides within the nine-layered palace,
should he not also be considered inferior to the hundred officials?"
In solemn silence, he swallowed his tears, for there was no one to oppose him;
the ministers all leaped for joy.
The Emperor then issued an edict.
Let those Daoist practitioners who claim to have attained the state of a transcendent immortal ascend the Three-Cup Terrace and soar far away;
as for those who cannot do so—
"You should go to the Chief Administrator of the Office of Monastic Affairs (Zhāoxuán Shàngtǒng) to receive tonsure and ordination.
Should anyone refuse, four people shall be executed.
Thereupon, he issued an edict stating:
As for those who call themselves "Sacrificial Masters," the flavors of this world are but false and illusory fermenting agents; where,
then, is the pure emptiness?
Gopu-si-gan’s compassion has been forever severed;
above, he differs from the benevolent shrines, and below, he deviates from the sacrificial rites.
It is fitting that all such practices be strictly prohibited and no longer observed.
Consequently, there were no Daoist masters throughout the territory of Qi.
Xu Shu stated:
"Xiu Jing was born at the end of the Jin dynasty and traveled with Master Huiyuan."
He underwent the "corpse-liberation" (shi-jie) during the Taishi era of the Song dynasty;
thus, Jianji spoke [of this period] from Taishi until the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty.
It has already been forty years;
it would not be right for you to practice tranquility again today.
If you say that because of Liang you abandoned the Way and fled from Liang to Wei—
It should be said that he was a disciple of Lu Xiujing;
this is indeed credible.
He was the layman Lu Faho of Jingzhou during the Liang dynasty.
Because Yuan Di had been defeated by Wei,
he subsequently returned to Qi.
The Emperor appointed him as Grand Marshal (Taishouwei) and granted him a prime residence.
He and his disciples converted it into a Buddhist temple;
seven hundred of his followers all practiced the methods of dhyāna.
One morning, while prostrating before the Buddha, he sat upon his bed and passed away.
He was about to wrap the body, which measured only three chi in height;
once the wrapping was finished,
the Emperor ordered him to open it again for inspection.
There was only a single empty coffin. He once inscribed on a wall:

"Ten years for a Son of Heaven is still permissible; ten days for a Son of Heaven is urgent as fire. A hundred days for an abdicated emperor; one year for a Son of Heaven who succeeds him. The reign of Emperor Xiaozhao did not even last a year. People feared it would be scraped away and erased.
In the end, they could not be extinguished.
After seven years,
the Emperor presented one thousand fascicles of Sanskrit scriptures from the inner treasury.

By imperial decree, the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas was commissioned to translate [the text] at T'ien-p'ing Temple; the Great State Preceptor Dharmaśāna and the Śramaṇa General Dharmaśūṇ were appointed as supervisors of the translation.
The Emperor personally paid homage to the Sanskrit manuscript.
He said to his ministers:
"This is the grand foundation of the Triple Gem;

according to propriety, it is fitting to show singular reverence—'singular' meaning exclusive devotion. The title for a śramaṇa is 'Venerable,' while that for a layperson (jushi) is 'Myriad-Heavenly Excellence' (Wàntiānyì)."
The lay devotee Zhi Xi also translated scriptures at Ye City for ten years.
The Emperor visited Liao Yang and resided at Ganlu Temple for profound contemplation.
He issued an edict stating that nothing but matters of great importance to the state and the military should be reported to him.
Sengshu said:
The world says that Wenxuan was cruel and indeed engaged in executions and killings,
to the point that some even wished to compare him to Jie and Zhou.
Yet, observing his translation of scriptures, cultivation of dhyāna, reception of precepts, prohibition of killing, honoring of the National Preceptor, and the dismissal of Daoism,
one sees that his reverence for the Buddha was indeed ultimate;
this was likely because in a previous life he had been a śrāmaṇera at a noble monastery.
By the power of his wisdom and vows, he appeared in the world;
occupying the throne of a king of men, he performed the works of the Buddha-dharma,
yet in his first year he was fond of killing.
This was merely the result of his residual habits;
it was not like that of Jie or Zhou, who, having never encountered the Buddha-dharma, committed acts of slaughter without remorse.
"Wucheng Wucheng" refers to Gaozu’s ninth son, Heqing, in the second year of the Heqing era.

By imperial decree, Dharma Master Huizang was to lecture on the sixty-fascicle *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* translated during the Jin dynasty in the Taiji Hall. Previously, Sun Jingde had fashioned an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
subsequently, he was condemned to death for a crime.
In a dream, a śramaṇa instructed him that reciting the sūtras could bring liberation from this fate.
Upon waking, he recited them a full thousand times;
when the execution was imminent, the blade broke three times.
The official reported this to the Emperor,
who issued an edict to pardon him.
Upon returning home, he saw [the mark] upon the neck of the image.
There were three sword scars [upon it],
and this scripture was subsequently circulated;
it was titled the *Gao Wang Guanshiyin Jing*.
The commentary states:
This sutra consists of only ten phrases;
it was [translated] by Wang Xuemu during the Song dynasty.
The text bestowed in the dream has now been published for sale in the marketplace;
it is that which Sun Jingde recited.
Later generations arbitrarily added to it,
making the text vulgar and confused;
consequently, those with discernment came to doubt its authenticity.
Furthermore, during the Jiayu era of our dynasty,
Mei Zhi, the Dragon Scholar, lost his wife's sight; he prayed at Upper Zhushan,
and one night he dreamed of a person in white robes who instructed him to recite the Ten-Phrase Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.
He then recited [the scripture] without ceasing,
and his two eyes were restored to sight.
Lord Zhao Qingxian published this account.
The Great Being has used this most concise sutra-dharma to rescue people from peril and distress;
there are three verifiable accounts of this that can be recorded throughout antiquity and the present.
Is this not to be believed?
Later Emperor Houzhu was the eldest son of Emperor Wencheng.
In the sixth year of the Wuping era, ten śramaṇas, including Baoxian, [were present].
Having traveled to the Western Heaven to seek scriptures and returned,
he obtained two hundred and sixty sections of the Sanskrit originals.
This was in the first year of the Longhua era.
By imperial decree, the White Horse Temple in Ye were restored; three śarīras were obtained from the stupa built by Fotudeng and enshrined in a precious vase.
Wang Yong of Guangwu placed them in a crystal bowl and performed circumambulations and prayers.
The śarīra suddenly floated upon the surface of the water, circling to the right seven times.

It circled northward toward the Northern Zhou capital of Chang’an. As for Emperor Min of the Northern Zhou, Yuwen Jue, he was the third son of Taizu; he received the abdication of the Western Wei, and his first year of reign was the twenty-fourth year of the Datong era of the Western Wei.

Upon his accession to the throne, he issued an edict changing the era name and appointing Master Sengshi as the Tripitaka Master of the State of Zhou. By imperial decree, the śarīra were enshrined in Changnian Temple in Puzhou;
they emitted a great radiance that issued forth from the reliquary jar.
He then constructed a stupa to commemorate this auspicious marvel. While the Emperor was hunting at Mount Tan,
he pointed toward the mountain from afar and asked his ministers,
"Do you see anything there?"
The Secretary-General Lu Guangdu said,
"I saw a śramaṇa.
The Emperor said:
This was so. He immediately lifted the siege and returned, ordering Guang to construct a stupa at the very spot where he had seen [the vision].
Upon digging one zhang deep for the foundation, they discovered a monk’s staff and a ceramic alms bowl.
Emperor Wu. Emperor Wu Yong was the fourth son of Taizu. In the third year of the Baoding era, an imperial edict stated:
"The year is Zhaoyang; it is the first month of spring when the dragon gathers at Tianping. 'The dragon gathers' means—"
The Azure Dragon of the East presides over the year;

Heaven and the Year both reside in the year of Shen. It is now commanded that the relevant authorities shall respectfully produce all the scriptural treasuries, beginning with the teachings on arising and ceasing and concluding with the discourse on Nirvāṇa, and so forth.
In the fourth year of the Tiānhé era,
the śramaṇa Zàngchēng translated scriptures in Cháng'ān.

The Śramaṇa Zhidu translated the "Verses on the Universal Gate" (Pumen) of the Lotus Sūtra. An imperial edict commanded Confucian scholars, Buddhist monks, and Daoist priests to expound upon the Three Teachings;
the Śramaṇa Dao’an then composed the *Ejiao lun* (Treatise on the Two Teachings).
He regarded the nine schools of Confucianism and Daoism as external teachings and Buddhism as the internal teaching.
The Emperor placed his faith in the praises offered by the Daoist practitioners Zhang Bin and Wei Yuansong.
Based on the prophecies of the *Chenwei* texts, which stated that those in black robes were destined to rule as kings,
he harbored a deep-seated resentment toward the Śākyamuni tradition.
Zhang Bin then advised the Emperor, saying:
In the eras of Tang and Yu, the state was secure despite the absence of Buddhist temples;
in the Qi and Liang dynasties, the mandate of heaven was short-lived despite the presence of monasteries.
However, that which benefits the people and strengthens the state accords with the Buddha’s mind.
The Buddha takes great compassion as his foundation;
he would never subject the common people to arduous labor for the sake of devoutly honoring clay and wood,
nor would he request the construction of vast monasteries to house the myriad sentient beings of the four seas.
He did not establish sectarian views, but installed the five scriptures of the Mahāyāna throughout the monastery;
as for those who extended [the teachings] with impartiality,
he made no distinction between monastics and laypeople, nor did he choose between enemies and kin.
They take city walls and moats for stūpas and monasteries;
they regard the Emperor as the Tathāgata;
they use the suburbs and towns as monastic dwellings.
The husband and wife serve as the holy assembly;
those of superior virtue are appointed to the Three Bonds,
and the elderly are honored as the Elder (Upadhyaya).
He selected the benevolent and wise to serve as administrators and sought the courageous and diligent to act as Dharma masters; thus,
throughout the six realms of existence, there was no heart of resentment like that of King Zhou.
There were songs from the eight directions and verses from the *Zhou* [Classic], and so forth.
In the second month of the fourth year,
he assembled the various officials, monks, and Daoists at Wende Hall.
In the first month of the first year of the Jiande era,
the Emperor visited Xuandu Monastery and ascended the seat himself to deliver a lecture discussing the similarities and differences between Śākyamuni and Laozi.
The high officials, monks, and Daoists posed questions and challenges to one another. At that time, there was a man named Li Lian in Chang’an whose spiritual anomalies were unfathomable;
every night he would wail loudly on the streets for Śākyamuni Buddha.
In this manner, several months passed.
Two years later, as expected, there was indeed an event concerning the abolition of Buddhism.
On the second day of the second month of that second year.
He assembled a hundred officials, monks, and Daoists to debate the sequence of the Three Teachings,
establishing Confucianism as primary and Daoism as secondary.
Shi Ju was seated at the rear. An imperial decree was issued for the ministers, śramaṇas, and Daoist masters to engage in a broad discussion on the Three Teachings within the inner palace.
Dharma Master Faming established a thesis that excelled in its reasoning.
Zhen Luan, Grand Master of the Office of the Imperial Scribe, presents the *Xiaodao lun* (Treatise on Laughing at Daoism),
consisting of thirty-six chapters,
modeled upon the thirty-six sections of the Daoist canon.
Since the teachings of Śākyamuni consist of twelve divisions, this [work] now surpasses them threefold;
thus ends the *Hongming ji*. The Emperor assembled the monks and Daoists and proclaimed his decree, saying:
The Six Classics and Confucianism are appropriate for the world;
true Buddhas have no physical form, yet people vainly venerate stupas and temples.
Foolish people follow this with blind faith, needlessly exhausting their precious wealth.
All scriptures and images should be removed and destroyed.
That śramaṇas do not revere their parents’ profound恩情 (en) is the height of rebellion and perversity.
"According to the laws of the state,
how could it be permitted to allow all of them to return to secular life so as to honor their filial support?
At that time, Dharma Master Huiyuan stepped forward from the assembly and replied with firm resolve:"
If it is argued that because an image is insentient,
serving it brings no merit,
then how can the seven ancestral temples of the state be considered sentient?
The Emperor said:
"Buddhist scriptures are the laws of foreign lands;
therefore, they ought to be abolished."
"The seven ancestral temples were established by those of former generations;
I, Your Majesty, do not consider them appropriate and intend to abolish them all.
The Master said:
If the laws of foreign lands are not applicable here,
then since what Confucius taught originated in the state of Lu,
they should likewise not be practiced in the territories of Qin and Jin.
"If the seven ancestral temples were abolished, the Five Classics would become useless.
If the Three Teachings were all abolished together, how could one govern the state?
The Emperor said:
Although the territories of Lu, Qin, and Jin differ,
they are all none other than the transformation of a single sovereign’s influence.
The Master said:
"If Qin and Lu were under the same royal transformation,
then China and India are likewise under the single transformation of a universal monarch within Jambudvīpa."
"Why do you not follow [the same path]?
The Emperor and the Master exchanged such words as many as twelve times,
yet the Emperor could not prevail over him.
In the fifth month of the third year,
the Emperor intended to abolish the Buddhist teachings unilaterally and ordered the Daoist Zhang Bin to employ deceptive rhetoric to undermine the Buddhist monks.
The Dharma Master Zhiyan’s responses were profound and his spirit vigorous;
the Emperor’s intent was unable to subdue him.
Thereupon, the Emperor manifested his celestial majesty and posed difficult questions.
The attendants shouted, "Listen to the decree!
Xuán remained composed and responded with measured calm;
his exposition of the principles was exceedingly profound.
Among the ministers attending the assembly, there was none who did not revere this as rare;
yet the Emperor alone did not speak of it.
The following day, he issued an edict.
Furthermore, he abolished the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism,
destroyed all scriptures and images,
and compelled both śramaṇas and daoshi to return to secular life.

At that time, more than two million monastics and Daoists within the borders of the kingdom reverted to secular dress. In the sixth month, an imperial edict was issued to establish the Tongdao Guan (Monastery for the Way) for those among the Buddhists and Daoists of renowned virtue;
one hundred and twenty scholars were appointed to serve there.
He donned ceremonial robes, a cap, a tablet, and sandals,
and appointed Yancong and others as Academicians.
The śramaṇa Da’an, who possessed long-standing renown, wished to be granted an official post.

Seng'an refused to comply with the summons, dying while wailing and abstaining from food; he had previously composed the *Treatise on the Two Teachings*. When the Dharma Master Jing’ai heard that the imperial decree had been issued, he went to the palace gate to present a memorial requesting an audience.
The Emperor summoned him for an audience.
[Huiyuan] recounted in great detail the matters of retribution for the destruction of the teachings.
The Emperor changed his expression, apologized, and dismissed him.
He then fled into Mount Zhongnan.
Wailing for seven days,
he sat upon a flat rock and drew a knife to cut off his own flesh.
She hung her intestines and stomach from the branches of a pine tree;
holding her chest, she passed away.
White milk flowed from her side and congealed upon the rocks.
Among those who heard this, there were none who did not shed tears. Shu said,
"The Way of the Buddha is fundamentally eternal."
That there are times of distress is merely the result of the karmic retribution of worldly beings. For this reason,
the great and small three calamities are the result of great karmic retribution.
The three instances of the suppression of the Sangha by Emperor Wu were minor karmic retributions;
yet whenever such a suppression occurred, there was invariably a sage or holy person who appeared.
During the Wei dynasty, there was Tan Shi;
during the Zhou dynasty, there were Zhi, Xuandao, Anjing, and Ai.
All of them forgot their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma, seeking to restore the Great Teaching.
Yet Seng’ai’s flesh was emaciated and his heart was burdened;
some of his contemporaries remarked that his followers were merely inflicting hardship and bitterness upon themselves.
Little did they realize that even if it had been of no benefit to their own court,
it was nonetheless sufficient to move the hearts of the people and make them aware that the urgency of upholding the Dharma was such as this.
Emperor Wu abolished it.
Emperor Xuan restored his [the master's] posthumous honors;
within fewer than a few years, his Way flourished once more.
Who would have known that this was not a response to the sincere spiritual resonance of Master Āryadeva?
In the sixth year,
he attacked Qi and destroyed it,
simultaneously demolishing all Buddhist scriptures and images within the borders of Qi.
At that time, there were more than three million monastics who had returned to lay dress.
In the sixth month of the first year of the Xuanzheng era,
the Emperor was stricken by a pestilential illness.
A severe eruption broke out on his body, and he subsequently passed away. A supplementary note cites the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*):
Emperor Xuan (Emperor Xuan Bin), the son of Emperor Wu, during the first year of the Dacheng era.
Prior to this, the śramaṇa Daolin had been granted an audience for his scholarly achievements.
He debated with Emperor Wu for twenty days,
exchanging seventy rounds of discourse;
the Emperor was unable to best him.
He subsequently granted permission for the restoration of the teaching.
However, the Emperor passed away;
it was only upon reaching this point that Daolin submitted his petition with renewed vigor.
The Emperor granted his request and subsequently issued an edict stating:
"The late Emperor was deluded by heterodox doctrines."
Because they considered the teachings of Śākyamuni to be of no benefit,
they abolished them and did not practice them.
However, as these are bound up with the Great Teaching, how could they be deemed fit for dismissal?
Now, two hundred and twenty venerable elders of virtuous character have been selected.
Without shaving their hair or altering their appearance,
they shall perform rites for the sake of the state at Shuzhu Temple in both the Eastern and Western Capitals.
He then issued an edict for Zhizang and others to grow their hair long to serve as Bodhisattva-monks, appointing them as temple masters;
they were adorned with flower crowns and necklaces to manifest the appearance of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. The imperial decree stated:
The Three Jewels are most venerable and should be especially honored with reverence.

He ordered that those former śramaṇas who possessed virtuous conduct be settled in peace at Zhengcheng Hall to practice the Way. He also posthumously conferred upon Confucius the title of Duke of Zou.
In the first year of the Dading era, Emperor Jing— Emperor Jing being the son of Emperor Xuan Di—
issued an edict throughout the empire to restore both the Buddhist and Daoist teachings and to re-establish images of the Buddha and the Celestial Honored One.
The Chancellor Yang Jian,
together with Zhizang and Linggan of Shuzhu Temple and others,
underwent the tonsure for a second time and ordained two hundred and twenty monks.

The *Fozu Tongji*, Volume 38, concludes: "Since the *Hetu* and *Luoshu* are manifestations of the Way of Heaven intended to instruct the world, how could they be dismissed as mere supernatural anomalies?"
Thus, the Sage Laozi may have been a sovereign in heaven,
or he may have manifested divided forms to teach below; in all cases,
he revealed his transformation in accordance with the times.
When Laozi descended to instruct Lord Kou,
he bestowed upon him the scriptures and laws and appointed him as the Celestial Master,
charging him with the task of eliminating the abuses of the Three Zhangs.
His words were indeed worthy of being adopted.
As for his exhortation regarding the principles for assisting in the realization of Great Peace (Taiping),
he was thus able to proceed to the imperial palace to present his treatise.
Cui Hao led him forward,
and Emperor Taizu trusted and accepted him;

Cen Wénběn served as the Director of the Secretariat. When he was young, he frequently recited the "Universal Gateway" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Once, while traveling by boat on the Wu River, he encountered a storm. Cen Wénběn then chanted the "Universal Gateway" chapter; immediately, a great wind arose from the southeast, and the boat was blown back to the shore. He subsequently built a stupa at that location. Later, when he was serving as the Director of the Secretariat, he dreamed of a monk who said to him, "The merit you have cultivated through your recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* has caused you to attain the position of Minister. Upon waking, he related this dream to his fellow officials. All were deeply moved and marveled at the spiritual efficacy of the scripture. Subsequently, he had a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* transcribed in gold ink and enshrined it within the stupa. It is said that the stupa emitted light from time to time. During the Kaihuang era, Emperor Wen summoned him to the capital, where he died shortly thereafter. His remains were returned to his native village, where they were interred. At that time, the local people saw a white cloud hovering over the burial site, which gradually grew larger until it reached the sky. They also heard the sound of chanting and music, which continued for several days before fading away. Thus, the miraculous response of the *Lotus Sūtra* was manifest even in the present life. This account is recorded in the *Fǎhuá Jīng Xuánjì* (Mysteries of the Lotus Sūtra). It is also mentioned in the *Guǎngzhōng Jì* (Records of the Expanded Canon) and other sources. Furthermore, the monk Zhìshān of the Northern Qi dynasty once dreamed of a man who told him, "I am the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Because you recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, I have come to protect you. how could one possibly disregard the Buddha’s regulations to conform to the laws established by a single generation?
The proposal for its abolition does not arise from this principle.
From the time of Emperor Ming through to our own dynasty,
no one has again raised such a non-meritorious objection.
In the third year,
an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Yixing for an audience.
The Emperor consulted him on the principles of securing the state and governing the people.

Furthermore, regarding the essential teachings of the supramundane Dharma, he was called the Teacher of Heaven and the Teacher of the Son of Heaven. When the Emperor questioned him, asking how the state's fortunes were, [he replied:
"As for the duration of the national reign..."
He replied, "The imperial carriage shall travel ten thousand li, and the state will ultimately meet with good fortune.
He then presented a golden casket, saying, "Upon reaching ten thousand li, you should open it; inside there will be only a small amount of *danggui* (angelica)."
During the rebellion of An Lushan, the Emperor fled to Chengdu;
upon reaching Wanli Bridge, he realized the significance of the "returning" prophecy and was suddenly cleansed of his sorrows.
The title "Zhongji" (Ultimate Auspiciousness) was discontinued with Emperor Zhaozong,
as he had previously been enfeoffed as Prince Ji.
In the fourth year [of the reign].
The Tripitaka Master Wufei arrived from the Western Heavens.
Previously, Emperor Ruizong had heard of the Master’s reputation and dispatched General Shi Xian to welcome him beyond the Yumen Pass.
At this time, the Emperor dreamed that a strange monk came to visit him and ordered his likeness to be painted on the wall.
When the Master entered and saw it, he found that he was no different from the image on the wall.
The Emperor delighted in him and established an inner ritual arena for him to reside in,
honoring him as the head of the teaching.
The Master translated the *Vairocana* Sūtra and other scriptures.
The Esoteric School flourished here [in China]. In the seventh year, the Japanese monk Genbō was sent to China to seek the Dharma.
From India, the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi arrived.
Traveling south along the coast, he reached Guangzhou.
He was summoned to the capital and granted an audience;
by imperial decree, he was assigned a residence at Ci'en Monastery.
Zhi transmitted the Yogācāra and Esoteric teachings of Nāgārjuna.
Wherever he went, he invariably established maṇḍalas and conferred empowerments (abhiṣeka) to deliver sentient beings;

his prayers for rain and rites for averting calamities were particularly renowned for their manifest efficacy. Huiji, a śramaṇa of Wangji Temple in Chang’an, returned from traveling to the Western Heavens.
He presented the Buddha’s true likeness and Sanskrit scriptures to the Emperor;
summoned to the inner palace, he preached the Dharma and enlightened the Emperor's mind,
whereupon the Emperor conferred upon him the title "Tripitaka Master Cimin."
The Dharma Master traveled through seventy countries over a period of twenty years. On the third day of the third month,
the Elder Li Tongxuan [observed that] the commentaries and interpretations of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* by various schools were overly prolix.
He then took the newly translated scriptures to the residence of Gao Shanu in Taiyuan and composed a treatise there.
After three years,
he consumed only ten jujubes and one plum-leaf cake each day.
The world called him the Great Being Zao Bo Dashi.
As he was carrying the scriptures toward Hanzhuang,
he suddenly saw a tiger blocking the road.
The elder placed the scripture upon his back and led him up to the earthen grotto on the square mountain;
there, within the chamber which lacked lamps or candles, light issued from his mouth, brilliantly illuminating the place where the work was being produced.
There were two women who daily provided her with a plate of food, as well as paper and ink.
On the day she passed away while seated in meditation,
a white light issued from the crown of her head and pierced through to the Taiwei Heaven.
Among the forty fascicles of the *Sōzō-ron* (Treatise on the Composition of Works) contained in the Tripitaka, there is one fascicle titled *Chōja-no-jiseki* (The Deeds of the Elder).
In the eighth year,
the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra from North India [arrived].

Traveling southward along the South Sea, he reached the capital, where at Ci’en Monastery he transmitted the Great Dharma of Yoga to Vajrabodhi. In the fifth month, many people in the capital suffered from an epidemic.
The King of Physicians, Master Wei, dispensed medicine to save them,
and there were none who did not recover.
The Master constantly maintained this intention and made vows.
Those who saw him regarded him as ill,
but when the Emperor heard of this, he summoned him for an audience and treated him with great courtesy;
thus he became known as the Bodhisattva Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja).
The Master was a native of Shule.
Those of the Western Regions commonly wear woolen robes and carry several hundred gourds at their waists.
Wearing a silk turban on his head and holding a staff of *ariṣṭa* wood,
he was accompanied by a single black dog;
he himself said that five hundred years had already passed.
From Yao and Shun to Yin Tang, Zhou, Qin, Han, and Tang—
seven times in total— he manifested his body to rescue those suffering from poverty and illness.
On one day, his dog transformed into a black dragon.
Carrying his teacher on his back, he flew up into the sky.
Nine years later,
an imperial decree was issued for the Zen Master Yi-xing to compile the Dayan Calendar.
Xing Hebo said to Yin Yin: "Han Luoxia Hong once remarked that eight hundred years from now,
there would inevitably be a discrepancy of one day in the calendar— a matter of error— and that a sage would surely appear to rectify it."
Now, Yi Xing has compiled the calendar and corrected its errors;
the words spoken in Luoyang are indeed true.
Six years later, he passed away.
Posthumous title: Chan Master Dahui. ○ The Yutian śramaṇa Zhìyán arrived and translated four sections of the sutras. ○ Yáo Chóng passed away.
His final instructions stated:
"The Buddha takes purity and compassion as his foundation."
Yet the foolish copy scriptures and fashion images in the hope of seeking blessings.
You all must not emulate these ignorant people who perform posthumous rites for the sake of冥福 (míngfú—merit for the deceased).
It is said:
"Where does the Buddha-way reside?
It must be found within the monasteries, the scriptures and images, and among the śramaṇas who uphold the Dharma;
it is there that one may perceive it."
Only then can one carry out the transformative influence of pure compassion.
Master Chong was unaware of this path,
yet he relied solely on abstract principles to gloss over his own shallow views.
Thus, while he held the central axis of power,
he prohibited the ordination of monks, the founding of temples, the casting of Buddha images, and the copying of scriptures.
When his breath was about to cease...
Thus, he issued a final injunction forbidding his sons to perform Buddhist rites,
seeking to make himself like Emperor Taiwu of the Wei dynasty so as to fulfill his stubborn and deviant will; in this,
he was merely a contemporary counterpart to Cui Hao.
He did not allow it to reach its conclusion.
In the fourteenth year,
the Japanese śramaṇas Ryoji and Fujo arrived in Yangzhou.
By imperial decree, he was presented with ten *saṃghāṭī* robes to bestow upon a Vinaya Master of high conduct in China.
When Ganjin received these robes,
he was moved by the presence of the Buddha-seed in the foreign land.
He then joined with Rui and the others, traveling eastward by boat.
Upon their arrival,
the King welcomed them and offered his congratulations.
He took up residence in the Vairocana Hall and requested the bestowal of the precepts of taking refuge;
the queens and ministers, in turn, received the transmission.
The Japanese Vinaya teachings first began to be practiced here.
In the fifteenth year,
an imperial edict was issued concerning small Buddhist chapels in the villages throughout the realm.
They were all demolished.
The merit was transferred to the larger halls of nearby temples,
all of which were ordered to be sealed off.
Both public and private parties waited for his signal;
consequently, large buildings and great statues were likewise destroyed.
An imperial edict was then issued to Yuzhou.
While Li Xufang, the Magistrate of Xinxi, was intoxicated, the official decree from the province arrived.
He became furious and vowed that any subordinate or official who dared to tear it up would be executed.
Li’s conduct in his duties was frequently contrary to proper norms.
It was not that he had intentionally built a temple for the Buddha.
Later, he died of illness;
after he had been encoffined, the sound of his finger scratching against the inside of the coffin was heard.
His mother urged him to open it, and he was born.
It was the height of summer, and his body was quite ulcerated; it took over a month before he recovered.
He spoke of this himself.
Initially, he was arrested by two officials and brought before the king’s court,
where he saw the former official of Xinxi,
whom he had not seen for years.
Xū said, "The high official harbored the intent to kill;
he shall now receive his retribution."
Xū heard this and was greatly terrified, pleading for rescue.
The official said,
"Last year you demolished a Buddhist hall."
The official’s jurisdiction alone is complete.
This merit fills the heavens;
it is not appropriate for him to be summoned and detained here.
"If the King asks, answer him only with this.
Shortly thereafter, he saw the King,
who was holding a formal document.
The clerk read it as:
"Li Xu exclusively practiced the art of cutting sheep's hooves;
he shall receive one hundred strokes of the rod and have flesh cut from his own body."
Xū said, "Last year,
when the imperial decree ordered the destruction of Buddhist halls,
the one within my jurisdiction alone remained."
"I pray that this merit may atone for my prior transgressions.
The king asked in astonishment,
"Is this truly so?"
The official reported, "There is a register of merit in heaven.
The King ordered it to be examined.
The official read it aloud:
Last year, when the Buddha hall was demolished,
only Xinxi County remained intact. For this,
he shall suffer countless evils throughout his entire life and have his lifespan shortened by thirty years.
When he had finished speaking, fire issued from the registers of sins and consumed them almost entirely.
He then commanded two officials to escort him back.
Thirty days later, he passed away without illness. (From the *Taiping Guangji*). [Record of the death of Bodhiruci.]
He was one hundred and fifty-six years old.
He was posthumously titled "Tripitaka Master Sarvajña" (All-Knowing) and granted the honorary rank of Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial. Fang Guan served as the Magistrate of Lushi.
The Daoist Xing Hepu went out on an excursion with him.
Passing through Xiakou, they entered an abandoned temple and sat beneath an ancient pine tree.
He sent someone to dig into the ground, where they discovered scrolls of calligraphy and paintings by Lou Shide and Master Yong hidden inside a jar.
He said to Guan, "Do you perhaps remember this?
Guan was suddenly enlightened and realized that his previous life had been as Master Yong. Subsequently, Ren Shan of Suizhou fell ill and died.
A certain number of laypeople and a monk arrived together at the abode of King Yama.
The monk said,
"I constantly recite the Diamond Sūtra."
The king immediately joined his palms in reverence.
Suddenly, five-colored clouds appeared to escort the monk up into the heavens.
The underworld official said to Shan:
"You have also recited [this] twenty-one times;
therefore, I shall order him to be released and sent back.
Furthermore, Zhao Bi of Lian-shui entered the capital to take the imperial examinations.
On the road, he encountered his deceased wife,
who said that she was currently undergoing unspeakable suffering in the underworld.
She added that her clothing and belongings were with her mother-in-law.
He was told, "You may take the money to purchase and commission a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He followed these instructions;
however, when he had reached the middle of the first fascicle, he happened to pass by a cemetery.
Seeing an old man who claimed to be the landowner, [the monk] said:
"According to the *Jingang Gan Yan Lu* (Record of Miraculous Responses to Vajra), your wife attained rebirth in heaven yesterday.
(The record was compiled in the seventeenth year.)
The imperial decree that monks and nuns throughout the empire must compile registers every three years and provide official accounts began with this.
[The author] states:
"The essential point of leaving home to study the Way lies in receiving the precepts from a teacher."
From its inception, the system for these [monastics] never required them to register their names in official government records;
this was the case from the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty until the beginning of the Tang.
It was not until the Yancai era of Empress Wu’s reign that an order was issued requiring the two communities [of monks and nuns] to be subordinated to the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu).
During the Zhenguan era of Emperor Ming, the practice was first mandated that registers be compiled every three years.
During the Zhide era of Emperor Suzong, the sale of registration certificates was reinstated,
and these were termed "incense-water money."
By the time our Southern Dynasty first crossed the river, they further established the tax on exempted laborers,
calling it "clearing fees" (*qingjian qian*).
Alas, the laws and regulations were not something we could control.
If one must necessarily act according to what is considered pure in other regions,
how could it be that the Tathāgata, observing those among my disciples in the final age with his Buddha-eye,
would not urge them to comply with the laws of the state?

Alas! In the eighteenth year, Chan Master Lang of Zuoxi expounded the Dharma-gate of *Zhiguan* for Chan Master Zhanran of Jingxi. [The Emperor] issued an edict to all monasteries and observatories throughout the realm.
On the occasion of the establishment of the T'ien-ch'ang Festival, a ritual service for longevity was held.
At Ch'ung-fu Monastery in the Western Capital, the śramaṇa Chih-shêng presented the twenty fascicles of the *K'ai-yüan Shih-chiao Lu* (Kaiyuan Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings) which he had compiled.
He fixed the number at five thousand and forty-eight fascicles and issued an imperial decree to include them in the Great Canon.
Su Gui, the Assistant Magistrate of Wugong County,
regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The entire family of fifty members all maintained a vegetarian diet.
His wife, Lady Cui, grew so emaciated that she would secretly eat meat;
as a result, her flesh turned into bone-marrow.
Ten days after his breath had ceased and his body was laid out,
he revived and said:
"I saw King Yama reprimand me, saying:"
"Your husband is an incarnation of a Bodhisattva in a physical body.
Why did you steal and eat his flesh?
It is only thanks to the merit of his reciting the sutras that [you have not suffered further]."
"His life shall be extended by twenty years;
you may return and inform the people.
When the Emperor heard this, he was delighted.

He also resolved to uphold this sutra, and those who were transformed by him were exceedingly numerous. The śramaṇa Haitong carved a stone image of Maitreya Buddha on the banks of the Great River in Jiazhou.
It was three hundred and sixty feet high and covered by a nine-story pavilion;
the temple was named Lingyun (Cloud-soaring).
Twenty years later,
the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi passed away;
he was posthumously honored with the title Imperial Preceptor of Empowerment (Guanding Guoshi).
The disciple Amoghavajra, the Tripitaka Master, respectfully followed the final instructions and returned to India, reaching the Kingdom of Siṃhala.

There he met Nāgārjuna and received the eighteen assemblies of the *Abhiṣeka* (Consecration) rites, as well as over five hundred sūtras and śāstras. Initially, during the Western Jin period, there was a monk named Yixing.
Thirty *li* southeast of Mao County, in a valley among the mountains, a Buddhist shrine was established upon a cliff.
Later, the eminent monk Faye followed these ancient traces and constructed a vihāra on the eastern foot of the mountain.
The Secretariat Official Wan Qirong erected a Many Jewels Stūpa in the southwest corner.
The Master resided there and recited the Lotus Sūtra daily;
he was moved by the manifestation of a celestial boy from Mount Tai, who brought him offerings.
One night, while circumambulating the stupa on his walking path,
people saw that the Master’s body was level with the top of the stupa;
consequently, he was given the title Chan Master Taibai (Great White).

It is erroneously handed down in tradition that Master Qi was the founder of this mountain, which is named Tiantong. As for the Mani [sect], it is originally of heterodox views and falsely claims affiliation with Buddhism;
since it is already the teaching of Master Xi Hu, [it should not be confused with the true Dharma].
His disciples acted on their own initiative;
there was no need for formal punishment. Shu said:
The Buddha said:
"Among the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths,
the Way of the Buddha is the correct one."
Thus we know that all others are heterodox teachings beyond the need for further discussion.
Since the maṇi is a product of false views,
the court must prohibit it.
Now, you allow them to act as they please without imposing any disciplinary measures;
yet you fail to consider that those who establish such practices will become tainted by their habits,
transmitting the heterodox through the heterodox, which is precisely what serves to corrupt and confound the Buddha-dharma.
Alas! One cannot fathom why the sovereign and his ministers at that time were so incapable of making such a distinction.
The twenty-first year.

In the twenty-third year [after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa], Vinaya Master Daoxuan of the Southern Mountains produced the *Sifen jieben* (Abridged and Revised Code of Precepts for the Four-Part Vinaya),
which enabled those who have left the household life to recite and study it.
The Tripitaka Master Wufei passed away and was interred in a stupa on the western mountains of Longmen in the twenty-fourth year.

An imperial decree was issued to promulgate the Imperial Commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra throughout the realm. The Secretariat memorialized that monks and nuns throughout the empire be placed under the jurisdiction of the Court of State Ceremonial. Wu Daoxuan, whose courtesy name was Daozi—
He excelled at the art of painting;
his general style followed that of Zhang Sengyou.
The Emperor summoned him to serve in the palace.
At Jinggong Temple, he painted the transformations of the hells;
all the people of the capital came to view them and, fearing their own transgressions, cultivated goodness.
Consequently, the butchers and wine-sellers in the two markets found they could no longer sell their goods. In the present day, there exists a stone copy of Daizi’s Avalokiteśvara.
In the twenty-fifth year,
an imperial edict was issued that monks and nuns should continue to be registered under the Ministry of Rites,
while Daoist priests were to be registered under the Court of the Imperial Clan.

Because the imperial clan was included within the imperial registry, in the twenty-sixth year, an edict was issued for all prefectures throughout the realm to establish two temples, named Longxing and Kaiyuan.
A śramaṇa named Fashou dreamed of a strange monk who exhorted him to provide five hundred cassocks as offerings for the dedication of merit at the temple; upon waking, he found this extraordinary.
He then began to beg from people until he reached their number.
Suddenly, one day he encountered a monk who said,
"I shall lead you to enter Huixiang Temple."
Following him, he entered Zhongnan Mountain.
There he saw a lofty vermilion gate halfway up a cliff,
with a signboard inscribed "Huixiang" (Dedication).
He hurried in to see the senior elder above;
the monks exchanged greetings with one another,
and Xiu took out his *kāṣāya* and distributed it throughout the monastery.
The elderly master led him into an empty room and said,
"This was the former chamber of the Tang Emperor.
He then commanded an attendant to fetch the jade flute.
He said, "Previously I dwelt here, fond of music and song.
I have been exiled as the lord of the human realm;
after a long time, I shall surely return."
He instructed Xiu, saying,
"Take this jade flute and the *kāṣāya* robe back to present them to the Son of Heaven of Tang.
Xiu returned to the capital and submitted them to the imperial court.
The Emperor took up the *xiao* flute and played it with such mastery as if he had practiced it for years; this is recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
In the twenty-seventh year, he issued an imperial edict to all monks and Daoists throughout the realm.
In the twenty-eighth year, he performed ritual circumambulations at Longxing Temple for the national memorial services,
and held a ceremonial fast at Kaiyuan Temple for the birthday celebration of the Emperor.
Chan Master Xingxi of Qingyuan in Jizhou passed away while seated.
Having received the Dharma from the Sixth Patriarch,
he was posthumously honored with the title Chan Master Hongji and interred in the Guizhen Pagoda during the reign of Emperor Xizong in the twenty-ninth year [of the era].
Qi Han, the Commissioner for the Inspection of Henan, submitted a memorial stating:
"The Ultimate Way is worthy of veneration;
it should be followed and revered."
It cannot be avoided that they will be subjected to whipping and flogging,
which brings disgrace upon their outward appearance and demeanor.
As for those monks and Daoists who have committed transgressions:

The Emperor decreed that the desires of monks and Daoists shall be dealt with according to their respective codes of discipline and assigned appropriate punishments; the prefectures and counties shall not arbitrarily inflict sentences or execute punishments.
This was approved by imperial edict. ○ The Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra returned from Siṃhala Island to Guangzhou.
The Imperial Envoy Liu Juji requested the establishment of the Abhiṣeka Maṇḍala ritual. Moved by this,
Mañjuśrī manifested his physical form to deliver sentient beings, numbering in the millions.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, the five kingdoms of Kangju, Yīnjú, Dàshí, and others from the Western Regions launched a raid on Anxī.
The Tang court had established the four prefectures of Andōng, Anxī, Nán'ān, and Nèiběi; the Emperor then summoned the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra to the inner palace.
He personally held the incense burner while the Benevolent Kings’ State-Protecting Secret Mantra was recited seventeen times.
Looking up, he saw a divine being, about five hundred feet tall, standing in the palace courtyard.
The Master said, "This is Bhīṣmaka,
the second son of Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Northern Heaven."
The Crown Prince prayed for the rescue and pacification of Anxi,
requesting that a meal be prepared and [the envoys] be dispatched.
In the fourth month, Anxi submitted a report, saying:
On the eleventh day of the second month,
within black clouds to the northeast of the city, a figure clad in golden armor was seen, over a zhang in height;
from the sky, the sound of drums and horns resounded throughout heaven and earth.
Within the enemy's tents and curtains, there appeared golden rats that gnawed through the bowstrings;
the five kingdoms immediately fled in total disarray.
In a mere moment, the Heavenly King manifested his form atop the city tower.
The Emperor ordered an investigation of this.
It was on the very day he recited the mantra that the city watchtowers and military camps were established; it was because of this that the Heavenly King (Tianwang) was installed.
This occurred two years later.
An Imperial Edict states: "According to the Buddhist scriptures, Mount Luofu is the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva Huashou.
A Yanxiang Temple, a Huashou Terrace, and a Mingyue Precept Platform shall be specially established there. [At that time,] the śramaṇa Chujin...
While reciting the Lotus Sūtra at Qianfu Monastery in the capital,
when he reached the "Jeweled Stupa" chapter,
his body and mind became serene and tranquil, and a jeweled stupa suddenly appeared.
He then sat in meditation for six years, vowing to construct this stupa.
On the day the foundation was laid, the multitude heard celestial music and an extraordinary fragrance.
In an imperial dream, he saw the characters "Chu Jin" (Buddha Gold) appear in the void.
He questioned his ministers,
all of whom replied that it was the Master;
he then personally inscribed the title of the Many-Jeweled Stūpa.
He was granted silk and coinage to assist with the labor for three years.
In the third year,
the construction of the Many Treasures Pagoda at Qianfu Temple was completed.
A five-colored cloud was perceived enveloping the top of the stupa,
and the myriad crowds gazed upon it in worship.
Bukong then assembled virtuous monks beneath the stupa to practice the Lotus Samādhi.

He was moved to receive three thousand and seventy grains of śarīra relics; by imperial decree, he ordered the various prefectures to cast golden-bronze images of the Emperor’s own likeness at Kaiyuan Temple; and he summoned Chan Master Benjing of Mount Sikong.
He arrived at the palace and was questioned on the essential tenets of the Chan school;
by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Bailian Temple. Master Nanyue Huairang entered nirvana.
The stupa of Chan Master Zuishenglun was posthumously titled Dahuì.
The Master received the Dharma from the Sixth Patriarch for four years.
An imperial edict stated: "The Buddhist scriptures of Persia originated from Da Qin;
therefore, the Persian temples in the two capitals should be renamed as Da Qin temples. [He] summoned the Daoist master Wu Jun of the Central Peak to have an audience.
He asked about the essentials of the Way.
[The Emperor] replied,
"Nothing is more profound regarding the Way than the Five Thousand Words of Laozi."
He asked again about the methods for cultivating and refining [the elixir] as practiced by immortals, to which he replied:
"This is the business of those from the wilds;
they seek it through the accumulation of years and months."
This is not something for a sovereign to take seriously.
At that time, the eunuch Gao Lishi, who had long been a devotee of Buddhism,
spoke disparagingly of it before the Emperor.
He then took his leave and returned to Maoshan.
Because he had been rejected,
Liu Yun composed a treatise to disparage the followers of Śākyamuni.
Chen Shaoyou, the Regional Inspector of Western Zhejiang,
requested that Dharma Master Shen Yong resolve his doubts.
Shen Yong agreed to discuss the heterodox and the orthodox face-to-face.
As soon as the banners and drums arrived, Jün was utterly defeated.
Yōng then composed the *Fanyelun* (Treatise on Turning Away from Heresy) to attack the remaining followers.
Shǎoyóu reported this to the court.
He appointed Daoyong as the Sanghasthavira; Daoyong succeeded Zuo Xi for five years.
At that time, the Kingdom of Siṃhala sent an envoy to court to present offerings of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* on palm leaves, jeweled necklaces, and white cotton cloth.

The Emperor issued five edicts for the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra to reside at the Court of State Ceremonial and enter the inner palace to perform the *abhiṣeka* (consecration) rite for the Emperor.
At that time, it had not rained for a long duration.
The Master established the altar and performed the ritual;
a great rain fell everywhere in abundance,
and he further prohibited the great winds.
The wind immediately ceased.
For six years,
an imperial edict was issued placing all monks and nuns under the jurisdiction of the Merit Commissioner (Gongde Shi) of the two streets.
He first ordered the Sacrificial Bureau to issue certificates made of patterned silk and plain white silk,
and issued an edict to all monasteries throughout the empire to select boys of genuine conduct and talent.
Three persons were ordained from each commandery every fourteen years.
The Emperor [considered that] because those in the north possessed a constitution of firm and resolute qi, many at the various monasteries were accustomed to horsemanship and archery.
An imperial edict was issued for the śramaṇa Biàn-cái to serve as an instructor presiding over the ordination platform, thereby providing further guidance and instruction. Sù-zōng (r.
756–762), whose personal name was Héng, was the third son of Xuán-zōng; this occurred in the first year of the Zhì-dé era.
In the first month, An Lushan, the Regional Inspector of Fanyang, rebelled.
In the fifth month, the Heir Apparent, the Emperor Xuanzong, and the officials departed from Chang’an intending to flee to Shu.
Upon reaching Mawei, several thousand commoners petitioned the Heir Apparent to remain in the east to destroy the rebels.
The śramaṇa Daoping of Jincheng earnestly urged that troops be mobilized at Lingwu in order to plan their recovery.
He was subsequently appointed General of the Household (Jinwu Dajiangjun).
Upon reaching Lingao, he engaged the rebels in battle several times and decisively defeated them.
When the matter was settled, he was offered a fief, which he firmly declined.
He was then commanded to reside at the two monasteries of Chongfu and Xingqing,
and was granted purple robes, gold, and silk.
In the seventh month, the Prince ascended the throne at Lingwu.
He honored Xuanzong as the Retired Emperor. While the Emperor was at Lingwu,
because military necessities were insufficient,
the Chancellor Pei Mian requested that the ordination certificates for monks and Daoists be sold.

This refers to the "Incense-Water Money Sale Deed" (xiāngshuǐ qián mài dié). At the beginning of this period, when the threat of banditry was at its height, some advised the Emperor that he should rely on the protection of the Buddha;
accordingly, an edict was issued for one hundred śramaṇas.
He entered the palace and recited the scriptures morning and evening.
One night, the Emperor dreamed of a śramaṇa with a golden body chanting the name of Ratnaśrī Tathāgata.
Upon waking, he questioned his attendants about it.
Someone replied,
"The monk Mulu from Silla constantly recites this name at Helan Baicao Valley.
We have summoned him to appear before Your Majesty."
