The Master said:
"How do you act throughout the twelve hours of the day, Great Officer?
Guàn replied,
"Not a single thread of silk hangs upon me."
The Master said,
"He is still a man standing below the steps.
When Lu Xun saw someone playing double-sixes, he picked up the dice and said:
"Whether it is so or not so— if one simply proceeds with such faith, how is it?
The Master picked up [the object] and said:
"Stinking bones, eighteen flowers.
Jueyan said, "Master Zhao is truly extraordinary; his understanding of the Way is marvelous."
"Heaven and earth share the same root; the myriad things are one body.

The Master pointed to a peony flower in the courtyard and said, "A person seeing this single stalk of a flower is like being in a dream. When Chan Master Weiyen of Yaoshan in Liuzhou passed away, [the Master said: "..."
The posthumous title of Great Master Hongdao was conferred;
he visited Shitou.
In the ninth year, auspicious clouds appeared over the Buddha-relic stupa at Famen Temple on Mount Qishan. In the fourth month, Li Xun, Academician of the Hanlin Academy...
He requested that the ritual altar within the Changsheng Hall be discontinued and that monks and nuns who were fraudulent or spurious be purged.
On that day, at night, a great wind blew through the imperial palace, and the four *chīwén* (ornamental ridge-end tiles) of the Hanyuan Hall were all shaken down.
Three trees in front of the palace were uprooted;
dozens of watchtowers, gatehouses, and city gates within and without the Golden Guard Barracks were destroyed,
and both the western walls of Gwanghwa Gate were demolished.
The officials and the people were struck with terror.
The Emperor, considering that Hui-xun’s request had offended the will of Heaven,
immediately issued an edict to suspend the previous purge.
Furthermore, he established grand ritual images within the inner palace.

The [unusual] winds began to subside. According to the *Wuxingzhi* (Annals of the Five Elements) in the old histories, in the seventh month, Li Xun petitioned that the monastics and nuns throughout the empire be tested on their mastery of the scriptures, and those who failed to meet the standards were to be dismissed.
In the eleventh month, Li Xun was executed for plotting to assassinate the eunuchs;
his head was displayed at the Kunming Pool.

An imperial decree exempted monks and nuns from the requirement to pass scriptural examinations. In the eighth month, an edict conferred the title Guifeng upon the śramaṇa Zongmi, designating him as the sixth patriarch of a collateral lineage of the sixth generation, who was summoned to the inner palace to discourse on the Buddha-dharma.
He was granted the purple robe and formal monastic attire.
In the first month of the first year of the Kaicheng era,
he served as the Left Street Monk Registrar (Zuoxie Senglü), an Inner Attendant (Neigongfeng) for the Discourse on the Three Teachings.
The Grand Master of the Imperial Procession,
Dharma Master Wudafu Duanfu,
passed away lying on his right side; upon cremation, three hundred śarīras were obtained.
The Master served as a model for the pure assembly for eleven years;
those among his disciples who transmitted his teachings numbered more than a thousand.

The stele inscription was composed by Pei Xiu, Compiler of the Historiographic Office. By Imperial Decree, the śramaṇa Cundyuan was appointed as the Head Monk (Senglü) of the Left and Right Quarters. The Emperor once said to his close ministers:
"In the world, there are those who contribute nothing to the transformation of the people through teaching and yet consume the resources of the state like wood-eating insects."
"You ministers may speak fully.
One who responded said,
"Since the time of our ancestors, we have extensively practiced Buddhism."
The number of monastics increased further,
becoming nothing more than a parasitic burden.
The Emperor immediately issued an edict to both the central government and the provinces to cease the monastics' lectures on Buddhist scriptures.
While the Imperial Kitchen was preparing the Emperor's meal and cooking eggs,
he suddenly heard an extremely faint sound from within the cauldron.
Upon listening, he found that it was the many eggs calling out the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The scene was so profoundly mournful that the supervising official reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor dispatched someone to verify it, and it was indeed as described.
The Emperor sighed in admiration, saying,
"I did not know that the spiritual power of the Buddha's Way could be such as this.
He issued an edict that from now on, chicken eggs were not to be used.
On another day, he ate clams;
there was one that he could not crack open,
so he burned incense and prayed to it.
Suddenly, he transformed into the form of a Mahāsattva.
The Emperor summoned Chan Master Weizheng of Zhongnan Mountain and questioned him.
The Master said:
Now, nothing in the world responds without cause;
this is merely to broaden Your Majesty’s faith.
As the Sūtra says:
"To those who are to be saved by this body,
he manifests this very body and preaches the Dharma for them.
The Emperor said:
The Great Being preached the Dharma concerning what has been heard and what has not yet been heard.
The Master said,
"Your Majesty, behold this."
"Is it permanent or impermanent?
Is it trustworthy or untrustworthy?
The Emperor replied:
"How could one not believe such a rare occurrence?
The Master said,
"The Dharma has already been preached."
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
He immediately issued an edict for all monasteries throughout the realm to establish statues of Avalokiteśvara,
and commanded the Master to reside at Shengshou Monastery.
When Emperor Wuzong ascended the throne,
he retired to live in seclusion on Mount Zhongnan.
When people asked him the reason for this, he replied:
"I was merely avoiding an enemy," said Wuzu, who then departed.
In the third month of the third year,
National Teacher Qingliang Chengguan passed away.
The Emperor suspended court for three days.
High ministers dressed in white mourning garments, and he was granted a state funeral at a stone chamber on Mount Zhongnan.
The Master served as the preceptor to seven emperors across nine successive reigns.
He was nine chi and four cun tall;
his hands reached below his knees when hanging down.
His talent was such that he could supply two brushes and compose ten thousand words daily.
He did not part from his robes while sleeping and maintained the practice of eating only once per day for as long as he lived.
Prime Minister Pei Xiu composed the inscription for his memorial stele by imperial decree.
In the fourth year,
the Secretariat submitted a memorial stating that,
by imperial decree for the Emperor’s birthday, the Chancellor and all officials were to visit the temple to provide a vegetarian feast for one thousand monks.
The imperial edict granted his request.
At that time, renowned monks gathered together;
the officials and commoners watched freely, all of whom were filled with profound reverence.
In the first month of the fifth year,
Chan Master Zongmi of Guifeng passed away;
Prime Minister Pei Xiu composed his funerary inscription.
Emperor Wuzong (r. 841–846). Emperor Wuzong was the fifth son of Emperor Muzong. In the third year of the Huichang era, the Emperor desired to eradicate the followers of Śākyamuni.

He issued an edict ordering the two monastic districts to recount the periods of rise and fall since the advent of Buddhism and what miraculous responses had occurred therein. Dharma Master Xuanchang, the Great Master, [was summoned].
He compiled the "Chart of the Five Dynasties of the Three Jewels" and presented it [to the throne]. By imperial decree, all Mani temples throughout the empire were ordered to be abolished.
Seventy women of the Mani sect in the capital were all executed.
Among those who followed the various Daoist sects in the Uyghur lands,
the majority died.
In the first month of the fourth year.
The Emperor, finding it objectionable that the prohibition of killing during the months of fasting originated from Buddhist teachings,
issued an edict stating that henceforth only the New Year, the three primary festivals (*sanyuan*), and the days of national mourning were to be restricted.
This was done in the first month of the fifth year.
Zhao Guizhen requested to debate with the followers of Śākyamuni.
An imperial decree was issued for a meeting of monks and Daoists at the Linqide Hall;
the Emperor personally handed the *Laozi* to him.

The Master Zhi Xuan ascended the lecture seat and extensively expounded upon the meaning of "governing a great state as one cooks small fish," detailing the principles of kingship and the fundamental basis of the Way and its teachings for transforming the world.
His eloquence was so vigorous and robust that the masters of the Way could not refute him. Consequently,
he spoke of the matters of transcendents ascending to immortality and commoners practicing solitary self-cultivation in mountain forests.
"It is not appropriate for an emperor to pay close attention to this.
The Emperor’s expression was displeased, and he sent him back to his native place.
The Emperor then constructed the Wangxian Terrace (Tower of Longing for the Immortal) at the southern suburb.
Returning to the True Vehicle, he favored [Daoism] while disparaging and destroying Buddhism;
this is not something that should be venerated in the Middle Kingdom.
It ought to be eliminated and abolished.
The ministers all said that Gui Zhen was treacherous and wicked and should not be trusted;
Gui Zhen himself felt that he had already become the subject of public censure.
He then recommended Luo Fu’s Deng Yuanchao and others to join him in consolidating their efforts to plot the destruction of the Buddha-dharma.
In the fourth month, an imperial edict was issued to inspect the number of monasteries, monks, and nuns throughout the empire.
In the fifth month, an imperial edict was issued for the two capitals,
ordering that four monasteries be retained in each of the Left and Right Quarters, with thirty monks assigned to each;
furthermore, one monastery was to be retained in every prefecture and commandery throughout the realm.
Twenty persons for the upper temple,
ten for the middle temple,
and five for the lower temple.
In the eighth month, an imperial edict was issued ordering all monasteries to be demolished within a fixed period.
A census of the empire’s monasteries revealed four thousand six hundred temples and forty thousand *ārāmas*;
the timber from these sites was used to repair government offices and postal stations.
Images made of gold and silver were entrusted to the Ministry of Revenue;
those made of iron were cast into agricultural implements;
and those made of copper, including bells and stone chimes, were melted down to mint coinage.
He confiscated several million *qǐng* of fertile fields and one hundred and fifty thousand male and female slaves.
Twenty-six thousand five hundred monks and nuns were returned to lay life.
Furthermore, two thousand or more *mùhù* and *huǒfù* were all compelled to revert to secular status.
The Chancellor Li Deyu led the hundred officials in submitting a memorial to offer congratulations. Many monks from the Five Terraces (Wutai) fled in all directions;
Li Deyu of Youzhou said to the official on duty:
Upon his return, he reported to the Chief Envoy that he must not allow wandering monks to enter the territory.
Zhang Zhongwu, the Military Commissioner, carried out this command.
Weibo, the Court Gentleman for Guest Reception, said to Du Yu:
The method of purging officials should not be excessive.
In the sixth year, Li Deyu, enraged, dismissed Bo Wuling as a judicial secretary.
In Chang'an, there was a man walking at night who passed by the tomb of King Mu of Zhou and saw a person descend from the sky.
A man in vermilion robes holding a tablet proclaimed, "Where is the Director of the Tomb?
Two officials emerged from the tomb and said:
At this, the one in the red robe said,
"When will the envoy of the Lord of the Western Sea arrive?"
The official said,
"By calculation of the distance, it should take eighteen days.
The one in the crimson robe said:
"Why have you detained us for so long?
The official replied, "Li Yan has been condemned for destroying the Buddhist teachings; his life span has been forfeited and he has been removed from office."
"I shall record his soul together with the Lord of the Western Sea.
Then, the sound of a merchant's bell came from the east,
and the two officials in vermilion robes suddenly vanished.
A few days later, Shangguo fell ill and passed away (*Taiping guangji*). Lu Zhen, a Palace Attendant, had a son who had formerly been a monk;
due to the suppression of the monastic order, he was subsequently appointed as a Counselor to the Guangwang Prince.
One night, he dreamed that his former teacher came to his home.
Lu told him,
"To be a lowly official and toil in such petty matters is not what I desire."
Reflecting further on donning the black robes, he did not know what day it would be.
The Master said, "The restoration is imminent; you should firm your resolve."
Suddenly, ten thousand cavalry appeared with banners and streamers, shouting as they approached, saying:

"We come to welcome Prince Guang as the Son of Heaven. (From the *Tongji*). In the fifth month, an imperial edict appointed Yang Qin-yi as the Commissioner for Merit and Virtue (*Gongde Shi*) of the Two Streets.
It was ordered that eight additional temples be established in each of the two streets,

and that the monks and nuns ordained therein be granted official certificates by the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu). An imperial decree was issued stating that on the memorial days of the various emperors, officials shall proceed to Buddhist monasteries to offer incense,
in accordance with the established ritual.
Because these Daoist practitioners had deluded the previous reign and destroyed the Buddhist teachings,
an imperial edict was issued to Yang Qin-yi, the Commissioner for Meritorious Works,
to arrest Zhao Gui-zhen, Liu Yuan-qing, Deng Yuan-chao, and eleven others, totaling twelve persons.
They assembled at the court together and executed him, displaying his corpse.
This was in the third month of the first year of the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzhen, the thirteenth son of Emperor Xianzong. His name was Chen.
During the final years of the Huichang era, an imperial decree ordered the reduction and consolidation of monasteries;
the reforms were carried out with excessive severity,
affecting even these sacred sites of the Spirit Mountain.
If there are veteran, renowned monks capable of performing repairs and construction, the relevant authorities must not prohibit them.
○ Li Deyu had monopolized power for a long time;
the Emperor detested him and demoted him to the post of Sima in Chaozhou.
Shortly thereafter, he was demoted once more to the post of Assistant Magistrate of Yachou.
He died of a loathsome disease.
Initially, there had been a monk who possessed knowledge of past lives.
He said to Deyu,
"In your journey southward for ten thousand *li*, you have consumed ten thousand sheep in your lifetime;
now you have reached nine thousand five hundred."
"As long as the sheep are not yet exhausted, there will still be a day for their return. Deyu said,
"I once dreamed of walking through the mountains of Jin."
Seeing that the entire mountain was filled with sheep as far as the eye could reach,
the herdsman said,
"These are the very things you have eaten throughout your life."
Ten days later, Li Ji, the Military Governor of Zhenwu, sent four hundred sheep as a gift.
The monk said,
"The ten thousand sheep are now nearly complete."
"It appears that Your Excellency will not return.
Subsequently, he indeed passed away on Zhuyi.
Shu said:
Since ancient times, whenever a sovereign has sought to disparage the Buddha,
there have invariably been ministers and aides to assist in carrying out such matters;
thus, Emperor Taiwu of the Wei dynasty relied upon Cui Hao.
Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty employed Zhang Bin and Wei Yuansong;
Emperor Wu of the Tang dynasty employed Li Deyu and Zhao Guizhen.
Ultimately, these actions caused the Great Dharma to be disgraced, and both the sovereigns and their ministers were met with evil retribution.
How unfortunate this situation is for both sides!
As for the implementation of a purge,
it was like that of Huan Xuan during the Jin dynasty.
Fu Yi during the Tang dynasty;
Yao Chong during the reign of Emperor Ming;
and Li Xun during the reign of Emperor Wenzong.
However, all were constrained by the exigencies of the times; once implemented, they were again obstructed.
For this reason, a temporary minor setback was not as cruel in its calamity as the three suppressions of Buddhism under the Wu emperors.
As for Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty, his nature was such that he reviled Buddhism.
Yet they did not find capable assistants.
Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu were by nature opposed to Buddhism,
yet they did not encounter a sovereign who would support them.
Had Emperor Sejong obtained Cui Hao,
his suppression and execution of śramaṇas would have been even more severe than the cruelty of Emperor Taizu (Wu).
Had Han Yu and Ou-yang Hsiu encountered the three emperors of the Wu dynasty...
Thus, by destroying the images and extinguishing the Sangha,
[the cruelty] would not fall short of that of Cui Hao and Li; indeed,
Cui Hao was executed by having his waist severed.
Deyu was exiled and died;
not allowing him to live out his natural term was itself sufficient retribution.
Lu Ji (Ruzhi) said:
When Tuō Móu (Túshuō) saw Dàtián, he was discouraged by his refutation of Buddhism;
Zǔ Xiù remarked that Yǒngshū saw Yuántōng and his internal opposition was thereby diminished.
That Han and Ou were able to achieve a favorable outcome later on was also due to their spiritual knowledge and power of the Way, which served to turn [the situation] around.
Yang Han-gong, who commanded the Left Imperial Guard, [acted accordingly].
He submitted a memorial to establish merit by requesting the restoration of Buddhism,
petitioning for the search and discovery of the Dharma Master Zhi Xuan; thereupon,
the monastic community was reinstated.
He entered and resided at Baoying Temple.
Coinciding with the Longevity Festival, he was appointed as the Head Seat for the Three Teachings at the Lecture and Praise Bureau.
The Emperor constructed Fagan Temple using the materials from his former residence.
He appointed his teacher to reside there. Bai Juyi passed away;
he was posthumously honored with the title of Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs.
In his later years, Bai Juyi revered Buddhist scriptures and abstained from meat for months at a time.
He established his residence at Xiangshan Temple and styled himself the Layman of Xiangshan (Xiangshan Jushi).
He once composed a eulogy, saying:
I now know completely the worlds of the ten directions, both above and below the heavens.
There is none like the Buddha;
majestic and sublime,
he is the teacher of devas and humans.
Therefore, I prostrate at his feet,
offer praise, and take refuge.
At the beginning of the Huichang era, a merchant ship encountered a storm and was driven by the wind to a great mountain.
A Taoist said,
"This is Mount Penglai;
one courtyard has its locks and keys very firmly secured."
He replied, "This is where Bai Juyi lived;
it has simply not yet reached China.
Upon hearing this, Bai Juyi composed a poem, saying:
I study the True Emptiness, not the path of immortals;
I fear these words of yours are but empty rumors.
The seas and mountains are not my place of return.
Upon returning, he must indeed return to Tuṣita Heaven.
The Joyful Deva once made a vow, saying:
"I shall exhort one hundred and forty-eight people to share a single resolve."
Having formed the aspiration for rebirth in the higher realms, one should practice mindfulness by reciting the name of Maitreya and visualize his countenance while seated;
one should vow that in a future life, one will certainly be born in Tuṣita.
In his later years, suffering from wind-induced paralysis,
he commissioned an artisan to paint a depiction of the Western Pure Land,
which he venerated day and night.
For this, a hymn of praise is spoken:
"In the Pure Land of the World of Ultimate Bliss,
there are no evil realms nor any manifold sufferings."
May those who are old and sick, such as my own person,
be born together with me in the land of Amitāyus Buddha;
may they recite the Buddha’s name for even a single night.
He passed away suddenly.
In the second year [of his reign],
an imperial edict was issued to the capitals of Chang'an and Luoyang, as well as to the prefectures of Jingzhou, Yangzhou, Bianzhou, and Yizhou.
He established monasteries and erected square *sīmā* ordination platforms (*kaidan*) for the purpose of administering the precepts again to monks and nuns who had received them previously.
He also constructed five monasteries on Mount Wutai.
Each ordained fifty monks.
Shu states:
According to the *Sengshi lüe* (A Brief History of the Sangha):

Those who embrace the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras need not be restricted by physical deficiencies or differences in conditions; provided they simply resolve their minds toward the Great Vehicle, all may receive [the precepts].
When the Sengni were suppressed during the Huichang persecution and returned to secular life, how could they have been free from various transgressions?
First one causes them to repent of their transgressions, and afterwards increases their observance of the precepts.
Were it not for the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] teachings, how could re-ordination be permitted?
Thus spoke Pei Xiu, the Regional Inspector of Xuanchuan.
Many temples and monasteries throughout the realm have been desecrated by visiting officials and guests.
From now on, no one shall reside within these temples;
those who violate this decree shall be severely punished.
The imperial decree was granted. The śramaṇa Xiuhui of An guo Temple,
who had been summoned for his ability to compose poetry on imperial command,
once petitioned the Emperor for purple robes.
The Emperor said,
"It is not that I am being stingy with you;
it is simply because your physical marks are incomplete."
Furthermore, [the Emperor] was granted [an audience], but died suddenly one night.
On the day of the fast in the first month of the third year,
eight thousand people, both monastics and laypeople, gathered from Siming.
At the Aśoka Monastery, he made offerings at the Buddha’s reliquary stūpa;
heavenly flowers fell in profusion like snow,
and as soon as they reached his hands, they dissolved.
At nightfall, it emitted light of five colors,
causing the great assembly to rejoice and leap for joy.
The following year, a monk from Silla stole the stupa at night, carrying it aloft in his hands.
He walked around the pavilion without leaving his original spot,
until he was noticed by the crowd.

An imperial edict appointed the śramaṇa Lingyan as the Monastic Registrar for the Left and Right Quarters. On the birthday of Emperor Shouchang, an edict commanded the Court Counselor Li Yisun, the Dharma Master Zhixuan, and Daoist practitioners to engage in discourse on the Three Teachings at the Lindian Palace.
Xuánzòu submitted a petition requesting that the temples throughout the empire which had been abolished be restored;
the Emperor, who had long held the Master’s virtue in high esteem,
ordered his portrait to be painted and enshrined within the imperial palace.
In the fourth year [of the reign],
by imperial decree, the Chan Master’s Monastery of Qi'an in Yanguan, Hangzhou,
was granted the name Qifeng Temple.
Originally, when the Emperor was Prince Guang,
Wuzong became jealous of him and confined him in the rear garden.
He was about to be executed when the eunuch Qiu Shiliang falsely claimed that the Prince Guang had fallen from his horse and died;
he then escaped and fled.
He went to the assembly of Chan Master Xiangyan Xian,
where he shaved his head and became a śrāmaṇera;
together they traveled to Mount Lu.
Master Xian inscribed this on a waterfall:
Piercing clouds and penetrating rocks, it does not disdain its toil;
Only from afar can one know how high its source lies.
As Xian paused to reflect,
the śrāmaṇera continued:
"How could a mountain stream ever remain still?"
In the end, it returns to the great ocean to become waves and billows.
It was only in leisure that he realized he was no ordinary man.
Later, he went to Haichang in Yanguan to see Chan Master Qian'an.
He claimed to possess supernatural light.
Dao’an marveled at this and immediately appointed him as his secretary.
At that time, Chan Master Huangbo Yun was serving as the Head Seat (Shouzuo).
One day, he paid his respects to Master Foguang and asked him:
"If one does not seek the Buddha, what is the use of prostrating?
Yunbian held up his palm.
He asked again.
"Without being attached to seeking the Buddha, one should constantly perform such deeds as these.
Yunzhuang then took charge of the affairs.
Guang said:
It arises from being too coarse.
Yun also took charge,
saying, "To speak of such coarseness and fineness here."
One morning, Master An said to him:
"The time has come;
do not linger in the mire."
He then entrusted him with the Buddha-dharma.
Not long after, Emperor Wuzong passed away.
The various officials welcomed the Prince to ascend the throne.
The Emperor repeatedly dispatched envoys to summon Huian with the etiquette due to a teacher,
but Huian declined resolutely.
Upon his death, an imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Wukong (Awakened to Emptiness).
The Emperor bestowed upon Huangbo the title Chan Master Chuxing.
Pei Xiu memorialized that the name be changed to Duanji; Xuedou’s verse on Huangbo says: "The Great Zhong Emperor once lightly provoked him."
Three times he personally encountered the play of [the deity’s] claws and fangs;
this is it. ○ A śramaṇa named Jōkō was dispatched from the land of Japan to enter China to seek the Secret Teachings of Śākyamuni.
In the fifth year,
an imperial decree was issued that the various prefectures, commanderies, and kingdoms must offer incense during memorial services for the deceased,
and that no one shall carry wine or meat into temples. He summoned Hongbian of Jianfu Temple in Jingzhao to have an audience with him.
The Emperor asked,
"What is meant by 'sudden realization,' and what is called 'gradual cultivation'?
He replied, "Sudden realization means clearly understanding one's own nature as being equal to that of the Buddha."
Nevertheless, because there are defiled habits from beginningless time, one must employ gradual cultivation as an antidote to cause the inherent nature to arise in its function.
It is like a person eating rice: they do not become full from a single mouthful.
The Emperor was pleased and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Yuanzhi. In the sixth month, Sun Qiao, a jinshi of the capital, submitted a memorial stating:
"The common people, with men plowing and women weaving, cannot provide for their own warmth and fullness."
Yet the multitude of monks sat at ease in magnificent dwellings with an abundance of fine food;
on average, ten households could not even support a single monk.
Emperor Wuzong was indignant at this state of affairs.
When twenty-seven hundred thousand monks have shaved their hair,
then two million seven hundred thousand people throughout the world will finally find relief.
"Your Majesty, even if you cannot eliminate long-standing abuses as Emperor Wuzong did,
why must you revive them after they have already been abolished?
I pray that you issue an edict stating that those monks who have not yet returned shall not return."
"Temples that have not yet been repaired shall not be repaired.
The Emperor was angry and did not accept [the request].
In the ninth month, a woman from Wuzhou once made a vow to open the stupa of the Great Being of Shuanglin.
He saw that the crown of the head, the feet, the rings of the fingers, and the teeth were all intact.
He brought the remains out to offer worship for forty-nine days,
after which he reinterred them within the stupa.
In the sixth year,
an imperial decree was issued to rebuild Mount Lu’s Donglin Monastery,
and the Dharma Master Huiyuan was posthumously honored with the title Bianjue (Discerning Enlightenment).
During the Huichang persecution of Buddhism,
two monks carried a statue of Mañjuśrī and concealed it atop a peak in Jinxiong Valley;
when the temple was restored later, they searched for it but could not find it.
The two monks suspected one another and believed the light had vanished;
suddenly, they beheld an auspicious sign of a circular halo surging above the surface of the sky.
From that time forth, this radiant phenomenon was constantly visible at the summit of the peak, at the Buddha’s Hand Rock, and by the Heavenly Pond.
It is said that Tianchi (Heavenly Pond) is exceptionally lofty and steep.
It lies thirty li from Donglin.
At night, one may see sacred lamps appearing in the sky, approaching from afar.
At first there was a single torch;
in a short while, it became hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of lamps.
Sometimes, one would see the Great Being Mañjuśrī within the clouds.
Appearing and disappearing without constancy, if one prostrates with a sincere heart, one will surely behold the sacred form. The minister said:
"If the ordination of monks is not performed with purity, the precepts and the Dharma will fall into ruin."
The construction of temples without restraint results in excessive expenditure of wealth.
Henceforth, permission shall be granted for the construction of temples only at famous sites and sacred mountains.
Furthermore, the former palaces shall be restored and monks and nuns ordained.
In the seventh year, it was decreed that the provincial *rishi* (vinaya master) should look upward and carefully select those possessing the nature of the Way.
It was thus authorized.
In the seventh year.
Chan Master Lingyou of Mount Gui in Tanzhou entered nirvana.
He had studied under Baizhang.
In the eighth year [of the reign], by imperial decree, Bianzhang, the Head Seat of the Three Teachings, was appointed as the Director of Monks for the Left Ward.

The śramaṇa Sengche was appointed as the Director of the Right Street (Youjie Senglü). The śramaṇas Shuyan and Shu of Yuelu Monastery in Tanzhou traveled together to Taiyuan to seek the Great Canon (Tripitaka).
There, they met with Lu Jun, the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Sikong) and Regional Inspector (Jiedushi) of Hedong.
The Vice Commissioner Wei Zhou offered it as a religious donation. Li Jie,
the Circuit Inspector of the Military Command, composed its record, saying:
Those who study Confucianism take pleasure in disparaging the followers of Śākyamuni.
Their argument invariably states:
"In the eras of Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius, there were no followers of Śākyamuni."
The rise of the Śākya clan originated in the Han dynasty,
flowed through the Jin,
and spread extensively throughout the Song, Wei, Qi, Liang, Chen, Sui, and Tang dynasties.
This is what is venerated in this degenerate age;
it should be swept away entirely so that it may not proliferate.
The arguments of those who discuss this are superficial.
I shall now explain this in detail.
Once there was a man whose skin was plump and his complexion harmonious;
his spirit was clear and his vital energy vigorous.
He remains composed and maintains his harmony;

medical treatment and prayers are of no use. (The character *cū* is pronounced with the initial *hú* and final *-chē*; *tún* is pronounced *tuò*, meaning "fat"). Furthermore, a man suffers from the ailment of wind-moisture (*vāta-śleṣman*).
With backs hunched and legs crippled,
ears deaf and eyes blind,
they consequently employ moxibustion and cauterization, and perform rites of exorcism and propitiation.
Why are these two men so contrary? They differ only in being ill and not ill. *Bì* (pinyin: bì):
unable to walk. *Kuài* (pinyin:
kuài, with the initial *wù* and the final *guài*): deaf.
"Deaf. (Míng, with the phonetic "mò" and "dìng" as the initial rhymes;
it means the eyes are closed. Alas! Before the Three Dynasties, the world was peaceful.
The final ages of the Three Dynasties were plagued by illness.
Before the Three Dynasties, Yu, Tang, Wen,
and Wu disseminated virtue and righteousness.
The Duke of Zhou and Confucius upheld the classical teachings;
though the influence of the Way has become slight, it still persists through gradual permeation.
For this reason, falsehood cannot overcome trust,
and the wicked cannot know how to avoid the good.
This continued until the end of the Three Dynasties.
Social customs were utterly ruined;
deceit and force multiplied against one another.
With the abolition of the well-field system, people pursued only the accumulation of land through annexation.
If one covets land and dwellings, then warfare will occupy one's daily affairs;
therein, the wicked and devious will run rampant,
and the virtuous scholar will find no place to shelter his person.
For this reason, superiors and inferiors are at odds with one another,
and their animosity is stirred up to become the common custom.
The teaching of the Śākya [Buddha] dwells in purity itself.
If one is gentle and self-restraining,
then enmity and strife can be brought to rest.
This is spoken of in terms of cause and effect.
When success and failure are accepted as one's lot, then nobility and meanness can be lived with equanimity.

When resentment and strife cease, then weapons and banditry will not arise. When nobility and meanness are lived with equanimity, then the distinctions between ruler and minister, and between the common people and the elite, will be maintained.
This is why the Buddha, the Sage, provides the means to rescue the world from its decline.
Were it not for the followers of Śākyamuni, how else could it be saved?
Yet, contemporary debaters do not hold the customs of this degenerate age to be difficult to transform.
To further disparage the followers of Śākyamuni as being useless is like failing to pity a man suffering from illness,

yet reviling the physician and the one who offers prayers for him; it shows no consideration for the great benefit of Śākyamuni’s work in saving the world and transforming beings through his teachings.
Furthermore, you take offense at the splendor of their monastic compounds and the abundance of their followers;
you seize upon those who are vulgar and unrestrained as grounds for criticism,
and you seek to abolish them all without exception.
This is to see the branches while neglecting the root.
During the final years of the Huichang era, Emperor Wuzong extensively eradicated the followers of Śākyamuni;
he bound their heads with lay turbans, demolished their dwellings, and cast those images fashioned from wood and clay into the water.
Those who had written these doctrines on paper were to be cast into fire.
Imperial Censors were ordered to travel throughout the empire by relay station to investigate anyone who dared to conceal them; such persons were to be punished.
Consequently, the famous monasteries and sacred edifices throughout the empire were demolished as if swept away.
Now, at the beginning of the present Emperor’s reign,
it was declared that the teachings of Śākyamuni ought not to be abolished.
He immediately issued an edict to restore them;
thereafter, those from distant regions south of Lake Dongting, fearing the law,
came to embody the solemn intent of the imperial court.
The scriptures and images were burned away until almost nothing remained.
Consequently, although imperial edicts have now been issued to clarify the matter,
it has been impossible to recover their canonical texts.
Dolinsi is a place of sublime excursion in western Xiangxi.
There was a monk named Shuyan Du who said:
"Among the old capitals of the state, Taoyuanfu has the greatest number of Buddhist shrines."
The Grand Marshal, Minister of Works, Lord Lu, is a man of universal benevolence throughout the world;
I shall go to his residence to seek his collected writings, for they may perhaps still be found there.
Having thus presented himself at the military gate, he entered.
The Duke indeed granted his request.
He dispatched messengers in all directions to seek out missing texts.
Before a month had passed, he obtained five thousand forty-eight fascicles of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras.
He carried it back on a palanquin.
Ah! The way of the Śākya to save the world has now been described.
Had it not been for our sagacious sovereign, who clearly discerns the source of principle,
how could this Way have been practiced again?
Had it not been for Minister Sīkāng, who was able to honor the Great Dharma, [this would not have been possible].
How could one possibly preserve this scripture in its entirety?
Were it not for Master Shu, a śramaṇa who deeply understands the course of the Dharma,
how could he have refrained from the arduous journey to seek it out and thus bring this grand ceremony to fulfillment?
By carrying out the Imperial decree to promote the school of Śākyamuni,
its benefits extend to future generations;
its efficacy is beyond words.
This may be left as indeterminate.
The commentary states:
"This passage establishes its terminology and constructs its principles."
This is sufficient to enlighten those in the world who do not know the Buddha.
If Lu Tong (Tui-zhi) were to see it, he would have no leisure but to feel ashamed and submit.
This is the preface by Zi-thou and Hao-chu.
Tu Yun merely states that [this work] accords with the *Yi Jing* and the *Lun Yu*, yet he cannot so clearly articulate its merit in saving the world.
Thus, this record likely surpasses his.
As for Li Jie, his name was Wei, and he is not recorded in the *Tang Shu*.
In the ninth year,
Chan Master Xiyun of Huangbo in Hongzhou passed away;
he was posthumously titled Chan Master Duanjì.
The Master received the Dharma from Baizhang.
When Pei Xiu, the State Councilor, was serving as the governor of Xin'an,
he invited the Master to enter the commandery.
He inquired about the methods of Chan and performed the rites of a devoted disciple.

He propagated the essential teachings of the Mind-to-Mind Transmission based on what he had heard throughout the world; he was the fourth generation under Mount Nanyue and remained there for ten years.
The Imperial Edict decreed that every year, when ordaining monks according to the fundamental teachings,
those who possess the nature of the Way and are proficient in the Dharma-gates among the three studies of precept, concentration,
and wisdom shall be ordained. Beyond this, all miscellaneous arts are strictly prohibited.
In the twelfth year,
an imperial edict was issued for all monasteries throughout the realm to repair and maintain the stupas of the various ancestral masters.
A Japanese śramaṇa named Huìbò paid homage at Mount Wutai and obtained an image of Avalokiteśvara.
Dao Siming was about to return to his country when his boat passed Mount Putuo; it became stuck against a rock and could not proceed.
The assembly, filled with apprehension, prayed to him, saying:
If the sacred image has not yet reached the time for its karmic conditions to ripen in the lands east of the sea,
please remain on this mountain;
then the boat will immediately begin to float away.
Wu Ai mourned him so deeply that he could not leave;
he subsequently built a hut by the sea to pay his respects.
Hearing of this, a general from Silla named Wen requested the statue and returned it to Kaiyuan Temple on the nearby mountain, which people today still call Wutai Temple.
It is also called "The Avalokiteśvara Who Refused to Depart. Later,
a monk of extraordinary character arrived at the temple carrying a piece of *jia* wood,
which he carved into a replica of that image.
He bolted the doors and applied his efforts for over a month until the image was completed;
suddenly, he lost sight of the monk,
who had then been invited to Mount Potalaka.
The mountain is situated in the midst of the great ocean,
six hundred *li* by water route southeast of the city of Yincheng;
it is precisely the solitary and remote place on the southern coast mentioned in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
There is a mountain named Potalaka where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara dwells;
this is what is referred to in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* as the palace of Avalokiteśvara on Mount Potalaka.
This is the place where the Seal of Great Compassion was taught by Śākyamuni Buddha.
On that mountain is the Cave of the Sound of the Tide;
as the ocean tides ebb and flow, they thunder and roar day and night.
At the stone bridge before the cave,
those who come to pay their respects offer earnest prayers;
some may see the Great Being seated in meditative repose.
In some instances, he saw Sudhana bowing and gesturing with courtesy;
in others, he saw only a pure jade pitcher;
and in yet others, he saw only kalaviṅka birds flying and dancing.
Six or seven *li* from the cave, there is a great monastery (*āranya*).
This is where envoys from the various kingdoms of the Eastern Sea come to pay court, and where merchants travel back and forth;
all who pay their respects and offer their sincere devotion find salvation, as recorded in the *Ca’ān-lù*.
In the thirteenth year,
the Emperor consumed an elixir of the Daoist master, and a carbuncle broke out on his back.
In the eighth month, the Emperor passed away.
The commentary states:
Emperor Wuzong destroyed Buddhism and followed the Way of the Daoists; he ingested cinnabar and died with carbuncles breaking out on his back.
At that time, the world took this as a warning.
Xuanzong had taken refuge as a monk to avoid his enemies;
he eventually ascended the throne and,
resentful of the Huichang persecution of Buddhism, executed Li De and Zhao Tingwei.
He established the cubic *jietan* (ordination platform) and mandated that monks and nuns receive the precepts again;
his intention was most profound.
Yet, in his final years, he again adopted the attire of a Daoist priest.
By ingesting cinnabar elixirs, an abscess broke out on his back.
His fault lay in his desire for longevity while failing to comprehend the principle that worldly phenomena are impermanent;
thus, he ultimately met with disaster and became a laughingstock for future generations.
Yizong (r. 859–873). Zai, the eldest son of Emperor Xuanzong, was born in the third year of the Xiantong era.
By imperial decree, the four monasteries of each of the two streets were ordered to establish ordination platforms (*jietan*) to confer the precepts upon monks.
The Emperor established a lecture seat within the inner palace and personally chanted the titles of the scriptures.
He personally transcribed Sanskrit texts and frequently visited various monasteries to distribute alms for six years.
In the seventh year, Chan Master Xuanjian of Deshan in Langzhou passed away.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Jianxing and was the fifth generation descendant of Qingyuan of Longtan.
Chan Master Linji Yixuan entered nirvana;
he was posthumously titled Chan Master Huizhao.
His followers refer to him as the fourth patriarch of the Linji school, following Huangbo and Nanyue.
In the first month of the eighth year,
Chan Master Chuanzhen of Xiangshan in Yongzhou sat upright and passed away.
The Master was a native of Chen.
While traveling, he arrived at Mount Xiangshan and established a Buddhist monastery called Jingtu (Pure Land).
Monks from all quarters gathered like clouds to receive his teachings.
At the beginning of the Huichang era, he suddenly said to his disciples:
When the Sangha was beset by calamity, it was appropriate to change their attire.
One night, his beard and hair grew long all at once;
he donned a purple robe called the "Infinite Life Robe."
The crown atop his head was azure and empty, called the "Crown of the Dharma of True Emptiness.
Subsequently, Emperor Wuzong indeed abolished Buddhism,
while Emperor Xuanzong restored the Buddhist teachings.
The Master no longer removed his robes or cap.
The world proclaimed that Amitābha Buddha had manifested his transformation and arrived here.
This lasted for ten years.
Chan Master Liangjie of Dongshan in Ruizhou entered nirvana;
he was posthumously titled Chan Master Wuben, the fifth generation descendant of Qingyuan of Yunyan. By imperial decree, Vinaya Master Daoxuan of Nanshan was posthumously titled Chengzhao.
In the eleventh year,
the Chancellor Pei Xiu passed away.
Xiu had studied under Huangbo and attained his essential teaching.
In his daily life, he abstained from wine and meat.
He composed the "Exhortation to Arouse the Bodhicitta" to inspire worldly people and authored various Buddhist texts.
His prefaces to the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*, the *Dharma-realm Contemplation*,
and the *Exposition on the Source of Chan* were universally esteemed for their essential profundity. On the eleventh month, during the Longevity Festival,
an imperial decree was issued for the two monastic communities to enter the Linde Hall to lecture and debate upon the Buddha-dharma.

[The Emperor] conferred the title of Great Master Qinglan Huizhao, Director of the Left Street Monks, and Great Master Yanchu Mingche, Director of the Right Street Monks. His Majesty had long heard of the reputation of Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun.
He was bestowed the imperial title of "Great Master Zhengjue.
The Master resided in the mountains for forty years,
and his Dharma assembly was preeminent throughout the land.
The assembly reached fifteen hundred.
The King of Min, the Wang family, served him with the etiquette due to a teacher for twelve years; he was the sixth generation descendant of De Shan Qingyuan.

The Emperor visited An Guo Temple and bestowed upon National Teacher Zhi Xuan a precious throne of agarwood. The Emperor also established a vegetarian feast for ten thousand monks within the imperial palace.
While he was seated upon the throne performing a chanted hymn of praise, an elderly monk with long eyebrows came to receive alms.
Having accepted the offerings, he ascended into the air and departed; this was Piṇḍola-bharadvāja.
In the third month of the fourteenth year,
[the Emperor] commissioned the construction of jeweled canopies for the stupa, colored banners, and flowered parasols.
He issued an imperial decree for the two monastic streets to go to Fengxiang to welcome the Buddha’s relics.
For three hundred li, chariots and horses never ceased their passage.
Among the ministers who offered remonstrances, there were those who spoke with utmost candor.
Yet Emperor Xianzong welcomed the Buddha’s relics and shortly thereafter passed away.
The Emperor said,
"Having lived to see this, I have no regrets even in death.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, the Buddha’s relics arrived.
Led by the imperial guards and accompanied by the magnificent display of public and private music and ceremonial retinues,
they passed beyond the Southern Suburb.
The Emperor presided over the Anfu Gate.
He descended from his palace tower to welcome and pay homage to them.
He bestowed gold and silk in varying amounts upon the śramaṇas and elders who had witnessed the welcoming ceremony during the Yuanhe era.
The Buddha’s relics were kept within the imperial palace for three days and offered worship.
He was welcomed and enshrined in the two temples of Anguo and Chonghua,
allowing both officials and commoners to pay their respects.
In the twelfth month, as per the previous rites, he welcomed the Buddha’s relics back to Fengxiang.
Emperor Xizong (r. 888–904), the fifth son of Emperor Yizong, ascended the throne in the third year of the Qianfu era.

At Guoqing Temple, the Outer Dharma Master expounded the *Zhiguan famen* (Treatise on Stopping and Contemplation) for the Dharma Master Yuanxiu. The stupa of Chan Master Wuliao of Guiyang in Quanzhou enshrined his entire body for twenty years.
It was submerged by a mountain spring;
when the disciples went to retrieve it, they found that it had not been damaged.
When the King of Min heard of this, he [sent for it].
He dispatched messengers to carry it into the courtyard of the palace for veneration.
Suddenly, a foul odor was smelled from afar.
The King burned incense and offered prayers to it.
He may return to the former site at Kwi-yang to build a stupa;
immediately, a wondrous fragrance will pervade everywhere, and the entire city will come to gaze upon it with reverence. This should be reported to the local government.
The Emperor bestowed upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Zhenji;
his stupa was named Lingjue.
His disciple Huizhong encountered the purge of the monastic community and ended his life as a layman.
To the east of the funerary stupa is the one true-body relic (ekadhātu-vigraha) at Guiyang, which the people and officials rely upon as their refuge;
it is like the lingering transformation of the Saṃgha.
In the first year of the Zhonghe era,
Huang Chao attacked Chang’an and proclaimed himself the founder of the Great Qi dynasty.
The Emperor traveled to Chengdu.
He issued an edict for National Teacher Zhixuan to attend him at his temporary residence, where the Emperor received him in private audience and was greatly pleased.
The Emperor personally composed the title "National Teacher Wuda" for him.
After remaining in the temporary palace for some time, he took his leave to return to Jiulong.
While in meditative concentration, he saw a Bodhisattva touch his crown and preach the Dharma;
as soon as the words were finished, the Bodhisattva vanished.
Suddenly, he saw a pearl enter his left undergarment;
it rose up with extreme pain,
and upon it were the two characters "Chao Cuo."
Xuan, aware of his past karma,
lay down on his right side and passed away.
It is said that Xuan’s previous incarnation was Dharma Master Zhixuan of Sanxue Mountain in Hanchuan.
The illness he experienced at the time of his death is precisely analogous to the account in the *Hanshu*:
during the reign of Emperor Wen, the Prince of Wu was seen by others as he was being admitted into the presence of the Imperial Heir.
While drinking and playing board games, they vied for the path and behaved with irreverence.
The Crown Prince pulled him down by the gaming board and struck him to death.
From this incident, the King of Wu claimed illness and ceased attending court.
Consequently, a plot for rebellion first emerged.
Chao Cuo, the Household Steward of the Crown Prince, repeatedly submitted memorials stating that the transgressions of Wu could be curtailed.
Emperor Wen was magnanimous and could not bear to punish him.
When Emperor Jing ascended the throne,
Xiao Cao said to the Emperor:
Previously, the King of Wu had the Crown Prince removed from office;
he enticed fugitives from all over the world to plot a rebellion,
and even when the King ordered his territories to be reduced, he still rebelled.
Even those who had not been stripped of their territories rebelled;
furthermore, the three kings of Chu, Zhao, and Jiaoxi were all deprived of their commanderies and counties due to crimes.
While the court officials were currently debating the reduction of Wu’s territory, [the situation unfolded as follows].
The King of Wu consequently dispatched an envoy to coordinate with the seven states to rebel together,
using the execution of Chao Cuo as their pretext.
When Yuan Ang, the Chancellor of Wu, entered for an audience,
the Emperor was then engaged with Jiao Cao in discussing military affairs and provisions.
The Emperor questioned Ang.
Dong Ying wished to have those around him cleared away.

Lü Cao hurried to take cover in the eastern corridor, feeling deeply resentful toward Dong Ying, and said to him: "I beg you to dismiss those on your left and right. Lü Cao then stepped aside to avoid him in the eastern wing, harboring great bitterness. Dong Ying replied: "I am speaking to you."
The states of Wu and Chu sent letters to one another saying:
"The treacherous minister Chao Cuo has arbitrarily expelled the feudal lords and confiscated their territories;
for this reason, they have rebelled."
We wish to join forces to execute Zuo and restore their original territories.
If we now calculate our strategy, there is only one way: execute Zuo, dispatch envoys to grant amnesty to the seven kingdoms, and restore their former lands.
Then the armies may be withdrawn without shedding a drop of blood.
After a long silence, the Emperor said, "I do not begrudge one man in order to appease the world.
The Emperor then ordered the Chancellor to indict Jiao Xiao for execution by decapitation at the Eastern Market. Master Xu of Longxing Temple remarked:
The world claims that Zhixuan was the reincarnation of Yuan Ang.
From Emperor Wen of the Han to Emperor Xizong, more than seven hundred years had passed;
thus, Ang’s obligation to repay [the debt for] Chen Qiao must have been fully discharged by now.
Why is it that even now he still suffers this evil retribution and perishes?
It is likely because Zou Yang and Xiao Cao first harbored private resentments against one another,
and when Xiao Cao proposed the reduction of the territories of the seven kingdoms, those seven kingdoms rebelled.
At that moment, Liu Ang requested that Chang’e be executed immediately;
Emperor Jing, out of fear, complied with him,
though it was certainly not his original intention.
Furthermore, had the execution been carried out erroneously and the armies of the seven kingdoms not retreated,

"How can one not stand in awe?

The Dharma Master Zhi Xuan was renowned for his vigorous and spirited debate;

When he reached the twenty-first day, the third seven-day period, [he attained realization].

The Emperor questioned him regarding his visions and conferred upon him the title "Constantly Diligent Bodhisattva" (Cháng Jīngjìn Púsà) and the noble rank of Duke (Kāiguó).

Emperor Zhaozong was the seventh son of Emperor Yizong.
