The world calls this the Guiyang School.
At first, when he led his disciples to dwell on Wangmang Mountain, one day his meditation seat sank into the ground;
it was because the mountain deity could no longer bear his presence there.
To the southeast there was a great Mount Yang,
a place of worldly merit;
he subsequently moved his residence there.
After a long time, the community grew so large that their dwelling became cramped.
One night, the mountain deity moved the temple thirty *li* away to Dutián to make way for them.
This was the fifth generation under Mount Nanyue.
In the first year of the Jingfu era,
the King of Wuyue, Qian Liu, established Ruixiang Temple at Shicheng Mountain in Shan County to enshrine the stone image of Maitreya from his third birth.
In the second year of the Qianning era,
Chan Master Wenju went to visit Chan Master Da'an of Xiyuan.
Seeing him from afar, [Da'an] smiled and said:
"Go to the Nirvana Hall.
The Master assented and immediately entered.
At that time, five hundred monks were all afflicted with a seasonal epidemic.
The Master marked them one by one with his staff;
as soon as he marked them, they rose. The King of Min, filled with reverence and wonder, established the Guanhuan Monastery for him to reside in.
In the third year [of the Yongchu era],
an imperial decree was issued to rebuild Cao Tang Temple at the site where Dharma Master Kumārajīva had translated the scriptures. In the fourth year...
Chan Master Congshen of Zhaozhou Guanyuan Monastery entered nirvana at the age of one hundred and twenty.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Zhengji; he had studied under Nanquan.
The Fourth Patriarch of Nanyue: When Lord Wang, the Governor of Zhao, entered the monastery to pay his respects,
Zhaozhou sat there and asked him,
"Does Your Majesty understand?"
The King said,
"I do not understand.
The Master said:
Having observed the fast since childhood, his body was already aged;
when he saw others, he lacked the strength to descend from his meditation seat.
The King treated him with even greater courtesy.
The next day, he ordered an attendant to deliver a message.
When the Master descended from his seat to receive him,
an attendant asked for the meaning of this.
The Master said:
"When those of the highest caliber come, I receive them upon the meditation seat;
when those of the second caliber come, I receive them after descending from the meditation seat."

When those of lower rank came to the outer gate of the mountain monastery, they received the imperial decree appointing the śramaṇa Juehui as the Vice-Registrar (Fusengl) for the Left and Right Quarters; this office began from that time.
This was in the second year of the Gwanghwa era.
A report from Fuzhou stated that a group of foreign monks had gathered on the summit of Mount Cao;
the local villagers pursued them.
They all flew away, leaving behind their rain hats, which were of an exceptionally strange and ancient design. An imperial edict was issued to establish He-yu Chan Temple on that site.
This was in the first year of the Tianfu era.
The mountain bandit Xu En rose in rebellion;
he went to Jing Mountain in Hangzhou and opened the stupa of National Teacher Guoyi Chan Master.
Inside, he saw two jars containing the master’s incorruptible body, with his hair grown so long that it covered his face.
The rebel soldiers were all terrified and fled.
The King of Wu-Yue ordered that he be reinterred with due solemnity.
In the second year.
Chan Master Daoying of Yunju in Hongzhou passed away.
His posthumous title was Hongjue (Great Enlightenment).
He was a descendant of Dongshan in the sixth generation of Qingyuan.
In the third year [of the Tianxi era],
Chan Master Benji of Caoshan in Fuzhou entered nirvana;
he was posthumously granted the title Yuanzheng (Original Realization).
The Master received the Dharma from Dongshan;
the world calls this the Cao-Dong School. Upādhyāya Xihe of Jingzhao personally had his mind certified by Dongshan.
He mingled with the common folk in Min,
where he spent his days foraging along the riverbanks for shrimp and clams to sustain himself,
and at night he slept amidst the paper money offerings in the Baima Temple.
Chan Master Jing of Huayan entered at night with paper money to observe him.
When the Master arrived,
Jing seized him and asked:
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said,
"The wine table and tray before the deity."
He performed his formal bows of gratitude and withdrew.
Later, he entered the capital city, feigning madness among the people;
his spiritual wonders were unfathomable. ○ Chan Master Wenyuan of Yunmen in Shaoyou gathered a thousand disciples.
The Han Emperor of the Liu clan summoned him into the inner palace at Guangzhou to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma,
treating him with the rites due to a teacher.
The Master had received the Dharma from Xuefeng.
He was known as the seventh patriarch of the Yunmen School at Qingyuan.

Jingzong was the ninth son of Emperor Zhaozong; in the first year of the Tianyou era, on the anniversary of his birth, an imperial edict was issued for all monasteries and observatories throughout the realm to establish vegetarian feasts.
A Prohibition on Slaughter and Fishing among the Common People.
Lü Dongbin traveled to Mount Hua, where he met Zhongli Quan, who bestowed upon him the Golden Elixir and the methods of swordsmanship.
Later, he passed through Huanglong Mountain in Ezhou.
When Chan Master Zhiji was ascending the hall, Qingyuan’s eighth-generation descendant Yan’i asked:
“Within a single grain of millet lies a world;
within half a pint of a cooking pot, one boils mountains and rivers.”
"What do you think of this?
The Master said,
"A corpse-guarding ghost."
Lü Dongbin said, "Alas,
there is an elixir of immortality within my bag.
The Master said:
"Even if one passes through eighty thousand kalpas, in the end one will surely fall into emptiness and perish.
The guest did not submit;
at night, [the Master] flew his sword to threaten him.
The Master already knew this beforehand;
he sat in the abbot’s quarters with his dharma robe covering his head,
while the sword circled him several times.
The Master pointed at it with his finger, and it immediately fell to the ground.
The guest came forward to apologize for his error.
The Master interrogated him, saying:
He did not inquire further about the half-sheng cauldron.
"How is it that within a single grain of millet the world is concealed?
Suddenly, the guest attained realization.
He then composed a verse in thanks, saying:
"Since the moment I first beheld Huanglong, I have only then realized that all my efforts hitherto were misdirected. (From *Xianyuan yishi*).

The Five Dynasties Liang: The Liang dynasty was based in Luoyang. Its founder, Taizu Zhu Wen, was granted the name Quanzhong. In the first year of the Kaiping era, an imperial edict decreed that monks and nuns were to be transferred from the supervision of the Court of State Ceremonial to the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu).
The śramaṇa Zhixuan of Quanzhou traveled to Western India to seek Buddhist scriptures. Upon his return,
he presented to the imperial court the relics of a pratyekabuddha, palm-leaf manuscripts, and Sanskrit sutras.
In the second year [of the Tianxi era], in the second month,
Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun passed away.
In the eleventh month, Chan Master Xuansha Shibei passed away.
The Master received the Dharma from Xuefeng.
In his later years, he resided at Xuansha,
where he had a thousand disciples.
He responded to the capacities of others and engaged with sentient beings for twenty years.
The King of Min treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
Upon his death, the King bestowed upon him the posthumous title "Zongyi" (One of the Patriarchs).
In the third year,
on the Great Brightness Festival (Damingjie), an imperial edict was issued for the hundred officials to visit the temple to offer incense and pray for [the Emperor's] longevity.
In the fourth year...
The youngest son of the King of Wu, Qian Liu, named Lingyin, entered the monastic order;
by imperial decree, he was granted purple robes and the title of Great Master Wuxiang,
with his seniority increased to thirty years of ordination.
In the first year of the Zhenming era of Emperor Mo Di (Muzong),
the śramaṇa Guixu of the East Pagoda Monastery presented the *Jinglun huìyào* (Essentials of the Scriptures and Treatises).
By imperial decree, it was compiled and included in the Great Canon.
In the second year [of the Tianfu era], he was conferred the title of Great Master of Propagating the Teaching (Yanjiao Dashi).
King Qian Liu of Wuyue dispatched the śramaṇa Qingwai, along with his younger brother Qian Hua.
He traveled to Mount Ayuwang in Siming to welcome the Śākyamuni Sarīra Stūpa.
When the boat moored at Xiling,
the stūpa emitted light at night, making the Qiantang River as bright as day.
The King personally went out to welcome him to Luohan Temple,
where he extensively prepared offerings.
[There was also] the Master Budai of Fenghua in Siming.
At the eastern corridor of Yue-lin Temple, he sat upon a flat rock and passed away; he was buried at Feng-shan.
After his burial, there were those who saw him again on the road to Dong-yang.
He entrusted him, saying,
"I have mistakenly brought this single sandal;
you may take it back for me."
Upon his return, he learned that the Master had passed away;
when the assembly looked at the cave, only a single shoe remained there.
When the Master first arrived, he did not know where to go.
He called himself Qici;
with his furrowed brow and protruding belly,
he spoke of people's fortune and misfortune, and all his pronouncements were proven accurate.
He constantly wandered through the markets with a staff and a cloth bag, begging for anything he saw;
whatever he obtained, he placed entirely into the bag.
A group of sixteen boys would clamorously pursue him.
They vied with one another to pull at the bag;
some opened the bag in the midst of the crowd,
producing from it alms bowls, wooden sandals, fish, rice, vegetables, meat, tiles, stones, and other such items.
He scatters the clouds. Look!
Then he picks them up one by one and says:
"What is this? Then, wrapping some excrement in paper, he said,
"This is the Inner Court of Maitreya."
Once, he was standing on the road.
A monk asked, "What are you doing?
The Master said:
When an individual came,
he said, "I have come.
The Master took an orange from his bosom and gave it to him.
The monk prepared to receive him,
but [the Master] withdrew his hand and said,
"You are not that person."
A monk asked,
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master dropped his sack, stood with his hands clasped, and remained there.
The monk said,
"Is there not something else?
The Master picked up the cloth bag and walked off on his shoulder.
The Master followed behind the monk and patted him on the back.
The monk turned his head,
and the Master said:
"Give me one coin.
He once showed [this bowl] to the assembly while at the latrine, saying:
"I have traveled about to solicit offerings, yet I cannot even perform these two matters [of defecation and urination] here."
Jiang Mahā, a local man of the commandery, was frequently in his company.
One day, they bathed together at Changting;
seeing a single eye on the Master’s back, Jiang touched it and said:
"You are a Buddha.
His teacher stopped him, saying,
"Do not speak of this to others."
The Master frequently recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*,
so people of the world called him "Mahā Upāsaka.
Formerly, the Master traveled through Min.
There was a layman named Chen who served the Master with great diligence;
he asked the Master how old he was.
He said, "This cloth bag of mine has been coeval with empty space.
He was asked again for the reason why,
and he replied, "My surname is Li."
He was born on the eighth day of the second month during the early Tianli era of the Jin dynasty.
Wang Ren, the Magistrate of Putian, encountered him in Min.
He left behind a verse which says:
"Maitreya is truly Maitreya;
he manifests thousands, tens of thousands, and billions of transformation bodies."
At that time, he appeared to the people of his age, yet none of them recognized him.
Later, someone found a blue, pure alms-bowl and a six-ringed mendicant’s staff beside a stupa.
He stored it in the temple.
Four years later,
the Tripitaka Master Bhadra from India arrived in Shu.
He himself stated that he had traveled from the kingdom of Magadha to Yizhou,
passing through a distance of ninety-nine thousand three hundred and eighty li.
At that time, Wang Jian was the ruler of Shu.
This was the first year of the Guangtian era.
The Tripitaka Master himself stated that he was already two hundred and seventy years old.
The commentary states:
There are two routes from this land to the Five Indias.
The first is the northwestern route.
From Dunhuang and Yangguan, he traveled through the various kingdoms of the Western Regions,
crossed the Pamir Mountains and the Snow Mountains, and entered the territory of Northern India.
Since the time in antiquity when An Shigao, Dharmaratna, and An Sheng came from the West, [the Dharma has spread].
This is the route by which the Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty and others traveled eastward.
The second is the southwestern route:
departing by ship from the South Sea, one reaches the kingdoms of Fo-shih (Śrīvijaya) and Ka-ta (Kāṭha).
Traveling northwest for one day, one reaches the kingdom of Damā, which lies within the borders of East India; it constitutes the southern boundary of East India.
This is the very place from which, in ancient times, those departing by ship from the sea mouth returned to the Tang. It was here that Bodhidharma of the Liang dynasty came from the West.
The places traveled by the Tripiṭaka Master Jing during his journey to the East are those;
now, the route from Bhaṭṭāraka to Shu lies directly to the West.
This is precisely what Zhang Qian meant by his statement that Daxia was not far to the southeast of Shu;
compared to the two other routes, it should be somewhat closer,
yet the distance currently traversed is approximately one hundred thousand li.
It was because the mountains and rivers were winding and convoluted,
local customs were not in communication with one another,
and the routes taken were circuitous.
Thus, it was only after more than ten years that he finally reached Shu.
For this reason, those who arrived were merely a single *pātra*.
Yet, in this region, not a single person took this path for six years.
In the sixth year,
Mani of Chenzhou gathered a multitude and rose in rebellion.
They installed Mu Yi as Son of Heaven;
however, the court dispatched troops to capture and execute him.
His followers, because they abstained from meat and wine, [were spared].
At night they gathered for lewd and impure acts;
during the day, the Māra-king sat in a haughty posture.
The Buddha washed his feet for them.
He claimed that the Buddha belonged to the Mahāyāna while his own teaching was of the "Supreme Vehicle" (Anuttarayāna).
Such was his arrogance and lack of Dharma. In the first year of the Longde era, an imperial edict was issued throughout the realm prohibiting the private ordination of monks and nuns.
The one who wished to leave the household life entered the capital to undergo an examination of his mastery of the scriptures.
This was in the first year of the Zhuangzong era (the same as the Zhuangzong Li Cunxu of the Tang dynasty) at Luoyang.

On his birthday, an imperial decree was issued for the Buddhist Registrar Huijiang and the Daoist Cheng Zixiao to enter the inner palace for discussion and to provide a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks.
A śramaṇa from Fengxiang named Daoxian dreamed of traveling to the Five Indias and beholding the Buddha.
He pointed out a certain country and a certain village, whereupon he immediately understood the languages and sounds of the Five Indias.
He transmitted the methods of the powdered altar to the world;
people called this the Dharma of the Fuxiang Ajari.
At the beginning of the Qingtai era,
he followed the last emperor to Luoyang and passed away there;
his stupa was erected at Longmen.
In the second year,
by imperial decree, Zen Master Huìràn of the Three Sages was summoned to the inner palace to consult him regarding the methods of Chan.
The Emperor said, "I have recovered a priceless jewel from beneath the Great Liang, yet no one has offered a price for it.
Rannyo replied: "Indeed."
"Please, Your Majesty, examine this closely.
The Emperor reached out his hand to lift the corners of his *fàtóu* (headgear) and said:
"Who would dare to offer a price for the treasures of an Emperor?
The Emperor said this,
and then he passed away.
An imperial edict conferred the posthumous title "Great Master Guangji Tongji" upon his stupa.
In the third year,
the cavalry general Shi Yinqiang, who had achieved merit in battle, accompanied the imperial entourage into Luoyang.
He suddenly attained awakening to the Way of Chan.
He requested the name Chiqing for his monastic ordination and was granted the title Great Master Wuxue.
He established his residence as Dede (Establishing Virtue) Monastery.
In the first year of the Tiānchéng era (936), during the birthday celebrations of Emperor Míngzōng— who was the younger brother of Emperor Zhuāngzōng by birth—
the Imperial Edict was issued to the Registrar of Monks, Yúnbiàn.
He entered the inner palace with the Daoist master to engage in discussion.
In the second month of the second year,
the Emperor burned incense every evening within the palace and prayed to Heaven, saying:
A certain Hu man, having been thrust forward by the masses due to the chaos, prayed:
"May a sage-ruler arise early in heaven to be the lord of the living.
Three years passed.
The ruler of Min, Wang Yanyun, had long revered the Buddha.
In this year, twenty thousand monks were ordained. Chan Master Guichen of Luohan Monastery in Zhangzhou entered nirvana;
the Master had received the Dharma from Xuanyuan.
In the reign of Emperor Mo (Emperor Mò), he was posthumously titled Chan Master Zhēnyīng. He was the eighth-generation descendant of Qīngyuán.
In the second month of the first year of the Qīngtài era, Emperor Mò’s adopted son, Emperor Āmíngzōng, issued a decree.
The Commissioner of Merit submitted a memorial.
On every occasion of a festival celebrating a birthday, I request that the prefectures and commanderies be ordered to recommend monks and nuns who excel in four categories:
lecturing on the sutras, meditative concentration, recitation of mantras,
and literary composition and debate, so as to test their competence.
From *Hong Rongzhai Sanbi*, citing the *Old History of the Five Dynasties*: Regarding the Ancient Buddha Koubing of Chong’an County in Jianzhou, whose name was Zaoxian.
He first visited Xuefeng.
He brought a bundle of wild ducks and a jar of sauce as an offering.
Feng asked,
"What is inside the bundle?"
He said, "A wild duck.
"Where did you find this?
"In the mud."
"How deep is the mud?
"It is beyond measure.
"Is there anything further beyond that?"
"Deeper and deeper, more and more existent.
He asked again,
"What is inside the jar?"
The Master said, "Soy sauce. "Where did you get it?
"I made it myself."
"Is it ripe yet?
It is not much different.
Feng said:
"In another life, you will surely become a teacher to kings and nobles.
In the summer months, you shall always sit upon paper garments;
in the winter months, you shall bathe by striking the ice."
For this reason, he was called "Knocking on Ice.
King Yanjun of Min invited him to reside at Ruiyan.
He subsequently passed through Jianzhou.
The Provincial Inspector Chen Hui provided a meal for a thousand monks and asked the Master,
"Is there anyone extraordinary among those gathered today?"
The Master said,
"There is none.
Tomorrow I shall bring a Great Being for you."
The next day, Huì prepared a full vegetarian feast in expectation.
An elderly woman arrived from outside;
he invited her to take the seat of honor.
When he had finished eating and departed,
the Master said,
"This is the Bodhisattva Suvarṇaprabhāsa."
After a short while, the old woman came again and pointed at the Master, saying,
"Why does the Pratyekabuddha, an ancient Buddha, speak so much?
Having said this, she vanished.
In the second year,
the śramaṇa Zilin of Siming traveled to the various kingdoms of Goryeo, Baekje, and Japan.
He was entrusted with the transmission of the Tiantai teachings.

The Goryeo kingdom dispatched the envoy Li Renri to escort Lin back; the Prince of Wuyue, Qian Liu, ordered the construction of a monastery within the prefectural city to provide a dwelling for his followers.
In the second year of the Tiānfú era of Emperor Gāozǔ Shí Jìngtáng of the Later Jin dynasty,
when the capital was Bìndu, the Zhū Xuānhuī general Zhū Chóng excavated the ground beneath his residence in Luoyang and discovered ten large stone Buddha statues.
An inscription states:
"In the sixth year of the Chuigong era of the Tang dynasty, Jingfu Temple was constructed;
its magnificence was so great as to evoke a profound sense of awe."

He immediately vacated his residence to establish it as a monastery. Dharma Master Song expounded the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (*Zhiguan*) dharma-gate to Dharma Master Xi Ji at Guoqing Monastery for three years.
Yang Guangyuan was appointed as the Commissioner of Merit for the Realm.
All temples were subordinate to it.
In the fourth year,
an imperial edict was issued for the state memorial services involving the chief ministers and the hundred officials.
He went to the monastery to offer incense and provide meals for the monks,
establishing this as a permanent practice.
This was done by the śramaṇa Kehong of Hanzhong.
He presented four hundred and eighty fascicles of the *Dazangjing yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning of the Great Canon),
by imperial decree they were included in the canon. At Tiantzhusan in Hangzhou,
the śramaṇa Daoyi obtained a rare piece of wood and carved an image of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.
There was a śramaṇa named Congxun who,
from Luoyang, brought a relic of an ancient Buddha and placed it within a jeweled crown.
Thereafter, the relic was constantly visible upon his headgear.
The white light from his *uṣṇīṣa* shone brilliantly,
manifesting great spiritual efficacy.
During the first year of the Kaoyun era, when the young Emperor Shao Di Li Gui was the grandson of the High Ancestor (Gaozu).
By imperial decree, the Tripitaka was transcribed for the High Ancestor and enshrined at Mingsheng Temple to provide merit for his vast blessings. In the sixth month, Qian Hongzuo, the King of Wuyue,
dispatched the monk Huigui to the stupa of the Great Master Kaishan Hui at Shuanglin.
Sixteen fragments of sacred bone and countless purple-gold *śarīra* relics were obtained.
Purple mushrooms grew upon the brick bed,
and two tigers lay prostrate beneath the tomb.
Auspicious clouds shrouded the mountains and sweet rain fell upon the earth.
Thereupon, they brought forth the sacred relics and remains, along with a pure flask, an incense burner, a door-knocker, a mallet, and other items.
They arrived at Qiandang and enshrined them in the An-guang Hall for veneration.
He established Longhua Temple and used his bones to sculpt an image of the Bodhisattva;
this took three years.
A man from Shàngyuán County in Jīnlíng died suddenly and was mistakenly summoned to the underworld.
There he saw the former ruler of the Táng dynasty, who was bound with five wooden stocks most severely.
The people were greatly alarmed and asked,
"Master, why do you act in this way?
The Master replied:
I was misled by Song Qichu.
I executed a thousand surrendered people from Hezhou,
for which I have been accused on account of their grievance.
The people said,
"Your servant followed by mistake and ought to return.
The lord wept and said:
"I am imprisoned here;
when I hear the sound of the bell, my suffering briefly ceases.
Return and tell the successor of the throne."
In all monasteries, one should ring the bell to cause [the suffering] to be delayed;
furthermore, it is even more effective for alleviating suffering to cast a new bell.
The people asked,
"How may we, the common folk, verify this for ourselves?
The Master replied:
I once received this auspicious jade from the Great King of Khotan;
I buried it in the fragrant mud at the left knee of the Buddha in Waguan Temple,
where at that time no one knew of it.
After the people returned and reported this,
the later ruler personally went to Waguan Temple and cut open his knee;
indeed, he obtained the jade image.
Moved to tears and struck with deep grief,
he immediately commissioned a bell for Qingliang Temple and inscribed upon it:
He offered sacrifices to the late Emperor Xiaogao, his heroic ancestor;
having escaped obscurity and emerged from distress,
he erected a pagoda at Jiangshan with a jade image.
During the Han Dynasty, the capital was at Jinyang. In the twelfth year of the Tianfu era, the High Ancestor Liu Yao—
whose original name was Zhìyuǎn— and the Grand Marshal Guò Lìngwēi erected a stele for the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* at Shòuchūn.
The Emperor Yindu, Chen You, was a paternal cousin of the High Ancestor (Gaozu). In the first year of the Qianyou era,
the King of Wuyue, Qian Chu,
honored the Tiantai śramaṇa Deyun as State Preceptor.
In the second year, he observed the rites for a junior disciple.
Chan Master Yunmen Wenyuan passed away while seated.
The entire body [of the relic] was enshrined in a stupa within a chamber one zhang square.
During the first year of Guangshun of Emperor Taizu (Gaozu) of the Later Zhou, when Li Shouzhen rebelled in Hedong, Gaozu Guo Lingwei... [text fragment].
When Taizu was personally leading a military campaign,
the Madman of Mái went to tell Zhao Pu:
"How can Minister Li endure for long?"
Beneath the city, there were the three "Son of Heaven" vapors.
Before long, the city fell.
At that time, Emperor Shizong and the Taizu of our own dynasty were both in attendance and traveling together.
In the second year,
by imperial decree, on the Emperor’s birthday,

On that day, by imperial decree, all followed him into the monastic life; ten youths from throughout the empire were universally ordained, one for each [of the ten directions]. By imperial decree, [a temple] was established at Jiamaying in Luoyang, the site where the Great Ancestor was born.
In the third year, he established Yingtian Temple to enshrine the divine icons and issued an imperial decree for Taiping Xingguo Temple in the capital.
He established the Ganlu (Nectar) Precept Platform for Honoring Ancestors;
precept platforms were subsequently established throughout all the provinces of the realm,
totaling seventy-two locations.
A separate Mahāyāna ordination platform was established at Cixiao Temple in the capital.
The author states:
According to the *Neitonghui Sengshilüe* (Brief History of the Sangha by Ning Tonghui), it says:
Amṛta (the deathless) is used as a metaphor for Nirvāṇa.
Since the precepts constitute the initial gateway for entering Nirvāṇa,
they are designated by this name based on their fruit.
Regarding the present statement about establishing a separate Mahāyāna ordination platform:
it refers to first receiving the full precepts of a Śrāvaka in various regions,
and subsequently coming to this site to further receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

This was in accordance with the principle that, following the period of the revealed teachings, in the final age those who have left the household life must be equally urgent in both their observance of the precepts and their practice.
An edict was issued to all provinces and prefectures stating that for any monk or Daoist who has committed a public offense:
The ransoming method was adopted for hearing [the case].
An edict was issued stating that no official of the various ranks shall, without cause,
insult or humiliate monks or nuns by vocally uttering the word "bald."
Those currently in office were suspended from their duties;

commoners were banished for a thousand *li*. By imperial decree, Li Wei, Director of the Bureau of Memorial Drafting, was ordered to provide scriptural and doctrinal topics for the examination of *śramaṇas*, based on which they were promoted or appointed to positions within the Left and Right Streets.
The Xiangguo Monastery was on the Left Street, and the Kaibao Monastery was on the Right Street.
By imperial decree, Chan Master Yunhuo of Xifeng in Jizhou was invited to reside at the Northern Imperial Garden.
He entered meditative absorption for over a month.
He requested permission to return to his native mountains,
and the Emperor granted his request.
Whenever the Master entered meditative absorption, he would sometimes remain there for an entire year before emerging.
The śramaṇa Saṃghadeva from the Western Heaven came to court, presenting śarīra relics, Sanskrit scriptures, and the Bodhi-seal. The śramaṇa Juecheng Fajie from Central India came to court.
He presented the Śarīra relics, the Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscripts, the portrait of the Vajrāsana, and leaves from the Bodhi tree;
the Emperor summoned him to the private audience hall, where he was treated with great courtesy and reward,
and provided lodging in the Translation Institute.
He recited the "Hymn in Praise of the Holy One" (Shengzan shengsong).
He issued an imperial decree for Weijing to translate it.
He then addressed Scholar Yang Yi, saying:
Upon entering this country, I saw pigs and sheep being slaughtered and meat hanging in the market stalls;
it was so painful that I could not bear to look.
In India to the west, those who eat meat or the five pungent vegetables are driven out of the city.
Therefore, those without wealth did not wish to dwell here for long;
they aspired to travel to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī and then return to their own lands.
Duke Ding Wei of Jin asked him,
"Having come from as far as tens of thousands of li, what further purpose do you have?
He replied:
He also wished to pay homage at the stupa of Vinaya Master Xuanshi.

Upon his return, the Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya* robe to be enshrined upon the Vajrāsana, as well as funds for its construction and offerings of tea and fruit.
[Omitted] Fourth, Dharma Master Zhili of Mingzhou.
At first, he followed a different tradition from that of the śramaṇas.
He resided at Ba'en on the south lake, where he gathered disciples and expounded the Way.
In this year, the temple was granted the name Yanqing.
He then composed two pieces of admonitory oaths,
intended to serve as a place for the perpetual study and recitation of the Tiantai school’s teachings.
In them, he stated that his own tradition possesses five virtues.
I shall bestow it upon him so that he may dwell therein;
thus, all subsequent schemes will be entirely successful.
These are the five virtues.
First, those who have long studied the Tiantai teachings should not engage in lecturing on multiple subjects concurrently.
Second, they should refine their studies and contemplate deeply, remaining far removed from superficiality and falsehood.
Third, they should be renowned for their precepts and virtue, rectifying themselves before dealing with others.
The fourth was his ability to distance himself from honors and not bend his Way.
The fifth was his excellence in both rhetoric and eloquence, and his skill in leadership and guidance.
In the third month of the fourth year.
The Emperor visited Guanghua Temple on Mount Longmen in Luoyang to pay homage to the stupa of the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi;
he composed a eulogy which was engraved upon stone and placed at the site of the stupa.
He further visited Baima Temple to pay homage to the physical remains of the Tripitaka Master Kāśyapa Mātanga.
The Emperor said to his close ministers:
"Since Kāśyapa Mātanga arrived until now, a thousand years have passed,
yet his entire body remains undecayed."
This is truly worthy of veneration.
It is fitting that the temple monks be strictly instructed to guard it with diligent care.
Consequently, the Emperor composed a work to praise it and issued an edict bestowing three thousand taels of gold.
He renovated the Puxian Monastery on Mount Emei and provided vegetarian meals for thirty thousand monks;
four monks were ordained annually. By imperial decree, the monk Daojian of Lianshui Commandery was summoned to the audience.
He ordered all the palace ladies to come forth and burn incense.
As each lady approached him,
the Emperor deceived her by saying, "This is the Empress."
The masters all said it was not so.
After about a dozen people had spoken thus,
the master suddenly rose and said:
"Your Majesty likes to nurture this person; he will surely become the head of the house in the future.
This refers to Empress Dowager Zhangxian, née Liu, the consort of Emperor Zhenzong.
When Renzong ascended the throne...
Because he was young, he honored Lady Liu as Empress Dowager.
He presided over the court and exercised imperial authority for eleven years.
Then, Master Qi requested to return to the mountains.
The Emperor issued an edict granting his request.
While in the mountains, he constantly wore paper robes and kept his door closed, never seeing anyone.
There were those who placed food before the courtyard;
when people withdrew, they would take it for themselves.
This was in the fifth month.
In the eleventh month, the śramaṇa Jixian arrived from the country of Baṅni and presented the Sanskrit scripture *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra*;
he was granted purple robes.
In the second month of the fifth year, Li Shiheng, the Governor of Yizhou,
presented forty fascicles of the *Shishi huiaoyao* (Essentials of Buddhist History), compiled by the śramaṇa Renzan of Daci Temple.
An imperial edict summoned the śramaṇa Mózhen of Mount Emei in Jiaozhou for an audience.
The Emperor bestowed a poem upon him and provided him with lodging at Jingde Temple.
Prince Yuancheng of Shu dreamed that a youth dressed in black robes presented him with a letter and entrusted it to an imperial messenger;
the Prince’s feet then stepped upon yellow clouds, which gradually faded into obscurity.
The Prince questioned the Master about this dream.
The reply stated:
"There shall soon be the auspicious celebration of the descent of an heir;
before long, Renzong was born. At that time, Yue Shi was serving as the Imperial Commissioner for the Western Capital.
In a dream, the Lord of Devas summoned him and said, "The Lord of the World seeks an heir; I shall select one for him.
After a short while, a man arrived.
The Emperor said, "The Central Plains seek an heir; go there and do not decline.
He then assented and departed.
An attendant standing nearby said,
"This is the barefoot immortal Li of Mount Nanyue.
The following year, Renzong was born, as recorded in Zhang Shizheng’s *Kuaiyi ji*.
An envoy dispatched from the Kingdom of Japan presented a tribute, stating:
"In the eastern part of our country, there is an auspicious light.
According to ancient traditions, this omen appears when the Son of Heaven of the Central Plains is sagacious and enlightened."
The Emperor was delighted and issued an edict to construct a temple in Japan,
granting it the name Shinkō.
He commanded his literary ministers to compose a record of the temple.
In the second month of the sixth year,
he issued an edict that officials throughout the empire must examine the scriptural studies of novice monks.
Only then was he permitted to undergo tonsure. In the fifth month, a golden light was seen atop the wheel-ornament (cakra) of the Fusheng Pagoda at Kaibao Temple;
furthermore, holy monks were seen circumambulating the pagoda.
On the following day, five-colored śarīras were obtained.
The Emperor personally visited and paid reverent homage;
he beheld the śarīra atop the stūpa,
as large as the moon.
Its color was like crystal;
it moved back and forth, flying and gliding upon the bell-ropes,
while the commoners and officials alike gazed upon it from the earthen tiles on the ground.
He obtained over five thousand grains of sarira relics.
By imperial decree, the pagoda was granted the title "Pagoda of Miraculous Response" (Linggan Zhi Ta).
At that time, there was also the Xingci Pagoda at Tianqing Temple in the capital.
Furthermore, śarīra were seen atop the wheel-ornament (cakra).
[The Emperor] remarked:

"The auspicious signs of the Image-Dharma (Hīnayāna/Iconic Teaching) are the blessings for the people. In the eighth month, Zhao Anren, Vice Minister of the Ministry of War and Official for Polishing the Texts of the Translated Scriptures, [submitted a memorial].
Having received the imperial decree to compile the catalog of the Great Canon,
it was completed in twenty-one fascicles.
It was bestowed the title *Dazhongxiangfu Fabao Lu* (Record of the Dharma Treasures of the Dazhongxiangfu Era).
An imperial preface was further bestowed, stating:
"Since the Taiping Xingguo era, a total of four hundred and thirteen fascicles of sutras, vinayas, and śāstras have been translated.
These were compiled by Yang Yi, Director of the Imperial Library, and the Great Dharma Master Wujing, among others."
Furthermore, he requested that the collected writings on the Buddha-vehicle composed by the imperial pen of two reigns be included in the Great Canon;

an edict was issued granting his request with praise. An edict was also issued posthumously bestowing upon the Great Being Sengqie of Sizhou the title of Grand Master Puzhaomingjue (Universally Illuminating and Enlightening).

Neither public nor private officials were permitted to mention his name by title. In the ninth month, the śramaṇas Jñānabhadra and others from West India arrived to present śarīra relics and Sanskrit scriptures;
they were granted purple robes. In the eleventh month, the śarīra relics appeared at the Shengzu Mingqing Hall of the Yuqing Zhaogong Palace.
Some may think that in the Way of the Buddhas there is no matter of *śarīra* (relics).
The Emperor said to his chief minister Wang Dan:
"The establishment of the Three Teachings has but one underlying purpose."
In general, all [teachings] exhort people to do good;
only those who have attained insight through Consciousness-Only can unify them.
Those whose emotions are stagnant and who cling to partiality remain ever further removed from the Way.
The commentary states:
The śarīra of the Dharmakāya is omnipresent;
it manifests whenever there is a great occasion for spiritual resonance.
Even from stubborn emptiness and decaying soil, one may still obtain [the fruit];
how much more so within the palaces and halls of the Daoist tradition?
Only our True Teaching honors Heaven and reveres the Buddha, its virtue moving both the hidden and the manifest.
Recently, śarīra relics have been repeatedly obtained from various pagodas and temples;
now they are seen once more in the Hall of the Sacred Ancestor.
This truly serves to manifest the sincere devotion of the Sagely Ruler toward the two teachings.
This was brought about by the power of sincere devotion reaching the divine.

At that time, the Śramaṇa Pūrṇamitra from Vārāṇasī in India presented a Sanskrit scripture written on leaves of the Aśoka tree. The Dharma Master Fushizhongju, a disciple of Fazhi of Siming, arrived at the capital.
The Emperor heard of his reputation and summoned him into the inner palace,
where he lectured on the Sutra of Forty-two Sections.
He eloquently expounded upon profound principles,
greatly delighting the Emperor's mind.
The Emperor bestowed upon him purple robes, gold, silk, incense, and medicinal herbs.
In the first month of the eighth year,
the ministers and officials submitted a memorial stating:
"Every year during the Yuanxiao festival, the Imperial Carriage visits more than thirty temples and observatories, where the Emperor performs more than a hundred prostrations."
He hoped that from now on, the various palaces would have their subordinate officials perform prostrations in rotation.
The Emperor said to Wang Dan,
"I am praying for blessings for both the central court and the outer regions."
He rose from his prostrations with such devout reverence that he never showed the slightest laxity.

Your desire to propose reductions is not my intention; as stated in the *Guochao huiyao*: [The Emperor] rose from his prostrations with such devout reverence that he never showed the slightest laxity. Your desire to propose reductions is not my intention;
as stated in the *Guochao huiyao*:
According to the *Gui tian lu*:
When Emperor Taizu entered a temple, he asked Zanning about Tonghui,
"Should one prostrate before the Buddha?"
The answer is:
One does not bow to past Buddhas when facing a Buddha of the present.
Indeed, during the Taizong era, [the Master] followed the King of Wuyue upon his initial return to the capital.
It has never been seen that [the Emperor] ever prostrated himself before Taizu;
thus, what the Ouyang family recorded is erroneous.
Now, observing that with Zhenzong, [the number of prostrations] was already one hundred or more.
He did not wish to delegate authority to his close ministers;
this was likely because he was thoroughly accustomed to the family laws established by his ancestors.
Later, for instance, Emperor Huizong prostrated himself before the Buddha’s tooth relic.
Since the successive dynasties of the Southern Song, emperors have paid homage to the Great Being (Mahāsattva).
From this, one knows that since the founding of the state, there has never been a reason not to worship the Buddha.
Ou-yang [Hsiu] was arrogant toward the Buddha.
Because he did not wish for the ruler to pay him respect,
he specifically fabricated this doctrine; it is a groundless discourse that,
above, slanders the sovereign and, below, slanders Master Ning.
How great it was!
An imperial edict was issued to construct Jingling Palace on the Bing site within the Great Interior (the palace) to serve the Holy Ancestor.
Furthermore, an imperial decree was issued naming the Nan'an Cliff in Tingzhou as Junqing Monastery.
One hundred and twenty scrolls of the Emperor Taizong’s calligraphy were bestowed [upon him].
Previously, the monk Zicheng had resided on the upper cliffs;
his spiritual manifestations were unfathomable.
It is said that he was an emanation of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Seeing that a dragon in the Huairen River was harming people,
he wrote a verse and threw it into the pool.
The waters surged and the sands rose, blocking the pool and forming an island;
thus, the monsters were finally extinguished.
We then passed through the Huangyang Gorge at Meizhou.
When the people lacked water for drinking, he truly pointed his staff toward a stream,
which then shifted closer to the road.
Whenever there was a drought each year, [he would do the same].
He wrote a verse and cast it [into the air];
wind and rain followed immediately.
In subsequent instances, he always wrote this verse as a gift, using the four characters from its middle.

The people of this world do not understand its purport. An imperial edict was issued to entrust the five fascicles of the *Miaojue ji* (Collection of Wondrous Enlightenment), composed by the Emperor Taizong, to the Translation Court (*Fayuan*) to be included in the Great Canon (*Dazang*).
The preface states:
As for the school of the Daoists, that which they study consists of the *Daode jing* and the *Yinfu jing*.
These constitute the foundation for governing the mind and cultivating the person.
Furthermore, there are the ultimate words regarding the inner elixir (*neidan*), the outer elixir (*waidan*), the timing of the firing process (*huohou*), and the oral instructions (*koudue*).
Thus, it is not transmitted to those who are not of the human lineage.
As for the other peripheral methods, such as the techniques of fetal breathing (*tai-xi*) and herbal prescriptions,
these were all established by the supreme sages and taught by those below to provide for and transform the world of humans.
It cannot be said that this is mere emptiness or nothingness.
As for the establishment of altars and the transmission of registers, which originated with the Celestial Master,
these are further methods for the celestial deities to protect the state and its people, to govern ghosts, and to restrain malevolent spirits.
Both can assist in teaching and transforming the world;
for this reason, this Way is ranked among the state's institutions and is considered one of the Three Teachings alongside Confucianism and Buddhism.
As for the distinctions between small and great, superior and inferior, internal and external,
these can be clearly discerned. Thus,
Kan Ze addressed the King of Wu, saying:
The Way serves Heaven;
Heaven serves the Buddha.
Li Shiqian’s discourse on the Three Teachings states:
Confucianism is the five stars;
Daoism is the moon;
Buddhism is the sun.
If one can penetrate this meaning, then the positions of the three teachings are established.
The worldly parlance of "Confucianism, Daoism,
and Buddhism" is fundamentally based upon this.
That Confucian scholars and Daoist priests fail to distinguish between the fundamental and the derivative,
and thus seek to disparage and insult the followers of Śākyamuni,
is entirely the fault of those who have studied only the superficial branches of learning.
If you, O follower of the Way, support such ancient falsehoods as the claim that Laozi converted the barbarians and that the Buddha served as his attendant,
you slander Laozi and profane the World-Honored One.
"What would be the fault in this? Then,

offering a Sanskrit Buddhist scripture from India.

"For forty years now there has been no wind or waves at sea;
this suggests that a sage has appeared in the Middle Kingdom."
In the second month of the ninth year,
the śramaṇa Tianjue from the country of Udyāna in Northern India and the śramaṇa Miaode from the country of Siṃhala in Southern India [arrived].
In the fourth month, śramaṇas from the kingdom of Kaśa in Western India arrived, each presenting śarīra relics and Sanskrit scriptures;
each was granted purple robes and gold brocade. Also in the fourth month, the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema from the kingdom of Sarvāla in Central India arrived, presenting Sanskrit scriptures.
Bestowal of Purple Robes: In the fifth month, the śramaṇa Puzhi from Varṇu in East India arrived and presented Sanskrit scriptures;
he was bestowed with purple robes.

as for the Śramaṇas from the Five Indias gathering in competition at the imperial court,
none has ever been as magnificent as this present occasion.
Could it be that the flourishing of the Dharma’s destiny is also a response to the Emperor’s virtue?
Among the five kingdoms of India, it is only the Kingdom of Siṃhala that can be clearly identified through the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions).
The rest cannot be verified.
Indeed, the vicissitudes of affairs from antiquity to the present are like those from the Han and Tang dynasties to the current Song dynasty.
In truth, it is but a single realm.
The śramaṇa Jiquan returned from the Western Heaven with Buddhist relics and erected a stupa in Yangzhou.
[There is also] the stone niche Buddha at Longmen Mountain in the Western Capital.
After many years, it had fallen into ruin.
The Emperor commanded the śramaṇa Xiyuan to provide craftsmen for its restoration;
in total, there were seventeen thousand three hundred and thirty-nine statues. In the ninth month, no rain fell.
An imperial edict summoned the śramaṇa Zhìwù of Mount Guishan in Sīzhōu to the capital to reside at Kāibǎo Monastery and pray for rain.
Zhìwù had previously been moved by his efficacy in praying for rain in Sīzhōu;
he had once severed one of his arms.
At this point, he spoke again, saying,
"If it rains within seven days, I shall further sacrifice another arm.
On the fifth day, there was a great rain.
He then cut off one of his arms.

to which Huiguo replied:
He was unharmed.
When people saw that his severed arm was bloodless,
they found it most extraordinary.
The Governor of Sishou and the people of the commandery all had the same dream.
Śāṇakavāsin said to them,
"Wu is one among five hundred arhats."
He has come here to save the world.
In the fourth month of the first year of the Tianxi era,
an imperial edict was issued, stating:
The Golden Immortal bestowed his teachings, truly benefiting all sentient beings;
the texts transcribed upon palm leaves ought to be supported through translation and transmission.
Should the lineages of their masters differ...

having already lost precision and detail, errors gradually come to prevail.
This is all the more so when sacrifices involving meat and blood are utterly profane toward the True Vehicle.

From this time forward...

Such scriptural passages as these may not be translated. In the seventh month, an imperial edict was issued granting four thousand six hundred and twenty fascicles of printed copies of the *Teachings of the Wise One* (Zhìzhě Jiàowén) from Mount Dōngyè in Tāizhōu.
While residing at Mount Shouzhuang, Zhenru encouraged the people of the commandery to construct a library pavilion to enshrine [the scriptures].
In the ninth month, Chancellor Wang Dan passed away; on the day before his death, he instructed Yang Yi, the Hanxue Academician, saying:

"I am deeply weary of this toilsome life.

"Do not place gold or jewels inside the coffin.

"The Duke was one of the Three Dukes."
How could the ceremonial robes of a Duke (*gong*) used for burial be added to the body of a monk?
One should simply place the three monastic robes (*tricīvara*) within the coffin, rather than burying precious gems or jade.

— *Xiangshan Yalu* Prime Minister Wang Qinruo concurrently served as the Commissioner for the Polishing of Translated Scriptures. In the eleventh month, an imperial edict was issued to all prefectures and commanderies to re-establish the Ponds for Releasing Living Creatures (*fangsheng chi*).

In places where there were no existing ponds, fishing was prohibited for five li along the upper and lower reaches of the waterways near the cities of the provinces along the Yangtze and Huai Rivers; Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty established eighty-one such "Ponds for Releasing Living Creatures."

Yan Zhenqing composed an inscription to record his virtuous deeds. At Yanqing Monastery in Siming, Dharma Master Li gathered ten monks to perform the Lotus Sūtra Repentance ritual for a period of three years,
intending to cremate his own body as an offering to the Dharma.
Yang Yi, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, had long admired his reputation for the Way;
he sent a letter urging him to remain in the world,
stating that it was precisely the time for the revival of the Tiantai teachings.
Relying solely on you to maintain the transmission as an excellent guide for the world,
I have further composed letters to the Prefect Li Yigeng and to Ciyun of India,
requesting that they likewise provide counsel to dissuade him.
Shortly thereafter, Prince Nuptial Li Zunxū also submitted a letter with earnest exhortations.
Because the intentions of both the public and the private were so persistent, the Master ultimately abandoned his former resolve;
he then again gathered ten monks to perform the Mahākaruṇā-pūjā (Great Compassion Repentance) for three years.
To fulfill his supreme vow,
in the second year [of the reign], he issued an imperial edict for Changgan Temple in Shengzhou,
Jiangning Prefecture, to be renamed Tianxi.
The stupa is named Shenggan (Holy Response).
It is one of the nineteen stupas containing the relics of King Aśoka preserved within the Eastern Land. The stupa is located outside the city walls.
In the eighth month of the third year.
In offering sincere thanks for the Great Amnesty throughout the Realm by the Imperial Ancestor,
the text states:
"The wondrous Way of the Supreme Sovereign and the True Vehicle of Western India."
As we all originate from the source of transformation, we dare not forget to revere and uphold it.
May all monks, nuns, Daoist priests, female priests, and their affiliated apprentices throughout the empire be universally ordained.
Lin, the Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs,
was specially appointed as the Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices for the issuance of official documents.
In this year, 230,127 persons were ordained as monks.
There were 15,643 nuns, 7,081 male Daoist practitioners,
and 89 female Daoist practitioners (nüguan).
By imperial decree, a Daoist altar was established in the Tiān'ān Hall to offer thanks to Heaven and Earth.
The great assembly consisted of 10,308 Sha-men and Daoists.
The Emperor personally bestowed upon them large silver coins made of medicinal silver; this "medicinal silver" is quicksilver.
The *Yinshi* (Silver World) calls it "dry mercury. During the period when the imperial court extended its grace for a universal ordination,
the śramaṇa Daocheng of Moon-Disk Mountain in Qiandao compiled the three-fascicle *Essentials of Buddhism*.
For those who have left the household life, these various dharmas must be known and practiced in the world. [Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa and others.
We respectfully request that the Imperial Commentary on the Sutra of Forty-two Sections and the Imperial Commentary on the Sutra of the Bequeathed Teachings be included.
It was entered into the Imperial Library and promulgated.
The Emperor’s decree was granted. Prime Minister Wang Qinruo departed for the military governorship of Qiandang.
He led his subordinates to visit Master Ciyun Zunshi at Mount Ling in India to request him to lecture on the Lotus Sutra,
whereupon he sighed and said:
"This path has never been heard of before;
it has never been seen by such a person.
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial using the ancient name of India for the bestowal of the title.
The Master petitioned the Emperor to designate West Lake as a sanctuary for the release of living beings.
Every year on the eighth day of the fourth month,
the people of the commandery would gather upon the lake to release fish and birds.
To offer prayers for the longevity of the Sovereign. In the eleventh month, the kingdom of Dongnuzhen (Eastern Jurchen) presented tribute and requested that the Tripitaka be granted to them;
an imperial edict was issued to provide it.
In the first month of the fourth year,
Miyan and others of the Right Street (Right Ward) Lecture Hall requested that the Emperor’s own composition,
the *Shidian fayin ji* (Anthology of Dharma Sounds from the Buddhist Scriptures), be annotated by monks; the work comprised thirty fascicles in total.
He requested that it be included in the Great Canon (Tripitaka).
An imperial decree granted permission.
Initially, Yang Yi had been presiding over these matters.
Within this concentration, there are six kinds of expressions regarding trembling.
A monk has annotated them,
totaling approximately three hundred characters.
Obscure and fragmented, it cannot be contemplated.
[The character] "yi" (億) is deleted; the original note states:
"The substance of the earth is fundamentally quiescent; movement necessarily entails change."
People marveled at his simplicity. ○ The Śramaṇa Puxian from Western Heaven came forward to present Sanskrit scriptures;
he was granted a purple robe. ○ Prince Nui Zunchu submitted a memorial stating that the Dharma Master Siming Zhili possessed lofty conduct and sacrificed his body for the Dharma.
The Emperor praised him incessantly and specially conferred upon him the title "Dharma-Wisdom" (Fazhi).
He further issued an imperial decree that he should remain in the world to propagate the teachings.
He did not permit his body to be left behind.

At that time, twenty-three individuals from the Translation Institute, including the Chief Proofreader Jianchang and others, each composed a verse poem to praise his virtue and conduct; these poems are recorded in the *Siming Jiaoxing Lu*.
And a stone inscription was carved at Nanhu. In the twelfth month, Yang Yi, the Hanlin Academician, passed away.
Yi had devoted himself to Chan meditation;
from the time he fell ill, he immediately abstained from meat and pungent vegetables.
On the day of his death, he composed a verse on the "Empty Gate" (śūnyatā) to manifest his resolve;

On Mount Muping in Yuanzhou, a stone stūpa containing śarīras appeared spontaneously.
At night, it emitted five-colored rainbow light,
and within a lunar disc, a sixteen-foot Buddha was visible.
Avalokiteśvara and the Arhats stood in attendance on his left and right.
In the second year,
images of Arhats appeared upon a stone cliff at Mount Dongshan in Yanzhou.
In the fourth month of summer, there was no rain.
Wang Gu, the local governor of Yuanzhou, went to pray at the Holy Pagoda on Mount Muping.
A light shone forth from within the rock.
He saw the body of the Great Being clad in white robes, adorned with golden necklaces, from which he obtained śarīra relics.
They were five-colored and as large as jujube fruits;
within them was the form of a multi-storied pavilion.
He went again to the stupa site at Mount Yangshan,

and by imperial decree, the name of the Mupyeong Pagoda was bestowed as Hye-gyeong,
and that of the Angsan Pagoda as Sae-gyeong.

the Chan Master Foguo Weibai of Fayun Temple compiled the *Xudenglu* (Continued Record of the Lamp) in thirty fascicles and presented it to the throne.

A new refinement through a hundredfold adamantine smelting;

The third year.

How great!

May scholars of future generations who are able to infer this significance and present it to the central court petition for the implementation of regulations regarding avoidance.
Is this not a case of having a teacher and model within the Confucian gate?
The śramaṇa Huìhóng of Yǒngjū, whose courtesy name was Juéfàn, was exiled to Yáizhōu for his association with the Chancellor Zhāng Shāngyīng and the Regional Commander Guō Tiānxìn.
Upon hearing this, Chan Master Lingyuan Qing sighed and said,
"When orchids are planted in the middle of a path,
they will certainly not remain verdant for long."

yet it retains its crimson heart for many years;
as the ancients said:
Those who are clever and profoundly analytical yet come close to death are those who delight in criticizing others;
this was the case with Juefan.
In the second year,
Bian Zhibai, a Court Gentleman,
traveled from the capital to Linchuan.
Having contracted an illness due to the summer heat,
he suddenly dreamed of a celestial being dressed in white who sprinkled water upon him;
from his crown to his heels, he was cooled by its refreshing chill.
Upon awakening, he felt an immediate sense of clarity and refreshment.

Thereupon, he compiled accounts of miraculous responses from both ancient and modern times, producing the *Guanyin Ganying Ji* (Collection of Avalokiteśvara’s Responsive Manifestations) in four fascicles for circulation in the world; these were carved onto wooden printing blocks at Upper Zhong. The Governor of Jiazhou submitted a memorial regarding this.
A wind and thunderstorm snapped down an ancient tree.
Inside it was a monk in meditative concentration, his hair and beard covering his body.
An imperial decree ordered him to be carried by palanquin to the inner palace.
The Tripitaka Master Jin Zongchi, who was translating the scriptures,
struck a golden chime to awaken him with its sound and asked his name.
He replied, "I am Huichi, the younger brother of Dharma Master Huiyuan."
Having traveled to this place from Mount Emei,
I asked where he intended to return.
He replied, "To within the ancient tree in Chenliu."
The Emperor issued an edict to escort him with full ceremonial honors.
He subsequently had the Master’s portrait painted and composed a eulogy for it, which read:
"For seven hundred years, this ancient patriarch."
Who can know the news from within meditative concentration?
How could it compare to departing westward with a single sandal?
What need is there to labor over the wooden skin of birth and death? Three verses in total; here I record one of them, as cited in the *Pudeng lu*.
The commentary states:
According to the Master’s own biography,
he entered parinirvāṇa at Longyuan in Xian County.
There was a final testament left at the time of his death;
yet now it is said that he traveled to Mount Emei and arrived here.
This suggests that the Holy Master has undergone a divine transformation.
One must not allow oneself to be constrained by the traces of birth and death.
[This was written] three years later by the Tripitaka Master of Sūtra Translation, Mingyin Miaoshan Pujie Dashi, Jin Zongchi.
The same person served as the *yenyi* (translator of meaning) while Zongzheng acted as the *bishou* (scribe).
He traveled south through Jiangzhe to Chexi in Xiuzhou.

it never says to hang it over the shoulder.

The commentary states:

Regarding the discussion from antiquity concerning "right circumambulation" (*pradakṣiṇa*), the term "circumambulation" (*yào*) implies encircling, while "to circumambulate" (*zàoyào*) implies winding around. This is not like the terminology used for constructing a grass hut, which has two distinct meanings.
[In this context], it refers to being to the right of the Buddha.
To the right of the self,
it is exhausted. Yet,
Cao’an mistakenly clings to the right of the self.
That is to say, baring the right shoulder is convenient for manual labor, and lying on the right side is an auspicious posture for sleep.

Turning to the left signifies remoteness to represent evil;
turning to the right signifies ease to represent goodness.
Turning to the left is like an examination.
Turning to the right, as the hair of the Sage turns to the right while that of ordinary people turns to the left— only the Buddha’s hair turning to the right being entirely for the sake of the self—
he then circumambulated the golden coffin of his parinirvāṇa to the right, proceeding from the east toward the south.

yet he was unaware that he had erred himself.

people mostly use "circumambulating from oneself" (or "starting from oneself") when performing circumambulation to the right.

therefore, I cannot help but clarify this.
