He saw that the number of śarīra relics within the ceramic vessel was beyond calculation. In the eleventh month, Zonggao was demoted to Hengzhou and subsequently transferred to Meizhou.
Shu stated:
"From antiquity, high officials who associated with the Śākya clan..."
It is simply that they revere the Way and honor the person; in our own dynasty, those among the high officials who engage with the Śākya teachings are especially numerous.
I have never heard of anyone being mutually implicated by the transgression of their speech.
Hong Juefan was exiled to Zhuya for his association with Zhang Wujin;
Daoyuan and Dahui were sent to Hengyang.
Zuo Jiao associated with Zhang Zishao,
yet both were charged with the crime of their speech. Indeed,
such was the nature of the association between Confucians and Buddhists.
It was merely a matter of responding to one another’s verses and discussing the Way;
otherwise, it would have been nothing more than the kind of social gathering held at Mount Lu.
How could we allow ourselves to involve a worthy man in the machinations of the treacherous and wicked, or to form a faction among those dwelling in the forest?
It is a misfortune for the Dharma-gate that there are those like these two masters,
who in their discourse on affairs overstep the bounds and fail to examine the ninefold layers of subtlety.
In the tenth month of the twenty-third year,

Ping Jie (courtesy name Jichuan, style name Budong Jushi), a Palace Attendant serving as Prefect of Luzhou, was appointed by the Commissioner of Grain Transport to act as the acting governor of the prefecture.
The subordinate officials and assistants donned their robes and caps;
facing the palace gate, they performed two prostrations.
Then, wearing monastic robes, [the Master] ascended the seat.
He rested his staff across his knees and transformed [the people] by reciting a verse.
He first sought the Way from Fojiao Gaofodiri.
Having attained sudden enlightenment into the essential meaning of the mind,
after the relocation south of the Yangtze River,
he provided support for the preservation of the Tripitaka wherever it was incomplete or missing; he personally funded and encouraged the laity to produce forty-eight sets of the Great Tripitaka.

The four great sections of the Minor Canon (Kṣudrapiṭaka) were likewise established according to that number; the world regarded the *Avataṃsaka*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Ratnakūṭa*, and *Śūraṅgama* as these four great sections. Wherever they reached, eminent monks, recluses, and contemporaries of the Continued Lotus Society all followed his transformation.
In the twenty-fourth year,
an imperial edict designated Upper India as the Imperial Court’s Place of Practice (*dōjō*),
exempting it specifically from levies, assessments, and other such matters. ○ Kong Ji, the Duke of Sheng (the Confucian lineage holder) residing in Quzhou, passed away.
An imperial edict appointed his son, Jin, to succeed him as Duke of Sheng (Yansheng Gong).
This was the fiftieth generation.
In the twenty-fifth year [of the reign].
At the beginning of the Zhiping era, Chan Master Feishan Jizhu,
following the *Three Biographies of Eminent Monks*,
collected accounts of those who cultivated pure practices and were reborn in the Pure Land at the time of their death.
He composed the *Zhengtu zhuan* (Biographies of the Pure Land) in three fascicles.
During the Yuanfeng era, the Minister Wang Gu supplemented it with new accounts,
resulting in a total of four fascicles.
In this year, Lu Shishou of Qiantang compiled a continuation of those who attained rebirth in the Pure Land into eight fascicles,
changing the title to the *Baizhu ji* (Jewel-Bead Collection).
This was in the twenty-sixth year.
Zhang Jicheng was appointed as the Prefect of Wenzhou.
Having been exiled to Nan’an Commandery for fourteen years,
he had been residing in a Buddhist monastery at Hengpu.
He spent his days discussing the classics and composing writings for his own edification.
He once said, "The Six Classics are all sublime teachings. In the ninth month, Wu Bingxin, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, passed away.
At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, the Chancellor avoided speaking of military affairs and branded Bingxin as a partisan; consequently,
Bingxin returned to the south of the city of Siming.
He built a hermitage and sat in meditation;
he fashioned a coffin and slept within it at night.
At the fifth watch, he ordered a youth to knock on the coffin and sing:
"Wu Xinsou, come back!
There is no peace in the three realms; it is not a place where one may dwell."
In the Pure Land of the West there are lotus wombs;
go back, return!
Upon hearing this chant, immediately rise for meditation and recitation.
After a long time, Qin Hui passed away.
[He] was summoned to serve as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
At that time, the state treasury was depleted.
Bingxin requested permission to sell ordination certificates (dujie) in order to enrich the state;
however, he was subsequently impeached for his association with the Qin faction.
Because he had sought blessings through devotion to Buddhism, he was dispatched to serve as the Governor of Changzhou.
Shortly thereafter, he was summoned again to the Pingshan post station.
He ordered his family members to listen quietly, and they all heard the sound of celestial music.
He then said:
"Having lost mindfulness within the Pure Realm, I have arrived here.
Now that the golden platform has reached me, I shall proceed.
Having spoken these words, he passed away. In the tenth month, an imperial decree ordered Zonggao to be transferred to Meizhou.
He resumed his secular appearance and was released to return home.
In the eleventh month, an imperial edict ordered him to reside at Ayuwang Mountain in Mingzhou.
In the eighth month of the twenty-seventh year.
He Yunchong, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, ascended the dais.
The Emperor asked,
"How many monks and Daoists are there in the empire?"
The answer was:
"There are two hundred thousand monks and ten thousand Daoist practitioners."
The Emperor said,
"I have observed that among the scholar-officials who serve the Buddha,
many beg for the issuance of ordination certificates."
Currently, many agricultural lands lie fallow.
There are two hundred thousand people who consume food without tilling the soil.
If more ordination certificates were issued, [the situation would worsen].
This is to drive away farmers and turn them into monks.
Since the Buddha-dharma entered China during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty,
its Way has been vast and great, and can never be abolished.
"It is not that I have any intention to sever [the monastic order].
I simply fear that if the number of monks becomes too great, those who do not till the soil will be many.
Therefore, I have temporarily suspended the ordination of monks," so it is recorded in the *Shengzheng Lu* (Record of Sacred Governance).
The commentary states:
Emperor Gaozong was intelligent and adept at the way of expedient means;
therefore, he did not issue *du-cao* (ordination certificates).
The intention is to suppress the monastic community in order to assist agriculture;
this is precisely like the ancients who excluded Buddhism on the grounds that those who do not farm are a parasitic burden upon the state.
This may be called knowing the root of governance.
Nevertheless, I have often deliberated upon this:
as for those who are monks today.
I have not yet had the leisure to speak of them in terms of studying the Way.
Some are pressed by the large number of brothers,
while others lack fields and thus do not cultivate.
They are all the indigent and vagrant people of the world.
They dwell in deep mountains where snakes and tigers roam,
and in coastal lands of salt marshes and barren soil.
This is not a field of agriculture.
Those who have left the household life rely on the collective strength of the community and the power of their own vows.
Fortunately, these can be opened up for cultivation as fields;
they are all fallow lands throughout the empire.
Let the idle people cultivate these fallow lands for their sustenance.
They have never suffered from farming; moreover,
those who now farm are already numerous,
and they constantly lament that the arable land in the world is too scarce.
The assets of the monasteries were always fixed;
by not allowing commoners to become monks, agriculture increased.
With more farmers and fewer permanent fields, [the state's revenue grew].
Agriculture first fell into distress;
people left it to become merchants and traders,
or artisans of the hundred crafts.
Some wander about begging for alms;
some become performers or courtesans;
those who pursue such trivial ends do so in great numbers.
Furthermore, when they are unable to do so [legitimately], they plunder at sea and raid on land;
there is nothing they will not do.
Thus, one must drive out these idlers and organize them into a monastic community.
This is also a strategic method of governance;
how can it not be studied and clarified?
On the sixth day of the tenth month.
Chan Master Zhengjue of Mount Tiandong bathed,
changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away.
From his teeth, hair, and meditation implements, śarīras spontaneously emerged.
His entire body was interred in the Eastern Valley,
and his stupa was posthumously named "The Stupa of Chan Master Hongzhi Miaoguang.
There were those who came to pay respects at the stupa seeking śarīra relics.
All were fulfilled according to his wishes.

Nine generations after Dongshan, in the second month of the twenty-eighth year [of the Shaoxing era], an imperial decree was issued for Chan Master Zonggao, "Buddha-Sun," to reside once again at Mount Jing. In the seventh month, Hong Zun, Secretary of the Bureau of Remonstrance, [submitted a memorial].
When the discussion regarding the casting of coins had not yet reached its quota,
the Emperor issued an edict to his ministers,
ordering that copper utensils among the common people be replaced with other materials.
Thereupon, bronze vessels from the Imperial Treasury were sent to the Minting Office.
All bronze objects among the populace, including Buddhist and Daoist statues, bells, and chimes from temples and monasteries,
were ordered to be inventoried and recorded in registers.
Twenty [coins] were collected for each jin.
Shu said: "During the Shaoxing era, I resided in the office that sold ordination certificates."
He did not consider this a profit;
moreover, he levied taxes on monks and Daoists to exempt them from corvée labor, and collected fees for temple bells and chimes at monasteries and observatories,
yet the proceeds were not great.
Yet they merely cause later generations to point to them as antiquities.
It is because the subordinate official Zhan Shuyi understands that the root of revenue and taxation lies in the mind of the sovereign.
At that time, however, the ministers were unable to explain the relative gravity of the benefits involved.
In the eleventh month of the thirtieth year,
Chan Master Daochang of Lingyin Temple submitted a memorial to the throne.
He requested that ordination certificates be issued,
but no response was received.
In the thirty-first year.
Wu Zicai, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites,
submitted a memorial requesting the issuance of ordination certificates (*duce*).
Those who commented on the matter dismissed him as a sycophant for Buddhism.
He retired to his fields and village. In the seventh month, the Jurchen ruler Yuan Yanliang moved his residence to Bianjing.
In the ninth month, he personally led an army to invade.
The army numbered one million.
The śramaṇa Tanyi of Zhongzhu Temple studied Chan and attained insight into the *Yi* (Book of Changes);
he was frequently summoned to the imperial court.
At this point, he divined by means of the *Yi* numerals and declared that Zhuge Liang would perish north of the Yangtze River.
In the tenth month, he issued an edict for a personal campaign against Zhexi.
General Li Baozhou defeated them.
Yu Wenwen, Secretariat Drafter of Mizhou,
gathered the scattered troops of Commander-in-Chief Wang Quan and defeated them at Caishi.
Liang intended to cross at Guazhou and issued an order to his subordinates, saying,
"If I do not cross the river within three days, you shall all be executed."
The people suffered under his tyranny.
At midnight, several chieftains shot him within his tent and fled.
In the first month of the thirty-second year.
The Emperor returned from Jiankang.
In the fifth month, he issued an edict to abdicate the throne in favor of the Crown Prince. In the tenth month, torrential rain did not cease;
the Emperor dispatched an inner attendant to pray at Upper Zhushan.
As the smoke from the sacrificial fires first rose and the morning sun broke through the clear skies,
the Emperor was delighted and presented three types of jade vessels from the Inner Treasury to be bestowed upon the Hall of the Great Being (Bodhisattva).
Empress Dowager Shoucheng bestowed a crown of the seven precious gems upon Chan Master Dahui Zonggao of Mount Jing.
This was on the twenty-second day of the tenth month, the Huiping Festival, during the reign of Emperor Xiaozong.
In the first year of the Longxing era at Yongfou Ling,
the seventh-generation descendant of Taizu, named Zhen, was serving as the Magistrate of Jiaxing.
His wife, Lady Zhang, dreamed of a divine being who identified himself as Lord Cui and presented her with a sheep.
He subsequently conceived.
Initially, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Puan. When the Emperor was first at the royal residence, he dispatched an Inner Supervisor to Jingshan.
He asked about the Way of Chan Master Gaō,
who replied with a verse:
"A great root, a great vessel, and great power."
He bore the great responsibility in an extraordinary manner.
Later, while residing in the Imperial Residence,
he dispatched an inner attendant to the mountain to bestow upon him the three characters for "Miaoxi Hermitage" (Wondrous Joy) along with a portrait eulogy.
At this point, [the Emperor] took all the previously bestowed insignia and applied the Imperial Seal to them.
On the tenth day of the eighth month of that year,
the Master passed away.
The Emperor’s grief and lamentation were unceasing;
he bestowed upon him the posthumous title Pujue and named his stupa Baoguang.
The recorded sayings were included in the Great Canon.
[This was done by] Right Minister Tang Sisuì and Senior Councillor Li Bing.
Neihan Wang Zao,
Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites Zhang Jiu-cheng,
and Palace Attendant Peng Ji.
Everyone sought instruction, and there were those who attained realization. Zhang Jun, Duke Wei, composed the inscription for his stupa.
In the second month of the first year of the Qiandao era, he summoned the Dharma Master Lingshan Zilin to have an audience with him.
The Emperor asked, "I wish to read the sutras; what should be considered essential?
The Master replied:
"The Vajra-samādhi and Perfect Enlightenment are the most essential paths.
He then asked about the method of Chan meditation.
The Master said:
One must realize this for oneself.
The above was spoken.
He was granted the title Cishou [Zen Master]. In the second month, Princess of Zhengguo left the household life.
By imperial decree, should any official or commoner insult or humiliate a monk or nun,
addressing them by the derogatory term "bald-head," they shall be dismissed from office in accordance with the edicts of the Xiangfu and Xuanhua reigns.
The common people have wandered for a thousand li;
they look upward to the prefectures and armies throughout the realm.
Post notices everywhere to inform and instruct them.
It was further permitted that the records of monks and nuns,
along with their official decrees and ordination certificates (*duce*), be kept with them at all times as permanent documents of identification.
Regarding any offenses committed by these monks and nuns:
The judicial authorities shall not adjudicate such matters privately;
they must report them to the throne for imperial edict before proceeding.
The second month of the third year.
When the Emperor visited Shang Tianzhu to pay homage to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara),
he asked the mountain abbot Ruone:
"Before the Great Being, is it appropriate to prostrate or not?"
The Master said:
"If one does not bow, each person regards themselves as superior;
if one bows, they show mutual respect."
The Emperor joyfully paid his respects and further inquired about the meaning of performing the *Guanming Chan* (Repentance of Radiant Light) on the New Year’s Day.
The Master replied:
The Buddha expounded the path of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-samādhi* for Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings,
entrusting them with the protection of the nation and its people.
Later, the patriarchs established it as a ritual for repentance (*chanyi*).
On the first day of the year, one should practice this rite to pray for blessings upon the state;
this is the ritual of a flourishing age.
As previously mentioned,

he was appointed as the Right Street Monk Registrar (youjie senglu) and further granted money to construct the Hall of the Sixteen Contemplations (shiliu guan tang) on the site of the former residence of Dharma Master Daoyi.

The Inner Secretary Lou Yao was commissioned to compose the record. In the third month, an imperial decree was issued to construct the Neiguan Hall within the Forbidden City, strictly following the architectural regulations of Upper Zhi.
An envoy from Japan sent a letter to the administration of Ming Prefecture to inquire about the general principles of the Buddha-dharma.
He requested that eminent monks be assembled to open the casket and read its contents before the imperial envoy.
The prefect gathered a great multitude,
yet the monastics were all cowed with fear and none dared to accept the summons.
Qixin the Venerable Master emerged from his quarters with joy.
The script of Japan is identical to that of China;
how could there be any cause for doubt?
He immediately bowed to the Governor, tore open the seal,
and read it with his fingernails, making seven indentations in the paper.
Having finished reading, he said to the messenger:
Although the Japanese may wish to study literature, they are not without errors and omissions;
I have therefore analyzed each point for them,
causing them to withdraw in shame and trepidation.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the fourth year, Shu leaped for joy and exclaimed, "The world's *vina*! (World-Organizer).
He summoned the Dharma Master Zhunuo from Upper Zhu and led fifty monks into the Inner Contemplation Hall to perform the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* Samādhi for the Protection of the Nation.
After the meal, he preached the Dharma.
The Emperor said,
"The Buddha-dharma is indeed wondrous."
"How can there be so many volumes of scriptures?
The Master said,
"Those who possess the fundamental source are like this."
As previously stated,
he was subsequently appointed as the Director of the Left Street (Zuoxie Senglù),
the Dharma Master Huiguang.
From that time on, every year on the Buddha’s birthday, fifty bolts of silk were granted to the monks who entered the palace to perform Buddhist rites.
Song Zhi composed the inscription for the stupa. In the ninth month, the Emperor said to Li Tao, the Minister of Rites:
The texts for the civil service examinations must not employ the language of Buddhism or Daoism;
however, if one cultivates oneself in the mountain forests,
there is no harm to the Way.
If this were employed in the imperial examinations,
it would likely hinder the administration and the revitalization of state affairs. In the *Shushi* (Discourse on the Mirror of Revitalizing Affairs),
it is stated:
The Confucians have long employed the language of Laozi and Zhuangzi;
therefore, it cannot be abruptly discarded.
As for the subtleties of investigating principle (li) and the profundities of exhausting one's nature (xing), [these remain essential].
That which rises above the mundane world and yet encompasses all things without exception is none other than the scriptures of the Śākya school. Nevertheless,
the Confucianists seek to clarify the principles governing the relationship between Heaven and humanity.
The *Yi*, *Hongfan*, *Zhongyong*, *Daxue*, and the *Analects* and *Mencius* are sufficient for one’s own inquiry;
should one venture into the words and meanings of Buddhist scriptures, [one will find them therein].
Thus, one would contradict their own fundamental tenets and fall into unrestrained license without any refuge.
How great are the admonitions of the Greatly Virtuous King (King Sejong)!
They surely possess profound significance.
In the fourth month of the sixth year,
the Emperor discussed with his ministers the cycles of order and chaos, and of decline and growth, regarding the Eastern Capital.
The Emperor said:
Whenever I reflect upon the period before the establishment of peace and order, the state was free from affairs.
Since An Shi-shi first brought disorder to the established laws,
this was followed by Zhang Zhi-thou (whose name was changed to Dun to avoid taboo), Cai Jing, and their ilk.
By the time of the Jingkang era, the assisting ministers were for the most part mediocre and deluded,
leading to a total collapse.
Cai Jing died in exile in Huxiang forty-two years later.
On the day of the relocation of the burial, his skin and flesh had completely decayed;
only on his chest did a swastika (*svastika*) emerge,
appearing as if it had been carved there.
According to the Buddhist scriptures, the Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks;
the *svastika* on his chest is one of them.
It is accomplished through the gradual cultivation of morality, concentration, and wisdom;
its characteristics are luminous and wondrous.
Even Māra possesses the thirty-two marks.
Its characteristics have become somewhat obscure;
now that the situation in the capital is like this,
could it not be the work of Māra?

Furthermore, is it not the case that this demonic being was produced by the great cosmic cycles of Heaven and Earth as a calamity for the living people? [This is from] *Liangchao Shijian* (Mirror of State Affairs of the Two Dynasties) and *Rongzhai Sanbi* (Three Notes from the Studio of Containment). Written in the eleventh month at Deokjeon Hall, His Majesty personally inscribed the names of "In-gwang Gwan-jeom Temple" and the "In-gwang Gwan-jeom Treasure Hall."
He bestowed upon Shangzhu [Monastery] the six characters as its plaque.
In the second month of the seventh year,
Chan Master Huiyuan of Lingyin entered the Xuande Hall for an audience.
The Emperor asked,
"How can one escape birth and death?
He replied:
"Without awakening to the Mahāyāna, one can never escape [suffering].
The Emperor asked,
"How can one attain awakening?"
He replied,
"The nature that has existed from the beginning is naturally realized through polishing it over the course of years and months.
The Emperor said:
"After awakening, what is it like?
He replied,
"After awakening, one finally realizes that all the questions and answers of today were not [the truth]."
The Master said,
"If there is nothing that is not so in all places,
what then? He replied:
The manifestation of liberation was present before him, with no further signs to be seen.
His superior acknowledged this with a nod.
In the first month of the eighth year.
The imperial carriage visited Lingyin Temple,
where the Emperor bestowed increased gifts and honors. In the eighth month, he summoned Dharma Master Ne of Tiantong,
Chan Master Yin of Mount Jing, Bao Yin of Biefeng, and Chan Master Yuan of Lingyin.
He also assembled scholars of the Three Teachings in the Neiguan Hall to bestow upon them a vegetarian feast;
furthermore, he ordered Master Yuan to enter the Dongge Pavilion alone to be granted a seat.
Question:
The other day, while asleep, I suddenly heard the sound of a bell;
I did not know whether I was dreaming or awake.
"Are they the same or different?
He replied, "Dreaming and waking are no different; whom would you have teach to distinguish them?"
The Emperor asked,
"From where does the sound of the bell arise?
He replied:
Beginning from Your Majesty’s inquiry:
In the tenth month, the title Chan Master Fohai Xiatang was bestowed upon Huiyuan of Lingyin.
In the first month of the ninth year.
The Dharma Master Zhuneng of Shangzhu was summoned and granted an audience alone in Xuande Hall.

He was offered a seat, and the Emperor questioned him regarding the miraculous traces of Great Beings throughout successive dynasties and the essential meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra*; this is recorded in the *Dengduilu*. Meanwhile, Duke Wei Shi Hao retired from public life in Siming.
He styled himself the Recluse Zhenyin.
He frequently sought out Master Zhilian of Nanhu to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma.
Master Jueyun once remarked to him, "Does the Master also have a thorough mastery of both Chan and the Vinaya?"
The Master said,
"When the ice melts and the snow dissolves, it is surely but one water.
He asked again.
The Avataṃsaka and Prajñāpāramitā sutras—how excessively fragmented they are!
The Master said:
"It is precisely because they are fragmented that they are simple and easy."
The Duke suddenly attained a profound realization.
Upon returning to his native village after serving as the Governor of Min,
he established Mount Yuebo at Donghu.
He was sent to Mount Potalaka,
where a cave-dwelling was constructed for him to reside as a Great Being (Mahāsattva),
and he was honored with the title of Deśou Dian.
He inscribed "Chaoyindong" (Cave of the Sound of the Tide) as its plaque.

He first invited Master Ze-yue, a senior disciple of Jueyun Gao, who specialized in lecturing on the teachings of Zhiyi and was titled Yuan'an Cizhi Haishi. Initially, this master had served as the Superintendent of Salt for Changguo.
Accompanied by Cheng Xiufu of Poyang, he sailed across the sea to visit Mount Putuo.
Suddenly, a monk pointed to the summit of a cliff,
where there was a crevice from which one could look down.
While he was gazing and waiting in expectation, the Duke and the assembly beheld the Great Being’s golden physical form;
furthermore, the Duke saw two teeth protruding from the corners of his lips like white jade.
Reassured by this, he paid homage and withdrew.
When he returned to the monastery, it was already dusk.
A tall, lanky monk came to visit him and told him that his official career had culminated in the rank of Grand Preceptor (Taishi).
Furthermore, it was said:
"Lord Wen Lugu was one who met a good end;
in days to come, he will enter the相位 (the position of Chancellor)."
The Sovereign intends to employ military force;
you must remonstrate with him earnestly.
Twenty years hence, he shall meet with you at Yue.
Having finished speaking, he departed.

At the beginning of the Qiandao era, while the former Chancellor was stationed in Yue, a man of the Way arrived who called himself Master Yangsu; he claimed to have been an old acquaintance of the Duke.
He immediately ordered him to be invited in.
He took up paper and wrote in large characters:
"Black-headed Prime Minister of Lu, you further enhance the splendor of ten thousand miles."
The blue-eyed barbarian monk once shared intimate conversation with him for an entire night;
he then cast down his brush and departed abruptly,
leaving the Master greatly astonished.
Reflecting upon these matters concerning Putuo, I realized that both the tall-bodied monk and the Daoist practitioner were manifestations of Great Beings (Mahāsattvas).
This occurred twenty years prior to the present year. Thus it is recorded in the *Yijianzhi*.
Record of the Potalaka Wall Painting. ○ Currently, in the Gyōdō Hall, there is a single scroll depicting the manifestations of Potalaka as seen by the Grand Master.
It states:
At the beginning of King Gye’s official career...
Ascending Mount Potalaka to behold the Great Being,
he heard the words of a tall-robed monk,
who promised that one day he would serve as his teacher.
Furthermore, he entrusted him with the advice that His Majesty should not employ military force.
Later, when Zhang Weigong Xu indeed urged Emperor Xiaozong on a northern expedition,
the Prince of Yue remonstrated against it, but his words were not heeded.
When Fu Li’s troops were defeated, Xuun returned to see the Emperor.
The Emperor welcomed him and said to Xuun,
"This expedition was very pleasing to Shi Hao."
It was because the Great Being had foreseen the timing of events and knew that the north and south were divided and could not yet be reunified; thus,
he instructed you to offer remonstrance in order to spare the living beings from being reduced to a state of ruin and suffering.
When Lord Wei of the Shih family passed by Mount Jinshan,
he observed the grandeur of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty’s ritual for the Water and Land (shuilu) offerings and remarked that the Way of repaying kindness and saving the world lies herein.
Thereupon, he established a hall on Mount Yuebo (Moon-Wave Mountain) and installed images of the ten realms;
together with renowned monks, he researched and compiled four fascicles of ritual texts for the performance of ceremonies,
which were offered as worship according to the four seasons.

For the Universal Salvation Great Fast (Pudu Dazhai), which has continued for a hundred years until now, the sacrificial vessels have been refined through a balance of complexity and simplicity; the musical ensemble is appropriate to the occasion, and the sounds of the hymns and chants are modulated with rhythmic restraint.
In the various monasteries of the countryside and cities, there was none that did not regard this as the Dharma [text]. Wang Rihui,
a student of the National Academy from Longshu,
composed several hundred thousand words of exegesis and transmission for the Six Classics.
Once he renounced them, he said:
"These are all merely habitual karmic tendencies and not the ultimate Dharma.
Shall I not rather seek my return to the Western Land?"
From that time on, he single-mindedly practiced mindfulness of the Buddha,
reciting the name a thousand times daily as his regular practice.
One night, he recited the name of the Buddha with a resolute voice.
Suddenly he said, "The Buddha has come to receive me," and stood upright, passing away.
The people of the region dreamed that two youths dressed in green led him westward.
Nichiyo composed the *Jōdōmon* (Treatise on the Pure Land), which has circulated throughout the world.
He once provided a commentary for it, stating:
"Among Confucianists, there are some who disparage the teachings of the Buddha because they claim that his followers lack moral discipline."
How can one disparage Laozi because the Way has flowed to those who are unworthy,
or disparage Confucius because scholars have been unworthy?
The teachings of the Śākya [Buddha] comprise both mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas.
Regarding the worldly dharmas of refraining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct,
Confucianism and Buddhism have never differed.
That which differs is as follows:
The Dharma of the Śākyas transcends the world,
whereas Confucianism remains within the world; therefore,
it speaks only of a single lifetime and attributes all to Heaven.

Li served as State Preceptor. Emperor Xuanzong summoned Chan Master Jing to the palace to inquire about the Way. Emperor Suzong summoned Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra to bestow the consecration and precepts. An imperial edict invited Chan Master Zhong of Nanyang to inquire about the Way. He summoned Dharma Master Lin into the inner palace to lecture on the sutras. Emperor Daizong issued an edict to establish the Ullambana Assembly.

The imperial ancestral shrines were established with spirit seats, and processions were held along the ceremonial roads. An imperial edict summoned Chan Master Qin of Mount Jing to an audience; he was granted the title Chan Master Guoyi.

Emperor Dezong visited Anguo Temple to establish offerings for the *Ullambana* festival. Emperor Shunzong issued an edict for Chan Master Śīla to inquire about the principles of Chan. Emperor Xianzong questioned Master Guan regarding the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm.

Suddenly he attained realization. [The Emperor] conferred upon him the title of Great State Preceptor Qingliang. He summoned Chan Master Yi of Ehu to inquire about Buddha-nature; he summoned Chan Master Dan of Zhangjing to consult on the methods of Chan; and he summoned Chan Master Kuan to consult on the essentials of Chan. Emperor Muzong dispatched officials from the two monastic districts to welcome and invite Chan Master Fenyang Wuye.
In the middle of the night, he preached the Dharma and passed away while sitting upright. Emperor Jingzong visited Xingfu Temple to observe Master Xu’s lecture on the sutras.

Emperor Wenzong issued an edict for Chan Master Guifeng Mi to inquire about the Buddha-dharma. Emperor Xuanzong dispatched an envoy to summon Chan Master Yanguan An with the etiquette due to a teacher.

He declined the appointment with firm resolve. An imperial edict was issued to establish Qi-feng Temple at his residence. Emperor Wen summoned Chan Master Bian to the palace for an audience to inquire about the Way. During the reign of Emperor Yizong, the Emperor invited renowned monks into the inner palace to establish lecture halls; he personally announced the titles of the sutras and transcribed the Sanskrit texts by hand. He also hosted a vegetarian feast for ten thousand monks, ascending the seat himself to lead the chanting of hymns and praises.
A monk with long eyebrows came to receive offerings and then departed,
soaring through the air.
This was during the reign of Emperor Zhuangzong of the Later Tang in the Five Dynasties period.
The Great Song Taizu summoned Chan Master Rengan of Sansheng to inquire about the Dharma;
he then issued an edict to Shen Yilun.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was transcribed with characters in gold and silver;

Master Yun was summoned to lecture upon it. An imperial edict ordered Dharma Master Chao and others to enter the palace to recite the *Tripiṭaka* written in golden characters. The Emperor himself frequently read and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He said to Zhao Pu, "I do not wish for those in armor to know of this;
simply say that I am reading books on military strategy. Emperor Taizong then summoned the barefoot Daoist to an audience.
Question: Regarding the Chan and Vinaya traditions of the South, how do they transform sentient beings? [And so forth. [The Master] said: "Fortunately, open the treasure pagoda.
He asked: "Who is this monk? He replied: "I am the master of the pagoda."
The Emperor said,
"For what reason did Your Majesty appoint you as the master of my stupa? The Emperor asked,
"Where have you come from, monk?"
The Master replied,
"At Woyun Hermitage on Mount Lu.
The Emperor said:

Reclining deep within the clouds, he did not attend court. An imperial edict was issued for the Monastic Records of the Two Streets to submit the *Yulanpen* ritual procedures. True Zong summoned the Dharma Master Fushijiu to lecture on the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*. Ren Zong wore a jade crown while viewing the Avalokiteśvara image.
He presided over the assembly of officials at court; he issued an imperial decree to welcome the robe and alms bowl of the Sixth Patriarch from Shaozhou to the capital for veneration;
he issued an edict summoning Chan Master Lian of the Left Street to have an audience in the Huacheng Hall; and he summoned Chan Master Shun to have an audience in the private palace.
Bestowed purple robes and a silver bowl. ○ Imperial decree for the Qianyuan Festival: to establish a great vegetarian feast at Fusheng Stūpa Monastery and bestow *kāṣāya* robes.
○ Imperial decree of Emperor Shen宗: to provide a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks within the inner palace.
Bestowal of a *Kāṣāya* from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. An Imperial Edict appointing Chan Master Ben of Jingci to reside at Huilin Monastery in the Capital.
He entered the audience at the Yanhe Hall. Emperor Huizong praised his discourse.
An ancient tree had a designated monk who,
when summoned by imperial decree to the inner palace,
declared, "I am Hui-chi, the younger brother of Dharma Master Hui-yuan."
The Emperor ordered the production of portraits and the composition of hymns.

When the Qinzhong and Gaozong emperors ascended the throne, they dispatched eight carriages to summon Chan Master Qín of Jīnshān to the imperial encampment to preach the Dharma. Gaozong visited the Great Being Hall at Upper Zhù.

Incense sticks were bestowed for the "Ten-Thousand-Year Old Incense Mountain" to serve as an offering for the Great Being (Bodhisattva). Emperor Xiaozong dispatched an Inner Palace Supervisor to Jingshan to seek the Way from Chan Master Gaofeng.

Dharma Master Lingshan Lin entered the imperial presence to inquire about the Way. [The Emperor] visited Shangzhu to inquire with Dharma Master Nan about the principles of the *Guangming Chan* (Luminous Repentance) performed on New Year’s Day.
He was granted money to construct the Hall of the Sixteen Contemplations (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā-śālā*).

The Palace Secretary Lou Yao composed a commemorative inscription. By imperial decree, the Inner Hall of Contemplation (*neiguan tang*) was established within the central building, strictly following the regulations of Upper Zhusi.
On the Buddha’s birthday, Master Ne of Upper Zhusi was summoned.
He led fifty monks into the Inner Contemplation Hall to perform the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* Samādhi for the Protection of the State,
for which he was granted fifty rolls of silk.

This was established as an annual custom. He summoned Chan Master Lingyuan of Linji to an audience at Xuande Hall; he also summoned masters from Tianzhu, Lingyin, and Jingshan, as well as scholars of the Three Teachings.

He assembled at the Neiguan Hall to bestow a vegetarian feast. He summoned the Dharma Master Neng of Shangzhu Monastery for a private audience at Xuande Hall, where he inquired about the sacred traces of the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) and the essential meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
He summoned Chan Master Zhongren of Mount Yan to enter the inner palace for an audience. He visited Shangzhu Monastery to pay homage to the Great Being.
He bestowed the seal of Baiyun Hall and commanded that practitioners of all three studies and various schools should proceed together to Baiyun Hall to be selected for its use.
He then summoned Chan Master Guang of Lingyin to an audience.
He was bestowed the title "Buddha-Reflection" (Fozhao). He summoned Chan Master Guang of Lingyin to have an audience;
[Guang] presented the *Direct Pointing at the Source of the Chan School* (*Zongmen Zhizhi*). He summoned Chan Master Yin of Xuedou to have an audience;
[Yin] presented a grand discourse in response.

On that very day, while residing at Mount Jing, the Emperor [Shizu] addressed the Dharma Master Nan as "His Majesty the Retired Emperor" and summoned him to the inner palace to provide a commentary on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
He attended the Buddha’s altar repeatedly; he attended the Buddha’s altar repeatedly—just as when Han Wudi visited the Ganquan Palace.
Regarding the ritual worship of the "Golden Man" (Jinren) at the sacrifice to Heaven: because the Han people did not yet know of the Buddha, they referred to him as the Golden Man.

Emperor Ming [of the Later Han] prostrated before the sacred tomb and the stupa of the Buddha’s *śarīra* in Luoyang. Sun Hao, the King of Wu, prostrated before the śramaṇa Kang Senghui and received the precepts. Emperor Wu of Liang faced north to pay homage to Master Yiyue and received the precepts from him. Emperor Wu of Chen led his ministers to prostrate before the Buddha’s tooth relic. The Last Ruler [of Chen] thrice summoned Zhiyi.

Please recite the Benevolent Kings Sūtra. During the reign of Emperor Taizu of the Northern Wei, whenever he passed through various commanderies and kingdoms, he would pay his respects to all śramaṇas.
Emperor Xiaowen welcomed the various statues from the capital to Luoyang.
Entering the palace to pay respects; Emperor Wenxuan of the Northern Qi commanded the Tripiṭaka Master to translate the scriptures, and the Emperor personally prostrated before the Sanskrit texts;
Emperor Wen of the Sui issued an edict inviting Dharma Master Yan to ascend the imperial throne.
Prostrating and kneeling to receive the precepts; Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty welcoming the Buddha’s bone from Fengxiang and entering the palace to pay homage;
Suzong establishing a dharma hall within the palace to pay homage, lecture, and offer praise;
Dezong casting a golden image upon its completion.

He led the hundred officials to pay their respects. Emperor Dezong welcomed the Buddhist relics from Fengxiang into the inner palace to pay them homage. Emperor Xianzong welcomed the Buddhist relics into the inner palace to pay them homage. Emperor Yizong welcomed and bowed before the Buddhist relics.
During the Shangyuan era of the Great Song Zhenzong, the Emperor visited temples and observatories and performed more than a hundred prostrations.

During the reign of Huizong, he welcomed the Buddha’s tooth relic into the palace, paid reverent homage, and composed hymns of praise. During the reign of Xiaozong, he visited the Great Being Hall at Upper Zhuzi.
He asked Master Nü whether it was appropriate to bow or not.
The Master said,
"If one does not bow, each person will claim to be superior."
In their prostrations, they showed mutual respect.
The Emperor joyfully returned their bows.
[The text includes] the *Celestial Writings* composed by the Emperor, and the *Ritual Text for Water and Land Offerings* (*Shuilu Yiwén*) composed by Emperor Wu of the Liang Dynasty.
At Mount Jinshan, he cultivated offerings; Master Sengliang composed a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

The Emperor personally composed a preface [for it]. The Emperor also personally composed commentaries on the meanings of various sutras, including the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Tri-vidyā-sūtra*. During the Tang Dynasty, Emperor Taizong [patronized] Master Xuanzang’s newly translated sutras and śāstras.

The Imperial Preface to the Sacred Teachings; the Stele for Ci'en Monastery composed by Emperor Gaozong; the Preface to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra composed by Empress Wu; and the Translation of Scriptures by Tripiṭaka Master Jing of the Zhongzong era.
The Imperial Preface to the *Sūtra of the Heap of Jewels* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra), translated by Bodhiruci under Emperor Ruizong;

the Imperial Commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* by Emperor Xuanzong; the Imperial Preface to the re-translation of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* by Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra under Emperor Daizong; the Imperial Preface to the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-cittabhūmi Sūtra* translated by Tripiṭaka Master Prajña under Emperor Xianzong; and the Imperial Praise for Vinaya Master Nanshan composed by Emperor Muzong, which is used in ritual feasts to this day.
During the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Tianxizai translated the scriptures.

The Emperor composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings" (Shèngjiào xù). He further issued an edict ordering the two monastic communities (liǎngjiē) to provide annotated commentaries on the "Exegesis of the Secret Treasury" (Mìcáng quán), the "Treatise on Causal Consciousness" (Yuánshí lùn), and the "Odes of Leisurely Roaming" (Xiāoyáo yòng).
The scriptures were entered into the canon and promulgated. ○ The Tripitaka Master Faxian of the True Sect translated the scriptures.
The Imperially Composed Preface to the Holy Teachings. ○ The Imperially Composed Treatise on the Veneration of Śākyamuni. The Emperor ascended Mount Tai to perform the Feng sacrifice.

Imperial Preface to the Record of the Dharma-Treasures of Taiping Xiangfu, Compiled by Zhao Anren under Imperial Order; Imperial Decree to Include the *Miaojue ji* (Collection of Wondrous Enlightenment) Composed by Emperor Taizong in the Tripitaka; and the Imperial Commentary on the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*.

The Imperial Commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (Yi-jiao jing). To the right, the Secretariat of the Right Street requested that the *Imperial Compositions on the Sound of the Dharma* (*Fa-yin ji*) be annotated and included in the Tripitaka. The *Hymns to the Triple Gem* (*San-bao zan*) composed by Emperor Renzong.
He bestowed upon the Translation Institute for the Monastic and Secular Officials the Imperial Preface to the *Source of Indic Characters*.

He bestowed upon the Translation Institute the Imperial Preface to the *Jingyou Catalogue of the Dharma-Treasury*. Emperor Gaozong visited the National University and composed eulogies for Confucius and his seventy-two disciples. Emperor Xiaozong calligraphed the name of the Temple of the Responsive Avalokiteśvara.
The Imperial Calligraphy "Taibai Famous Mountain" was bestowed upon Shangzhusan.
Chan Master Tiantong Pu was bestowed [the title] by the Emperor. Chan Master Fozhao Guang resided at Ayuwangshan.
He bestowed the imperial calligraphy for the plaque of the Miaosheng Hall as the Śarīra Hall; he composed the "Discourse on the Original Way" (Yuandao lun);
and he composed the "Imperial Commentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment," which he bestowed upon Chan Master Yin of Mount Jing.
"May the Sage Ruler protect the Dharma! May the Sage Ruler protect the Dharma!

Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty issued an edict stating that anyone who destroys images of Buddhas or Celestial Sovereigns shall be charged with the crime of high treason and unrighteousness. He further issued a decree regarding all locations where Buddha images, fragments of their bodies, or their remaining shadows were found.
The officials inspected and sent it to the temple for adornment during the period following the destruction of the Dharma by Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou.
During the reign of Emperor Dezong of the Tang,
Yuwen Ji was the Magistrate of Jingzhao.
He requested that the materials from a ruined temple be used for a school building, but the imperial decree did not permit it.
An edict was issued stating that temples and monasteries must be kept strictly clean and shall not allow outsiders to reside there. Xuanzong’s minister Pei Xiu stated:
Temples and monasteries were frequently trampled upon by officials and guests staying there.
Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty issued an edict that from now on, no one shall reside within these temples.
An edict was issued stating that temples which had not been destroyed during the Zhou dynasty were permitted to remain;

as for those temples already destroyed, their Buddha images were allowed to be relocated and preserved. An edict was issued stating that bronze statues in various prefectures were to be maintained according to previous custom. An edict was issued regarding the reported state of the Daochang Temple.
Gathering men and women at night is of no benefit to spiritual practice;
all such activities must be strictly prohibited. Emperor Taizong said to his close ministers, "Confucian scholars often disparage Buddhism."
Previously, when Su Yi-jian was commissioned to compose an inscription for the Buddha’s Diamond Throne in Central India, he referred to the Buddha as a "barbarian" (yi).
Consequently, the Emperor ordered another person to compose it instead. An imperial edict was also issued permitting monks in Lingnan to maintain wives and children.
The local magistrates everywhere should strictly exercise caution and restraint.
Emperor Zhenzong’s attendant reader, Sun Xi, requested that the construction of temples and the ordination of monks be reduced.
The Emperor said:
The two gates of Buddhism and Confucianism both assist the teachings of the world;
how could they be abolished? [The Emperor] issued an edict that those selling wine and meat in the capital must remain more than one hundred paces away from temples and monasteries.
Regarding those who sell goods to the Sangha, their offenses shall be discussed in detail. The ministers and officials submitted this statement:
"The ignorant masses are sycophantic toward the Buddha, and this corrupts and harms state governance."
The Emperor said:
"Buddhism causes people to reform toward the good.
How can it be prohibited? He then issued an edict that the steps of the halls and terraces of all temples and monasteries [should be restored].

It was prohibited for the people to sit or lie down with their bodies bared. An imperial edict ordered that the newly translated *Pinayega Sūtra*—which prescribes the use of meat and blood in sacrifices—be excluded from the Tripiṭaka.
During the Xiangfu era, an edict mandated that officials of rank should not insult or humiliate monks and nuns.
Those who verbally call [monastics] "bald-heads" shall have their current posts suspended;
commoners so offending shall be exiled a thousand li. ○ An edict from Emperor Huizong of the Xuande era states: "Princess of the Wu Kingdom reveres the Empty Gate (the Buddhist faith)."
Regarding those among officials and commoners who insult or humiliate monks and nuns:
this follows the decree of the third year of the Shengxiang era. Regarding the renunciation of the world by Princess Zheng of the Xiaozong Emperor:
by imperial edict, it is forbidden for officials and commoners to insult or humiliate monks and nuns.
In accordance with the imperial edicts of the Xuanhe era of the Shaoxing period,
officials and courts shall not investigate or take legal action against violations committed by monks and nuns.
It must be memorialized to the throne to await imperial decree.

Regarding the examination for monastic ordination: at the beginning of the Jinglong era of the Tang Emperor Zhongzong, an edict was issued throughout the empire to conduct examinations for the ordination of monks.
Da Yi, a novice monk at Lingyin Monastery in Shanyin, was ranked first in the examination for reciting the Lotus Sūtra.
During the reign of Emperor Suzong, he was commanded by imperial decree to recite five hundred sheets of scripture;
as a layman, he was granted the rank of "one who has mastered the classics" (mingjing chushen) and ordained as a monk.

At that time, Sengbiao was ranked first among those who passed the examination. Emperor Daizong issued an edict to test the three categories of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma (Śāstra) for novice monks;
those who passed were granted certificates and ordained. Emperor Jingzong issued an edict requiring monks to recite one hundred and fifty sheets of scripture from memory.
One hundred sheets of paper for nuns;
permission granted for tonsure and ordination. Emperor Xuanzong’s edict:
every year, ordain monks according to the three studies of precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
He selected those who possessed the nature of the Way and were proficient in the Dharma-gates.
At the end of the Liang dynasty, the Emperor issued an edict to all monks and nuns throughout the empire,
requiring them to enter the capital for an examination of their mastery of the scriptures.
At the end of the Tang dynasty, Emperor Mian established the system of the Four Categories for the ordination of monks:
exegesis, meditative concentration, recitation, and literary discourse.
This was during the reign of Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty.
The imperial decree stated that men aged fifteen must recite one hundred sheets of scripture, while women must recite seventy sheets.
Those who passed the examination at the commandery were to be granted certificates by the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibù).
This was during the reign of Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty.
An imperial edict decreed that śramaṇas be tested in ten questions on the sūtras, vinaya, and treatises;

those who passed all were granted purple robes. In the Yongxi era of Emperor Taizong, an edict was issued that all tonsured novices (tongxing) throughout the empire were to be granted full ordination.
Henceforth, one shall be permitted to register [for ordination] only after having read three hundred scrolls of the scriptures.
An imperial edict was issued to the circuits of Zhejiang and Fujian,
mandating that each monastery maintain a quota of three hundred persons.
One person was ordained annually;
for every hundred nuns, one person was ordained;
and one hundred scrolls of scripture were recited.
Reading five hundred sheets of scripture constitutes passing the examination.

Regarding the imperial decree concerning the annual ordination of ten persons each for the Buddhist and Daoist traditions, one person was specifically exempted from the requirement to test their mastery of scriptural studies.
An imperial edict was issued to all novice practitioners throughout the empire.
Examination for Ordination through Scriptural Mastery: Emperor Renzong issued an edict to examine the young novices (*tongxing*) throughout the empire on their recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Those who passed the selection were granted ordination.
Song Sou and Xia Song, the two Councilors of State, supervised the examination.
Emperor Xiaozong [issued a decree] to the Upper Tianzhu Monastery’s Chief Registrar of Monks, Nenguo,
requesting that the practice of testing candidates for the monastic ordination be reinstated.
The Special Edict for Ordaining Monks: Emperor Han Ming [of the Later Han] was defeated in a contest of religious methods by the Daoist masters of the Five Peaks.
Subsequently, the Minister of Works Liu Jun, the commoner Zhang Zishang, the consort Yin, and the Daoist master Lü Huītong, among others, petitioned for the special edict to ordain monks.
They also requested to leave the household life.
Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty issued an edict permitting both officials and commoners to renounce the world.
In this year, five hundred thousand monks were ordained. Emperor Yang issued an edict for seven days of ritual practice, during which one thousand monks were ordained in total.
This was the first year of the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty.

In the ninth year, an imperial edict was issued to ordain three thousand monks and nuns throughout the realm, with a mandate to select only those whose virtue and practice were refined and brilliant. In the twenty-second year...
Master Xuanzang remarked that the propagation of the Dharma requires people, and that the ordination of monks is essential;
he therefore petitioned the Emperor to permit five persons to be ordained at each monastery.
In total, seventeen thousand people [were ordained]. Emperor Xuanzong established an initiation altar (guanding tan) with the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra, whereby millions of people were saved.

By imperial decree, three youths of true practice were ordained in each prefecture. Emperor Ruizong universally ordained thirty thousand monks and Daoists. Emperor Wenzong issued a decree that monks and nuns must not be ordained except through formal authorization.
It was permitted for those with names to apply to the provincial government for official certificates (*jiedie*).
At that time, seventy thousand people applied daily;
later, this continued under Emperor Mingzong of the Later Tang and the Kings of Min.
Twenty thousand monks were ordained.
On the occasion of Emperor Taizu’s birthday, known as Changchun Jie, eight thousand novice monks (*tongxing*) were ordained.
Emperor Taizong universally ordained one hundred and seventy thousand novices. Emperor Zhenzong ascended Mount Tai for the ritual of *dengfeng*.
An edict was issued for all temples and monasteries throughout the empire to ordain one person each;
monks and Daoists in attendance were each permitted to ordain one disciple. Princess Wuguo Dachang was ordained as a nun.

An edict was issued to ordain one person for every ten child-attendants. An edict was further issued that all child-attendants registered under the monastic and Daoist establishments were to be granted full tonsure and ordination.
In this year, twenty-four thousand five hundred and seventy-seven monks and nuns were ordained.
Seven thousand one hundred and seventy Daoist priests and nuns. Emperor Renzong decreed that those with tattoos or bodily markings must not be admitted into the monastic order.
Emperor Shenzong issued an edict for the Tianzhu Guanyin Temple in Qiantang.
One person was ordained each year to maintain the incense and lamps.
Regarding the "payment for ordination" (jin na du seng): at the beginning of the Zhide era of the Tang Emperor Suzong, Chancellor Pei Yuan petitioned that ordination certificates be sold.

This was called "incense-water money" (xiāngshuǐ qián). It was permitted for laypeople (*báiyī*) to recite sutras and be granted official status (*chūshēn*), or to pay one hundred *mǐn* of cash to request a certificate for tonsure.
During the reign of Emperor Shenzong of the Song dynasty.

Qian Gongfu, the Director of Remonstrance, petitioned that during years of famine and river flooding, the government should request the sale of *ducao* certificates. Emperor Gaozong issued an edict to sell the four-character monastic titles. This began at the end of the Zhiping era.
The sale of ordination certificates (du-die) began;
previously, many had been forged on yellow paper.
At this time, Zhu Yi of the Ministry of Revenue submitted a memorial.
He ordered that the Buddhist and Daoist clergy use imperial silk certificates (*chiling*). ○ Zhan Shuyi submitted a memorial requesting that the sale of ordination certificates (*dudie*) be halted.
○ An imperial edict was issued requiring the clergy to begin paying taxes to exempt them from corvée labor.
This is called "money for leisure.
When a gentleman leaves the household life— such as when Emperor Han Mingdi,
the Minister of Works Liu Jun, Lady Yin, and others all left the household life— [this applies].
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty received a memorial from the Court Attendant Liu Siran requesting permission to leave the household life;
he was granted the name Huidi.
He paid homage to the Emperor.
Zong Dai, a Court Counselor, resigned his office to become a monk,
taking the name Wuming.
The "Inscription on the Cessation of Mind" (*Xixin ming*) circulated throughout the world.
During the Northern Wei dynasty, Prince Xing of Jingzhao, the Crown Prince, submitted a memorial requesting permission to leave the household life;
he was granted the name Sengyi. Empress Dowager Feng [also requested ordination].
She left secular life to become a nun and resided at Yaoguang Temple. Empress Dowager Gao of the Xuanwu era also left secular life to become a nun.
She resided at Yaoguang Temple. Pei Zhi, the Minister of Revenue, whose mother was Lady Xiahou, reached the age of seventy and left the household life to become a nun;
she entered Mount Songgao. Empress Dowager Hu, the posthumous title of Emperor Xiaozhuang’s mother, [did likewise].
She left secular life to become a nun and resided at Yaoguang Temple during the reign of Emperor Gaozu of the Tang dynasty.
Shi Zhiyan was originally a General of the Household;
he resigned his office to become a monk.
A strange monk said to him:
"You, Minister, have left the household life at eighty-one.
Emperor Gaozong gave the crown prince born to Empress Wu the name Prince Foguang.
After more than a month,
an imperial edict was issued for her to leave the household life and shave her head at the temple of Dharma Master Xuanzang. Empress Wu had initially been a palace attendant.
She left Kaiye Monastery to become a nun.
Emperor Gaozong saw her and took her into the inner palace.
During the reign of Emperor Daizong, the Chancellor Du Hongjian was on his deathbed.
He ordered that the morning robes be donned over the saṃghāṭī and that his hair and beard be shaved;
then, departing from the community, he passed away.
In accordance with the dharma of śramaṇas, his body was cremated.
Emperor Muzong: Liu Zong,
the Military Governor of Youzhou, shaved his head to become a monk and was conferred the title of Grand Enlightened Master (Dajue Shi).
He was granted fifty *la* [years of seniority] by Emperor Xuanzong.
Initially enfeoffed as Prince Guang, he fled because Emperor Wuzong resented him and became a *śrāmaṇera*.
He eventually reached Yanguan and served as a secretary.
Emperor Wuzong passed away.
The hundred officials welcomed the Prince to ascend the throne as the Taizu of Liang.
The youngest son of the King of Wu-Yue, named Lingyin, became a monk together with Saṃgha at thirty years of *la*.
Emperor Zhuangzong of the Tang had a cavalry general named Shi Yingqiang,
who awakened to the Way of Chan and left the household life, taking the name Qicheng.
During the reign of Emperor Zhenzong of the Song dynasty, Princess Chang of the Wu Kingdom entered the monastic life;
her dharma name was Qingyu. Prime Minister Wang Dan passed away.
The final instructions requested that a virtuous monk be invited to bestow the precepts,
that his hair be shaved, that he be dressed in the three robes, and that he be cremated.
Yang Yi discussed these matters with his son.
He merely placed the three monastic robes inside the coffin. ○ Emperor Gaozong.
Feng Jia, a Palace Attendant serving as Governor of Luzhou, dressed in monastic robes when bidding farewell to his subordinates.
He ascended the seat and preached a verse to pass away.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty conferred the title of "Duke" upon the śramaṇa.
By imperial decree, the śramaṇa Huichao was appointed as a Scholar of the Shouguang Hall.
During the reign of Emperor Mingyuan of the Northern Wei,
the śramaṇa Faguo was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Yicheng and subsequently promoted to the Marquis of Ancheng.
He was posthumously titled Lord Ling.
Emperor Taizong of Tang issued an edict appointing the śramaṇa Zhìwēi as one of the Four Great Masters.
Enfeoffed as the Court Dispersing Grand Master (Chaosand Dafu). During the reign of Gaozong, an imperial edict appointed Huiwei as one of the Four Great Masters;
he was the same Fawei who had been enfeoffed as the Court Dispersing Grand Master, along with the two masters Fahua and Tianguan. Empress Wu enfeoffed nine individuals, including Falang.
He was enfeoffed as a County Duke.

He was granted a *kāṣāya* robe and a silver tortoise-shaped belt buckle. Emperor Zhongzong conferred upon him the title Dharma-Cloud, Duke of Wan-hui. An imperial edict appointed Hui-fan as Minister of Justice (Zheng-yi Da-fu) and Duke of Shang-yong Commandery.
The nine Hui-zhens were all conferred the rank of Chao-san-dafu and enfeoffed as County Dukes. By imperial decree, Hui-fan was additionally granted the rank of Yinqing-guanglu-dafu,
and Wan-sui was granted the rank of Chao-san-dafu.

He was enfeoffed as Duke of Xian County and appointed as Palace Attendant of the Guangqing Hall and Commissioner of Merit. When Empress Wu Zetian’s son, Ruizong, passed away at Wanhui Temple, he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Education (Situ) and Duke of Guo.

Dharma Master Fazang passed away; he was posthumously granted the title of Court Councillor of the Ministry of Rites (Honglu Qing). Empress Wu Zetian’s son, Xuanzong, passed away at Puti Liuzhi Temple.

Bestowal upon the Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial: During the reign of Emperor Suzong, the śramaṇa Daoping served as Grand General of the Golden Myriad (Jinwu Dajiangjun) and defeated the rebel An Lushan.
During the reign of Emperor Daizong, the śramaṇa Amoghavajra was enfeoffed as Special Advancement (Teci) and Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
He was further granted the title of Jia Kaifu Yitongsan si,
promoted to the rank of Duke of Su with a fief of three thousand households.

At his death, he was posthumously bestowed the title of Minister of Works (Sikong). During the reign of Emperor Dezong, the śramaṇa Yuanzhao served as an Inner Attendant and was appointed Court Gentleman for Ceremonial (Honglu Qing). During the reign of Emperor Xizong, the śramaṇa Miaoxing recited sutras and beheld the Buddha and Great Beings (Mahāsattvas).
He was granted the title Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent and the noble rank of Duke of Kaiguo. [This concludes the entry for] Tian Xizai,
Tripitaka Master of the Translation Bureau under Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty.
Shi was appointed as Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices;
Fata and Shihu were both appointed as Acting Ministers of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Monthly allowance for ghee and curd. ○ The Dharma Protector (Fahù), Silver Light and Rank of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, who had translated scriptures, passed away. ○ Under the imperial decree of the Acting Regent of the Eastern Capital, Emperor Qīnzōng, the śramaṇa Fādào was appointed.
He was promoted to the rank of Xuanjiao Lang (Imperial Messenger of Propagation). He participated in military affairs.
Regarding his monastic titles and posthumous names: [the first] is the Monastic Title of the Jin'an Emperor.
The ruler of Qin appointed Sengqie as the National Preceptor (Guo-sengzheng) and Faqin as the Registrar of Monks (Senglü).

Emperor Wen of Song issued an edict appointing the nun Baoxian as the Preceptor of Nuns for the Capital (Jingyi-nisengzheng). Emperor Xiaowu issued an edict appointing Daoyou as the Dharma Master of Xin’an Temple. [He] issued an edict appointing Daowen as the Preceptor of the Metropolitan Area (Duyi-sengzheng). Emperor Shun issued an edict appointing Fachih as the National Preceptor of All Under Heaven (Tianxia-sengzheng).

Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty issued an edict appointing Faying as the Monastic Head (Sengzhu) of the capital. Emperor Wu issued an imperial decree appointing Xuanchang and Faxian as Monastic Heads, assigning them respectively to oversee affairs in the regions south and north of the Yangtze River.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty issued an edict appointing Dharma Master Yun Guang as the Great Sangzheng (Chief Administrator of the Monastic Community).

Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty issued an edict appointing Baoqiong as the Great Sengtong of the Capital. Emperor Xuan issued an edict appointing Tan Yuan as the National Sangzheng. Emperor Houzhu issued an edict appointing Huikong as the Great Sangzheng of the Capital. Emperor Wencheng of Northern Wei issued an edict appointing Shi Xian as the Shamentong (Director of the Clergy). He further issued an edict appointing Tanyao as the Shamen Dutong of the Zhaoxuan Commandery.

The Northern Qi Emperor Wenxuan issued an edict appointing the eminent monk Fachang as State Preceptor; he also decreed that Dharma Master Tanyan be appointed as the Upper Director of the Office of the Orthodox Doctrine (Zhaoxuan Shangtong), establishing ten directors for this office.
He appointed Sha-men Fa-shang as Grand Overseer and honored him as National Preceptor under Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty.
The Emperor decreed that Sengmeng be the Great General Overseer (Dàtǒng) of the Sui State; he issued an edict appointing Tánqiān as the Great Śramaṇa General Overseer of the Śāo Xuán Commission.
Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict summoning the Venerable Dúshùn for an audience.
Bestowing a Title by Imperial Decree: Empress Wu issued an edict for Chan Master Shenxiu to enter the capital to propagate the Way;

he served three successive reigns and was honored as National Preceptor. Emperor Xuanzong bestowed the title "Celestial Master" upon the śramaṇa Yixing. By imperial decree, Biancai was appointed as the Instructor for the Shuofang region. Suzong summoned Chan Master Huizhong of Nanyang to have an audience.

He was titled National Teacher [Guoshi]. Emperor Daizong issued an edict appointing Fazhao of Mount Nanyue as National Teacher. Emperor Dezong bestowed the title of Qingliang Dharma Master and Professor Upādhyāya upon Chengguan. Emperor Xianzong bestowed the title of Wudao National Teacher upon the śramaṇa Zhixuan. He further conferred upon Chengguan the rank of Great Steward (Datong) Qingliang National Teacher.
○ An imperial edict appointed the śramaṇa Duānfǔ as Recorder of Monastic Affairs for the Left Street;

Língsuì was appointed as Recorder of Monastic Affairs for the Right Street. ○ Emperor Mùzōng issued an edict appointing the śramaṇa Wéiyīng as the Monk-Patriarch (Sēngtǒng) of the Two Streets. ○ Emperor Wénzōng [honored] Duānfǔ—Dàdà Fǎshī, Inner Attendant for the Three Teachings’ Discourses, Grand Master of the Imperial Procession—as the Recorder of Monastic Affairs for the Left Street.

He passed away reclining on his right side. ○ An imperial edict appointed the śramaṇa Cúnduán as the Superintendent of Monks for the Left and Right Quarters. ○ An imperial edict appointed Língyàn as the Superintendent of Monks for the Left and Right Quarters. ○ An imperial edict appointed Dharma Master Zhīxuán as the Head Seat of the Three Teachings. ○ An imperial edict appointed Biànzhāng, Head Seat of the Three Teachings, as the Superintendent of Monks for the Left Quarter.

Sengche was appointed as the Monk Registrar of the Right Street. During the Yanqing Festival of Emperor Yizong, an imperial edict appointed Qinglan as the Great Master Huizhao, Monk Registrar of the Left Street, and Yanchu as the Great Master Mingche, Monk Registrar of the Right Street.
He lectured and discussed the Buddha-dharma. By imperial decree, the śramaṇa Juehui was appointed as Vice Superintendent of Monks for the Left and Right Quarters.
Qian Chu, the King of Han, Wu, and Yue, honored the śramaṇa Deshao as National Teacher.
Zanning, the State Preceptor of the Wu-Yue Kingdom, was granted an audience with Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty and bestowed the title of Great Master Tonghui.
Zanning was appointed as a Compiler in the Office of the Historian and later promoted to Right Street Registrar of Monks.
Zhili of Yansheng Temple in Siming was bestowed the title of Great Master Fazhi. Benru of Dongshan in Tiantai was also bestowed a title.
National Teacher Shenzhao; Emperor Renzong bestowed upon him the title Tripitaka Master Fahu Puming Cijue.
National Teacher Tianzhu Haiyue Huibian; Emperor Shenzong bestowed upon him the title Supu Master. National Teacher Fadao Baojue Yuan Tongfaji; Emperor Gaozong bestowed upon him this title.
He bestowed the title Chan Master Dahui Zonggao upon [the master of] Mount Jing. Emperor Xiaozong.
Bestowed upon Lingshan Zilin the title *Dashi Cishou*; bestowed upon Shangzhu Ruone the title *Youjie Senglü*;
bestowed upon Shangzhu Ruone the title *Zuojie Senglü Hui Guang Fashi*; bestowed upon Lingyin Huiyuan the title *Fohai Chanshi*;
bestowed upon Lingyin Deguang the title *Fozhao Chanshi*.
Regarding the matter of not bowing to the sovereign or one's father, during the reign of Emperor Cheng of Jin,
the Chancellor Yu Bing proposed a decree requiring śramaṇas to pay full respect to the king.
He Chong opposed this argument, and it was not carried out. During the reign of Emperor An,
Huan Xuan proposed that śramaṇas should show full respect to the sovereign.
Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu adamantly opposed this and would not comply.
Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty then issued a decree requiring śramaṇas to pay full homage to their sovereign.
The former Emperor Fei issued a decree suspending the practice of paying homage [to the throne].
Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty issued an edict requiring śramaṇas and Daoist priests to pay homage to the sovereign.
The śramaṇa Mingzhan defied the imperial decree,
asserting that monks have no ritual code for showing reverence to the laity;
consequently, the matter was suppressed.
Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict requiring monks and Daoists to pay homage to their parents;
after more than a year, the requirement for paying homage was suspended. — Emperor Gaozong.
The Emperor [Xuanzong] issued an edict that monks and Daoists must not receive prostrations from their parents or elders.
Emperor Xuanzong then issued an edict requiring monks and Daoists to pay respect to their parents;
after more than a month, he rescinded the requirement for them to pay such respect.
Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty did not address the śramaṇas as "Your Subject.
When the śramaṇa Sengzhong addressed the Emperor as "this poor man of the Way" (pindao),
the Emperor questioned Wang Jian about it.
He replied,
"Since the Jin and Song dynasties, most have addressed me as 'the Poor Monk' (pindao),
yet you have allowed me to take my seat."
During the reign of Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty,
an imperial edict was issued stating that monks and nuns must not address themselves as "ministers" (*chen*) in their petitions to the court. According to the *Book of Rites* (*Liji*),
among the Confucians, there are those who do not serve as ministers to the Son of Heaven above, nor do they serve as officials to the feudal lords below.
Han Wang Ruzhong addressed Emperor Guangwu by his given name rather than as a subordinate.
Song Mingdi honored those of lofty conduct;
he issued an edict granting Dharma Master Meng a monthly stipend of thirty thousand coins, as well as a carriage and the services of attendants.
Sengjin was granted one set of Dharma manuals by Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty.
Whenever Dharma Master Huiyue entered the imperial court, [the Emperor would bestow these upon him].
A special couch was necessarily provided;

the Emperor’s seat was situated beside it. An imperial edict appointed Dharma Master Fayun as the Great Sangha Rectifier (Daisengzheng), with government officials providing the necessary labor and resources.
Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty issued an edict to allocate the tax levies of Shifeng County to provide for Master Zhiyi.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, Vinaya Master Lingzang resided at Daxingshan Temple.

By imperial decree, the Left and Right Vice Directors of the Chancellery were to inquire after his health twice daily. Dharma Master Tanyan ascended the imperial throne and bestowed the Dharma upon him from the south side.
During the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty,
Chan Master Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch, did not rise for the four imperial summons;
consequently, the Emperor bestowed upon him precious silks.
To commemorate his Way, Emperor Daizong issued an edict summoning Chan Master Qin of Mount Jing to an audience and conferred upon him the title Guoyi (National One).
Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty issued an edict to the high official of Hangzhou,
ordering that he report on [the Master’s] well-being every month.
Zanning, the Monastic Director of Wuyue, was granted an audience.
On one occasion, he was summoned seven times,
and was bestowed the title Tonghui.
The Monk’s Book on Monks; the Monk’s Book on Monks compiled by Emperor Wu of the Liang Dynasty.

The *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) in fourteen fascicles was compiled by the monk Huìjiǎo, covering the period from the Yǒngpíng era of the Han dynasty through the Tiānjiān era of the Liang dynasty.
The opening of virtuous deeds is divided into ten sections.
[This was compiled by] Fei Changfang, a scholar-translator under Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty.
He further compiled the *Kaihuang Sanbao Lu* (Record of the Three Jewels of the Kaihuang Era).
During the reign of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang,
the śramaṇa Daoxuan authored the *Xu Gaoseng Zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) in thirty fascicles.
From the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty to the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the śramaṇa Daoshi compiled the Fayuan zhulin in one hundred fascicles.
It comprehensively covers the entire Tripitaka by categorizing matters according to their respective sections. [Emperor] Dezong.
Yu Di, the Prefect of Huzhou, presented the *Collected Poems of the Śramaṇa Jiaoran* from Zhushan to the Emperor.
During the late Liang dynasty, the Śramaṇa Gui presented the *Preface* and the *Essential Compendium of Sūtras and Treatises* for preservation in the Imperial Calligraphy Hall.
By imperial decree, he was admitted into the Great Canon and bestowed the title of Master of Propagating the Teaching (Yanjiao Dashi).
This was Sha-men Ke Hong of the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty.
During the reign of Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty, the śramaṇa Yichu presented the *Dazangjing yinyi* (Phonetic Meanings of the Great Canon) in four hundred and eighty fascicles;
he also presented the *Shishi liutie* (Six Categories of Buddhist Records), which was by imperial decree entrusted to the Historiographic Office.
He was granted purple robes and silk currency.

During the Song dynasty, Emperor Taizu [bestowed honors upon] Chan Master Shou of Wuyue, who authored the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) in one hundred fascicles. The śramaṇa Wensheng, by imperial decree, compiled the *Dazang suihan suoyin* (Hidden Meanings Sought According to the Case Bindings of the Great Canon) in six hundred and sixty fascicles. [This was undertaken by] Li Fang and others of the Hanlin Academy under Emperor Taizong.

Zeng presented the *Taiping guangji* (Extensive Records of the Taiping Era), among which thirty fascicles record matters concerning the Buddha-dharma. Zanhui Dashi Zan Ning presented the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) in thirty fascicles.
Beginning in the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty,
he was commanded by imperial decree to include his works in the Great Canon.
He also compiled the *Record of Sages and Worthies on Vulture Peak* in fifty fascicles.
*Monk History Simplified* (Sengshi lüe), three fascicles. [Compiled during the] Zhenzong reign.

The śramaṇa Daoyuan presented the *Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* (Jingde chuandeng lu), thirty fascicles. [The official who revised the translation was] Zhao Anren, an official for refining translated texts.
The *Xu zang jing lu* (Supplementary Catalogue of the Tripiṭaka) in twenty-one fascicles was compiled;

it was granted the title *Dazhongxiangfu fabaolu* (Record of the Dharma Treasures of the Great Zhongxiangfu Era). The śramaṇa Daocheng authored the *Shishi yaolan* (Essentials for Buddhists) in three fascicles. The śramaṇa Renzan of Yizhou submitted the *Shishi huiyao* (Essential Matters of Buddhism) in forty fascicles. [This was during the reign of] Emperor Renzong.
The Tripitaka Master Weijing submitted the *New Translation of the Phonology and Meanings of the Scriptures* in seventy fascicles.
The Tripitaka Master Weijing also submitted the new translation of the *Catalogue of the Great Canon* in two bundles,
which was granted the title *Tiansheng Record of Translated Teachings*.

The Great Master Fabian was granted the purple robe; concurrently serving as State Councilor, Wang Sui presented the revised *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* in fifteen fascicles; and Li Zunxu, Prince Consort, expanded the *Chuandeng Lu* into thirty fascicles.
He was granted the title *Tiānshèng Guǎngdēnglù* (The Extensive Lamp Record of the Tiānshèng Era). The śramaṇa Qìsōng presented the *Fǔjiào biān*, the *Dìngzǔ tú*, and the *Zhèngzōng jì*;
by imperial decree, these were included in the Great Canon (*Dàzàng*).
He was granted the purple robe and silk fabrics with the title Master Míngjiào. — Emperor Huīzōng.
The śramaṇa Weibai submitted the *Xùdēnglù* (Continued Record of the Lamp), which was by imperial decree included in the Tripitaka;
