the Buddha-Country Chan Master was granted a golden-embroidered robe. The Minister Wang Gu read through the Tripitaka and compiled the eight-fascicle *Fǎbǎobiāomù* (Catalogue of the Dharma-Jewels). Shimen Huìhóng compiled the thirty-fascicle *Chánlín Sēngbǎozhuàn* (Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest).
*Fozu Tongji*, Volume Fifty-one, End.
*Fozu Tongji*, Volume Fifty-two.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhipan of Fiquan, Mingzhou, during the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty.
*Compendium of Essential Matters Through Successive Dynasties*, Section Nineteen, Part Two:
Karmic Destiny and Previous Lives; Releasing Living Beings and Prohibiting Killing; Prayers for Calamities and Marvels;
Historical Anecdotes of the Imperial Court; Tribute from Various Kingdoms.
Regarding the previous lives of Emperor Wu of Jin:
it is said that Yang Hu was a monk who built a temple on Mount Wudang in a former life;
consequently, his current provisions and honors are exceptionally abundant, and so forth.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
when Prince Yueyang Xiao Cha was stationed in Yue,
learned that his previous incarnation had been Xu Xun; he and Tan Yan then constructed a stupa for him, and so forth.
During the Northern Qi dynasty,
Emperor Wenxuan sent someone riding a camel out of the city;
suddenly, it was as if he were dreaming.
When they reached the temple on the mountainside to retrieve the scripture cases,
a group of śrāmaṇeras said,
"Gao Yang has arrived with his camels."
The Emperor summoned the old monk for an audience and asked,
"How was it that Gao Yang became the Son of Heaven? and so forth.
Empress Wu Zetian.
Master Wei was a previous incarnation of Xu Ling of the Chen dynasty.
Having heard Master Zhi lecture on the sutras, he made five vows.
Later he was reborn as a member of the Zhu family of Jinyun;
he entered the order under Master Zhang’an as his teacher. As for the "Pine-Planting Wayfarer," he took birth as the daughter of the Zhou family.
He met the Fourth Patriarch and left the household life;
he was the Fifth Patriarch Ren.
During the Xuanzong era, Fang Guan and the Daoist Xing Hepu visited Xia Mountain.
He entered an abandoned temple and had someone dig into the ground.
There they discovered letters addressed by Lou Shide to Master Yong, which had been hidden inside a jar.
Greatly delighted, he realized that his previous life was that of the śramaṇa Fa-xiu of Yong... An extraordinary monk led him into Mount Zhongnan.
Seeing a vermilion gate with a plaque that read "Dedication of Merit" (Huixiang),
the elder monk pointed to a palace chamber and said,
"This was the former residence of the Tang Emperor."
He commanded his attendant to fetch a jade flute and said,
"In my former dwelling, I enjoyed fine music;
now I have been banished to be the lord of the human world."
During the reign of Emperor Dezong,
when Wei Gao was first born as the Regional Inspector of Xichuan,
a foreign monk said:
This was the reincarnation of Zhuge Wuhou.
Emperor Xianzong gave a date fruit to the foreign monk Qijun, who ate it.
He immediately realized that his previous life had been that of a monk who lectured on the sutras;
he then entered the monastic order at Lingyin, taking the name Jiankong.
(Emperor Xizong).
National Teacher Zhixuan saw a pearl enter his left thigh, causing him intense pain.
Upon it were the two characters "Chao Cuo.
Realizing this was the result of his past karma, Zhixuan passed away while lying on his right side.
The world claimed that Xuan was the reincarnation of Yuan Ang, and so forth.
During the reign of Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty,
Chancellor Zhang Fangping was appointed as the Governor of Chuzhou.
Upon arriving at the monastery, he saw the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* with his own handwriting still clearly visible;
thus he knew that his previous life had been that of a monk who transcribed the scriptures. (The Prime Minister, Lord Zeng Gongliang.)
Her previous incarnation was Qingcaotang of the Chan school.
She was a courtesan from Yingzhou whose mouth emitted the fragrance of lotuses.
A monk from Shu said:
This woman was previously a nun who recited the Lotus Sūtra for thirty years.
Emperor Zhezong [was formerly] the Chan Master Wuzu Jie; Su Shi [was formerly] the same.

Releasing Life and Prohibiting Killing: During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Sui Dynasty, an edict was issued throughout the realm that on the first, fifth, and ninth months, as well as during the six days of the *poṣadha*, it was forbidden to kill living beings.
When the Zen Master Zhiyi arrived at Yuezhou to lecture on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, he [established this practice].
He converted one prefecture and five counties;
more than one thousand locations all abandoned fishing and hunting.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty...
An imperial decree was issued that the Court Physicians were not permitted to use living creatures as medicine;
furthermore, the sacrificial animals for the suburban and ancestral temple rites were all replaced with flour-based effigies.
The ancestral temples used fruits and vegetables.
Emperor Xianwen of the Northern Wei issued an edict that sacrificial animals should not be used for offerings to Heaven, Earth, or the ancestral shrines.
Each year, seventy-five thousand animal lives were spared.
Emperor Wenxuan of the Northern Qi received the precepts and abstained from eating meat.
The slaughter of animals was prohibited within the precincts. Emperor Gaozu of the Tang dynasty issued an edict [prohibiting killing] on the first,
fifth, and ninth days of each month, as well as on the days of the ten-fold fast (*daśa-vārṣika*).
The practice of execution, butchery, and fishing was prohibited [during the reign of] Empress Wu;
she issued an edict to ban butchery and fishing throughout the empire.
Emperor Suzong issued a decree establishing "pools for releasing living beings" (fangsheng chi) throughout the realm.
There were eighty-one such sites in total.
Yan Zhenqing composed the inscription.
Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty...
The Emperor decreed that from the second month to the ninth month of the year, the common people were not permitted to hunt or shoot;
this was recorded in the legal statutes. — Zhenzong.
An imperial edict was issued to all provinces and prefectures throughout the empire to fully restore the fish-releasing ponds (*fangsheng chi*).
In places where no such ponds existed, within a five-li radius of the city walls in the prefectures along the Yangtze and Huai rivers, fishing and hunting were strictly prohibited.
— By Pan Hua, Magistrate of Zhujia.
In accordance with the *Samantabhadra Repentance Ritual*, he prohibited the catching of fish in rivers and lakes.
When he returned to the capital by imperial decree,
he dreamed that tens of thousands of fish had taken human form.
Their wailing resounded to the heavens as they all cried out, "The elder is gone!
We shall not escape being cooked!"
...and so forth. The Dharma Master Ciyun of India petitioned for the West Lake to be established as a sanctuary for the release of living beings (*fangsheng chi*).
Every year on the eighth day of the fourth month, the people of the commandery would gather by the lake to release fish and birds.
On behalf of the Sovereign, he offered prayers for his longevity.
This was the Dharma Master Fazhi of Yanqing Monastery in Siming, during the Renzong era.
Every year on the Buddha’s birthday, fish and birds were released to pray for the Emperor’s longevity.
The Prefect reported this to the throne,
and an imperial edict was issued for Liu Yun, a member of the Bureau of Military Affairs, to compose an inscription for a stele erected at the temple gate.
Regarding Prayers for Calamities and Anomalies during the Jin Dynasty:
Emperor Jianwen of Jin had a crow nest in the Taiji Hall.
He summoned the nun Daorong to bestow upon her the Eight Precepts of the Fast.
A crow flew away with its nest. A malevolent star manifested as an anomaly;
the Emperor summoned the śramaṇa Fakuang to perform a rite of repentance, and the star vanished because of it.
[This occurred during the reign of] Emperor Xiaowu.
The Indian master Shesheng arrived in Chang’an;
he frequently invoked dragons to bring rain,
and the ruler of Qin honored him as his teacher.
Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty fell ill.
He summoned various śramaṇas to pray to the Buddha;

moved by their devotion, a celestial fragrance filled the hall, and holy monks appeared shaking their staffs. Lu Jingyou, the National Preceptor and Doctor of the Guozijian during the Jiemin era of the Northern Wei, was well-versed in the Buddha-dharma.
His elder brother incited a rebellion which repeatedly implicated Jingyou;
yet through sincere recitation of the sutras, his shackles fell away of their own accord.
[This was the case with] Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty.
During a severe drought,
Dharma Master Tanyan ascended the imperial throne;
the Emperor and his ministers received the Eightfold Precepts of the *Guanzhai* fast.
Before long, rain fell in torrents.
Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict to the monks and Daoists of the capital and its various prefectures.
For seven days and nights, they shall perform the recitation of scriptures and circumambulation to pray for a bountiful autumn harvest;
this shall be established as the annual rite for the first and seventh months. [The Emperor] issues this decree to the śramaṇas of the capital.
On the twenty-seventh day of each month,
they performed the ritual practice and recited the Benevolent Kings Sutra to pray for blessings upon the nation. [The Emperor] issued an edict summoning Master Jing to the capital to pray for rain.
A white rainbow appeared in broad daylight as an omen,
and heavy rains fell throughout the region.
Emperor Zhongzong issued an edict for Bodhiruci to establish a ritual altar to pray for rain.
For three days there was torrential rain.
Emperor Xuanzong [ruled] when the Kangju entered as raiders into Anxi.
Emperor Daizong issued an edict for Amoghavajra to recite the Benevolent Kings’ Dhāraṇī.
In response, divine soldiers from the Prince of Northern India appeared,
and the five kingdoms were utterly defeated and dispersed.
When the Tufan forces pressed upon the capital,
the *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* (Renwang jing) was issued from within the palace;
an imperial edict was issued to establish one hundred high seats for the preaching of this sūtra.
When the rebels were pacified, an imperial edict was issued to establish a Consecration Ritual Chamber (Guǎngdìng Dàochǎng),
where twenty-seven śramaṇas were selected to recite the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī* for the long-term benefit of the state. A comet appeared in the eastern sky.
The Emperor issued an edict to Amoghavajra to perform a ritual;
however, the stars fell as meteors,
and there was no rain during the spring and summer.
An altar was constructed and prayers were offered,
whereupon a great rain fell in abundance. Zhang Zhao, the Military Governor of Dangyang,
invited the śramaṇa Zizhao and said:
He heard that the dragon deity, having relied upon his teacher to listen to the sutras, had forgotten its duty of bringing rain.
He prayed for the deity to give rise to great compassion;
the teacher then burned incense and offered prayers from afar.
Clouds arose and a great rain fell.
Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty visited Xiangguosi Temple to pray for rain.
He established a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks. When the Emperor visited Xiangguo Temple to pray for rain, he offered vegetarian food and a great downpour ensued.
Later, when rain did not cease as he was about to perform the suburban sacrifice to Heaven, he dispatched an envoy to pray at the Vajra-body Stūpa.
When the appointed time arrived, it cleared. During the Zhenzong era, there was a severe drought;
a foreign monk established an altar at Jinming Pool and recited incantations for the dragon, and in a mere moment, rain fell. During the Shenzong era...
During a summer drought,
the Emperor performed a fast and prayers within the inner palace.
He dreamed that a divine monk spat forth mist from mid-air.
Upon waking, a great rain fell.
An imperial edict was issued to seek out the image, and it was found as the thirteenth of the Arhats in the pavilion of Sōgoku-ji. Master Jōshō of the Shō sect resided at Kōfuku-ji.
When Lord Zhao Qingxuan was the military governor of Yue,
there was a severe drought and a great epidemic.
He welcomed the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) and prayed with earnest devotion.
One night, as rain poured down, the epidemic also subsided.
Consequently, he memorialized the Emperor regarding his residence, naming it "Yuantong" (Perfect Penetration).
When Empress Meng left the court, she faced southward.
One should enshrine an image of Marīcī to protect the body. Li Yüel avoided the rebels by encountering a person riding in a carriage, who instructed him to recite the name of the Honored One Marīcī;
thus he escaped the calamity of war. When the Jin rebels entered Hangzhou, [he likewise relied on her protection].
The Emperor personally visited the Hall of the Great Being at Upper Zhuzhi to offer solemn prayers.
For those who had perished in battle, he performed the Water and Land Offerings (*shuilu gongyang*).
In a dream, he was informed that the deceased warriors were celebrating their rebirth in a favorable realm. At that time, there was a great drought.
The Emperor issued an edict for Dharma Master Dao to pray for rain.
The Master recited incantations over four fresh carp and cast them into the river;
the rain fell in great abundance. However, the excessive rain did not cease.
An inner attendant was dispatched to pray at the Great Bodhisattva [Guanyin] of Upper Zhu.
A jade vessel and a seven-jeweled crown were bestowed.

Regarding the historical precedents of our dynasty: on the occasion of the Imperial Birthday, at the Inner Daochamber (Neidaochang) and the Gongdeyuan, the national taboo name is that of Emperor Taiwu of the Northern Wei.
On the occasion of his birth,
Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty first issued an edict for all Buddhist temples throughout the empire to establish long-life *dharmapūjā* assemblies (*zhòushòu dàochǎng*).

An imperial edict was issued for all temples and monasteries throughout the realm to establish Daoist and Buddhist ritual assemblies (*daochang*) to pray for longevity on the occasion of the Tiāncháng Festival.
By imperial decree, monks and Daoists were to perform rites and distribute offerings at Kāiyuán Monastery during the Qiānqiū Festival. This was the birth festival of Emperor Dēngzōng.
Emperor Wenzong issued an edict for Dharma Master Chengguan to enter the inner palace to lecture on the sutras. Emperor Zhaozong issued an edict that,
on the anniversary of his birth, the Chancellor and the various officials were to visit the monastery to provide a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks.
The Imperial Birthday.
An edict was issued for the monks and Daoists of the two streets to enter the inner palace for discussion. [The Imperial Birthday of] King Jungjong.
An imperial edict ordered monasteries and temples to hold vegetarian feasts and prohibited hunting and fishing.
During the Daying Festival of Emperor Taizu of the Liang dynasty,
an edict was issued for the hundred officials to visit the temples to offer incense and pray for the Emperor’s longevity.
On the anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday during the Tang dynasty,
an imperial edict was issued for the Buddhist Registrar Yunbian and Daoist priests to enter the inner palace for discussion.
On the anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday during the Zhou dynasty...
The ministers and the hundred officials went to the temple to observe the establishment of a ritual altar for the Emperor’s longevity.
On the occasion of Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty’s birthday, Prime Minister Fan Zhi composed the ritual prayer for the Longevity Offering, which stated as follows: [text omitted].
On the Longchun Festival (the Emperor’s birthday),

an edict was issued for śramaṇas to undergo an examination in the palace on ten topics concerning the sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras. Emperor Qinzhong issued an edict that the celebration of Daojun’s birthday should continue to be held at a Daoist monastery,
while the Qianlong Festival should continue to be held at a Buddhist temple.
First, it follows the ancient laws of our ancestors.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty, the Buddha was venerated within the inner palace;
śramaṇas were summoned to reside there and practice the Way.
Emperor Daizong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict for one hundred śramaṇas to perform recitations within the palace,
which was called the "Inner Sanctuary" (neidaochang). He further issued an edict to establish a sanctuary at Daming Palace.
Moved by the manifestation of the Buddha’s light,
Song Taizong summoned the monastic chief Zanning to an audience in Zifu Hall.
An image of the Buddha and a collection of scriptures were installed there, along with the erection of a banner-pole (*kṣetra-dhvaja*) and the sounding of a bell.

This was the inner *maṇḍala* hall. By imperial decree, monks from the two monastic districts were commissioned to establish a *maṇḍala* within the inner palace to pray for the blessings of the people. Emperor Xiaozong constructed the Inner Contemplation Hall (*Nei-guān-táng*).
An imperial edict was issued for Dharma Master Zhunai to lead fifty monks into the practice of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* repentance ritual;
this was established as an annual custom.
Emperor Ruizong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict for the Imperial Consorts and Princesses to establish Gongde Temples (Merit Monasteries).
Emperor Daizong issued an imperial decree to the Chancellor and high ministers.
The Gongde Monastery was first established.
Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty issued an imperial decree to follow the established laws of the founding ancestors.
For the meritorious tombs and monasteries of meritorious ministers and members of the imperial clan, one should permit them to construct their own buildings and establish fields;
they shall be granted official titles and exempted from levies and impositions,
and it is permitted for their respective families to appoint the abbots.
Regarding the prohibition against appropriating monasteries with fixed endowments: During the reign of Emperor Gaozong,
Chen Gongfu, the Palace Counselor,

submitted a memorial stating that for those officials who had previously petitioned to have a monastery with a fixed endowment converted into a funerary temple for the merit of their ancestors, [the government should take action].
I beg that you examine the established laws of our ancestors and grant a rectification throughout. [Emperor] Lizong:
A memorial submitted by a court official stated:
I beg that the monasteries claimed by the current ministers and high officials be investigated and restored to their original status. — Sung Xiaowu.
On the anniversary of Emperor Wen’s death,
an Eightfold Precept fast was held at Zhongxing Temple; however,
the minister Yuan Min-sun further presented fish and meat.
The Emperor was enraged and demoted him from office.
Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty issued an imperial edict regarding the memorial days of the former reigns.
During the incense-offering and vegetarian feast at Zhangjing Monastery,
Zhongzong issued an edict that on the memorial days of the seven successive reigns,
vegetarian feasts and incense offerings were to be held within the inner palace. — Emperor Xuanzong.
The Emperor decreed that on the days of the national memorial services for the deceased emperors,
the monks and Daoists were to perform rites at Longxing Temple and observe the period of fasting.
Emperor Xuanzong decreed that the same should apply to the memorial days of all the successive sovereigns.

They proceeded together to the monasteries to offer incense according to the ancient rites; this was during the period following Emperor Wuzong’s suppression of Buddhism. An imperial edict mandated that when performing incense offerings for the anniversaries of the state’s founding or the deaths of emperors in the prefectures, commanderies, and kingdoms, no one was permitted to carry wine or meat into the temples.
During the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty, an imperial edict was issued regarding the observance of the national memorial day:
the ministers and all officials were to proceed to the monastery to offer incense and provide a meal for the monks.
Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty issued an edict regarding the national memorial days for deceased emperors,
stipulating that from the Chancellor downward [must observe the rites].
He visited temples and monasteries to perform the incense ritual and abstained from meat and wine.
Various countries sent tribute to the Jin Emperor Wu;
the Kingdom of Funan dispatched an envoy.
A golden Buddha and an ivory stupa were presented by Emperor An.
A jade Buddha image, four chi and two cun in height, was presented by the Kingdom of Siṃhala.
Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty;
the kingdom of Kapilavastu;
the kingdom of Siṃhala.
The kingdoms of Harada, Haruṇḍa, and Śrīvijaya—
these five nations all dispatched envoys to present tribute.
During the reign of Emperor Donghun of the Qi dynasty,
the monk Huishen from the country of Fusang came to the capital. [Later,
during the reign of] Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty...
The Kingdom of Youtouli presented tribute, reporting: "A Sage King has appeared in the eastern lands.

A śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Funan presented a coral Buddha image. The Kingdom of Panpan dispatched an envoy to present a Buddha tooth. The Kingdom of Dandan dispatched an envoy to present a Buddha image. The Kingdom of Funan dispatched an envoy to pay court and present tribute.

[Emperor Taizong of Tang] requested Buddhist images, sutras, and śāstras; the Kingdom of Baekje dispatched an envoy to present tribute and request sutras and śāstras; the Kingdom of Khotan dispatched an envoy to offer jade Buddhist images.
Emperor Taizong of Tang.
The Silla monk Sengwon of the Three Kingdoms period entered China to study the Buddha-dharma during the reign of Emperor Dezong.
The Tibetan ruler sent an envoy requesting that a śramaṇa skilled in expounding Buddhist principles be granted to them.
Emperor [Tang] Xuanzong ordered Liangxiu to go there.
Emperor Taizu of Song [did likewise].
The Korean śramaṇa Diguan traveled to China carrying the commentaries on the Tiantai treatises to pay his respects to Master Luoxi. The King of Goryeo dispatched thirty-six monks to China.
The lineage of Chan Master Yongming Yanshou was studied;

to this day, the single school of Fayan flourishes abroad. The Śramaṇa Kazhi and others from India came to court. The Śramaṇa Sugata from India came to offer Buddhist relics and Mañjuśrī flowers. The Śramaṇa Mīra from India came to offer Sanskrit scriptures. Seven Śramaṇas from Khotan, including Shanming, arrived. The Kingdom of Gaochang dispatched the monk Fayuan.
An ivory tooth of a Pratyekabuddha was offered. Emperor Taizong:
The Śramaṇa from the Western Heaven, Śrī, came to present Sanskrit scriptures.
The Śramaṇa Jizong returned from the Western Heaven and presented Sanskrit scriptures and a stūpa containing śarīra relics. The Śramaṇa from Central India, Padma, arrived.

Offering of a Śarīra Stūpa; the Indian śramaṇa Húlu arrived to offer Sanskrit scriptures; the śramaṇa Guǎngyuǎn returned from his journey to the Western Heaven and presented the memorial of the Prince of West India.
An offering of Śākyamuni’s śarīra relics. ○ The śramaṇa Fayu returned from the Western Heaven with an offering of a *buddhōṣṇīṣa* śarīra relic and a Sanskrit sūtra.
○ The śramaṇa Chongda returned from the Western Heaven with an offering of a *buddhōṣṇīṣa* śarīra relic and a Sanskrit sūtra.
The Śarīra and Sanskrit Sūtras were presented by the Śramaṇa Potala from Central India.

The Śarīra and Sanskrit Sūtras were presented [by another]. The Śramaṇa Jingjie from the Kingdom of Champa went to the palace to offer a gold-copper bell and *vajra*. The King of Goryeo dispatched an envoy.
I beg that you graciously grant me the Imperial Compositions on the Buddha Vehicle from the Great Canon.
An imperial edict was issued to bestow [these works] upon the Japanese monk Ryōnen,
who came to court and stated that his country has transmitted [the Dharma] for sixty-four generations.
During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty,
an envoy was dispatched to China to seek the Lotus Sutra.
In the fourth year of the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty...
He dispatched the monk Dàozhào to enter China to receive the Dharma from Dharma Master Xuánzàng, as detailed at length in the *Tōnsai-shi*.
Eien then returned to his own country.
An edict was issued granting the Tripitaka.
In the ninth year of the Xiangfu era of the Zhenzong reign,
the Japanese Dharma Master Fajie (Ryōnen) dispatched his disciples Jiayin and Qiqian to the imperial court.
The śramaṇa Tiānjué from North India;
the śramaṇa Miàodé from South India;
and the śramaṇas from West India.
Each presented Sanskrit scriptures:
the Śramaṇa Tanyao from Central India came to present Sanskrit scriptures;
the Śramaṇa Puzhi from Eastern India came to present Sanskrit scriptures.
Within a single year, all five regions of India presented tribute.

A śramaṇa from the kingdom of Japan named Jikishō arrived and offered a statue of Amitāyus Buddha and the *Lotus Sūtra* written in golden characters. A śramaṇa from Central India named Nivini also arrived.

Śāriputra-brāhmaṇa-sūtra presented. ○ The Śramaṇa Buddhagupta from Western India arrived and presented a Sanskrit sūtra. ○ The Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa from Western India arrived and presented a Sanskrit sūtra.

○ The Śramaṇa Śīlabhadra from Northern India arrived and presented a Sanskrit sūtra. ○ The Śramaṇa Mūlaśikṣita from Kaśmīra arrived and presented a Sanskrit sūtra. ○ The Śramaṇa Dharmapāla from Western India arrived and presented a Sanskrit sūtra. ○ The Śramaṇa Guṇamati from Western India arrived for audience.
The Śarīra-vibhaṅga-sūtra was presented by the Śramaṇa Juecheng and Fajie from Central India.
The True Image of the Vajrāsana was presented by the Śramaṇa Jixian from the country of Pāṇi. The Śramaṇa Zhixian from the Western Heaven (India) arrived and presented Sanskrit scriptures.
The *Śarīra-brahma-sūtra* was presented; the Kingdom of Eastern Jurchen submitted tribute and requested the bestowal of the Tripiṭaka;

the Śramaṇa Āryabhadra from the Western Heaven presented the Sanskrit *śarīra-sūtra*; the Śramaṇa Prajñāśrī from the Western Heaven came to present Sanskrit scriptures; and the State of Xixia submitted a memorial.
A newly constructed monastery was established within the realm;
[the Emperor] requested that the Tripitaka be bestowed.
During the reign of Emperor Shenzong, the Japanese monk Jōjin came to court. During the reign of Emperor Zhezong.
Prince Yi Tian, the State Preceptor of Goryeo, came to court;
Su Shi served as his host,
and by imperial decree, Yang Jie was sent to escort him to Qiantang.
He received the Dharma from Master Yuan;
he transmitted the Tiantai teachings to Master Jian of Tianzhu;
and he transmitted the Vinaya to Master Zhao of Lingzhi. [Emperor] Xiaozong.
An envoy was dispatched from the Kingdom of Japan to deliver a letter.
At the court of Siming County, the Venerable Qixin read it aloud to the envoy and refuted its textual meanings and errors.
There are seven locations in total.

The *Fozu Tongji*, Volume 52, concludes with the following entry: "The Holy Ancestor Opens the Way First. Regarding the Holy Ancestor Opening the Way First: during the Song dynasty, the Great Ancestor, a celestial deity, descended into the home of Zhang Shouzhen, saying: [text continues].
The duration of the state’s mandate shall exceed that of the Tang dynasty.
An imperial edict was issued to enshrine him as the True Lord Who Assists the Sage and Protects Virtue (Ciyingsheng Baode Zhenjun).
During the Zhenzong era, the court sorcerer Wang Zhongli encountered a Daoist practitioner surnamed Zhao.
He styled himself the True Lord of Destiny (Siming Zhenjun).
When auspicious omens or anomalies appeared throughout the nine realms, he would invariably inform Zhongli [Midian]. Then, a celestial deity descended into his private chamber and said to him:
"A heavenly book is about to descend; it is fitting that you observe fast and purification to receive it.
The Imperial Household Office reported that a silk scroll was trailing from the *chīwén* (ridge-end ornament) atop the Right Gate of the Heavenly Court.
An attendant picked it up and examined its text, which read:
The Zhao dynasty received its mandate and rose during the Song era for seven hundred and ninety-nine years;
its founding was proclaimed by Wen,
and its name was Da Zhongxiangfu.

In three sections total. Having completed the Feng and Shan sacrifices at Mount Tai, he issued an edict appointing Siming Zhenjun as the Nine Heavens Lord of Fate, the Venerable Sovereign Who Preserves Life.
Emperor Zhao then commissioned Ding Wei, the Commissioner of the Three Departments, to construct the Yuqing Zhaoying Palace.
The front hall was named Taichu (Great Beginning),
established to serve the Jade Sovereign;
a pavilion was constructed to enshrine the Celestial Scripture.
The rear hall was named Mingqing (Bright Celebration),
established to enshrine the Holy Ancestor, the Most High Lord of Destiny of the Nine Heavens.
By imperial decree, Tianqing Observatories were constructed throughout the empire.
He offered these to the Three Pure Ones and the Jade Emperor, and additionally established the Hall of the Sacred Ancestor (Shengzu Dian).
A celestial deity descended into the inner palace and said to the Emperor:
"I am one of the nine Human Sovereigns (Renhuang)."
This is the second descent of the progenitor of the Zhao clan;
he was Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor Xuan Yuan.
I have descended during the Later Tang period.
Having governed the lower regions in total, he was born into the Zhao clan; now a hundred years have passed.
The Emperor has skillfully nurtured all living beings, and he shall now depart upon yellow clouds.
In this month, there was a great amnesty.

The Emperor assumed the honorific title of "Suzhu Shangling Gao Dao Jiutian Siming Baosheng Tianzun" (Holy Patriarch, Supreme Spirit, High Way, Lord of the Nine Heavens, Preserver of Life, Celestial Honored One).
The Holy Patriarch’s Consort was titled "Yuantian Dasheng Hou" (Great Sage Empress of the Primordial Heaven).
The personal name of the Holy Ancestor was Xuānlǎng.
By imperial decree, none within the realm were permitted to utter it in disparagement or violation.
An edict was issued for all prefectures to construct additional halls for the Holy Ancestor at their Tianqing Observatories.
He dispatched Li Pu to Jian’an Commandery to supervise the casting of two statues of the Jade Sovereign and the Holy Ancestor.
By imperial decree, Ding Wei was commissioned to escort them to the capital,
where they were enshrined in the Yuqing Zhaoying Palace.
○ Śāri saw [the Emperor] at the Mingqing Hall of the Shengzu Temple in the Yuqing Zhaoying Palace.
○ An imperial edict was issued to construct the Jingling Palace on the Bing site within the Great Inner Palace to enshrine the Sacred Ancestor.
Regarding auspicious portents recorded in the dynastic histories: the lay practitioner Lu Faho of the Northern Qi once inscribed on a wall, saying:
"Ten years for the Son of Heaven is still tolerable; ten days for Wenxuan is as urgent as fire; a hundred days for the deposed Emperor. (The deposed Emperor reigned for one hundred days.)
The successive reigns of the Heavenly Son (Emperor) for a full cycle— namely, [Emperors] Xiaozhao and the two others—
feared that they could not eradicate [the heresy] through mere suppression.
Then, Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, Śrīṣeṇa of the Western Heaven, came forward and submitted this petition:
According to the account obtained from a stone inscription in India:
"In the east lies the land of China, named Da Sui;
its capital city is named Da Xing."
The king's name was Jianyi (Firm Resolve).
He established the Three Jewels.
[This corresponds to] Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty.
The Prefect of Yuanzhou submitted a report:
"In Hongchizhu Valley there are five stones with a blue substance and white inscriptions which read: [followed by the inscriptions].
The Heavenly Sovereign of Great Peace, Li Shimin, and the Crown Prince, Li Zhi; the Seven Buddhas and Eight Bodhisattvas.
By imperial decree, an envoy was dispatched to offer sacrifices of thanks. The Emperor obtained a secret prophecy which stated:
"Three generations after the Tang..."
A female ruler, King Wu, shall succeed to the throne of all under heaven.
The Grand Astrologer Li Chunfeng said:
"The omens have already been established; she is currently within the palace."
The Emperor said, "Kill those who are suspected.
He replied,
"The Mandate of Heaven cannot be altered."
Thereupon he desisted. Emperor Suzong issued an edict for the śramaṇa Yuanjiao to establish a Bhaiṣajyaguru-pūjā altar;
suddenly, forty-nine peach trees sprang forth. The nun Zhenru ascended to heaven and beheld the Heavenly Emperor.
He bestowed thirteen heavenly treasures to pacify the lower realm.
Thereupon, the era name was changed to Baoying. From Emperor Suzong to Emperor Zhaozong, there were thirteen reigns. [Emperor] Ruizong was the Prince of Xiang.
Every time he went out ten thousand times, he would announce to people,
"The Son of Heaven is coming!
When Emperor Xuanzong was still a prince, he went to pay his respects to him.
He patted his back and said,
"The Son of Heaven who has enjoyed fifty years of peace is Song Taizu."
He was born in Luoyang;
a divine light filled the room,
and his body was clothed in golden radiance.
Once, while staying at Chángshòu Sī (Longevity Monastery) and resting upon the pillow-platform of the Hall of the Emperor,
the monk Shǒuyán saw a red snake entering and exiting his nostril. In Sòngchéng,
there was an extraordinary monk who pointed to the ground of the prefecture and said:
"In less than twenty years, there shall be an emperor.
For this reason, the title 'Great Ancestor' (Dazong) was established.
In the fourth year of Taiping, two dark stones were obtained by a commoner from Jiajiang County in Jiazhou.
All were written in vermilion characters.
One read: "The King and Lord live ten thousand years.
The other read: "The Twenty-first Emperor of Zhao."

*Jianqishi lai xian benchao tongjian* (The Sealed Stone Presented to the Present Dynasty’s Comprehensive Mirror). In the seventh year of Taiping, Shuzhou submitted a memorial reporting the offering of an *duan* stone.
It was engraved with the record of Master Zhigong of the Liang dynasty, which states:
"I observe that after four or five dynasties, in the next *bingzi* year, the Zhao will be called Taiping, spanning twenty-one emperors."
One day, Master Zhigong descended into the imperial palace.
The Emperor personally heard his instructions and subsequently dispatched an envoy to Mount Zhong to offer a vegetarian feast.
He was posthumously bestowed the title Bodhisattva Zhijue of Daolin.
Emperor Zhenzong took the inscription on the auspicious stone by Master Zhigong and showed it to his close ministers.
The Chancellor Wang Qie said:
The auspicious destiny of the state began during the Liang, Chen, Sui, Tang, and the Five Dynasties periods;
the year of Emperor Taizong’s accession was the *bingzi* year,
and all current events regarding the descent of the Honored One correspond perfectly with these.
Thus we know that Heaven’s mandate for our Song has been with us for a long time.
[The Emperor] was delighted. The Japanese Kingdom submitted an offering, stating:
"In the eastern part of our country, an auspicious light appeared; this omen corresponds to the sagely brilliance of the Son of Heaven of the Middle Kingdom."
An imperial edict was issued to establish Shinkō-ji Temple in Japan.
○ A tribute mission from Chulnyun-guk arrived,
reporting that for forty years there had been no wind or waves at sea.
It was said that a sage would appear in the Middle Kingdom;
previously, when the former sage [the Buddha] left home, and likewise when the Han High Ancestor passed through Lu,
he offered sacrifices to Confucius.
He enfeoffed Teng, a ninth-generation descendant, as Lord of the Sacrificial Service (Fengci-jun).
○ Emperor Yuan enfeoffed Yi, a descendant of Confucius, as Lord of Baicheng (Baocheng-jun).
○ Emperor Ping enfeoffed Kong Jun, a descendant of Confucius, as Marquis of Baicheng (Baocheng-hou). ○ Emperor Guangwu visited Lu and sacrificed to Confucius.
He enfeoffed Houzhi as Marquis of Baicheng.
During the reign of Emperor Ming, when he visited Queli to sacrifice to Confucius,
he enfeoffed the nineteenth-generation descendant, Xi, as Marquis of Baicheng.
Emperor Ming of the Han visited Lu and sacrificed to Confucius;
he appointed Kong Xi as Langzhong.

Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty enfeoffed Kong Xian, the twenty-first-generation descendant of Confucius, as the Marquis of Chongsheng. Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict designating Confucius as the First Sage.
His descendants were enfeoffed as the Marquis of Bao Sheng.
Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty issued an edict enfeoffing Xuan, the forty-fourth descendant of Confucius, as the Duke of Wenxuan.
○ Emperor Zhenzong issued an edict enfeoffing Kong Shengyu as Duke Wenxuan.
○ Emperor Renzong issued an edict enfeoffing Kong Zongyuan as Duke Wenxuan.
○ An imperial decree was issued enfeoffing the forty-sixth-generation descendant, Zongyuan, as Duke Qiansheng.
Emperor Shenzong issued an edict conferring the title Duke Qinsheng upon his forty-seventh-generation descendant, Ruomeng.
Emperor Huizong issued an edict conferring the title Duke Qinsheng upon his forty-eighth-generation descendant, Danyou.
Emperor Gaozong issued an edict concerning the death of the Forty-ninth Generation Grand Master of the Confucian Temple, Yan, who was residing in Quzhou.
His son, Jin, succeeded him as the Grand Master of the Confucian Temple, becoming the Fiftieth Generation.
A great Confucian who brought fame to the age: Zengzi of the Zhou dynasty.
His name was Shen;
he studied under Confucius.
He composed the *Xiaojing*.
○ Zisi was the grandson of Confucius;
his name was Ji.
He studied under Zengzi and composed the "Zhongyong" (The Doctrine of the Mean). — Mencius.
His name was Ke.
He studied under Zisi and authored seven chapters of a book,
expounding upon the Way of Yao and Shun.
Ji (Ji Kang) stated that human nature is good.
○ Xun Qing, whose given name was Kuang.
His written work is titled the *Xunzi*.
He honored the King and rejected the barbarians,
asserting that human nature is evil.
During the reign of Emperor Ai of the Han dynasty,
Yang Xiong modeled his *Taiyan* after the *Yijing* and composed his *Fayan* based on the *Lunyu*.
It is said that human nature is a mixture of good and evil.
Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty and Wang Tong continued the Six Classics.
His disciples posthumously conferred upon him the title Wénzhōngzǐ (Master of Literary Excellence).
His disciples compiled his words of questions and answers,
titling the work Zhōngshuō (Discourses of the Middle).

In the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, an imperial edict decreed that Mencius be enshrined as the Duke of Zou alongside the former sage [Confucius] in the temple;
however, he was not included in the ranks of those participating in the sacrificial offerings. As for Zu Qiu Ming, the Grand Scribe of Lu—
Contemporary with him,
Confucius used the Annals of Lu as the basis for the Spring and Autumn Annals and composed commentaries upon them.
Furthermore, Guo Yu was composed by Gu Liang Chi, a man of Zhou and Lu who transmitted the *Chunqiu*; Gongyang Gao, a man of Zhou and Qi, also transmitted the *Chunqiu*.
Both Chi and Gao were disciples of Zi Xia. Fu Sheng served as a *boshi* under the Second Emperor of Qin.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Han, he was ninety years old.
He orally transmitted the *Shangshu* to Chao Cuo.
Initially, when Fu Sheng encountered the proscription of books during the Qin dynasty, [he hid them].
He stored it in the wall-shelf of the Imperial Library.
After the Han dynasty was established,
twenty-nine chapters were recovered and used to instruct Zhang Sheng of Jinan, Ou-yang Sheng Mao-lang, and the scholars of the River-Interval Prince Xian-wang.
Shizi Xia composed the *Gaoxun* commentary on the *Mao Shi*. Gao Tangsheng, a native of Lu, served as a *Fushi* (Assistant Official) at the beginning of the Han dynasty.

The *Zhuan Shili* (Seventeen Chapters on the Rites of the Officer) consists of seventeen chapters. Kong Anguo was the Governor of Linhuai under Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty and the eleventh-generation descendant of Confucius;
he composed the *Shangshu Zhuan* (Commentary on the Book of Documents).
The *Commentary on the Ancient Text of the Classic of Filial Piety* and the *Exegesis of the Analects*.

by Amoghavajra in the eighth year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong; and by Master Wei.
The Maiden of Ma (Mālabhāryā) during the eighth year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong;
the Emanation Body of Samantabhadra during the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong; and the Great Holy One (Mahāsiddha) who followed [the Buddha].
Emperor Wenzong, Taihe [Era]:
Song Renzong added a title for Qiyu.
Emperor Dezong, Jianzhong [Era]: Lan Can.
Emperor Dezong’s Zhenyuan era: Fudashi.
Emperor Xuanzong’s *Zengzhiyuan*: Opening the Stupa. Emperor Shaodi of Jin:
The King of Wuyue Questions the Stupa. Xiangshan Amitābha.
In the eighth year of the Yizong era,
the Chan Master Quanzhen of Mount Xiang was an emanation of Amitābha Buddha; [the remains of] the two *dharmakāya* bodies at Guiyang were from the third year of the Xizong era.
The two stupas of Chan Master Wuliao of Quanzhou and his disciple Huizhong; Xiazizi;
during the Tianfu era of Emperor Zhaozong; the manifestation of Pudu Maitreya at Yuelin.
Wudai Liang: Daoyuan.
Wudai Tang: Koubing Gufu. Wudai Tang: Mayi.
Emperor Taizu of Zhou (Guǎngshùn); Emperor Taizu of Song (Jiànlóng); the Ascetic Lou;
Emperor Zhenzong of Song (Chúnhuà);
[he] trod upon the jeweled flower, an emanation of the Buddha; summoned by the Emperor for an audience; the four worlds.
Loudao said: "This is an emanation of the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha;
he speaks of the Lotus Sūtra."
Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty;
Emperor Renzong silently offered prayers and invited him to a vegetarian feast; Maozhen of Mount Emei;
Emperor Zhenzong summoned him for an audience; the Master of Nanan Rock.
During the True Sect (Shinshū) period,
Kishō Chigo was an emanation of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
During the True Sect period, he severed his own arm as a prayer for rain.
It is said that among the five hundred arhats was one named Jie Xiang (Fragrance of Precepts), who was mute.
During the reign of Emperor Renzong,
the ancient Buddha Jie Xiang Weiyu of Siming appeared as Li Shineng.
During the reign of Emperor Renzong, [the Master] said to Wei Kai at Luoyang:
"The 'Fragrance of Precepts' and the 'Mute Woman' refer to the Buddha Vipaśyin. — Cai Junmu.
The Illusory Eyes Dream of Nāgārjuna and Pán'áng.
During the reign of Emperor Shenzong, Pan’ang spoke regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*, saying: [text continues]
This is the Sunlight Buddha (Rìguāng Fó).
During the reign of Emperor Shenzong,
[he] followed Pán’āng and traveled with Fótuōbōlì.
During the reign of Emperor Zhezong, Su Shi, the Governor of Yingzhou, requested that the imperial court grant the plaque for the monastery’s courtyard, naming it "Guangfan" (Radiant Dharma).
He established an altar there to receive the precepts. Regarding the establishment of an altar to receive the precepts, it was first practiced during the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.

The Minister of Works Liu Jun and others all requested to leave the household life; at that time, they merely received the Three Refuges. When the Western Indian Dharmakāla arrived in Luoyang during the Wei dynasty, he translated the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and established the *mahāsaṃgha-karman* for the conferral of precepts. Duke Gaogui (Yuan Shao) invited Dharmakāla to perform the rite for receiving the precepts, with the śramaṇa Zhu Shixing acting as the officiant for the ordination. This was the beginning of the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*).

During the reign of Emperor Kang of the Jin dynasty, the nun Jingjian attained the precepts through her original method; this refers specifically to receiving the precepts from the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty...

When Saṃghavarman arrived in Jiankang, he conferred the full ordination a second time upon the śramaṇa Huizhao and others while they were on board the ship; this opened the way for receiving the precepts repeatedly. ○ Guṇavarman.
He established a *kṣetra-maṇḍala* (ordination platform) at Nanlin Monastery to confer the precepts upon monks and nuns,
including the nun Huiguo and others.
Regarding the re-ordination of full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon the *śīlakaṇḍa* according to the two assemblies— consisting of ten monks and ten nuns as the two assemblies—
the *Sengshi lüe* (Abridged History of the Sangha) states:
"In the Han dynasty, Apan received the Three Refuges."
Jin Du and Jing Jian followed the tradition of the single assembly (*ekasamgha*).
The two assemblies (*dvisamgha*) represent the beginning of attaining the fruits of precepts and wisdom.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty.
He received the full precepts from Master Yao. Among the crown prince, high officials, monastics, and laypeople who received the precepts from the Master, there were forty-eight thousand people.
These included venerable śramaṇas who were already recipients of the Bodhisattva precepts and who now received the dharma of the precepts again; this was their reception of the full precepts.
During the reign of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty,
Vinaya Master Xuan established a stone *śīlaskandha* altar at Jingye Monastery,
where śramaṇas from the mountains and rivers received the full ordination once again.
The Compilation of the *Platform Sūtra*.
Emperor Daizong issued an imperial decree for the construction of a Fangdeng Precept Platform at Daxingshan Temple. Emperor Muzong [reigned];
Wang Zhixing, Grand Secretary of the Secretariat.
He established a Fangdeng (Vaipulya) ordination platform at Sizhou and requested that on the Emperor’s birthday, the monk Jingzong be ordained.
By imperial decree, Fangdeng ordination platforms were established in both monastic districts.
An Guo Temple in the Left Ward;
Xing Fu Temple in the Right Ward.
○ Emperor Xuanzong.
Following the suppression of Buddhism during the Huichang era,
imperial edicts were issued for the capitals and the provinces of Jingzhou, Yangzhou, Bianzhou,
and Yizhou to establish ordination platforms (jie tan) for the Fangdeng school.
Regarding the method for receiving the precepts again for those who have already been ordained as monks or nuns:
Emperor Yizong issued an edict to the four monasteries of the two streets,
ordering each to establish a *śīla-maṇḍala* (ordination platform) to ordain monks.
Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty,
because there was no distinction between monks and nuns,
issued an edict that nunneries should establish altars for the conferral of precepts.
The Great Virtuous Bhikṣuṇī presided over the True Sect.
At Chongsheng Monastery in Shenzhou, it was granted the name "Ganlu Ordination Platform. By imperial decree, the Ganlu Ordination Platform for Honoring the Ancestors was established in the capital.
Precept platforms were established throughout all the circuits of the realm,
totaling seventy-two locations;
a separate Mahāyāna precept platform was also established in the capital.
They established images and placed scriptures; Prince Zhou Mu established an image of Kāśyapa at the Qinshui Grottoes.
Duke Mu of Qin fashioned a bronze image of the Buddha.
Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty cast a golden stupa and an image of Laozi.
Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty...
Xun Xu, the Palace Attendant,
commissioned twelve golden images in Luoyang.
Emperor Xiaowu’s Dharma Master An commissioned a bronze image at Tanxi Temple.
He was able to initiate the practice himself.
The Recluse Dai Kui emitted light that illuminated the heavens;
he personally fashioned a statue of Amitābha Buddha and enshrined it at Lingbao Monastery.
Xi Chao gathered incense and performed a prostration;
suddenly, smoke rose upward. Emperor An of the Jin dynasty had Jiang Yi commission a statue of Avalokiteśvara through Dai Yong.
In a dream during the night, a person commanded him to recast the Maitreya statue;
as soon as it was touched by his hands, it became a marvelous image of Emperor Gao.
The Emperor then issued an edict for the Waguan Temple to cast a sixteen-foot golden image.
Radiant light filled the temple. During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, a sixteen-foot golden Buddha was cast in Xuzhou;
whenever there was a threat of invasion, the image would perspire. During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu.
Empress Dowager Lu commissioned an image of Samantabhadra at Zhongxing Temple.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty visited Tongtai Temple and cast golden-bronze images of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions.
During the reign of Emperor Xianwen of the Northern Wei,
an imperial edict was issued to cast five statues of Śākyamuni Buddha,
each one zhang-six feet tall, to represent the Five Emperors of the Taizu lineage. During the reign of Emperor Xiaoming...
For Empress Dowager Hu, he constructed the nine-story pagoda of Yongning Temple, housing a sixteen-foot golden image; it stood ninety zhang high.
By imperial decree, pagodas of five tiers were established in all commanderies. — Emperor Xiaozhuang.
Meng Zhonghui fashioned a buddha image of lacquered cloth.
Every night he circumambulated the seat while practicing the Way.
Emperor Xiaowu established a stupa at Pingdeng Temple and hosted a vegetarian feast for ten thousand monks.
The stone Buddha kept its head bowed all day long.
Emperor Gaozu of the Tang dynasty commissioned three life-sized statues of the Buddha for Taizu. Emperor Taizong dreamed of Yu Shinan.
An imperial edict was issued to create one statue of a Buddha to provide merit for the deceased.
Emperor Gaozong issued an edict to carve a stone niche for Vairocana Buddha, eighty-five feet in height, at Longmen Mountain in Luoyang.
The śramaṇa Zhìyùn carved fifteen thousand stone Buddhas at Longmén Mountain.
Empress Wǔ collected one coin per day from every monk in the empire to create a Great Image on Báisīmǎbǎn. Emperor Xuānzōng [did likewise].
An imperial edict was issued to all prefectures to cast a gilded bronze statue of the Emperor, equal to his own height, at Kaiyuan Temple.
The śramaṇa Haitong carved a stone image of Maitreya Buddha, three hundred and sixty feet high, from the Great River at Jiazhou.
The upper pavilion has nine stories.
During the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty,
the Indian śramaṇa Daoyi [constructed it].
A statue of Avalokiteśvara was fashioned from a rare wood, and ancient Buddha relics were enshrined within its *ūrṇā-kośa* (hair-treasure).
A brilliant white light radiated forth. [This was commissioned by] Zhu Chong, General of the Propaganda Bureau.
While digging the earth, a great stone Buddha was discovered;
it was converted from its original site into a temple.
At the beginning of the Kaion era, an imperial edict was issued to transcribe the Tripitaka for the High Ancestor.
Enshrined at Mingsheng Temple:
Han Gaozu and Shangzhuguo Guo Lingwei.
Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty erected a stone stele for the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṃitā Sūtra* at Shouchun;

he issued an imperial decree to have the woodblocks for the Tripitaka carved at Yizhou; he issued an imperial decree to go to Mount Emei to adorn Buddhist statues; and Emperor Zhenzong performed the Feng sacrifice at Mount Tai.
The Emperor decreed the restoration of thirty-two Buddha images;

he personally composed the "Record of the Restoration of Images. ○ By Imperial Edict, the śramaṇa Xiyan was commissioned to restore seventeen thousand Buddha niches at Longmen Mountain. ○ Emperor Zhezong.
An imperial decree was issued for Donglin Temple to fashion divine images and transport those of the Five Halls. Su Shi painted the Water-Land (Shuilu) images and composed sixteen eulogies for them.
Su Shi obtained a painting of the Eighteen Arhats by Zhang and wrote eulogies for them.
He bestowed [the title] upon his younger brother Zhe.
Emperor Gaozong granted the *gishi* (Court Attendant) Feng Jie permission to produce forty-eight sets of the Great Canon (*Dazangjing*).
He constructed temples and erected stupas; Prince Zhou Mu built Zhulin Monastery on Mount Gu.
Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty first established the Baima Temple;
there were ten temples within and outside the capital city of Luoyang.
To the east of Baima Temple, a stūpa for the Buddha’s śarīra was constructed.
During the Wei dynasty, Sun Quan, Prince of Wu,
established Changle Temple in Wuchang.
Lady Pan founded Huibao Temple. [This was during the time of] Kan Ze,
the Grand Master of the Secretariat.
His residence was converted into Dejun Temple, which is the present-day Puji Temple.
During the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, Zhuge [Shi] of Kuaiji established Lingbao Temple. During the reign of Emperor Cheng...

Li Miao, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, took the Lingyao Temple at Juyong and Wang Xizhi’s Lushan Temple to establish Guizong Temple. Xu Xun constructed a four-story pagoda, but it lacked a *xianglun* (finial).
One day, amidst wind and rain, the wheel and basin appeared spontaneously. Emperor Kang:
the Grand Secretary He Chong donated his residence to establish Jianfu Temple. Emperor Ai:
issued an imperial decree to establish Waguan Temple. Emperor Fei.
The Emperor issued an edict to establish Wozhou Temple for Dharma Master Zhi Dun.
Emperor Jianwen issued an edict to establish Xinlin Temple for the nun Daorong;
he also commanded Changgan Temple to construct a three-story pagoda. Emperor Xiaowu.
Tao Fan, the Regional Inspector of Xunyang,
converted his own residence to establish Xilin Monastery for Master Yong.
Huan Yi, the Regional Inspector of Jiujiang, [did likewise].
He established Donglin Monastery for Dharma Master Huiyuan. Furthermore, Huan Chong, the Governor of Jingzhou,
commissioned Dharma Master Tanyi to establish two monasteries, East and West,
where the number of monks regularly reached ten thousand.
Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty:
Fan Qin founded Jihuan Temple;
Xie Lingyun founded Zhaoti Temple. Emperor Wen.
He established Ba’en Temple for the sake of the High Ancestor.
By imperial decree, the śramaṇa Daohu was sent to Maò County to construct a three-storied stūpa. The śramaṇa Dharmamitra...
The Aśoka King Stūpa was constructed in Mao County.
During the reign of Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty,
the śramaṇa Xuanchang established Qilong Temple.
He was moved by a divine being in green robes who circumambulated the mountain to protect it;
Emperor Wu [of the Liang dynasty] and the lay practitioner Ming Sengshao then donated their residence at Mount She to establish Xiqia Monastery.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty:
His former residence emitted light for seven nights;
by imperial decree, Guangzhai Monastery was established. He issued an edict to repair the Longgan Stupa.
He obtained a lapis lazuli jar to enshrine the śarīra, nails, and hair.
When the stupa of Tongtai Temple was destroyed by fire, he rebuilt it as a twelve-story stupa. [This was done by] Tao Hongjing, the Immortal of Huayang.
He built a stupa and a white pagoda at Mount Sanmao. When Prince Yueyang Xiao Cha governed Yuezhou,
he renovated both the brick and wooden stupas,
recognizing that [the former master] had been Xu Xun in a previous life.
During the reign of Emperor Wencheng of the Northern Wei,
the Buddha-dharma was extensively restored.
He issued an edict that each commandery and county must establish one Buddhist monastery (futu), and he decreed the construction of Luye Monastery.
He practiced and studied meditative concentration for several hundred days with Zen monks.
Emperor Xiaowen built Baode Temple for the Empress Dowager and for Dharma Master Luoshi.
A three-story pagoda was built at the former residence of Caotang.
During the Xuanwu era, Duan Hui of Luoyang heard the sound of bells underground and discovered one golden Buddha and two Bodhisattvas.
He subsequently donated his residence to become a monastery. During the Northern Zhou dynasty, at Changnian Temple, a śarīra was enshrined in a reliquary;
its radiance spontaneously emerged from the vessel.
A stūpa was constructed and enshrined therein.

During the Sui dynasty, Emperor Wen issued an edict to establish a temple at the site of the battle in Xiangzhou to offer merit for the soldiers who had died in service. Xin Yanzhi erected a fifteen-story stūpa there.
Zhang Yuan traveled by spirit to the heavens and saw a hall.
A celestial being said, "The Prefect Xin shall dwell here. [He then issued] an edict for all famous provinces under heaven to construct stupas of numinous power.
The śarīra relics were enshrined within one hundred and eleven stupas;
the records of these miraculous and auspicious traces are fully contained in the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*). [Regarding] Li Yuan, the Duke of Tang:
The residence was converted into Qingchan Temple. By imperial decree, Chandeng Temple was established;

Master Tanqian was summoned, and one hundred and twenty men of renowned virtue were gathered to reside there. When Master Zhiyi of Zhizhe arrived at Yuquan, [the Emperor] likewise sent an envoy to invite him.
Gan moved the divine soldiers of Guan Yu to build a temple; Zen Master Zhiguan established Tianzhu Temple on Mount Hulinsi;
and Emperor Yang received the final testament of Zhiyi.
He founded Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai.
Emperor Gaozu of the Tang dynasty established Shengye Temple for the śramaṇa Jinghui.
He established Cíbēi Monastery for the śramaṇa Tánxiàn;
he established Yìxīng Monastery for those who had raised righteous banners in Bìngzhōu.

Emperor Tàizōng issued an edict to designate the former imperial residence as Xīngshèng Monastery; he also issued an edict to establish monasteries at each site where military engagements had occurred since the beginning of the Jiànyì era.
Having defeated Liu Wuzhou at Fenzhou, he established Hongji Temple there;

Li Baiyao composed its inscription. Regarding twenty-seven temples, it says: "By imperial decree, Qingshan Palace was converted into Cide Temple for the construction of a memorial for Empress Dowager Mu."

He established Puguang Temple for Crown Prince Chengqian; he issued an edict to convert his former residence in Luoyang into Tianguan Temple; he issued an edict to establish Hongfu Temple for Empress Dowager Mu; and Crown Prince [Gaozong] established Cien Temple for Empress Wende. Emperor Gaozong.
Thirteen Great Halls of Ximing Monastery were built by imperial decree. [Regarding] Ruizong:

he issued an edict designating Jianguo Monastery in Bianzhou—originally constructed by the śramaṇa Huiyun—as Daxiangguo Monastery; because the Emperor ascended the throne as the Prince of Xiang, it was named accordingly. [Regarding] Xuanzong: [...]

An imperial edict was issued to construct the Maitreya Hall of Jiangu Temple using the timber from the imperial bedchamber. An imperial edict was issued for all prefectures throughout the empire to establish Kaiyuan Temples and Longxing Temples.
Regarding Suzong: the Retired Emperor traveled to Chengdu.
The śramaṇa Yinggan provided gruel to relieve the poor and hungry, vowing that the national destiny might once again be purified.

By imperial decree, ninety-six monasteries and eight thousand five hundred quarters were established at Dàshèngcí Temple. The Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs, Wang Wei, along with his younger brother Wang Jin, both served the Buddha.
Upon the mother’s death, the Wangchuan residence was converted into a monastery. During the reign of Emperor Daizong, he dreamed of traveling to a mountain temple;
the following day, a monastery was established on Langye Mountain and its plan submitted for imperial inspection, whereupon it was granted the name Baoying Monastery.
Furthermore, the Emperor dreamed that a Pratyekabuddha from Mount Niushou came to visit him.
An imperial decree was issued to construct a seven-storied pagoda within the mountain.

Li Chongqian, the Military Commissioner of Huaixi, donated his residence to establish a Buddhist scripture hall, which was granted the name Baoying. [This occurred during the reign of] Emperor Xuanzong.

An imperial edict was issued for all temples throughout the realm to repair and maintain the stupas of the various patriarchs. Emperor Zhaozong issued an edict to rebuild Cao Tang Monastery at the site where Kumārajīva had translated the scriptures.
During the Jin dynasty, a group of Indian monks gathered on the summit of Mount Cao.
He flew away.
[The Emperor] decreed the construction of He-yu Chan Temple.
[This was during the reigns of] Emperor Taizu of the Song and King Chu of Wuyue.
He constructed eighty-four thousand stupas made of gold and copper and distributed them throughout the kingdom.
Emperor Taizong of the Zhou dynasty converted Longxing Temple into an official granary.
The monks of the temple beat drums to petition for its restoration.
By imperial decree, it was restored as a temple, and the title "Taiping Xingguo" was bestowed upon all unnamed temples throughout the realm.
It is recorded: An imperial decree was issued to go to Mount Wutai to cast gilt-bronze statues of Mañjuśrī and ten thousand bodhisattvas;

an edict was issued to establish Kaisheng Chan Temple and to enshrine an Indian sandalwood miraculous image, a tooth relic of Śākyamuni Buddha, and the true body of Master Zhigong. An imperial decree was issued to go to Mount Tiantai to rebuild Shouchang Temple.
Five hundred and sixteen statues of arhats were fashioned.
A nine-story pagoda, thirty-six *zhang* in height, was constructed at Kaibosi;
the uppermost hand-hold chamber enshrines a relic stūpa.
The radiance of his light illuminated heaven and earth.
Emperor Zhenzong issued an edict granting gold for the restoration of Mount Emei’s Puxian Temple.

The śramaṇa Jiqian returned from India and obtained Buddha-relics with which he constructed a stupa in Yangzhou; by imperial decree, it was designated as the Stupa of Changgan Temple in Jiangning Prefecture.
He was granted the name Shenggan. An imperial edict ordered the establishment of Zisheng Monastery in Bingzhou to perform rites for the posthumous merit of soldiers who had perished in battle.
Emperor Renzong issued an edict to establish Cihua Temple in the capital.
To offer merit for the late Emperor, by Imperial Decree the Linggan Pagoda was rebuilt.
The Inner Attendant Li Yun-ning memorialized that he had established the Sifang Jingyin Monastery on his own estate.
The Emperor issued a decree for Chan Master Lian to reside there.
Emperor Yingzong issued an edict prohibiting the private construction of temples throughout the realm.
He also bestowed the plaque "Shousheng" (Longevity and Sagehood).

Emperor Shenzong issued an imperial decree for the Linggan Pagoda of Kaibosi to be inscribed with the calligraphic plaque "Hongfu Yuancheng" (The Fulfillment of Great Blessings). Emperor Zhezong [did likewise].
The śramaṇa Jieran of Yanqing in Siming established the Hall of the Sixteen Contemplations;
Chen Guan composed its record. Emperor Huizong [reigned].
Chan Master You of Yunju constructed three pagodas.
When Chan Master Baiyun Congshan established the Patriarchs’ Hall,
Hong Juefan commented on it, saying:
"Yunjian Baiyun’s insight was lofty and far-reaching."
This may serve as a model for the world.
Emperor Gaozong issued an edict to establish Baoen Temples throughout all prefectures and commanderies to perform memorial services for Emperor Huizong.
He also issued an edict to construct Tianshen Wanshou Yuanjue Temple on the northern mountains of Xihu. Emperor Xiaozong [did likewise].

An imperial decree granted funds from the Inner Treasury for the construction of a Sūtra Repository Hall at Upper Zhushan. An imperial decree granted money for the construction of a Hall of the Sixteen Contemplations at Upper Zhushan;
the record was composed by the Palace Secretary Lou Yao. An imperial decree established an Inner Contemplation Hall within the Forbidden City.
First, following the regulations of Upper Zhù (India):
Seeking the Dharma in the Western Heavens, during the reign of Gao Guīxiāng Gōng of the Wèi dynasty,
the śramaṇa Zhū Shì...
During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, the śramaṇa Faxian traveled west to Khotan and obtained the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra of the Radiant Light.
Having traveled from the Western Regions to the Five Indias, he obtained scriptures and images;
he then crossed the South Sea on his return.
[This was during the reign of] Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty.
Dharmodgata went to Western India and returned after twenty years;
he translated scriptures at the capital of Yangdu. Later, during the reign of Emperor Fei.
The śramaṇa Faxian traveled west to Khotan and obtained the *Devaparivarta*.
The Liang dynasty śramaṇa Zhixuan traveled to Central India,
obtained the Sanskrit manuscript, and returned.
During the reign of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty,
the śramaṇa Zhiyuan traveled to Western India;
during the time of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, he returned with Sanskrit scriptures.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaoming of the Northern Wei,
he dispatched the envoy Song Yun and the śramaṇa Fali to the Western Heavens.
Having obtained one hundred and seventy sections of the Brahma-sūtras, he returned.
During the reign of the Later Ruler of Northern Qi,
the śramaṇa Baoxian and others traveled to the Western Heaven (India).
The Sanskrit original was obtained and returned.
During the Sui dynasty,
the monk Zhizhou and others from the Chen court [collated it].
Upon his return from seeking scriptures in India,
Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict appointing Li Yibiao and Wang Yuance as envoys to India.
An inscription was carved upon Mount Qi to record the majestic virtue of the Tang dynasty. Tripitaka Master Xuanzang, having returned from seeking scriptures in India,
was summoned for an audience.
An imperial edict was issued to compile the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions).
Regarding Empress Wu:
initially, the Tripitaka Master Yijing had traveled by ship from the South Sea.
He traveled to India in the Western Regions to seek the Dharma;
upon his return, he deposited the Sanskrit manuscripts in the kingdom of Fo-shih (Sumatra) and composed the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of the Inner Law Sent Home from the Southern Seas).
Biographies of Eminent Monks Who Sought the Dharma ○ Emperor Xuanzong:
The śramaṇa Huiri returned from the Western Heaven;
the Emperor summoned him for an audience and he preached the Dharma.
He was granted the title "Tripiṭaka Dharma Master Cimin. During the Liang dynasty,
Emperor Taizu received Buddhist relics and Sanskrit scriptures brought back by the śramaṇa Zhixuan, who had traveled to Western India to seek out the sutras.
During the reign of Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty,

the śramaṇa Daoyuan returned from his travels through the five regions of India and presented śarīra relics and Sanskrit scriptures [to the throne]. The śramaṇas Xingqin and others [also made offerings].
He was dispatched by imperial decree to Western India to seek the Dharma;
all the kingdoms he passed through were granted imperial edicts ordering them to send guides to escort him. The śramaṇa Jian-sheng returned from Western India.
On the matter of advancing the *palm-leaf Sanskrit scriptures* [to promote] the True Dharma:
Chen Shu of Kaifeng Prefecture submitted a memorial stating that śramaṇas have traveled to the Western Heaven to retrieve the scriptures.
It is fitting to examine the talents of men. Emperor Renzong:

The śramaṇa Huaiwen requested permission to travel to Western India to erect a stūpa for the present Sovereign beside the Vajrāsana of the Buddha. The śramaṇas Huaiwen, Deji, Wuding, and others returned from Central India.
Presented are nineteen items: Buddha-relics, śarīra, palm-leaf Sanskrit scriptures, and inscriptions from the Western Heavens;
as well as records of scripture translations in the Eastern Lands, beginning with the arrival of Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.
The *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* was first translated.
Dharmaratna also translated five sections of the *Buddhacarita-sūtra*.
During the reign of Emperor Huan, Lokakṣema translated twenty-one works, including the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*. During the reign of Emperor Ling...
Zhu Foshuo translated the *Daoxing Banruo Jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra).
Throughout the Han dynasty, more than three hundred scriptural translations were produced. [There was also] the lay practitioner Yan Fotiao.
He translated the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* during the Wei dynasty under Emperor Qi.
Dharmakāla translated the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
Dharmadeva translated the *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra).
Kang Sengkai translated the *Wuliangshou jing* (Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra). The Shramana Bo Yan arrived in Luoyang during the reign of Emperor Gaogui of the Wei dynasty.
He translated the *Sutra on the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment*.
○ The śramaṇa Zhu Shixing obtained the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (the *Fangguang Prajñāpāramitā*) in Khotan.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty,
Zhu Fahu translated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and others.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu, Kumārajīva arrived in the Qin.
Translation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:

During the reign of Emperor An of the Later Qin, Dharmarakṣa translated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Śāriputra-parivarta-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Dharmakṣema arrived in Liang.
He translated the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Compassionate Lotus Sūtra) and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in forty fascicles.
Buddhabhadra, while in the Qin, translated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Buddhabhadra... [text continues]
In Jiankang, he translated the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* in sixty fascicles, with Huiyan and Huiguan serving as scribes.
During the reign of Emperor Shao of the Song dynasty, Buddhayaśas translated the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya). During the reign of Emperor Wen.
Dharmamitra translated the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra*.
Kuṅ-lǎng-yé-shè translated the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* during the reign of Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty.
Dharmayaśas translated the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings).
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty [commissioned] the śramaṇa Zhenshan to translate the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The Emperor personally received [the teachings] in his own hand. Paramārtha translated the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* for Emperor Jianwen.
During the reign of Emperor Xuanwu of the Northern Wei, [Paramārtha] also translated the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
Bodhiruci was translating the scriptures in the Ziji Hall when Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty personally received the dictation with his own hand.
The *Buddhacarita-sūtra* (佛本行經), thirty-two fascicles, translated by Jñānagupta,
with the scholar Fei Changfang serving as scribe,
during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty.
The eight-fascicle *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* translated by Guptaka and Kumārajīva is titled the "Supplementary Version" (*Tiānpǐn*).

During the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang newly translated the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and other works. Furthermore, Dharma Master Xuanzang translated the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
An imperial edict was issued bestowing [this] upon the Nine Circuit Commanders.
The Imperially Composed Preface to the Holy Teachings.
Translated by Buddhatoṭara: the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuanjue jing*), compiled by Emperor Gaozong.
An imperial edict was issued to Yu Zhining, Vice President of the Left, and Lai Ji, Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, to serve concurrently as translators and editors for the scriptures.
By imperial decree, Tripitaka Master Xuanzang translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in six hundred fascicles. The śramaṇa Huining sailed across the sea and reached the kingdom of Ho-ling.
Yùzhìxián translated the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra, Latter Part* in two fascicles; by imperial decree, the Tripiṭaka Master Rìzhào and Dúxíngyǐ jointly translated the *Buddhōṣṇīṣavijaya Dhāraṇī*.
The imperial edict did not avoid the national taboo [of the Empress’s name].
Empress Wu dispatched an envoy to the Kingdom of Khotan to welcome Śikṣānanda;
he arrived at the Eastern Capital.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in eighty fascicles was translated again; this was the second translation.
During the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, the Chancellor Fang Rong traveled to Nanhai, where he encountered Prajñāmitra, who translated the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Emperor Rong personally received [the teachings] in his own hand. ○ He issued an edict for Tripitaka Master Yijing to translate the *Saptabuddhaka-bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra*;
the Emperor personally received [the teachings] in his own hand.
○ He issued an edict for Bodhiruci to translate scriptures at the Foguang Hall.
The Emperor received it with his own hand.
The hundred officials sat in attendance. When Bodhiruci translated the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, Wu Pingyi, a scholar of the Xiuwen Pavilion, served as the Director of the Translation Bureau.
Lu Zangyong and others polished the text. When Bodhiruci presented his newly translated scriptures, an imperial banquet was granted at the Lingguang Hall;
by imperial decree, painters were ordered to depict the eminent monks who had translated the scriptures on the walls of the hall. — Emperor Ruizong.
Bodhiruci translated the Ratnakūṭa Sūtra.
The Chancellor Zhang Yue and the Court Gentleman Lu Xiangxian [were among those involved].
The text was polished by Dr. He Zhizhang and others.
Emperor Dezong composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings" (Shèngjiàoxù).
Tripitaka Master Prajñā translated the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra based on a manuscript presented from the kingdom of Oḍra.

The Emperor personally participated in the translation assembly, editing and correcting the texts as they were produced. Tripitaka Master Prajñā and Dharma Master Chengguan presented the newly translated forty-fascicle *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; this was the third translation. [Emperor] Xianzong.
An imperial edict was issued to Meng Jian, Counselor for Remonstrance,
and others to supervise the translation and refinement of the texts at Liquan Palace. —
Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty.
The Indian Śramaṇa Fātian translated the *Sūtra of the Holy Immeasurable Life*.
Emperor Wǔzōng summoned Fātian to the capital to oversee the work of translation.
At that time, the Tripiṭaka masters Tianxizāi and Shīhù arrived.
By imperial decree, he was summoned to the palace for an audience. An edict was issued to establish a Translation Institute (Yijingyuan), where Tian Xizai and others were ordered to reside.
He then composed the ritual procedures for the translation of scriptures.
From the chief translator to the editor of the text,
there were nine individuals in total;
the Imperial carriage personally visited [the site].
He was granted a seat and exhorted with words of encouragement.

Emperor Zhenzong visited the Translation Institute to observe the translation of scriptures. Zhu Ziaang, Director of the Office for Drafting Edicts, concurrently served as the Official for Polishing Translations. Chen Shu, Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, submitted a memorial stating:
The Translation Institute had long been a source of heavy expenditure for provisions and supplies;
[the Emperor] requested its abolition.

The Sovereign, considering it a grand ceremonial institution of the previous reign, did not permit it. Prime Minister Wang Qinruo concurrently served as the Commissioner for Polishing the Texts of Translated Scriptures. Prime Minister Ding Wei concurrently served as the Commissioner for Polishing the Texts of Translated Scriptures.
Chao Jing and Li Wei, both Hanlin Academicians, were concurrently appointed as Officials for Refining Texts.
Emperor Renzong [responded] when the Tripitaka Master Weijing requested that the translation of scriptures be suspended, saying:
How could I dare to abolish the ancient canons of the Three Sages?

Furthermore, the registers of precious tributes cannot be identified without the assistance of the Minister of State Ceremonies (Honglu). Chancellor Zhang Dexiang concurrently served as the Commissioner for Translating Scriptures and Polishing Texts; Chancellor Wen Yanbo concurrently served as the Commissioner for Translating Scriptures and Polishing Texts; and Xia Song of the Hanlin Academy and others [were appointed].

*Jinxinyijing yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning of Newly Translated Scriptures), seventy fascicles. Supervised by Lu Yijian, Right Vice President of the Department of State Affairs and Commissioner for Polishing the Text of the Translated Scriptures;
and Song Sou, Participant in the Administration of State Affairs and Official for Polishing the Text.
Imperial Decree to Compile the *Fǎbǎo Lù* (Record of the Dharma-Jewels). Prime Minister Fú Bǐ concurrently served as the Commissioner for Polishing the Texts of the Translated Scriptures.
Emperor Huīzōng. The Tripiṭaka Master Jīnzǒngchí, who had translated the scriptures, traveled south to the regions of Jiāng and Zhè.
The *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu* (Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings of the Kaiyuan Era),
compiled by the śramaṇa Zhisheng during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty,
contains a total of five thousand forty-eight fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty,
the Tripitaka Master Weijing presented the *Tiansheng Shijiao Lu* (Tiansheng Record of Buddhist Teachings),
comprising a total of six thousand one hundred and ninety-seven fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaojing of the Northern Wei,
there were two million monks and nuns and thirty thousand monasteries.
During the Wenxuan era of the Northern Qi dynasty,
there were four million monks and nuns and forty thousand monasteries.
During the reign of Emperor Zhenzong of the Song dynasty,
there were 397,615 monks and 61,240 nuns. During the reign of Emperor Renzong...
There were 385,520 monks and 48,740 nuns. During the Shenzong era,
there were 220,660 monks.
